case40v1-prob.validation:
Yojak Freight Works: The Night Before the Board Call

A decision case on evidence, instruments, and whether a problem exists at all. Pune, February 2026.

1. Sunday night

At twenty past eleven on Sunday, 15 February 2026, Poorvi Jasuja sat on the floor of her flat in Baner, Pune, with four printouts and a cold cup of filter coffee beside her. She was to bring them to the board call at half past two the next afternoon. One at a time each was persuasive; together they would not say the same thing.

Jasuja was chief product officer of Yojak Freight Works, a seven-year-old Pune company selling dispatch, toll-reconciliation and settlement software to road-freight operators of thirty to three hundred trucks. For ten months her team had tested one sentence, written in April 2025: that owners of such fleets cannot tell which lanes lose money until long after the money is gone, and would pay to find out sooner.

The board wanted one thing: was the problem real. Pradyot Potnis, the co-founder and chief executive, had told the investors he thought it was, and Rahil Sondhi had sold against it from New Jersey. At nine that evening Reema Barakat messaged from Toronto: Re-ran the pilot with fleet as the unit. The interval crosses zero. Call me before the board, not after.

2. How Yojak came to be shaped this way

Potnis had spent nine years in a Nagpur commercial-vehicle dealership before founding Yojak in 2019 with two Pune engineers. The first product generated GST e-way bills and dispatch memos without re-typing consignment details; it sold because the alternative was a clerk and a ledger. By 2021 the wedge was FASTag reconciliation, which found operators two to four per cent of their toll spend in wrong-class deductions.

The decision that constrains Jasuja today was taken in November 2022. Warsan Inland Logistics LLC, a Dubai forwarder moving cargo inland from Jebel Ali, wanted Yojak's dispatch engine white-labelled for its Indian subcontractors. The contract was worth ₹2.60 crore a year in licence plus ₹0.90 crore in services, ran four years, and came with Schedule C: a frozen definition of the canonical trip object. It lists eighteen events, including gate-in at loading point. It has no gate-out event at the consignee and no field for dock arrival or release (Figure A); any change needs ninety days' notice and Warsan's counter-signature.

In February 2025 Yojak raised ₹220 crore at a post-money valuation of ₹1,150 crore. The deck promised a second revenue line of ₹100 crore, and trip-level profitability was that line. By January 2026 recurring revenue was ₹61.80 crore across 1,340 paying fleets — ₹4.61 lakh a fleet on average — against ₹41.30 crore a year earlier; Trip P&L is ₹1.09 crore of today's figure. A growing share of it was not software: freight-settlement float fees had gone from ₹1.10 crore to ₹4.50 crore, and that line is the one exposed to the Reserve Bank's payment-aggregator and digital-lending directions.

3. The industry

Two-thirds of India's freight tonnage moves by road, most of it on trucks owned by operators too small for any league table. Yojak's customer is a family firm in Namakkal, Indore or Ludhiana, between the owner-driver and the organised 3PLs; its own customers are the shippers — Reliance Retail, Flipkart and Meesho sellers, Amul and its peers, cement and steel majors, and Zepto and Swiggy, whose dark-store replenishment has broken the weekly rhythm of dispatch.

Four forces press on the product. The data rails are public and improving: GSTN's e-way bill system, NPCI's FASTag feeds and the Vahan registry let a software firm know a great deal about a truck without installing anything on it. The OEMs give telematics away — new Tata Motors and Ashok Leyland tractors arrive with connected dashboards — which caps what location alone can be charged for. BlackBuck, Porter, Delhivery and the ONDC logistics pilots are channel and threat at once. And the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 makes a driver's continuous location a consented processing activity, not a telemetry stream.

Warsan's licence alone is 4.2 per cent of revenue, but close to a quarter of Yojak's schema. Engineering sits in Bengaluru and Pune, design in Berlin, data science in Toronto, customer success in Singapore and sales in New Jersey, so a Monday-afternoon decision in Pune is argued over by people for whom it is Sunday night.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The hypothesis, written on 14 April 2025 and never edited since, read: Owners of 30–300-truck fleets cannot identify loss-making lanes until month-end closing, so they continue running them; they will pay ₹60,000–₹80,000 a year per fleet for trip-level profit and loss.

Between May and July 2025 the team ran sixty interviews (Exhibit 1), coded independently by Jasuja and Rucha Shenoy for whether the owner named cost visibility among their top two pains (Exhibit 2). In August eleven fleets opened their books, and the decomposition that came out (Exhibit 4) was the one result nobody had predicted. In September the alpha shipped, built on Schedule C and therefore on the only cost fields the trip object carries. From October to December it ran as a pilot across forty-two customers, through the Diwali peak (Exhibit 3). In January came the usage telemetry (Exhibit 5) and the receivables ageing (Exhibit 6); Figure B sets out the sequence.

Three things believed in April are no longer safe. First, that the sample was neutral: 44 of the 60 participants (73.3 per cent) came from a broadcast to Yojak's own FASTag users, whose opening line read “Do you know where your trip money goes?” Second, that the pilot produced a result: by unit of analysis it is either decisive or absent. Third, that the instrument can see the problem. It cannot see the largest line in Exhibit 4.

5. The people

Poorvi Jasuja — chief product officer, Pune
Joined in 2023 from a payments firm. Position: the evidence is unclear and she will not call it validated. Incentive both ways: the ₹100 crore line was promised on her slide. Unsaid: she drafted the broadcast in April and did not re-read its wording until November.
Pradyot Potnis — co-founder and chief executive, Pune
Believes the problem is real because he has sat in the offices where it occurs. Position: validated; ship by June and stop studying. Incentive: a Series C conversation begun informally. Unsaid: two of the pilot's best fleets are his cousins' firms in Nagpur.
Rucha Shenoy — vice-president, engineering, Bengaluru
The second coder. Position: the module is cheap to finish and expensive to make correct, because correctness needs dock events Schedule C cannot carry. Incentive: seven engineers, three roadmaps. Unsaid: she disagreed with Jasuja on fourteen transcripts and said nothing.
Reema Barakat — senior data scientist, Toronto
Re-analysed the pilot with fleet as the unit of randomisation. Position: it is uninformative and must not be quoted as evidence of effect. Incentive: her standing suffers if a number she signed is wrong. Unsaid: she flagged the clustering in September; nobody replied.
Pia Reinecke — principal designer, Berlin
Position: the module asks the wrong person to do the work — the owner feels the pain, the driver and munshi enter the data, neither paid for accuracy. Incentive: rebuilding the consent and entry flows costs six weeks. Unsaid: she has an offer from a Berlin mobility firm.
Rachel Kurien — head of customer success, Singapore
Ran onboarding. Position: behaviour did not change — the dashboard was opened, the WhatsApp group still used. Incentive: her renewals include nineteen pilot fleets. Unsaid: she chased settlement closures herself in eight treatment fleets.
Rahil Sondhi — senior vice-president, sales, New Jersey
Sold two large logos in January on the Trip P&L roadmap, one with a written availability date. Position: validated enough; shipping late is the only risk. Incentive: 38 per cent of his pay sits on new-logo value. Unsaid: the clause was his idea, not the customer's.
Rami Al Mazrouei — head of inland logistics, Warsan, Dubai
Position: Schedule C is not to be touched before the November 2026 renewal; his team is mid-migration. Incentive: a clean renewal, no change requests on his record. Unsaid: Warsan has begun evaluating an alternative vendor.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

Two-thirds of the owners we spoke to told us they cannot see where the money goes. Two-thirds. I do not need an interval to know what that means. Pradyot Potnis, product council, 4 February 2026
Thirty-two of the forty-eight who answered that question said it — and forty-four of the sixty were recruited with a message that put the words in their mouth. I wrote the message. Poorvi Jasuja, reply in the same meeting
The seven-day number is real and it is also meaningless. Twenty-one fleets is the sample size, not seventeen thousand trips. Treated correctly, the effect is somewhere between slightly negative and quite large. That is a shrug with error bars. Reema Barakat, email to Jasuja and Shenoy, 11 February
Also it was Diwali. Everybody closes settlements in Diwali because everybody needs cash by Diwali. Rachel Kurien, same thread, 12 February
The owners have the problem. Nobody asks who has to type. The munshi types, the driver photographs the fuel slip, and neither gets anything if the number is right. Pia Reinecke, design review, 6 February
If detention is a third of the leak, we cannot measure a third of the leak. Schedule C has gate-in and nothing at the other end. I can build the geofence in five months with seven people. I cannot change Schedule C. Rucha Shenoy, engineering planning note, 9 February
I have a contract that says general availability by the thirtieth of June. If we tell the customer we are still studying the problem, I would rather lose the logo cleanly. Rahil Sondhi, chat message to Jasuja, 13 February
I do not need certainty. I need one number I can defend to my investment committee for three years. Prashant Bhargava, board member, January minutes

8. The options as Jasuja currently sees them

The first is to call the hypothesis validated and ship by 30 June. It honours Sondhi's clause, uses engineers already trained on the code — and rests on an interview base Jasuja contaminated and an interval crossing zero at the unit of randomisation.

The second is to call it unclear and run one properly designed study: fleets recruited outside Yojak's user base, randomised by fleet, with the lane decision as the primary measure rather than settlement speed, outside Diwali. A quarter, ₹85 lakh, and the June clause unmet.

The third is to call it invalidated as written and re-point Shenoy's seven engineers at detention — a driver-app geofence and a consignee-side event, five months, ₹1.40 crore over thirty-five engineer-months. It attacks the largest row in Exhibit 4 and needs the Schedule C change Al Mazrouei has asked in writing not to receive this year.

The fourth is to reframe the problem as working capital rather than visibility, on the evidence of Exhibit 6, and push the settlement line — which takes Yojak deeper into float and credit, and into the part of the Reserve Bank's rulebook it has only brushed against.

All four share an assumption Jasuja noticed on Sunday and has not said aloud: that the answer must be the same for all 1,340 fleets. Exhibit 1 does not look like one population — eight of fourteen small western fleets were coded yes, one of five eastern ones was — and Panel B's between-fleet deviations are about 40 per cent of its means. The hypothesis may hold for one segment and fail in another, and ten months may have gone on averaging two companies' customers into one verdict. Or this may be what a product officer tells herself when she does not want to choose.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board call is at 14:30 IST on Monday, 16 February 2026 — four in the morning for Sondhi. Yojak holds ₹148 crore of cash against ₹9.4 crore of monthly burn: 15.7 months of runway, and no room for a funding story that contradicts the last. Shenoy has seven engineers, not fourteen; at Bengaluru's senior band of ₹48 lakh a year, the same money buys roughly half an engineer in Berlin (Reinecke, €96,000, ₹91.2 lakh at ₹95 to the euro) or Toronto (Barakat, CAD 142,000, ₹87.3 lakh at ₹61.5). The Mumbai 3PL contract carries ₹1.9 crore of annual value and a pro-rated refund of ₹47.5 lakh if availability slips past 30 June. Schedule C needs ninety days' notice and Warsan's counter-signature, and a ₹2.60 crore licence renews in November. Detention measurement built on driver location needs DPDP consent: in a December test, 255 of 418 drivers consented, or 61.0 per cent, so the metric would be blind to the fleets with the least biddable drivers.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. State the hypothesis so that it could be falsified. What evidence, had Yojak collected it, would have shown the problem to be imagined?
  2. Potnis's “two-thirds” comes from Exhibits 1 and 2. Work out what share of what base each figure describes, and say which speaker in Section 7 quotes them correctly.
  3. Exhibit 3 reports one pilot three ways. Which interval should the board see, and what does that choice imply about what the pilot was designed to learn?
  4. Exhibit 4's largest line, a third of the total, is invisible to Yojak's instrument. Is the hypothesis wrong, or merely under-instrumented — and does the distinction change what Jasuja should do?
  5. Exhibits 4 and 6 rest on the same eleven self-selected fleets; Exhibit 5 shows what the wider base did. Using only the exhibits, build the strongest case that the problem is real and the strongest that it is not.
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Jasuja do, in what order — and in her four minutes at the board call, what exactly does she say, and what does she decline to say?

 

At a quarter to one she put the printouts in order, then re-ordered them. Last on the pile was Exhibit 5, whose twelve descending bars she could read as proof of anything: that the problem was imagined, that the module was bad, that onboarding was rushed. Her phone lit with a message from Barakat, where it was still Sunday: Did you decide what we are calling it? Jasuja typed validated, looked at the word, deleted it, typed unclear, deleted that too, and put the phone face down beside the coffee.
case20v1-prob.validation:
Yaazhi Pharmacy Network: The Forgotten Refill

A case on validating a problem hypothesis

1. Opening

At 8.40 a.m. on Tuesday, 13 October 2026, Paromita Jotwani sat at a corner desk in Yaazhi Pharmacy Network's head office in Nungambakkam, Chennai, with two documents open on her laptop. One was a four-page research summary titled "Why chronic patients stop refilling". The other was a staffing request for four engineers for four months. Ramanujam Meiyappan, Yaazhi's founder and chief executive, had asked her to choose between them by Friday, 23 October, when the quarter's planning closed. Diwali fell on 8 November, after which the engineers were committed elsewhere.

The product Paromita wanted was an automatic refill service: a patient would be reminded, confirm with one tap and have the medicines delivered or held at the nearest store. Her team had written the underlying belief on a wall in August: chronic-care patients over fifty fall out of monthly refills mainly because they forget to reorder. The question was whether the evidence had earned the word "mainly".

2. Company background

Ramanujam Meiyappan opened the first Yaazhi pharmacy in Coimbatore in 2011. By 2026 the chain had 214 stores across Tamil Nadu and Karnataka and annual revenue of ₹640 crore. It competed with Apollo Pharmacy and MedPlus on the high street, Tata 1mg and PharmEasy online, and Jan Aushadhi Kendras on price. Its edge was chronic care. Patients with diabetes, hypertension or thyroid conditions bought the same strips every month, and 96,000 of them held a Yaazhi loyalty card.

Regulation shaped what could be built. Most of these medicines are prescription-only, so any automatic service had to check that a prescription was still valid. Reminders over WhatsApp needed recorded consent under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

3. The situation

Paromita's belief rested on three pieces of evidence, assembled in different places by different people.

The first was refill data. Pooran Sengupta, a data scientist working from Toronto, took a panel of 12,000 loyalty-card patients on 30-day prescriptions and computed, from each dispensed quantity, the date their supply should run out. A refill more than seven days after that date was counted as late. Over the six months to September, 4,200 of the 12,000 patients, or 35 per cent, had at least one late refill. Of those 4,200, 2,520 (60 per cent) came back within 30 days and 1,680 did not. Those 1,680 were 14 per cent of the panel. The panel was one-eighth of the 96,000 card-holders.

The second was interviews. Priscilla Tan, who leads customer success from Singapore and manages Yaazhi's patient helpline, had her Tamil-speaking team phone 24 patients drawn at random from the 4,200 late-refill patients. Exhibit 1 shows what they said. Fifteen reported that they had actually run out of medicine; nine said they were not late at all, because they had bought the strip from another pharmacy or a hospital counter. Among the fifteen, six said they forgot, five said Yaazhi's store did not have the brand in stock, three said money was short that month and one had been travelling. Two of the six who forgot said a son or daughter in Dubai normally placed the order.

The third was a pilot. In April, product had switched on WhatsApp refill reminders in 14 stores chosen by their managers. Exhibit 2 compares those stores with 14 others.

Exhibit 2. Late refills before and during the reminder pilot, per six-month window
StoresPatientsLate beforeRate beforeLate duringRate during
Pilot (reminders)3,00090030.0%81027.0%
Comparison (none)3,0001,08036.0%1,08036.0%

Source: Yaazhi dispensing records. Rates are late patients divided by patients in that group (3,000). The pilot stores were chosen by managers, not at random, and these 6,000 patients are separate from the 12,000-patient panel above.

Naively read, Exhibit 2 shows reminders cutting lateness from 36 per cent to 27 per cent, a nine-point gain. But the pilot stores were already six points better beforehand; against their own starting line they improved by three points, while the comparison stores did not move.

Rhea Bergmann, the product designer in Berlin, reviewed the call recordings with subtitles and raised a different worry. Patients who said they forgot often described a remembered intention that failed on the day: the shop was far, the brand was missing, the cash was not there. "Forgetting," she wrote, "may be what people say when the real reason is awkward to explain to a stranger."

4. The people

Paromita Jotwani, head of product in Chennai, wants to commit engineers only to a problem she can defend in front of the board. Ramanujam Meiyappan, founder and chief executive, wants a visible answer to Tata 1mg's subscription push before Diwali and finds "another study" a poor use of a quarter. Pooran Sengupta, in Toronto, trusts the panel numbers and distrusts the interviews' small base. Priscilla Tan, in Singapore, hears patients every day and believes the stock-out complaints are under-weighted, since managers rarely log a missing brand as a lost sale.

5. What the exhibits say, and what they cost

Paromita translated the evidence into money. The average chronic patient bought ₹1,450 of medicines a month at a gross margin of 22 per cent, or ₹319 a month and ₹3,828 a year. The 1,680 patients who did not return therefore represented about ₹64.3 lakh of annual gross margin (1,680 × ₹3,828). If the forgetting share found in the interviews, six of 24 or 25 per cent, applied to those 1,680, then about 420 patients, or ₹16.1 lakh a year, were lost to forgetting on the panel. Scaled eightfold to all 96,000 card-holders, that was roughly ₹1.29 crore a year. The assumption that interviewees from the late list speak for the 1,680 who never returned was untested, and Paromita said so in her summary.

Exhibit 3. The three courses of action
OptionCostTimeWhat it settles
A. Build auto-refill₹48 lakh4 monthsNothing before launch; learning comes after the money is spent
B. Fix brand availability₹30 lakh3 monthsAddresses 5 of the 15 who ran out; ignores the 6 who forgot
C. Concierge test₹6 lakh7 weeks to read-outWhether reminders plus one-tap ordering change refill behaviour

Source: Yaazhi product and finance estimates, October 2026. Costs are one-time. Option C covers 400 patients.

6. The options

Option A: declare the problem validated and build. The panel showed a real leak, and six patients and a pilot pointed at forgetting. If right, the payoff was about ₹1.29 crore a year against ₹48 lakh. If wrong, Yaazhi would own a feature that solved the smaller part of the problem, and four engineers would spend the Diwali quarter on it.

Option B: treat forgetting as unproven and fix availability. Stock-outs were within Yaazhi's control, and Priscilla believed they were under-counted. But the evidence for them was five patients, and the plan would drop a hypothesis the pilot partly supported.

Option C: call it unclear and run a structured test. From 2 November, 400 patients whose supply ran out in the next six weeks would be split at random, 200 and 200, across the same stores. One group would receive WhatsApp reminders with a one-tap order; the other nothing. Paromita would publish the decision rule in advance. The cost was about seven weeks to a read-out, the pre-Diwali slot and Ramanujam's patience.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Exhibit 1 shows that nine of the 24 patients never ran out of medicine. What does this do to the 35 per cent late-refill figure as a measure of the problem, and what does it leave of the 14 per cent who did not return?

2. Why does the nine-point gap in Exhibit 2 shrink to three points, and which part of the pilot's design caused the difference?

3. Classify the hypothesis today as validated, invalidated or unclear, and state in one sentence what evidence would change your classification.

4. Which option would you take to Ramanujam on 23 October, and how would you answer his objection that another study wastes a quarter?

8. A note for the learner

This topic frames a problem statement as a claim that evidence can support, contradict or leave open. A hypothesis is validated when independent sources, gathered differently, agree on the same mechanism. It is invalidated when they agree against it. It is unclear when the sources disagree or are too weak to carry the specific word in the claim. A good answer separates the parts of the hypothesis: that patients drift from refills is well supported (the panel), that the drift costs money is plausible (the margin arithmetic), and that forgetting is the main cause is not yet supported. Six of 24 interviewees is one in four, and the reminder pilot, once its head start is removed, shows three points.

One defensible path is Option C. The problem is real enough to pursue, so Option B's retreat is unjustified, and the mechanism is uncertain enough that Option A bets ₹48 lakh on a guess. The decision rule matters more than the test. Paromita should write before launch that she will call the hypothesis validated if the reminded group's late rate is at least ten points below the control's, invalidated if the groups are within three points of each other, and unclear otherwise, and say plainly that 200 patients per group can only detect a large effect. Randomising inside the same stores avoids the pilot's selection problem. To Ramanujam she can say that ₹6 lakh buys a decision on ₹48 lakh, with an answer by Christmas and, if validated, a build already specified.
exp40v2-prob.validation:
Validating a problem hypothesis

Validated, invalidated or unclear — and what the verdict is on.

1. Two readouts, five days apart

On Thursday 16 April 2026, in Ahmedabad, Madhurima Bhatkal put one sheet of paper before Nandkishore Ambegaonkar, founder of Nishkarsh Field Systems, and Mukta Saraph. Nishkarsh sold work-order software to 640 mid-market Indian manufacturing plants. A draft proposal would build a Spares Readiness module for ₹1.85 crore at ₹18,000 per plant per month, on one undisputed sentence: maintenance supervisors lose production hours to missing spares and already keep private records to cope.

Exhibit 1 · The Nishkarsh stakes

She brought work-order logs from eleven plants covering Monday 2 February to Sunday 15 March 2026 and twenty-two interviews run between 16 and 31 March. Her instruction to herself, written on Monday 9 March, was to say which of three things the evidence supported.

Five days later, in Bengaluru, Ojaswin Kharche faced the same question with nothing else in common. Mahaul Air Works had shipped 12,500 of its ₹7,900 indoor air-quality monitors between 1 July and 31 December 2025. Narayani Puntambekar wanted a ₹249 subscription, built by Oskar Wasilewski's firmware team in Warsaw. The hypothesis: households with a monitor installed experience air bad enough to pay monthly about it.

Exhibit 2 · The Mahaul stakes

Price per household per month₹249

4,686 of the 9,000 registered households is 52.1 per cent: Nishkarsh needed one plant in seven, Mahaul one household in two.

The craft turns not on quantity of evidence but on precision of the sentence. A hypothesis conjoins three claims — a condition exists, a named population feels it, that population will act — each failing separately and diagnosably.

2. The idea, and the quarrel inside it

A problem hypothesis is a falsifiable statement that a specified population experiences a specified difficulty, at a specified frequency or intensity, and already pays some cost to cope. Validating it means comparing evidence against a standard set in advance and returning one of three verdicts: validated, invalidated, or unclear. A binary forces evidence to carry weight it rarely bears, in the direction the team wanted.

Steve Blank, teaching customer development from the early 2000s, argued the fatal risk was the assumption, not the execution; Eric Ries generalised the loop in The Lean Startup (2011); Rob Fitzpatrick's The Mom Test (2013) attacked the interview itself. Clayton Christensen moved the unit of analysis to the circumstance; Tony Ulwick turned that into survey instrumentation; psychology's replication crisis supplied pre-registration.

Exhibit 3 · What each school would and would not sign

SchoolWould signWould not sign
Pre-registration (Blank, Ries, Maurya)A claim with no disconfirming result is not a hypothesis.Validated means most of a sample agreed.
Outcome quantification (Ulwick)Importance and satisfaction scale across 180-plus respondents.Twenty-two interviews validate anything.
Research craft (Hall, Young)Frame the problem space first; most validation ratifies a decision.A three-signal rule is the discipline.
Continuous discovery (Torres)No verdicts; opportunities carry weights.Validation is an event with a date.
Risk-first prototyping (Cagan)Put something in front of people and watch what they do.Four weeks of interviews first.

Ulwick's apparatus is worth seeing worked: the opportunity score is importance plus the shortfall of satisfaction against it, negatives set to zero. For “time from fault to part in hand”, Bhatkal's survey of 214 supervisors returned importance 8.4 and satisfaction 4.1: 8.4 + (8.4 − 4.1) = 12.7, against a median of 9.6 across twenty-three outcomes. Reproducible — and entirely a report of what people said.

3. Mechanics in depth

Expert practice has five steps, two skipped and one faked. One, make every clause explicit. Bhatkal's read: maintenance supervisors at Indian plants with 80 to 400 employees lose at least 20 per cent of closed work orders to a spare missing from the plant store, and already keep records outside the ERP. Two, the faked step: fix the rule before looking. Three, gather mixed evidence including one costly signal. Four, compare mechanically and record the verdict with its date.

Exhibit 4 · Bhatkal's rule, written 9 March 2026

These four plants hold 232 of the 541 delayed orders, or 42.9 per cent and 1,194 of the 1,750 hours, or 68.2 per cent — but 672.62 of the 730.44 lakh, 92.1 per cent.

Four of the eleven plants therefore carry 92.1 per cent of the money, at ₹1.68 crore at risk each per year against ₹8.26 lakh each in the other seven. A ₹2.16 lakh product is trivially justifiable in the first group and arguably not in the second. Frequency validated a problem existing almost everywhere; intensity located the part worth selling to.

Rows overlap and do not sum. Four of the five budget holders signed; of the 17 without one, 14, or 82.4 per cent, needed the plant head's approval.

Signal one validated at 23.6 against 20 per cent, signal two at 16 against 11, and signal three returned 4 against a bar of 5 — so the hypothesis was unclear. Unclear has two causes, and only one is cured by more evidence.

Why the third threshold was never measurable

A sample proportion carries sampling error of roughly the square root of p(1−p)/n. For signal two, p̂ = 16/22 = 72.7 per cent, standard error 9.5 points, 95 per cent interval 54.1 to 91.3 — wholly above the 50 per cent bar. For signal three, p̂ = 4/22 = 18.2 per cent, standard error 8.2 points, interval 2.1 to 34.3 per cent, and the bar of 22.7 per cent sits inside it. Resolving a proportion near 18 per cent to ±10 points needs 1.96² × 0.182 × 0.818 ÷ 0.10² = 57.2, so 58 respondents; to ±5 points, 229.

The second tool is a signal's weight: how much likelier it is under a real problem than an imagined one.

Exhibit 8 · What each signal is worth

Posterior odds are prior odds times the ratio: from even odds, 2.80 gives 73.7 per cent. The last row is the product of the exact ratios, 0.90/0.70 × 0.70/0.25 × 0.55/0.15 × 0.35/0.03 = 154.0, or 99.4 per cent, and is least trustworthy: correlated signals overstate.

An unprompted account of a recent episode moves belief from 50 to 56 per cent; a signature with money behind it, to 92. Cheap signals are weak because people with no problem produce them too.

4. When it applies, as testable claims

One: a specific observation could refute it. True for both protagonists — a 6 per cent stockout-delay rate would have sunk Nishkarsh. False for “customers want a better experience”.

Two: evidence costs less than being wrong. Nishkarsh spent about ₹11 lakh of team time against ₹1.85 crore; Mahaul's trial cost ₹18 lakh against ₹1.40 crore. Where that ratio approaches one, validation is unavailable.

Three: the population named is the population you can reach. Nishkarsh failed here: the sentence named supervisors, the decision belonged to plant heads, and 5 of 22 held a budget line.

Four: condition and felt need move together. This is the claim Mahaul's evidence destroyed, and where validation turns actively misleading: where a condition is severe and felt need weak, severity data keeps validating what the market keeps refusing.

Exhibit 9 · Mahaul's rule and result

SignalValidated ifInvalidated ifObservedVerdict
Registered households still opening the app in week 1235% or morebelow 20%29.0%unclear
Paid conversion at ₹249 among registered households12% or morebelow 5%4.6%invalidated
Trial subscribers who paid a second month70% or morebelow 40%35.4%invalidated

Rule written 12 January 2026; trial 2 February to 29 March. Of the 418 subscribers, 148 paid a second month, or 35.4 per cent.

The chain compounds and must be read in order. 12,500 monitors sold; 9,000 registered, which is 72.0 per cent and the only denominator that matters thereafter; 2,610 of the 9,000 still opening the app in week twelve, or 29.0 per cent; and, with the subscription offered to all 9,000, 418 paying at least once — 4.6 per cent of registered, 3.3 per cent of units sold. Of those 418, 362, or 86.6 per cent, came from the 2,610 engaged households: 13.9 per cent conversion against 0.9 per cent among the 6,390 others. Annualised, that is ₹12,48,984, or ₹12.49 lakh.

5. Hard edges, and the organisational seam

Exhibit 10 · Mahaul telemetry, quarter to 31 March 2026

The two rightmost totals are monitor-weighted, not city-averaged: (2,520×71 + 1,080×62 + 1,890×34 + 1,530×22 + 1,170×27 + 810×25) ÷ 9,000 = 44.0 per cent, and the opens column weighted the same way gives 10,035 ÷ 9,000 = 1.12. Delhi NCR and Kolkata hold 3,600 monitors and 281 of the 418 subscribers, 67.2 per cent — 281 of 3,600, or 7.8 per cent, against 137 of the 5,400 elsewhere, or 2.5 per cent.

Even in the worst air in the country, conversion reached 7.8 per cent against a 12 per cent bar. The device had already extracted the household's willingness to pay, a ₹7,900 one-time act of concern. Hardware businesses mistake a large installed base for a validated recurring-revenue problem, and the telemetry proving the condition makes that feel rigorous.

Two-sided markets fail differently, because a platform hypothesis is two hypotheses in one sentence. At Nauka Cargo Exchange, a Visakhapatnam road-freight marketplace, Mohini Rasane tested whether waiting at the port gate was worth solving. On the shipper side it validated hard: 34 of 46 shippers named it among their top three cost problems, or 73.9 per cent, and detention invoices from eighteen came to ₹2.94 crore over twelve months — ₹16.33 lakh per shipper per year. On the carrier side it failed: of 150 truck owners, 23, or 15.3 per cent, raised it unprompted, their chief complaint being delayed payment, named by 109. The fix needed truckers inside a ninety-minute window at ₹620 a trip of idle time, against a take of ₹1,480 on a ₹37,000 load at 4.0 per cent — 41.9 per cent of that revenue.

In regulated settings the seam moves: at Nistar Device Labs in Coimbatore, clinicians can validate the problem a point-of-care analyser addresses while permission belongs to CDSCO, and a validated problem with no regulatory pathway is worse than an invalidated one, because it keeps attracting budget. In AI-native products the hazard is decay — Nehal Thatte at Mantavya AI Labs validated in October 2025 that credit analysts spent 40 to 55 minutes extracting figures from scanned statements, and by June 2026 a model release had cut that under four minutes. Mature companies say they pre-register and mostly run two tracks: an official ritual whose output is a slide, and an informal one where conviction substitutes for the rule.

6. Eight things that separate an expert

One: validated is a verdict on a sentence, not on a market. The tell is a team that cannot recite the population clause: Nishkarsh's condition validated for plants of 80 to 400 employees and no others.

Two: a real condition and an imagined problem look identical in the severity data. The tell is a readout rich in severity, thin in action: 44.0 per cent of hours above 60 µg/m³ against 4.6 per cent conversion.

Three: ask whose problem it is before asking whether it is real. Those who describe it most vividly can least afford to: 19 of 22 described a recent episode, 5 held a budget line.

Four: a threshold the sample cannot resolve is not a threshold. The obvious reading is that signal three failed; the correct one is that it was never measured.

Five: frequency and intensity are different variables, and the money follows intensity. Four plants held 42.9 per cent of delayed orders and 92.1 per cent of the money.

Six: unclear has two causes calling for opposite actions. Thin evidence calls for more evidence; clauses pointing at different people call for a rewrite. Bhatkal's was the second kind.

Seven: costly signals dominate cheap ones only to the extent of what was given up. The tell is a commitment artefact with no price. Nishkarsh's letter named ₹18,000 a month, which is why four signatures carried a ratio near twelve.

Eight: a convenience sample is not imprecise, it is biased in a knowable direction. The tell is a frame drawn from the product's own engagement data: Mitaan surveyed 400 of the 11,200 app-openers in a book of 68,000.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

Across product types the logic is identical; only the cheapest available evidence changes. In consumer products behavioural data is abundant, so willingness to pay is the whole question. In B2B the buyer population can be enumerated, and the dominant failure is Nishkarsh's: user and buyer differ while discovery talks to the user. On platforms every hypothesis must be written twice, once per side. In hardware the recurring-value claim is the weak one; in AI products the distinctive feature is the expiry. Stage changes the constraint, not the method: a pre-seed team validates with twelve conversations; a Series B company's pathology is the exercise convened to ratify a decision already taken, recognisable because the rule follows the first three interviews; an incumbent needs a business case, so ₹58 lakh loses to ₹6.73 crore.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Odhani Apparel Industries: validation done plainly

Nilima Dharap's Tiruppur label sold ethnic wear online. Her hypothesis: buyers return garments because the size chart does not match the garment, and already order two sizes to cope. From 1 October 2025 to 31 March 2026, 86,400 orders shipped and 19,872 returned — 23.0 per cent.

Exhibit 11 · Odhani return reason codes

Reason codeReturnsShare of returnsShare of orders shipped
Size or fit11,12856.0%12.9%
Fabric or colour differs from listing3,37817.0%3.9%
Changed mind2,38412.0%2.8%

11,128 of 19,872 returns is 56.0 per cent of returns and 12.9 per cent of the 86,400 shipped. The coping behaviour showed independently: 7,344 orders, or 8.5 per cent, carried one style in two sizes.

Validated on all three clauses, and the remedy was measurable. Garment-measured charts replaced generic ones, and size-or-fit returns next quarter ran at 7,560 of 84,000 orders, or 9.0 per cent — 3.88 points below 12.9, which on 84,000 orders is 3,259 returns avoided, worth ₹47.26 lakh at ₹1,450 each.

Mitaan Lending Services: the failure

Nawaz Tyabji's Raipur lender served small-shop borrowers. In April 2025 his team surveyed 400 and found 268, or 67.0 per cent, had missed an instalment because they did not know the due date. Declared validated, it drew ₹2.60 crore and seven months into a reminder product.

The failure was the sample frame. The 400 came from the 11,200 borrowers who had opened the app in thirty days, out of 68,000 active — the most engaged 16.5 per cent of the book. In the six months after launch 6,392 accounts went 30 days or more delinquent; of those, 895, or 14.0 per cent, had opened the app beforehand. The product could not reach 86.0 per cent of its target behaviour.

Recovery was a re-draw and a re-write. Tyabji sampled 120 borrowers from the collections ledger instead; 78, or 65.0 per cent, said money had not come in from their own customers. The rewritten hypothesis named working-capital timing, and a borrower-chosen due date cost ₹34 lakh and moved 30-plus-day delinquency from 9.1 to 7.6 per cent of the book. The late catch cost the ratio: ₹2.60 crore against ₹34 lakh, 7.6 times.

Nauka Cargo Exchange: valid problem, invalid business

Rasane's is the outcome practitioners find hardest to accept: every clause of the shipper-side hypothesis validated, the ₹16.33 lakh per shipper per year was real, and the product still could not exist.

9. Failure modes and early warning signs

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of a late catch
Bar set after the dataThreshold just below the resultWhere is the dated document?A build with no evidence behind it
Frame drawn from the productRespondents are “active users”Who could not appear in the frame?Mitaan: ₹2.60 crore, 86.0% unreachable
Condition measured, action notAll severity, no commitmentsWhat did anyone give up?Mahaul: ₹1.40 crore against ₹12.49 lakh
Wrong population namedVivid describers hold no budgetWho signs, and did we ask them?Nishkarsh: a quarter wasted
One side of a two-sided problemEvidence from buyers onlyWhat does this cost the other side?Nauka: 41.9% of take consumed

Each diagnostic needs no new research, which is why it belongs at the readout.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether a verdict should exist. The continuous-discovery position at its strongest is that the question is the wrong shape: problems do not have truth values, opportunities have weights, and a team re-weighting weekly never carries a stale belief. For it to be wrong, irreversible commitments must demand a go or no-go no weight can supply — Ambegaonkar's view.

How small a sample may be. The quantification school holds that under roughly 180 respondents nothing can be claimed about a population, and a bar of 22.7 per cent inside an interval spanning 2.1 to 34.3 is its best evidence. The craft school replies that interviews are a different instrument: Guest, Bunce and Johnson reported in 2006 that most themes in a sixty-interview study appeared within the first twelve, interviewing existing to find the categories a survey measures.

Stated versus revealed preference. The hard behaviouralist position is that speech carries so little information that problem interviews should give way to prototypes and pricing tests; Exhibit 8 is the steelman, enthusiasm worth 1.29 against a signature at 11.67. The counter is that such tests only reveal preferences about artefacts someone already thought to build — so for the behaviouralist to be wrong, interviews must reliably surface problems no prototype would find.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied validation writes a hypothesis, runs interviews, counts agreements and reports a verdict. Someone who has internalised it argues for an hour over whether the population clause says supervisors or plant heads, because that argument is the decision; checks the rule's resolution before collecting anything; and says in advance which result would most embarrass them. The first defends a verdict; the second defends the rule.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Bhatkal did not fund the ₹1.85 crore module. Her readout: the condition was validated — 23.6 per cent against a 20 per cent bar, 16 of 22 keeping shadow records — while the hypothesis as written was unclear for a diagnosable reason: it named a population without budget when 92.1 per cent of the money at risk sat in four plants the sentence never mentioned. She rewrote it as plant heads at continuous-process plants of 80 to 400 employees will pay to reduce stockout-driven downtime, pre-registered a new rule on 20 April, and proposed a five-week paid diagnostic with six such plants at ₹45,000 each.

Kharche declared the subscription invalidated and stopped the project. Two of three signals sat below their invalidation lines, and even where 44.0 per cent of monitored hours exceeded 60 µg/m³, conversion reached 7.8 per cent against a 12 per cent bar. The readout also surfaced a validated problem nobody had hypothesised: 2,104 of the 9,000 registered households, or 23.4 per cent, had bought a ₹1,190 replacement filter within nine months unprompted, generating ₹25.04 lakh — twice the ₹12.49 lakh the subscription would have produced, at no build cost. Puntambekar wanted to reprice; Kharche's rule did not permit it.

For discussion. First, Bhatkal's third signal returned 4 against a bar of 5, inside an interval of 2.1 to 34.3 per cent: was her verdict a finding or an artefact? Second, what should have been in Mahaul's 12 January rule to catch an absent demand in four weeks? Third, both protagonists acted on a population other than the one in their hypothesis: where is the line between Bhatkal's rewrite and the post-hoc rescue of a dead idea?

13. Going deeper

Writing a problem hypothesis is the upstream craft: both failures here were failures of the sentence. Synthesising research decides what counts as a signal. Surfacing assumptions and riskiest assumption first say which clause to test first — Nishkarsh's was the buyer, tested last. Frequency and intensity of the problem turned 23.6 per cent into 92.1 per cent; vitamin vs painkiller asks the same of willingness to pay. Problem framing and reframing and ‘how might we’ questions govern the rewrite; persevere, pivot or perish follows a verdict; sizing an opportunity answers the market question; problem–model fit asks whether the business can profitably serve it, where Nauka came unstuck. Opportunity solution trees, writing a solution hypothesis and ideation: brainstorming, Crazy 8s, HMW begin the next loop, and problem decay and re-validation closes it.
exp20v2-prob.validation:
Validating a problem hypothesis

1. A Friday readout, and ₹60 lakh

On Friday 27 March 2026, Deepa Bhosekar, the product manager responsible for new products at Chikitsa Clinic Systems, a Pune company that sells appointment and billing software to independent clinics, stood in front of her chief executive, Bakul Dixit, and her head of sales, Dinesh Chandwani. At a planning meeting on Monday 2 March, the company had drawn up a proposal: spend ₹60 lakh over two quarters to build an automated appointment-reminder product, sold to clinic owners at ₹1,500 a month. The proposal rested on one sentence that everybody in the room believed: independent clinics lose a meaningful share of their booked slots to patients who do not turn up, and their owners want that fixed.

Everybody believed it because everybody had heard it in demos and support tickets. Bhosekar had asked for time before any money moved. By the Friday she held two bodies of evidence: 24 interviews with clinic owners conducted between 3 and 20 March, and the appointment books of eight clinics covering the four weeks from 2 February to 1 March. Her task was to say what the evidence supported.

Exhibit 1. What was at stake on 27 March
ItemFigure
Proposed build cost, two quarters₹60,00,000
Proposed price per clinic per month₹1,500
Annual revenue per clinic (₹1,500 × 12)₹18,000
Clinics needed for one year of revenue to equal the build cost (₹60,00,000 ÷ ₹18,000 = 333.3, rounded up)334

The last row of Exhibit 1 explains why the question mattered. Chikitsa served roughly 2,100 clinics, so 334 was plausible, but only if the problem was real for a large fraction of them. If it was imagined, two quarters of engineering, including Caroline Wambui's team in Nairobi, would build something clinics politely admired and did not pay for. If it was real but declared imagined, a competitor would take the opening. The skill on trial was validation.

2. The idea

A problem hypothesis is a falsifiable statement that a specific kind of person has a specific problem that matters enough to act upon. Validating it means deciding, from evidence gathered for the purpose, which of three states it is in: validated (the evidence meets the bar you set), invalidated (the evidence plainly fails it) or unclear (the evidence falls between the two, or is too thin to say). The third state is not a polite no; it prevents the two usual errors, declaring victory on a pleasant interview and abandoning an idea on an unpleasant one.

The practice was invented to solve a problem of expensive enthusiasm: teams built what stakeholders requested and discovered afterwards that request and need were different things. Steve Blank, teaching customer development at Stanford in the early 2000s, told founders to get out of the building and test their hypotheses first. Eric Ries popularised the loop in The Lean Startup (2011), and Rob Fitzpatrick's The Mom Test (2013) sharpened the interviewing craft.

Bhosekar's sentence for the meeting was this: "We will call the problem real when it clears a bar we wrote down before we looked, and not before."

3. How it actually works

The mechanics have five steps, and the unglamorous ones are the ones most often skipped. First, write the hypothesis so it can fail. Bhosekar's read: "Independent clinics with one to three doctors lose at least 15 per cent of booked slots to no-shows, and their owners are already trying to fix it." A no-show is a patient who booked a slot and neither attended nor cancelled in time.

Second, decide in advance what would count. This is the step practitioners leave implicit, and it is where most self-deception enters. A pre-registered decision rule states, before the data arrive, what result would validate, what would invalidate, and what falls between. Third, gather evidence of mixed kinds: what people say (interviews), what records show (appointment books) and what people do when asked to commit (a paid pilot). Fourth, compare evidence with rule mechanically. Fifth, record the classification and next action.

Exhibit 2. The rule Bhosekar wrote on 2 March, before any interview
SignalSourceValidated ifInvalidated if
Pooled no-show rateAppointment books, 8 clinics15% or higherbelow 8%
Owners running a workaround today24 interviews12 or more (50%)fewer than 5
Signed paid-pilot letters at ₹1,500 a month24 interviews6 or more (25%)0

All three signals had to clear the validated column together; any one landing below its invalidation line alone would sink the hypothesis; anything else was unclear. A workaround is any effort the owner already makes, such as a receptionist telephoning patients the evening before.

4. A worked example, and a second pass

The appointment books came from eight clinics. Exhibit 3 gives booked slots and no-shows for each over the four weeks to 1 March, and the rate is no-shows divided by booked slots.

Exhibit 3. Appointment books, 2 February to 1 March 2026

Clinic 3 is 92 ÷ 510 = 18.04 per cent, shown rounded. The simple average of the eight clinic rates is 13.0 per cent; the pooled rate weights each clinic by its volume.

Read the bottom row first. The pooled rate is 420 ÷ 3,100 = 13.5 per cent, below the 15 per cent bar and above the 8 per cent floor. The simple average of the eight rates is 13.0 per cent; the pooled rate counts every slot equally, which is what revenue responds to. Both sit below the bar, though four clinics (1, 3, 6 and 8) individually met 15 per cent, which is why the story felt true to anyone who spoke to them.

Figure 2 shows the spread: rates run from 5 to 20 per cent, so "clinics lose 15 per cent" misdescribes half of them. The interviews then added their own counts, in Exhibit 4.

Exhibit 4. Interview signals, 24 owners, 3 to 20 March 2026

The workaround signal cleared its bar (13 against 12). The pooled rate and the pilot letters did not (13.5 against 15 per cent; 5 against 6). None fell to its invalidation line. The classification was therefore unclear, leaning favourable.

The second pass. Suppose one input changes: Bhosekar had written the bar at 12 per cent rather than 15. Clinics 1, 3, 5, 6 and 8 would then individually clear it, five of eight rather than four, and the pooled 13.5 per cent would pass. Two of three signals would be validated, though no appointment had changed. That is the argument for writing the bar before looking.

A further sensitivity concerns value. Suppose a reminder product removes one third of no-shows. In the eight clinics that is 140 slots in four weeks; at an average consultation fee of ₹600, that recovers ₹84,000, or ₹10,500 per clinic per four weeks, and about ₹1,36,500 per clinic across thirteen such periods in a year. Against the annual price of ₹18,000, the return is roughly 7.6 times. If the fee were ₹350, as at many physiotherapy practices, the recovered revenue falls to ₹79,625 a year and the multiple to about 4.4. The open question was not "does it hurt" but "does it hurt widely enough".

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Validated is relative to a bar, not to the truth

The word suggests certainty; it records only that evidence cleared a threshold someone chose, so the threshold deserves as much scrutiny as the data.

Unclear is a result, not a failure

Teams treat unclear as embarrassing and push it up or down. The right response is to name the cheapest further evidence that would resolve it.

Interest is not commitment

Fifteen owners described a recent no-show, but only five signed a letter. Compliments are cheap; costly commitments weigh more.

Validation is not solution validation

Confirming a problem says nothing about whether a reminder product, a deposit system or a waiting list is the best answer. That belongs to a separate solution hypothesis.

The sample is not the market

The 24 owners came from Chikitsa's own customers and referrals, a convenience sample. If they are unrepresentative, the pooled rate describes them, not the 2,100 clinics.

Averages hide the segment

Dental and dermatology clinics (3, 6 and 8) sat at 15 to 20 per cent; ophthalmology and physiotherapy sat at 5 to 9. A pooled number can fall below the bar while a subgroup clears it. Finding the subgroup afterwards yields a new hypothesis, not confirmation of the old one.

Records beat recollection, but records have limits

Recalled rates run higher than the books show, because bad days are memorable. Yet a book cannot reveal whether a no-show would have attended with a reminder.

What validation cannot tell you

It cannot size the market, price the product or predict adoption. A widespread problem can still be one customers refuse to pay to solve.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products

The logic is constant; the cheapest evidence changes. Consumer products can use behavioural data at scale. B2B products depend on interviews and workarounds, because buyers are scarce. Marketplaces must validate the problem on two sides, and a problem real on one may be imagined on the other.

Chikitsa's case was B2B; had the product later let patients rebook through a Practo-style directory, patients would become a second side needing its own validation. Scale matters too. An early-stage company can validate with a dozen conversations and a hand-built test. A large company has data but more opinions to defend, and its danger is a validation exercise convened to approve a decision already made.

7. Common mistakes

Exhibit 5. Four mistakes, their symptoms and the cheapest catch
MistakeSymptom seen from outsideCheapest diagnostic
Bar set after the dataThe threshold sits just under the resultAsk for the dated document in which the bar was written
Counting enthusiasm as evidenceDeck quotes praise, no counts of commitmentsAsk how many people paid, signed or changed behaviour
Confirmation interviewingQuestions name the solution; answers agreeRead three transcripts for leading questions
Forcing a binaryEvery finding is "validated" or "killed" within a weekAsk what result would have produced "unclear"

Behind them lie four misunderstandings: validation as persuasion rather than measurement; the belief that what people say predicts what they do; forgetting that an interviewer who describes a solution has told the respondent what answer is welcome; and taking decisiveness for rigour. Each diagnostic is a single question needing no new research.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Bhosekar writes Exhibit 2 on 2 March and circulates it with Dixit's initials beside it. She interviews without naming the product, asks for appointment books rather than recollections, and offers the pilot letter as a test rather than a pitch. She reports the three signals separately, shows the spread in Figure 2, and states the classification in one line. Nobody is surprised by the label because the rule was agreed in advance.

9. Closing

Bhosekar told the meeting that the problem was unclear, leaning favourable, and proposed a four-week test rather than a ₹60 lakh build. She would take the 4 weeks to run a manual reminder service, texting patients on behalf of 12 clinics, with Wambui's team spending days rather than quarters. The aim was to learn whether reminders measurably cut no-shows, and to widen the sample beyond Chikitsa's own customers. She estimated ₹4 lakh, under seven per cent of the original proposal, and Dixit approved it that afternoon.

The evidence supported neither spending nor stopping, and a cheap test could resolve it within a month. What to learn next: Persevere, pivot or perish for the decision after a test; Sizing an opportunity for the market question validation cannot answer; Writing a solution hypothesis for the claim that a reminder product is the right remedy; and Problem decay and re-validation, since a validated problem can fade.

Two questions to sit with. First, if Bhosekar had written the bar at 12 per cent and reached a validated verdict, what in the evidence would have been different, and what does that tell you about where the real judgment sits? Second, think of a belief your own team holds about customers that "everybody has heard". What would you write down, today, as the evidence that would make you drop it?
