Lakeer Fleet Energy: Forty-One Minutes of a 540-Minute Day

A case for class discussion. The company is fictional; the market is not.

1. The night before

At twenty minutes to midnight on Sunday, 18 October 2026, Hemali Zalavadia was at the dining table of her flat off Sarjapur Road in Bengaluru, with four printouts in front of her and a fifth she had deliberately not printed. Dussehra was on Tuesday, her stations were into their heaviest weeks of the year, and the board met at nine.

She was VP Product of Lakeer Fleet Energy, and the item against her name was one line long: Problem statement for FY28 — approval sought. Hiten Bhavsar, the CEO, had added "approval sought" himself. The sentence Lakeer had run on since March 2021 had been photographed off a whiteboard so often that it appeared, unattributed, in two investor memos:

A gig delivery rider in an Indian metro is unable to complete a ten-hour earning shift on an electric two-wheeler because recharging costs him four hours of downtime he cannot afford.

Everything Lakeer owned followed from that sentence: 61 swap stations in four cities, 11,200 battery packs, a pack standard frozen in 2023, and five-year site agreements she could not unwind without writing a cheque. The uncomfortable thing was not that the sentence had aged, but that in March 2026 a diary study had put a number on the downtime — 41 minutes of a 540-minute logged-in day — and nothing had changed.

She had four options on the page and a suspicion that all four answered a question she could no longer defend.

2. How Lakeer came to own 61 leases

Lakeer was founded in June 2019 by Hiten Bhavsar, who had run a 40-vehicle diesel three-wheeler cargo fleet out of Peenya, and Ruchira Mohile, an embedded-systems engineer from Pune. The first product was a 2.1 kWh lithium-iron-phosphate pack sold to e-rickshaw makers: small, thinly profitable, dependent on other people's vehicles. The turn came in 2021, when delivery fleets were electrifying fast and every conversation Hiten had ended in the same complaint about charging.

Then came the decision that still shaped every option on Hemali's page. In February 2022, racing two well-funded competitors into the same cities, Lakeer signed five-year agreements for 61 sites at once — forecourt corners from fuel-pump dealers, kirana-chain parking, two municipal contractors — each with a monthly minimum guarantee whether a pack moved or not: ₹38,000 on average, ₹23.18 lakh a month across the estate, six months payable on early exit. The land grab worked. It also fixed the product's geography in 2022, by a team optimising for signatures, and meant walking away from an average site cost ₹2.28 lakh.

The second constraint was quieter. In November 2023, to let riders swap at any station, Ruchira froze the mechanical and BMS interface of the L2 pack — the right call, and one that locked Lakeer out of fleets running factory-fixed batteries, by 2026 most of the market.

3. The industry around the sentence

By late 2026 the Indian electric two- and three-wheeler fleet market had three customers who were routinely described as one: the independent gig rider, financed, often migrant, switching between Swiggy, Zomato and Zepto within a week; the fleet owner, from six-vehicle operators to the organised rental fleets that supply riders to the platforms, Zypp Electric among them; and the platform itself, which owned the order flow and none of the vehicles. Lakeer competed for the first with Sun Mobility and Battery Smart, for the second with Ola Electric's and Ather Energy's ownership propositions, and for the third with nobody.

Regulation pulled several ways. The Ministry of Power's charging guidelines had made room for swapping and de-licensed the resale of electricity for charging, which was what made Lakeer legal at all; BIS interoperability work pointed towards a standard pack the frozen L2 interface might not satisfy; the Battery Waste Management Rules made Lakeer responsible for every pack it had fielded. And from September 2026 the DPDP Act's consent machinery covered the rider location traces Raquel Dufresne's team in Toronto had used since 2023.

Ronak Trivedi, hired into New Jersey in 2025 to sell the Fleet Desk software, had closed 41 fleet customers for ₹3.6 crore of annual recurring revenue — ₹8.78 lakh each on average — and then brought in Nawras Courier LLC of Dubai, a 900-vehicle last-mile operator whose August 2026 letter of intent was worth USD 1.7 million over three years: about ₹14.96 crore at ₹88 to the dollar, or ₹4.99 crore a year, 1.4 times Fleet Desk's ₹3.6 crore of annual recurring revenue.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

Figure 1 lays out the sequence; read it as a record of what Lakeer believed at each point, because the belief is what the money followed.

2021–23: the sentence is confirmed. Utilisation climbed in Bengaluru and Pune and riders who joined kept swapping. Nobody asked why those who stopped had stopped: the only riders Lakeer could see were the ones at its stations.

August 2024: the shift changes shape. Quick commerce pulled rider work into two peaks and shortened the modal day. The ten-hour shift became, for many, seven or eight hours in two pieces — and a rider working in two pieces often needs no mid-shift swap. Lakeer read the flat swaps-per-rider number as a pricing problem.

January 2025: Shift Planner. Hedda Keller's team in Berlin built an in-app planner telling a rider when and where to swap. Adoption was poor; the team blamed the interface, and v2 was commissioned and tested as Exhibit 5.

March 2026: the diary study. Harini Nagarkatti's team paid 38 riders to log five days each. Exhibit 3 is the result: swapping, with the ride and the queue, took 41 minutes of a 540-minute day; waiting for the next order took 118.

April 2026: the definition changes. "Active rider" was tightened from one swap in the trailing 30 days to four. Defensible — and it silently broke every cohort comparison in Exhibit 6.

September 2026: consent. Of the 7,610 riders active in September 2026, 2,180 — 28.6 per cent — re-consented to continuous location sharing, and they skewed towards the heaviest swappers. The data that might have falsified the sentence became harder to collect and biased towards the riders for whom it was most nearly true.

5. The people

Hemali Zalavadia — VP Product, Bengaluru
Position: nothing can be approved until the problem is stated so that evidence could disprove it. Incentive: her ESOP tranche vests against the FY28 plan. Not saying: she wrote the Shift Planner v2 brief herself, on the old sentence.
Hiten Bhavsar — co-founder and CEO, Bengaluru
Position: the sentence is right and density is the gap. Incentive: the ₹60 crore bridge is priced on the rider-network story. Not saying: he has asked Ronak what a Dubai-led plan would look like.
Ruchira Mohile — co-founder and CTO, Pune
Position: the L2 pack and the station firmware are the only defensible assets. Incentive: her 22 Pune engineers maintain them. Not saying: she expects BIS work to make the L2 interface a liability within three years.
Harini Nagarkatti — Head of City Operations, Hyderabad
Position: the diary study is unrepresentative — her logs show 31 of the 61 stations queueing past ten minutes at peak weekly. Incentive: city P&Ls judged on swaps per station. Not saying: Jaipur has been unviable for nine months and the exit cheque lands in her budget.
Raquel Dufresne — Senior Data Scientist, Toronto
Position: every number Lakeer owns comes from the point of swapping, so none of it speaks about riders who do not swap. Incentive: credibility; she has twice refused to sign a metrics slide. Not saying: her churn model improved on distance from a rider's home to the nearest station and barely moved on queue length.
Hedda Keller — Principal Designer, Berlin
Position: the planner tested well and needs distribution, not a new problem statement. Incentive: two years of her portfolio sits in it. Not saying: riders in her sessions kept re-framing it as an earnings calculator.
Reshma Velankar — Head of Customer Success, Singapore
Position: the paying customer is the fleet owner; of 214 Fleet Desk tickets in the September quarter, the biggest category was battery health and warranty. Incentive: renewals. Not saying: she has promised two customers a pack-degradation report that does not exist.
Ronak Trivedi — Head of Enterprise Sales, New Jersey
Position: take Nawras and let it define the roadmap. Incentive: commission weighted to value signed before 31 December 2026. Not saying: what Nawras needs is evidence for Dubai's RTA that its packs are within safe state-of-health limits.

6. Exhibits

Hiten takes Exhibit 1 to investors: 182,000 swaps, ₹100.10 lakh of revenue, four cities. Read against Exhibit 4 it says close to the opposite.

Exhibits 2 and 3 cannot both describe the same world. In Exhibit 2, 171 of 486 riders — 35.2 per cent of those who answered — name charging time as the biggest drag on earnings. In Exhibit 3, swapping with the ride and queue takes 41 minutes of 540, or 7.6 per cent of the day, while waiting for the next order takes 118 minutes, 21.9 per cent. Raquel reads Exhibit 2 as what riders say to a man handing them a battery.

Exhibit 6 made the board nervous in July, and Hemali trusts it least: every daggered cell sits on the new definition, and the apparent collapse from 36 per cent to 24 per cent at M3 runs along the boundary of the April change. Raquel has twice asked for budget to recompute it; twice it was deferred.

7. Voices

"Density, density, density. Twenty-two stations in Bengaluru and we are above water there. If a rider spends 41 minutes a day on us, it is because we are the best option he has — not because 41 minutes was the whole problem."Hiten Bhavsar, management call, 6 October 2026
"We have never observed a rider who does not come to a station. Not once, in seven years. Exhibits 1, 2, 5 and 6 all come from people already standing in front of a Lakeer battery. The sentence was a reasonable guess in 2021. It is still a guess."Raquel Dufresne, on the FY28 planning document, 9 October 2026
"Six points of retention is six points. I am not losing a product because a confidence interval touches zero."Ronak Trivedi, in the #fy28-plan channel, 10 October 2026
"In four of six sessions the rider asked the planner the same question: kitna banega aaj? — what will I make today. Not when to swap. I logged it as a feature request. I think I logged it wrong."Hedda Keller, email, 12 October 2026
"Thirty-one of my sixty-one stations queue past ten minutes at peak at least once a week. But the quieter thing: in Jaipur the queue is never the problem, and Jaipur is where the riders leave."Harini Nagarkatti, city review, 13 October 2026
"My customers do not have shifts. They have 900 vehicles and an auditor. If FY28 is about riders, I must tell Hamdan Al Hammadi that the state-of-health report in his LOI is not on the roadmap."Reshma Velankar, note to Hemali, 14 October 2026

8. The options as Hemali sees them

Option A — recommit to the rider. Keep the 2021 sentence, close Jaipur, spend ₹9 crore densifying Bengaluru and Pune with 18 new sites, and raise the blended price from ₹55 to ₹62. Exhibit 4's arithmetic works at density. The uncomfortable part is that this is the option the evidence supports least directly, and that closing Jaipur means ₹18.24 lakh of guarantees on eight sites in Harini's budget.

Option B — make the fleet owner the customer. Sign Nawras, build the state-of-health and compliance product Reshma has half-promised, and let enterprise revenue carry the stations. ₹4.99 crore a year is real money against an annual burn of ₹28.8 crore. It also writes a problem statement about an auditor in Dubai, for a job no Indian rider has named, using a station estate that customer does not need.

Option C — the platform story. Hold both customers, call Lakeer an energy-and-software platform, and put a two-sided problem statement to the board. This is what Hiten's deck already implies, and what Ramya Kothandaraman's term sheet appears designed to prevent.

Option D — stop and re-discover. Freeze the roadmap for six weeks and run the study Raquel has wanted since 2023: riders recruited away from stations, including riders who left. Six weeks is roughly ₹3.6 crore of burn, and the one thing the bridge timetable may not allow.

All four take the same shape — customer, job, obstacle — with the obstacle in the supply of energy. Exhibit 3 puts a rider's day in riding and in waiting for order flow Lakeer does not control, not in energy, and Hedda's riders keep asking about money, not minutes. If the job is "earn ₹1,000 before I go home", a ₹55 swap is 5.5 per cent of that day, and the lever is price.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Cash at 30 September 2026 was ₹41 crore against a net burn of ₹2.4 crore a month, a little over 17 months. Ramya Kothandaraman, who led the Series A, has tabled a ₹60 crore bridge at a flat valuation on one condition: that Lakeer name a single customer segment and show positive contribution in it by 31 March 2027. The 61 site agreements run to staggered expiries through 2027, carry ₹23.18 lakh a month of minimum guarantees, and would cost a ₹1.39 crore exit cheque if surrendered at once. The 11,200 packs stand at ₹20.61 crore and carry producer-responsibility obligations. Nawras requires signature by 15 November 2026. Headcount is 214, frozen since July, and Ruchira's firmware roadmap cannot carry both a compliance product and a rider planner before April 2027.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Write the 2021 sentence as [customer] is unable to [job] because [problem]. Which slot is least well evidenced by Exhibits 1 to 6, and what observation would break it?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 disagree. Say what each one can measure and what it cannot see.
  3. Exhibit 6 suggests retention is collapsing. How much of the fall could the April 2026 definition change account for, and what would you recompute?
  4. If no Lakeer dataset can speak about the rider who does not swap, what is the cheapest study that could falsify the sentence before 31 March 2027 on a ₹25 lakh budget?
  5. Ramya's condition forces Lakeer to name one customer. Rewrite the hypothesis for the rider and for the fleet owner, and say which exhibit would most quickly prove each wrong.
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Hemali put on the one line against her name, what does she ask the board to stop doing, and how does she answer Hiten when he says a sentence is not a strategy?

At ten past one she turned the printouts face down, took out her notebook, and wrote "A rider is unable to —", then sat with the pen on the page, because the next word was either earn or finish, and she could not tell which the last five years had been about.
exp20v2-prob.hypothesis:
Writing a problem hypothesis

Discovery & Design: Problem & Opportunity Definition

1. A budget and a sentence

On Monday, 3 August 2026, Mahima Siroya, head of product at Munim Khata House, opened a one-page document that her chief executive, Ojasvi Kher, had asked for by Friday. Munim Khata House sold a billing and bookkeeping app to small wholesale traders in Surat, Ludhiana and Coimbatore, and it had 1,20,000 active traders. The company had earmarked six months of its product team for a new bet, at ₹30 lakh a month, which came to ₹180 lakh, or ₹1.8 crore.

The draft sentence on the page read: "Small traders find GST compliance difficult, so they need a simpler filing app." Naveed Khatri, who led sales in Surat, liked it. Mahima distrusted it. Nobody could say what observation would make the sentence false: on-time filers "coped", late filers proved the difficulty. A statement that survives every possible fact is a mood, not a diagnosis.

What was at stake was concrete. Six engineers, two designers and a data analyst, Marguerite Tremblay in Montreal, would spend half a year on whatever the sentence implied. If it pointed at the wrong obstacle, the company would ship a polished feature that nobody's behaviour required. This page follows what Mahima did with that sentence, and the discipline she used is called writing a problem hypothesis.

2. The idea

A problem hypothesis is a single sentence that names who has a problem, what they are trying to get done, and what stands in the way, stated precisely enough that evidence could show it to be wrong. The standard form is: [Customer] is unable to [job] because [problem]. A job, in the sense used by the Jobs to Be Done school, is the progress a person is trying to make in a given circumstance, such as "file my monthly return before the deadline". The problem is the specific obstacle between the person and that progress. A hypothesis is a claim that makes a prediction, so that the world can answer it.

The habit descends from two older traditions. Karl Popper argued in the 1930s that a claim is scientific only if some observation could refute it. The lean-startup movement of the 2000s, associated with Steve Blank and Eric Ries, carried that idea into companies: treat every plan as a guess and test it cheaply. The problem hypothesis applies the test earlier, to the question of what is wrong.

Teams write problems that already contain their answer. "Traders need a simpler app" is a solution wearing a problem's clothes. The sentence Mahima could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib was this: "Before we build anything, I want a version of the problem that a trader could tell us is wrong."

3. How it actually works

The mechanics have five steps, and the last two are the ones practitioners leave unspoken.

Step one: pick the customer narrowly. "Small traders" covers a kirana owner in Coimbatore with a turnover of ₹40 lakh and a textile wholesaler in Surat with ₹4 crore. Their monthly return, the GST (Goods and Services Tax) form called GSTR-3B, due around the 20th of the next month, is a different chore for each. Mahima restricted the customer to wholesale traders with annual turnover between ₹50 lakh and ₹5 crore who file monthly.

Step two: turn the job into something observable. "Find compliance difficult" is a feeling. "Files the return by the due date" is an event, recorded by the portal that the Goods and Services Tax Network runs, and it can be counted.

Step three: name one cause. The word because is where most drafts hide a list. From fifteen early interviews she listed the candidates: supplier bills arriving after the month closes, a backlog of manual data entry, not knowing the deadline, and a few miscellaneous reasons. She chose the best supported as the claim and kept the others as rivals.

Step four, usually implicit: state the prediction. If the cause is real, something else must also be true, and that something is checkable. If late supplier bills cause late filing, then traders whose bills arrive late should file late more often than traders whose bills arrive early.

Step five, usually implicit: state the refuting result in advance. Before collecting any data, the team agrees what outcome would make them drop the claim. Mahima fixed it as: if the late-filing rate among late-bill traders is not at least 20 percentage points above the rate among early-bill traders, the hypothesis is rejected.

The hypothesis she took to Ojasvi read: Wholesale traders with turnover of ₹50 lakh to ₹5 crore are unable to file their monthly GST return by the due date because supplier bills for the month arrive after the 5th of the following month.

4. A worked example, and a second pass

Munim's field team, Naveed's group together with a colleague in Ludhiana, interviewed 60 traders and checked each one's filing history for the preceding six months against the portal. Of the 60, 36 had filed at least one monthly return late, a late-filing rate of 36 / 60 = 60 per cent. The interviews coded the main reason each of the 36 gave:

Main reason givenTradersShare of all 60
Supplier bills arrive late2135.0%
Data-entry backlog915.0%
Did not know the deadline35.0%
Other35.0%
Total late filers3660.0%

Check: 21 + 9 + 3 + 3 = 36; 36 / 60 = 60.0 per cent, and 35.0 + 15.0 + 5.0 + 5.0 = 60.0.

Stated reasons are testimony, so Marguerite tested the prediction against behaviour. She split the 60 traders by the date their supplier bills typically arrived: after the 5th (30 traders) or by the 5th (30 traders), and counted late filers in each group.

GroupTradersFiled lateLate rate
Bills arrive after the 5th302480.0%
Bills arrive by the 5th301240.0%
Total / overall rate603660.0%

Check: 24 / 30 = 80.0%; 12 / 30 = 40.0%; 24 + 12 = 36; 36 / 60 = 60.0%. The overall rate is computed from totals, not by averaging the two rates.

The gap is 80 − 40 = 40 percentage points, twice the 20-point bar Mahima had set in advance, and the late rate in the late-bill group is 80 / 40 = 2.0 times that of the other. The hypothesis survived a test that could have killed it. Survival is not proof.

Now the arithmetic of stakes. Applying the 60 per cent late rate to 1,20,000 traders gives 72,000 late filers. The interviews attributed 21 of 36, or 58.3 per cent, to late bills, so 72,000 × 21 / 36 = 42,000 traders. If Munim charged ₹3,000 a year for a supplier-bill capture feature and 15 per cent of them bought it, that is 6,300 buyers and 6,300 × ₹3,000 = ₹189 lakh a year, against a build cost of ₹180 lakh.

Second pass, one input changed. Suppose the field data had pointed the other way, so that the dominant cause was the data-entry backlog, with 9 of 36 traders. The same chain gives 72,000 × 9 / 36 = 18,000 traders, 15 per cent of whom is 2,700 buyers, and 2,700 × ₹3,000 = ₹81 lakh. That does not cover ₹180 lakh. A different "because" does not merely change the product; it changes whether the bet is worth making.

Named causeTraders affectedBuyers at 15%Revenue a year (₹ lakh)Build cost (₹ lakh)
Late supplier bills (21 of 36)42,0006,300189180
Data-entry backlog (9 of 36)18,0002,70081180

Price ₹3,000 per buyer per year. 6,300 × 3,000 = ₹1,89,00,000 = 189 lakh; 2,700 × 3,000 = ₹81,00,000 = 81 lakh. Rows are alternatives, not parts of a total.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Falsifiable is not the same as true

A good hypothesis is one that can fail. The point is to be exposed, not to be right. A sentence that survived one test remains a conjecture.

The cause and the solution are different things

"Because they lack a bill-capture tool" smuggles the answer in. The cause should be a fact about the customer's world, here the arrival date of bills, that exists whether or not Munim does anything.

Correlation is not the whole claim

The 40-point gap shows that late bills and late filing travel together. Traders with slow suppliers may also be traders with weaker bookkeeping habits. Only an intervention speaks to cause. The problem hypothesis tells you what to test; it does not run the test.

It is easily confused with a problem statement

A problem statement describes pain. A problem hypothesis commits to a mechanism and invites refutation.

It cannot size the pain

The hypothesis says why traders file late, not how much it hurts. Frequency and intensity, a later topic, answer that.

Questions a newcomer should ask before relying on it

Who was asked, and who was not? Is the outcome measured or reported? Was the refuting threshold set before the data arrived? And would a person who disagreed with me know what to bring as evidence?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and late stage

In a consumer product the customer is an individual and the job is often episodic, so the hypothesis leans on behavioural data at volume: "commuters are unable to find a seat on the 8:10 train because..." can be tested in analytics within days. In B2B, as with Munim, the buyer, user and payer may differ, and a hypothesis written about the user may be vetoed by the buyer. Mahima's trader files the return, but a chartered accountant often chooses the software, so a second hypothesis was needed. In a marketplace there are two customers, and the hypothesis must name which side is unable and which side's behaviour causes it.

Stage matters as well. An early-stage company, with fifteen customers and a runway of a few months, tests hypotheses through conversations and manual workarounds. A large company has the data but also stakeholders who each hold a favourite cause. Nils Overgaard, a designer in Copenhagen, put it thus: in a small firm the hypothesis is a bet; in a large one it is a treaty.

7. Common mistakes

The hypothesis that cannot lose. The symptom, seen from outside, is that every interview "confirms" it. The misunderstanding is that the sentence is vague enough to absorb any result. Diagnostic: ask the author to name an outcome that would change their mind. If they cannot, rewrite the sentence.

The solution in disguise. The symptom is a roadmap that matches the sentence one for one. The misunderstanding is treating "users need X" as a finding. The diagnostic: delete the product's name and check that the clause still describes a real obstacle.

Testing after the fact. The symptom is a refuting threshold that appears in the deck only after the results do. The misunderstanding is that the standard of evidence can be set once the evidence is in. The diagnostic: look for the date on which the threshold was written down, and compare it with the date of the data pull.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Mahima's Friday page contained four things: the one-sentence hypothesis with a named segment, a measurable job and a single cause; the two rival causes, listed with their counts; the refuting threshold of 20 percentage points, dated before the analysis; and the stakes table showing that the bet pays only if the main cause is the real one. A sceptical engineer could tell, from the page alone, what result would stop the project. That is the target.

9. Closing: what she decided

Mahima proposed a staged commitment, not the full ₹180 lakh. The first stage was an experiment, giving 300 traders an early-bill reminder service by hand through the app's existing chat, and watching their filing for two cycles. If their late rate fell by at least 15 points relative to a comparison group, the full build would proceed. The correlation had passed its test, but the causal claim had not. Ojasvi agreed.

What to learn next, in order: surfacing assumptions, which lists the beliefs a hypothesis silently rests on; then validating a problem hypothesis, which designs the experiment properly; then frequency and intensity, which asks how often and how much it hurts; and finally problem framing and reframing, for when the evidence says the sentence was the wrong one.

Two questions to sit with. First, think of a problem statement you have written or approved at work: what observation would have shown it to be wrong, and did anyone write that down? Second, if Munim's experiment had returned only a 5-point improvement, which part of the hypothesis would you suspect first, the customer, the job or the cause?
exp40v2-prob.hypothesis:
Writing a problem hypothesis

Discovery & Design › Problem & Opportunity Definition · near-expert treatment

1. Two desks, one week in July

On Tuesday, 7 July 2026, Urvi Tilve, head of product at Upkaran Diagnostics Works in Pune, laid the quarter's service-ticket dump beside a funding note. Upkaran sold benchtop haematology analysers at ₹4.2 lakh to tier-two pathology laboratories, plus cloud reporting at ₹1,800 per analyser per month: 2,840 analysers across 1,960 laboratories, an average of 1.45 each, since most are one technician and one machine.

The note asked for ₹1.4 crore and nine engineering months. Its justifying sentence read: "Labs are frustrated by analyser downtime and need better service." Vedika Tulpule, the chief executive, had written one word in the margin: "Which labs?" The sentence could not lose: complaints proved frustration, silence proved suffering.

Nine days later, on Thursday, 16 July 2026, Tanuj Vaswani faced a different version in Bengaluru. Utsav Venue Exchange, his company, was two-sided: families searched banquet halls, enquired, visited and booked, and Utsav took four per cent of venue value. In June 2026 it carried 1,62,000 venue page views and confirmed 534 bookings at an average venue value of ₹3.85 lakh — ₹20.56 crore of gross merchandise value and ₹82.24 lakh of revenue. The circulating hypothesis was: "Families don't trust online venue booking, so they need verified reviews." Vatsal Thakore, who ran venue supply, believed it; Ujwala Tambe, the growth analyst, could not name a number that would move if it were false.

2. The idea, and the quarrel inside it

A problem hypothesis is one declarative sentence naming a customer, the job that customer is trying to get done, and the obstacle preventing it, stated so that some reachable observation would show it false. The canonical form is [Customer] is unable to [job] because [problem]. A job is progress sought in a circumstance — "return a haemogram the day the sample arrives" — not a demographic. The obstacle is a fact about the customer's world, true whether or not you act. Hypothesis means a claim that forbids something.

The lineage is twofold. Popper's demarcation argument of the 1930s held that a theory earns standing by what it rules out. The customer-development tradition Steve Blank formalised in the 2000s carried plan-as-guess into the firm. What the problem hypothesis adds is the location of the test: lean practice tested solutions, while this insists the diagnosis is itself a conjecture, and the costlier one, since a wrong solution to a real problem can be iterated and a right solution to an imagined problem cannot. It was invented against the statement containing its own answer: "labs need better service" organises a roadmap, survives every review, and is never tested.

Three schools disagree about how early that bottom rung should be reached. The falsificationist school signs a claim no observation could contradict is not a finding, not the sentence should precede field exposure. The interpretive school signs the circumstance must be discovered before any clause is fixed, not a claim is worth holding only if falsifiable today. The decision-analytic school signs a test is worth running only if its result changes the next action, not every hypothesis should be tested.

3. Mechanics in depth: five moves, two of them silent

Urvi's first move was to stop writing about laboratories in general. "Small labs" spanned a collection centre in Jalna billing ₹18 lakh a year and a six-technician chain outlet in Nashik. She restricted the customer to laboratories with a single qualified technician, sited over 120 kilometres by road from a service hub — a circumstance, not a demographic. Her second move made the job a recorded event: not "frustrated by downtime" but "returns the haemogram the day the sample is drawn", which the cloud layer timestamps. Her third named one cause, since because is where drafts conceal a list.

Fault category, quarter to 30 June 2026TicketsShare of tickets
Reagent-line clog1,28444.6%
Calibration drift74325.8%
Printer and connectivity48716.9%
Power-supply board2137.4%

Total tickets2,880100.0%

Arithmetic: 1,284 + 743 + 487 + 213 + 153 = 2,880. Shares are each category over 2,880, to one decimal: 44.6 + 25.8 + 16.9 + 7.4 + 5.3 = 100.0.

Reagent-line clog took 1,284 of the 2,880 tickets, or 44.6 per cent, and became the candidate cause; drift and connectivity were written down as named rivals, because a hypothesis without rivals is a preference. The fourth move is usually implicit — state the prediction the hypothesis forces: if distance converts a clog into a missed report, the slip rate must be higher at distant laboratories. The fifth is rarer — state in advance what kills the claim. On 7 July, before any cross-tabulation, Urvi wrote that unless the distant rate exceeded the near rate by 25 percentage points, the ₹1.4 crore would go to calibration. Thijs Vonk, in Rotterdam, ran the split.

Laboratory groupLabsClog ticketsReports slipped past same daySlip rate
Within 120 km of a service hub1,27470216122.9%
Beyond 120 km of a service hub68658246680.1%
Total (all labs)1,9601,28462748.8%

Arithmetic: 1,274 + 686 = 1,960 labs; 702 + 582 = 1,284 tickets; 161 + 466 = 627 slipped reports. Rates: 161 ÷ 702 = 22.9%, 466 ÷ 582 = 80.1%, 627 ÷ 1,284 = 48.8% — from the totals, not by averaging 22.9 and 80.1, which would wrongly give 51.5%. Clog tickets per laboratory: 0.55, 0.85 and 0.66.

Two second-order effects deserve naming. Circumstance is not randomly assigned: distant laboratories are also poorer and stock fewer spare reagent lines, so the gap bundles distance with its travelling companions. And a surviving hypothesis raises the cost of its own revision, since people defend a number this large — which is why the rivals belong in the same note.

4. The conditions, stated as testable claims

Claim one: the job has an observable completion event. Upkaran passes, since the cloud layer timestamps every report; Utsav passes, because a booking is confirmed or it is not. Claim two: the cause varies across the population you can reach. Distance from a hub is recorded; answer latency varies by venue. Claim three: a wrong answer is expensive enough to justify the test. Upkaran passes at ₹1.4 crore; a copy change would not.

Where the idea actively misleads is worth saying plainly. In a new category the customer's behaviour holds no instance of the job, so "unable to" has no base rate and every test returns nothing; the instrument there is a prototype that creates the circumstance. In a compliance-driven purchase the person who is unable is often indifferent. And where the obstacle is price the sentence degenerates: "unable to buy, it costs too much" forbids nothing.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Utsav is instructive because its hypothesis crosses a seam: the family cannot confirm a venue, but the cause sits in a venue manager's inbox. Ujwala's restatement was: families with a wedding date inside 45 days are unable to confirm a venue on Utsav because the venue manager, who answers enquiries personally, does not reply within 12 hours. That sentence belongs to two teams at once, which is why the original survived: no owner was embarrassed by it.

Other seams bite differently. In regulated settings — Upkaran's analysers fall under medical-device rules administered by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, where any change to a measurement path triggers revalidation — the obstacle may be real and the intervention barred, so the sentence names the pathway the team may touch. In hardware-plus-software the cause lives in the physical layer while the cheap lever is in software: Upkaran's clog is mechanical, but the actionable version was on-device detection. In AI-native products the model's visible failure tempts teams to write the hypothesis about the model when the obstacle has nothing to do with model quality. Mature companies keep a register of three or four live claims per area, each with an owner, threshold and date.

6. Eight nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

One: the cause must be a fact about the customer's world, not about your product's absence. The tell is a because clause naming a missing feature — "because there is no bill-capture tool". That reads as clumsy phrasing; it is worse, since the world cannot contradict the absence of your feature. Experts delete every proper noun and check an obstacle still stands.

Two: "unable to" has degrees, and the degree decides the economics. Customers are rarely unable; they are able at a cost. The tell is that nobody can say what the customer does instead. Upkaran's distant laboratories couriered samples to a district-town chain at ₹60 to ₹90 each — the real competitor, and the cap on what a fix is worth.

Three: the refuting threshold must be set before the data and sized to the decision. The tell is a threshold that appears only after the results. Twenty-five percentage points was no confidence level; it was the gap at which ₹1.4 crore beat calibration. Significance answers a question about sampling noise, and the question here was allocation.

Four: the segment definition does silent work, and defining it by product behaviour corrupts the test. "Active users are unable to…" is circular, since activity is downstream of the obstacle claimed. The tell is a segment nobody could have named before your product existed; a stranger with a map could find Urvi's.

Five: surviving a cross-sectional test is not a causal licence. The tell is a team whose next step after a 57-point gap is a build rather than a manipulation. The hypothesis earns the right to intervene cheaply on one variable; it does not establish that the variable is the cause. A small deliberate intervention severs the obstacle from its companions.

Six: a hypothesis can be perfectly true and commercially inert. The tell is enthusiastic agreement followed by no change in behaviour. Truth lives in the because; value lives in the unable to. If the job is one the customer would rather skip than solve, removing the obstacle buys nothing — vitamin versus painkiller, a property of the job clause.

Seven: the cause has a depth, and the right depth is one you can act on and the customer cannot route around. The tell is a why chain stopping at the answer that matches the roadmap. Upkaran could have gone deeper — unreliable power damages the reagent line — but cannot change the grid. Too shallow yields a bypassed feature; too deep, an unusable insight.

Eight: specificity transfers risk from the market to the sentence, which is the point. The tell of expertise is a sentence embarrassing within a fortnight: it dies cheaply in a cross-tab rather than expensively in a launch. The sentence that stays defensible for a quarter is the costly one, because it survives long enough to be built.

7. Product types and company stages

In consumer products tests are cheap, so the binding constraint is the segment clause, which analytics will blur. In B2B and enterprise user, buyer and payer differ: Upkaran's technician cannot return the report, but the proprietor signs the subscription, so Urvi carried two sentences. In platforms and marketplaces the sentence must declare which side is unable and which supplies the cause. For hardware the obstacle is often immovable within the bill of materials, pushing the hypothesis toward detection. For AI products the obstacle may be probabilistic — unable to rely on an output right most of the time — forcing a threshold into the sentence itself.

Stage changes the instrument more than the idea. At seed there is no cross-tab to run, and the discipline lives in the pre-registered threshold. At growth the risk shifts to segment definitions borrowed from the analytics schema. At scale, as Vedika put it, a hypothesis becomes a treaty: legible to a sceptical reviewer elsewhere. "Too complex for hypotheses" usually means the user's inability has not been separated from the buyer's indifference.

8. Three worked examples

Upkaran: a hypothesis that bought a staged commitment

Urvi priced the claim rather than the feature. Over the year to 30 June 2026 Upkaran lost 137 of 1,928 analyser subscriptions at near laboratories, or 7.1 per cent, and 196 of 912 at distant ones, or 21.5 per cent — 333 of 2,840 overall, or 11.7 per cent. The near rate, as benchmark, isolates the obstacle's cost.

Of 1,860 abandoned sessions with a fixed date, 1,041 abandoned at the return-leg step, or 56.0 per cent, because the Sunday evening return sold out before office leave was confirmed. A hold-the-return-seat feature shipped in six weeks for ₹38 lakh. Over the 60 days from Monday, 2 March 2026 to 30 April 2026, among 24,600 date-fixed sessions, bookings rose from 1,796, or 7.3 per cent, to 3,197, or 13.0 per cent — 1,401 more bookings worth ₹8.69 lakh, annualising to ₹52.84 lakh.

9. Failure modes and the cost of late detection

The sentence that cannot lose. Sign: every interview confirms it. Diagnostic: name the observation that would make you abandon it. Cost after a build: the whole build, as Vihaar shows.

The solution smuggled into the cause. Sign: the roadmap maps one-to-one onto the sentence. Diagnostic: strike out your product's name and read the clause again. Cost: a feature that is used and changes no outcome metric.

The confounded test. Sign: the groups differ in acquisition source or geography as well as in the obstacle. Diagnostic: list three ways they differ apart from the cause. Cost: Vihaar's two weeks, and the whole analysis without the organic cut.

Side confusion. Sign: no function volunteers to own the sentence. Diagnostic: who owns the metric in the "unable to" clause, and who the lever in the "because"? Cost: a quarter of coordination before anyone notices the lever was never funded.

The true but inert claim. Sign: strong agreement, no behaviour change in the smallest test. Diagnostic: what do these customers do instead, and what do they pay for it? Cost: the highest, since the evidence looks like success until revenue is measured.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The falsificationist position, at its strongest, is an argument about incentives rather than rigour: organisations are biased toward their existing plans, and the only reliable discipline is a claim sharp enough for reality to embarrass it in public. Its evidence is Vihaar in reverse: teams that could not say what would change their minds shipped expensive things. It is wrong where premature precision costs more than bias.

The interpretive position treats that exception as the rule for early work. At its strongest: a hypothesis fixes attention, the scarce resource in discovery, and a team pre-registering a threshold on clogs will not notice that distant laboratories have begun couriering samples wholesale — a larger business. Its evidence is that the best insight arrives as a surprise. It is wrong if unstructured discovery reliably converged.

The decision-analytic position cuts across both. At its strongest, the only question is whether a test changes an action: if Upkaran would have built the fix at any gap above zero, the cross-tab was theatre and the ₹26 lakh pilot the only real experiment. Its evidence is the validation exercises whose results altered nothing. It is wrong if the sentence has value independent of the decision, as a device for making beliefs visible.

A fourth position, rarely defended in print, is that shipping a thin increment beats any interview programme, so the hypothesis is overhead: Utsav could test the latency claim by answering enquiries for 200 venues for a month. The falsificationist reply is that this still needs a pre-stated threshold, or the result is read however the roadmap prefers.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this fills in the template correctly. Someone who has internalised it converts any handed-down problem statement into a prediction about a split in data already held; names the rival causes, with counts, unasked; sizes the refuting threshold to the decision and dates it; and treats a surviving hypothesis as the start of an intervention, not the end of an argument — the tell being a ₹26 lakh pilot after a 57-point gap, not a ₹1.4 crore build.

12. Closing: the two decisions

Urvi took the staged commitment to the board on Monday, 10 August 2026: ₹26 lakh for the hand-run service across 300 distant laboratories, the ₹1.4 crore release contingent on a 20-point fall in slip rate. Her reasoning was that the 57.2-point gap established where to intervene, not that the intervention would work, and that the 60 per cent recovery assumption worth ₹92.43 lakh a year was the note's weakest number. Vedika approved it, Tarana Velankar's team in Nashik running the pilot.

Tanuj dropped the reviews project, rewrote Utsav's sentence around the seam, and refused to fund the build. For one month Utsav would answer enquiries for 200 owner-answered venues with its own staff, Teodora Vranic in Zagreb modelling the result — a direct manipulation of the obstacle, planned against the degraded ₹4.80 crore case, not the ₹7.10 crore one.

Three questions. First, Upkaran's gap is cross-sectional and distance travels with poverty, power quality and spare-part stocking: what is the cheapest study that separates them, and is it worth running before the pilot? Second, Vihaar's hypothesis was specific, measurable and true, and still destroyed ₹3.1 crore — which clause was wrong, and what question in March 2025 would have caught it? Third, Utsav's scenarios differ by ₹2.30 crore on one assumption about marginal intent: should it be written into the hypothesis, and how?

13. Going deeper

Jobs to Be Done supplies the job clause and circumstance, without which "unable to" collapses into a demographic. Pains and gains supplies the candidate obstacles and the substitutes customers already use. Surfacing assumptions enumerates what Urvi's sentence silently assumes; validating a problem hypothesis turns the prediction into a study design. Frequency and intensity of the problem answers how badly it bites, and vitamin vs painkiller makes that commercial. Problem framing and reframing is what Vihaar used; persevere, pivot or perish is the rule once a sentence is refuted. Riskiest assumption first orders the queue. Opportunity solution trees link a hypothesis to candidate solutions, and "how might we" questions open that space without reopening the diagnosis. Sizing an opportunity yields the number that competes for budget.
case20v1-prob.hypothesis:
Lodestar Chemist Exchange: A Hypothesis Before the Budget

A teaching case on writing a problem hypothesis

1. Opening

On the evening of Tuesday 20 October 2026, Rajeev Zope sat at a corner desk in Lodestar Chemist Exchange's Baner office in Pune, with two documents open that disagreed about what the company's problem was. One was a product brief that read: "Chemists find ordering on Lodestar difficult." The other was a spreadsheet of lapsed customers in which Rajeev had found no chemist who called ordering difficult.

Rajeev was Lodestar's head of product. On Friday 23 October, the funding committee would release a single tranche of up to ₹60 lakh for the quarter ending in December, and he had to tell it what to spend the money on. Diwali fell on 8 November, and the festive weeks were the busiest of the year for chemists. If the tranche went to the wrong problem, there would be no second chance until the new year.

2. Company background

Lodestar Chemist Exchange is an app and delivery network that lets independent pharmacies in Maharashtra and Gujarat order stock from licensed wholesalers. Its customers are owner-operated chemist shops, which typically buy from two or three local distributors whose salesmen visit on fixed days and extend credit of a few weeks. Lodestar offers the same stock in an app, with next-day delivery from three partner distributors and digital invoices that feed GST filing and the batch records state drug inspectors expect under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act.

It competes with the salesman on the stool, with PharmEasy's business-to-business arm and with distributors' own apps. In 2026 Lodestar signed up chemists faster than it could keep them, and the board's question had changed from "how do we acquire?" to "why do they not come back?"

3. The situation

Exhibit 1 shows the problem in outline. Of 4,000 chemists who registered between 1 April and 31 August 2026, 2,600 placed a first order, which is 65.0 per cent of registrations. Of those 2,600, 1,040 placed a second order within 30 days, which is 40.0 per cent of first-order customers and 26.0 per cent of registrations. Only first orders placed by 12 September are counted, so every chemist had a full 30-day window before the pull on 12 October; later first orders are excluded. The other 1,560 went quiet.

The product team's reading was quick and sincere. Helga Vogel, the product designer in Berlin, had watched session recordings and seen several chemists abandon a search. She proposed voice and vernacular search in Marathi, Hindi and Gujarati, costing ₹48 lakh over 14 weeks.

Reeta Chandrasekhar, the data scientist in Toronto pulled a different cut. She grouped the 2,600 first-time buyers by how much of their first order Lodestar actually delivered, measured as lines delivered divided by lines ordered. Exhibit 2 shows the result.

Rohini Ramaswamy, the customer-success lead in Singapore, supplied a third view. Her team dialled 150 of the 1,560 quiet chemists and 120 picked up, which is 80.0 per cent of those dialled. Exhibit 3 gives the main reason each of those 120 offered. These are shares of the 120 who answered, not of all 1,560 lapsed customers, and the 30 who did not answer may differ from the rest.

The app complaint is the fourth-ranked of five reasons in Exhibit 3, and the fill-rate gap in Exhibit 2 points at stock. Neither is decisive: a chemist whose item is out of stock and who pays more for the substitute may simply blame the price.

4. The people

Rajeev Zope, Pune, head of product, owns the recommendation.

Helga Vogel, Berlin, product designer, wants the voice-search work funded. She has the session recordings, and argues that a chemist with a queue at the counter will not tolerate a failing search box.

Hamid Haldar, New Jersey, who leads sales for the distributor side, wants a margin and credit scheme. His partners, he says, are being undercut by the salesman's credit.

Reeta Chandrasekhar, Toronto, data scientist, wants the question stated first. She can test almost anything, but not the word "difficult".

Rohini Ramaswamy, Singapore, customer-success lead, has the voice of the customer and a worry that her team's calls are being over-read by people who were not on them.

5. The sentence at issue

The disagreement is partly about words. "Chemists find ordering difficult" names no customer, no job, no mechanism and no result that could embarrass it. A team could spend ₹48 lakh and still say it had held. The discipline is to replace it with one in the form "[customer] is unable to [job] because [problem]," where each bracket is specific enough that evidence could prove the whole thing wrong.

Rajeev drafted a candidate that evening; Figure 1 shows how it is built.

In prose: "An independent chemist in Pune who uses two or more distributors is unable to restock the fast-moving lines of the shop in a single order on Lodestar, because lines the app lists often cannot be supplied within 24 hours, so the chemist returns to the salesman for the lines that matter." Exhibit 2 makes the claim plausible without proving it. It is wrong if, among chemists with similar basket sizes, those whose lines were filled and those whose lines were not reorder at about the same rate.

6. The options

Option A: fund voice and vernacular search. Spend ₹48 lakh over 14 weeks, leaving ₹12 lakh of the tranche. It would help chemists who do struggle to search. The cost is a bet on the fourth-ranked reason in Exhibit 3; if the problem is stock, the build lands after the festive weeks and moves reorders little.

Option B: fund a margin and credit scheme. Spend the whole ₹60 lakh, carried past December into a six-month scheme, offering 15 days' credit and a margin top-up. Margin and credit together account for 50 of the 120 chemists reached in Exhibit 3, and the scheme can start before Diwali. The cost is that subsidy buys reorders without fixing why a chemist left, and ends when the money does.

Option C: spend ₹9 lakh on a hypothesis sprint of about three weeks, ending 13 November, then decide. The sprint would run 40 structured interviews and compare matched cohorts from the order log, with disproof conditions agreed in writing before anyone looks at the result. The upside is a decision on a falsifiable claim; the cost is a delay past Diwali, with ₹51 lakh held back through the festive weeks.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Why does "chemists find ordering difficult" fail as a problem hypothesis? What evidence could prove it wrong?

2. What does each of Exhibits 1 to 3 support, and what does it leave open? Why might the margin and stock reasons describe one event?

3. In Rajeev's draft (Figure 1), is the customer narrow enough, the job observable, and the disproof condition testable?

4. Which option should Rajeev recommend on Friday, and what would he tell the committee about the festive weeks it costs?

8. A note for the learner

This topic frames the decision as one of order. A problem hypothesis comes before a solution, and it earns its place by being exposed to refutation. The test of a good statement is whether a colleague could say, in advance, which result would make you abandon it. The brief fails; Rajeev's draft passes provisionally, because it names a customer, a job and a mechanism and states a result that would count against it.

A well-reasoned answer has three marks. It separates what the exhibits show from what they suggest: Exhibit 2 is an association and Exhibit 3 is a sample of 120 of 1,560. It treats each stakeholder's proposal as a competing hypothesis rather than a request, and it states in advance what result would change the choice.

One defensible path is Option C, with Option B held ready. The sprint costs ₹9 lakh against a ₹60 lakh tranche, and the disproof condition in Figure 1 can be run on data Lodestar already holds. If the matched cohorts show no gap, Rajeev drops the stock hypothesis and returns with Option A or B; if they show one, the money goes to supply, not search or subsidy.

The honest cost is Diwali: Hamid is right that the salesman is not waiting. A mitigation is to run the interviews in the first week and keep the rest of the tranche in reserve.

The weaker answers are the confident ones, which turn the loudest explanation into the plan.
case20v1-prob.pivot:
Nazar Stockbook: Persevere, Pivot or Perish

A decision case on what to do when the founding hypothesis has failed

1. Opening

On the morning of Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Kamal Ahuja sat in the glass-walled meeting room of Nazar Stockbook's office in Baner, Pune, with a single page of numbers. The board of the company, two seed investors and one independent director, would meet on Wednesday, 28 October. Diwali fell on 8 November, and the stocking season before it is when a young company can least afford to waste a month.

Ahuja, co-founder and chief executive, had to bring the board one recommendation. The product he had spent three years building had just failed the test he had set for it.

2. Company background

Nazar Stockbook sells a phone app to neighbourhood grocery stores. The shopkeeper photographs a shelf or scans a barcode, the app keeps a running count of stock, and it nudges the owner when a fast-moving item such as Parle-G, Maggi or Amul butter is about to run out.

Kirana stores are not short of software vendors. Khatabook and OkCredit own the credit-ledger habit, Udaan and Jumbotail sell wholesale to the same shops, and ONDC promises open catalogues. Most owners already take orders and credit from a distributor's salesman and a WhatsApp catalogue. Nazar's bet was narrower: that the owner would pay ₹499 a month purely for stock visibility.

The company was founded in 2023 and raised ₹14 crore in seed funding. It employs 38 people, mostly in Pune. At the start of October 2026 it held ₹5.6 crore in the bank, against a net burn of ₹56 lakh a month.

3. The situation

In January 2026 the leadership team wrote down its founding hypothesis, and Ahuja wrote the kill criterion beside it: at least 30 per cent of kirana owners who are still using the app at week eight will pay ₹499 a month. The test began in February. Between February and July the team onboarded 1,200 stores: 680 in Pune, 320 in Nashik and 200 in Kolhapur. Every store received eight weeks free, then met a paywall; by the end of September all had reached it.

Exhibit 1 sets out the result. Of the 1,200 stores, 840 were still active at week eight, 70.0 per cent. Of those 840, only 84 paid, a conversion of 10.0 per cent against a threshold of 30 per cent, which would have required 252 payers. Against everything onboarded it is 7.0 per cent. Revenue is 84 stores at ₹499, or ₹41,916 a month, about ₹5.03 lakh annualised.

The 756 active stores that declined, 840 less 84, were asked why. Only 300 of them answered, 39.7 per cent of decliners, so Exhibit 2 describes those 300 and nobody else. The commonest reason, given by 135, was that the distributor already supplied catalogue and credit. Price was named by only 45.

There was one other signal. From July, Ahuja's team had shown anonymised, aggregated stock counts to stockists, the regional distributors who supply the shops. Fourteen stockists in the three cities saw the dashboard. Six signed non-binding letters of intent at ₹15,000 a month each; none was yet invoiced.

Locations read this differently. Pune blames pricing; Berlin doubts the shopkeeper needed a tool; Toronto wants to see whether stockist interest survives an invoice; Singapore doubts a lower price changes minds.

4. The people

Kamal Ahuja, is the co-founder and chief executive, based in Pune. He wants a recommendation investors will back and staff will not read as panic.

Imran Dastur, heads engineering in Pune. He wants a price cut and a credit ledger, because he believes shopkeepers will pay once the app also tracks what customers owe them.

Ingrid Falk, is the product designer in Berlin. After two weeks in Nashik shops she is convinced owners hold stock in their heads and distrust anything that adds a task.

Indu Wadia, is the data scientist in Toronto. She built Exhibit 1 and has pointed out that 840 active stores spread over 14 stockists is an average of only 60 stores per stockist, a thin slice of what any one serves.

Kushal Sethna, leads customer success from Singapore and calls shopkeepers in Marathi and Hindi in the evening. He opposes any plan that depends on shopkeepers changing habits.

5. The options

Option A, persevere. Keep selling to kiranas. Cut the price to ₹299 a month, add a credit ledger and spend six more months testing. Imran estimates the ledger adds ₹6 lakh a month to the current ₹56 lakh, so spend rises to ₹62 lakh. The upside is that the team stays intact. The cost is that only 45 of the 300 reasons concerned price, and that the ledger fights Khatabook and OkCredit on their ground.

Option B, pivot. Keep the kirana app but make it free, and sell the aggregated stock visibility to stockists at ₹15,000 a month. Releasing the Nashik and Kolhapur field teams (₹14 lakh a month) and adding two stockist-facing sales hires (₹3 lakh) brings spend to ₹45 lakh. The upside is six stockists who signed non-binding letters. The cost is a new customer, a new sales cycle and dependence on shopkeepers who no longer pay.

Option C, perish. Wind the company down in an orderly way while cash is still large. Closing costs of ₹95 lakh for notice pay, lease exit and vendor settlements would leave ₹409 lakh to return to investors. The upside is preserved capital. The cost is that the one encouraging signal is abandoned unexamined.

Persevering consumes the bank in about eight months (504 divided by 62 is 8.1) and would need a new round on a hypothesis that has failed once. Pivoting is ₹19.80 lakh short at month twelve, on inputs resting on six non-binding, uninvoiced letters.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What exactly did the 10.0 per cent conversion in Exhibit 1 disprove? Product, price, customer or channel?
  2. Exhibit 2 describes 300 of the 756 decliners. What can and cannot be concluded from it, and what would you ask the other 456?
  3. Which projection in Exhibit 3 rests on the weakest assumption, and how would you test it cheaply?
  4. Kamal must tell his team on 29 October what happens next. Which option would you recommend, what would make you change your mind, and by what date?

7. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. An invalidated hypothesis is information. The skill is to decide which part broke. Nazar's hypothesis bundled three beliefs: that kirana owners have a stock-visibility problem, that this app solves it, and that they will pay ₹499 for it. The data attack the first and third. A pivot changes customer, problem, solution or channel while keeping what has been learned; persevering means the hypothesis was close and the fix is tuning; perishing means no remaining signal justifies the next rupee.

What a well-reasoned answer looks like. It names the failed assumption, tests each option against evidence, and fixes a gate in advance. Seventy per cent stayed active, but 10.0 per cent against 30 per cent says value did not become willingness to pay.

One defensible path. Option B, staged. Persevering fails because the reasons are structural: a distributor already supplies catalogue and credit, and owners trust their own eyes. A lower price addresses 15.0 per cent of the 300 who answered. Perishing is premature: 6 of 14 stockists, 42.9 per cent, asked in writing to pay for something the company already has. But six non-binding letters are a new hypothesis, not a validated one, and Indu's coverage point stands. So Ahuja should pivot with a written gate, as he did in January: by 28 February 2027, at least 8 of the 14 stockists must be paying invoices of ₹15,000 a month. The gate is a lead indicator, not the projection of 9. Four months at ₹45 lakh costs ₹180 lakh, leaving ₹324 lakh before any revenue. If the gate fails, a wind-down at ₹95 lakh still returns ₹229 lakh. If it passes, the ₹19.80 lakh year-end shortfall is a cost trim or a small bridge, far smaller than A's.

Kamal should tell the team plainly that the hypothesis failed, not the people who tested it.
exp40v2-prob.pivot:
Persevere, pivot or perish

What an invalidated hypothesis obliges a product organisation to do.

1. Two rooms, four days apart

On Friday 9 October 2026 Feroze Divekar sat above a components warehouse in Coimbatore with a 90-day clock that had run out. Durbin Camera Works, founded 2023, sold a subsidised dashcam to Indian drivers and earned its money from a ₹199 monthly driver-coaching subscription. Between Thursday 1 January and Tuesday 30 June 2026 it sold 86,000 devices, of which 61,060 were registered in the app, an activation rate of 71.0 per cent. The July 2025 Series A plan carried a two-clause hypothesis: at least 20 per cent of activated devices would start a paid subscription within 90 days, and the hardware subsidy would be recovered inside twelve months.

The window on the last device closed on Monday 28 September, eleven days before Feroze opened the file. Subscriptions started within 90 days: 7,327, or 12.0 per cent of activated devices. The second clause had passed — a subscriber at ₹175 of monthly contribution repays the ₹660 subsidy in 3.77 months — while the first failed by eight percentage points. Durbin held ₹14.8 crore against ₹2.20 crore a month: 6.7 months.

Four days later Dhruti Elavia met a different failure in Ahmedabad. Fehrist Catalogue Systems sold product-information software to Indian brands publishing one catalogue to Flipkart, Amazon India and Nykaa. It held ₹26.40 crore against ₹1.65 crore a month, exactly 16.0 months. Its pre-registered hypothesis read: at least 12 per cent of self-serve sign-ups will become paying customers within 60 days. Between Wednesday 1 April and Friday 31 July 2026 it took 9,400 sign-ups, the last 60-day window closing on Tuesday 29 September. Of them 3,948 imported a product, 42.0 per cent; 1,316 published a catalogue, 14.0 per cent; and 329 paid, 3.5 per cent. Eshani Datar put the standard error at 0.19 percentage points: a gap of 45 standard errors. Farzana Dalmia, the board's investor, asked what they would do on Monday.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A problem hypothesis is a falsifiable claim about a customer, a problem or a mechanism, written with a threshold that says what would count as a refutation. It is invalidated when evidence from a fair test falls on the wrong side of it. To persevere is to keep the strategy and change only the execution, legitimate only when someone can name a mechanism and its predicted effect. To pivot is to keep the vision and the learning while changing one structural element: customer, problem, solution, channel, pricing or revenue model. To perish is to stop.

The frame was invented against two opposite pathologies. Steve Blank's customer development work of 2005 addressed the founder who executes an untested plan; Eric Ries, writing from IMVU, gave pivot its modern meaning in 2011: a structured course correction testing a new fundamental hypothesis rather than thrashing. The canonical stories are survivals — Burbn's photo feature became Instagram in 2010, Glitch's chat tool became Slack in 2013 — and what is carried across the discontinuity is what makes a pivot cheaper than a new company.

Three schools disagree about evidence, not words. The evidence-first school holds that a pre-registered number missed under a fair test refutes the strategy; it will sign that a threshold a team will relitigate was never one, and will not sign that such a number beats a founder's judgement. The conviction school holds that early metrics measure market readiness more than thesis, and would sign that most category-defining products would have been killed by a disciplined gate at month eighteen; it will not sign that conviction may override a cash constraint. The option-value school treats each path as a call option priced in cash; it will sign that runway alone can flip the right answer, and will not sign that its probabilities are anything but elicited guesses.

3. Mechanics in depth

Experts run six steps; amateurs compress the first four into a feeling. One: recover the hypothesis as written. Dhruti kept the March deck beside the results: the claim was about self-serve conversion, not about whether catalogue software is useful.

Two: audit the fairness of the test. Three things invalidate a verdict rather than a hypothesis: thin precision, a window shorter than the behaviour's cycle, and broken instrumentation. Precision is arithmetic: for a proportion p on n trials the standard error is the square root of p(1−p)/n, so at Durbin's 61,060 activations and 12.0 per cent attach rate it is 0.13 percentage points, making the eight-point gap to 20 per cent roughly 61 standard errors. Instrumentation is not arithmetic, and section 8 has a case where the verdict was wrong.

Three: decompose the chain. A funnel is a product of rates and fails at one factor. Fehrist's ran 9,400 sign-ups to 3,948 imports, 42.0 per cent; to 1,316 publishes, 33.3 per cent of importers; to 329 paid, 25.0 per cent of publishers. The collapse is not at payment but between import and publish, where two-thirds of those who had done the tedious work left.

Four: search for a subgroup, and pay the price for searching. Eshani split the cohort by customer size.
