4. When the frame applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions, each testable. The threshold preceded the data: true for both, Durbin in July 2025, Fehrist in March 2026. The test had the precision to separate result from threshold: 61 standard errors at Durbin, 45 at Fehrist. The window matched the behaviour's cycle: arguable at Fehrist, where catalogue work waits for seasonal cut-offs, solid at Durbin, where a driver who has not subscribed in 90 days never does. Cash allows one more attempt: true at Fehrist with 16.0 months, marginal at Durbin with 6.7, which is why Durbin's options are narrower despite the cleaner verdict.

The frame misleads when value accrues on a cycle longer than the test, as with a tax product tested outside the filing season, and when the metric is a proxy that has drifted. It misleads most when the three words are treated as equally reversible: with tooling committed, or a supply side that took two years to assemble, pivoting and perishing carry asymmetric, often irreversible costs.

5. Hard edge cases

In a multi-product company the hypothesis belongs to one line, and the hard part is political: its leader will call a pivot a roadmap adjustment and a wind-down a merge. In two-sided marketplaces the broken link may sit opposite the symptom: demand fails because supply liquidity is thin in the categories demand asked for, so the real pivot is a supply decision. In regulated products a filed construct cannot be pivoted in a quarter; only the distribution layer is available.

Hardware plus software is the hardest, because cost is committed ahead of the learning: the board ordered, the tool cut, 86,000 units landed. A pivot that keeps the device and changes the buyer is cheap; one that needs a different device is a new company with a used balance sheet. Hardware teams must front-load the attach-rate hypothesis into the smallest production run possible, which fights the per-unit economics of tooling — an unresolved tension, not a process failure. AI-native products add a confound: when a value hypothesis fails, absent demand and an insufficient model predict the same data. A pre-committed capability threshold lets failure be attributed; without it, teams persevere on the belief that the next model release is the mechanism.

At the seams, mature companies do not behave as described. The stated process is a quarterly review with a kill criterion; the actual mechanism is reallocation at annual planning, during which the invalidated line is starved rather than killed: it keeps its name, loses its best engineers and closes quietly eighteen months later. Starvation preserves optionality; the learning is never consolidated.

6. Eight distinctions that separate the expert

An invalidated hypothesis is a refuted sentence, not a refuted company. The tell is the leap from “twelve per cent did not happen” to “catalogue software is a bad business”. The test condemns only what it was powered to test, and Table 2 shows the survivors can be valuable.

The verdict and the hypothesis fail separately. An expert's first move on a bad result is to attack the measurement, on a checklist written before the result; writing the checklist afterwards is motivated reasoning.

Perseverance requires a named mechanism with a predicted effect size, and “more time” is not one. Durva Faleiro's cheaper board is: a ₹900 cut in landed cost turns Durbin's hardware margin from minus ₹660 to plus ₹240 per device, which at the observed 7.95 per cent owner-driver attach rate still loses ₹208 per device after acquisition cost.

A pivot changes one element and carries the rest across; changing two is a restart in disguise. The tell is the handover document: if nothing in the new plan cites evidence from the old one, no learning crossed the gap, and the only advantage pivoting has over founding is gone.

A subgroup is a lead, not a verdict, and the discount is quantifiable. Examine twelve subgroups at the five per cent level and the chance of a spurious winner is one minus 0.95 to the twelfth power, 46.0 per cent. Fehrist's distributors survive it because the segment was pre-specified, large in revenue rather than favourable in rate, and mechanically legible.

Averages must be rebuilt from first principles. Durbin's blended monthly churn of 8.56 per cent is not the midpoint of the owner-driver 12.5 and the fleet 2.8 per cent but the subscriber-weighted combination: 4,351 times 0.125 plus 2,976 times 0.028, divided by 7,327. The tell is a blend that moves while the segments hold still.

Sunk cost is not evidence, but a sunk asset is. Durbin's ₹5,67,60,000 of subsidy is gone under every option, while the 61,060 activated devices are an installed base with a continuing claim. A confused team cites the spend.

Perishing is a decision with a quality, and the verdict is silent on the new hypothesis. Returning ₹23.60 crore of a ₹26.40 crore balance with a clean data room beats returning nothing eleven months later; the tell is whether the option was priced in the same table. And Fehrist's cohort shows distributors convert and pay, but nothing about how many exist, so a subgroup pivot needs its own test.

7. Across product types and company stages

In consumer products evidence is cheap, fast and cohort-shaped, so the characteristic error is pivoting on noise; the corrective is pre-registration. In B2B and enterprise the evidence is slow and the sample small, so the error inverts: a verdict on eleven opportunities, or three years of perseverance because every loss had an excuse. The instrument there is a loss-reason taxonomy coded by someone off the deal. In marketplaces the frame applies per side. In hardware the committed cost structure makes the options asymmetric; in AI products attribution dominates.

By stage, the difference is who must be convened and what the decision costs outside the product. A seed company decides in one meeting, moving four people. A Series A company, as both protagonists are, must also reset a plan it sold to investors, which is why Farzana's presence changes the analysis. A large company must move budget lines, revise compensation tied to the old metric and manage careers, which is where most corporate pivots fail. The difference is overstated in the statistics: demanding more data on a 45-standard-error gap is politics dressed as rigour.

8. Three worked examples

A pivot that worked. Enaayat Elder Care Network, under Dipali Fotedar, sold a ₹7,500-a-month home-nursing subscription in Pune. Between 1 February and 30 September 2025 it ran 4,200 subsidised trial visits; 378 families converted to a monthly plan, 9.0 per cent against a pre-registered threshold of 30 per cent. Contribution was ₹1,650 per plan-month against an acquisition cost of ₹9,400: a payback of 5.7 months that worked only if conversion did. The pivot changed one element, the channel. From 1 October 2025 to 30 April 2026 Enaayat signed eleven NABH-accredited hospitals for post-discharge care; of 3,542 referred discharges, 1,346 converted to a 30-day plan, 38.0 per cent, at ₹2,100 of acquisition cost and a payback of 1.3 months. The carried asset — nurses, rosters, protocols — did that work.

A perseverance that was right. At Farmaan Compliance House, where Devanshi Firodia ran product, the activation hypothesis for its GST e-invoicing software was that 55 per cent of trial accounts would file a first return within 30 days. For the quarter to 30 June 2025 the dashboard showed 336 of 1,460 trials, 23.0 per cent. The team spent six weeks and ₹38 lakh on a prototype for another segment before an engineer found, on Monday 18 August 2025, that filings made through the bulk-upload path were never logged. Re-processing the logs gave 745 of 1,460, 51.0 per cent: still short, but with a visible mechanism, an HSN-code mapping step that pushed users into the unlogged path. Farmaan persevered on that fix and in the quarter from 1 October to 31 December 2025 reached 1,090 of 1,880 trials, 58.0 per cent.

A pivot that failed, and the recovery. Dhaatu Scrap Exchange, co-founded by Dhiraj Edulji, built a listings marketplace for metal-scrap dealers. Of 1,250 registered dealers, 113 ever listed inventory, 9.0 per cent against a threshold of 35 per cent. Fourteen had instead asked for working capital, and on that basis Dhaatu launched invoice discounting on 1 July 2024, disbursing ₹9.4 crore to 86 dealers over nine months. Delinquency beyond 90 days reached 11.8 per cent of the book, ₹1.11 crore, against an underwriting assumption of 2.5 per cent; the book closed on 31 August 2025, fourteen months after launch, having consumed ₹7.2 crore of equity. The subgroup was fourteen of 1,250 dealers, 1.1 per cent, found after the fact; two elements changed at once, the customer problem and the revenue model, so nothing carried across; and a lending book invalidates itself in nine months where a listings experiment takes six weeks, making the option costlier to hold than priced. The recovery: Dhaatu returned to the one service dealers paid for unprompted, weighbridge verification at ₹340 per truck, running 4,100 verifications a month by January 2026, ₹13.94 lakh of monthly revenue.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Moving the threshold. Early sign: the board deck's success metric differs in definition or denominator from the charter's. Diagnostic: may we see the dated document in which it was written? Caught late, later decisions are unfalsifiable.

Extending the window without a question. Early sign: “one more quarter” with no named mechanism. Diagnostic: what result would change the decision, and when would it show? Caught late, Durbin would spend ₹13.20 crore of its ₹14.8 crore reaching an unactionable gate.

Pivoting to the first bright spot. Early sign: a new strategy each quarter on a post-hoc subgroup of a few dozen. Diagnostic: how many, how chosen, and does it hold in a fresh group recruited on purpose? Caught late, it costs what Dhaatu's did.

Pivoting the product and not the organisation. Early sign: the strategy is announced while quota and compensation still reward the old metric. Diagnostic: whose incentive changes on Monday? Caught late, six months of effort change no behaviour, which is misread as evidence against the pivot.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Evidence-first, steelmanned: pre-registration is the only defence against a team's own motivated reasoning, and teams which relitigate thresholds learn nothing transferable. It would be wrong if early thresholds were so arbitrary that their informational content is near zero — and critics note that Fehrist's 12 per cent was a guess by people who had never run self-serve.

Conviction, steelmanned: venture outcomes are skewed, almost all returns come from products that looked wrong for years, and a rule tuned against false positives discards the few that matter. It would be wrong if those products had shown an early signal the gate would have caught — an open question, because near-misses are unobservable.

Option value, steelmanned: the same evidence should drive different decisions at different cash balances, and Table 3 makes the trade-off arguable rather than personal. It would be wrong if the elicited probabilities merely laundered a prior; its only answer is that break-even sensitivities, not point estimates, are the output.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied the frame produces the word pivot on cue and a three-option deck. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently four weeks before the result: they write the threshold down with a date and an owner, pre-commit the fairness checks, and say which belief they would abandon if the number came in low. When the result lands they are unhurried, because the branching was settled in advance; they discuss perishing in the same tone as the other options and can state what their experiment did not test.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Dhruti Elavia pivoted on one element: the motion. Fehrist would keep the product, the integrations and the 329 accounts, stop paid acquisition into small sellers, and build a nine-person enterprise team for large distributors. Spend of ₹15.48 crore over nine months at ₹1.72 crore a month leaves ₹10.92 crore at the gate on Tuesday 13 July 2027, 6.3 months of runway — enough to act, the binding constraint. The pass bar is a hypothesis: at least 40 new distributor contracts at an average ACV of ₹15 lakh or more, 70 per cent of them publishing a first catalogue within 60 days of signature. The 70 per cent haircuts the perfect renewal of the Q1 FY26 cohort's six distributors, because six accounts are not a basis for a plan. Persevering needed 43.9 per cent to beat pivoting and nobody claimed half; perishing was worth ₹23.60 crore against a pivot priced at ₹69.15 crore.

Feroze had less room to manoeuvre. 13. Going deeper

Validating a problem hypothesis is the prerequisite: the verdict is only as good as the test. Writing a problem hypothesis comes next: Durbin's two-clause hypothesis is the drafting error that made its verdict ambiguous. Surfacing assumptions unlocks the step before: Fehrist assumed distributors behave like brands. Riskiest assumption first would have had Durbin buy the attach-rate answer on 3,000 devices, not 86,000. Frequency and intensity of the problem explains why owner-drivers never subscribed — coaching earns money on a problem felt weekly, not after an accident — and vitamin vs painkiller is the same point more bluntly. Opportunity solution trees make a pivot a sideways move rather than a leap. And leading teams through reorganisations and pivots is where this ends: a decision made in Table 3 is half made until quota, roadmap and reporting lines change.

The five companies and all individuals named here are fictional. Flipkart, Amazon India, Nykaa, NABH accreditation, the GST e-invoicing regime and AIS-140 are real market context; Instagram, Slack and the frameworks of Blank and Ries are real.
case40v1-prob.pivot:
Nabz Telemetry: The Pack That Did Not Fail

A decision case — Bengaluru, October 2026

1. Sunday night, 25 October 2026

Nabz Telemetry’s office is the second floor of a building off 27th Main in HSR Layout, Bengaluru. At nine on Sunday evening Iravati Anklesaria, co-founder and chief executive, sat there alone with the window open, the generator below having run all afternoon.

On Monday at nine she would open a two-day leadership offsite; on Thursday 5 November she would face four board members. Between those dates she had to turn nine months of evidence into one recommendation, and the evidence said that the thing she had built the company around was not true.

In January, Nabz had written down one hypothesis and a kill criterion beside it, in the plainest language the team could manage: electric two- and three-wheeler fleet operators with 500 or more vehicles will pay ₹149 per vehicle per month for predictive battery-failure alerts, because an unplanned pack failure costs them a rider’s day of earnings. We will consider the hypothesis invalidated unless at least 35 per cent of the fleets that complete the ten-week pilot sign a paid annual contract at a price no lower than ₹120 per vehicle per month.

Twenty fleets completed the pilot. Four signed. On 9 October the leadership team had reviewed the numbers in this room, had not agreed on what they meant, and had not agreed since. Anklesaria had the sense that most of the disagreement was not about the numbers at all. Nabz held ₹24.6 crore against a net burn of ₹2.05 crore a month — twelve months, to the end of September 2027.

2. The company, and one decision from 2024

Anklesaria and Kinshuk Deshingkar founded Nabz in April 2022. She had spent six years in commercial-vehicle telematics; he had designed battery-management electronics in Pune, and had watched “good packs thrown away because nobody could prove what happened inside them.” The product is a sealed module clamped to the battery — the pack monitor — reading cell voltages, temperature and charge cycles, with a cloud service that scores each pack and alerts when it judges failure near.

The decision that shaped everything came in August 2024. Tapti Commercial Vehicles, a Nashik maker of electric three-wheeler load carriers, offered a three-year line-fit agreement: it would fit the monitor on the assembly line and pay ₹7.5 crore up front, recognised over 36 months at ₹20.83 lakh a month. In exchange, pack data from line-fit vehicles could be used only for warranty and service purposes, and could not be licensed to any third party — a lender, an insurer, a resale platform — without Tapti’s written consent; and if Nabz discontinued the hardware it would repay the unrecognised prepayment plus a tooling contribution. At 30 September 2026 that clawback stood at ₹3.20 crore: ₹2.29 crore of prepayment and ₹0.91 crore of tooling.

The agreement bought Nabz its Series A — ₹68 crore in January 2025, led by Satpura Growth Capital. It also put 11,400 of the 46,900 vehicles Nabz monitors, or 24.3 per cent, behind a clause forbidding the sale of what it knows about them. Figure 1 sets out the sequence.

3. The industry

India’s electric last-mile fleet grew up around quick commerce. Zepto, Blinkit and Swiggy Instamart pushed delivery density until two-wheeler fleets became infrastructure, and operators such as Zypp Electric and Yulu built rider-facing businesses on leased assets. In three-wheeler cargo, Mahindra Last Mile Mobility and Euler Motors sell to fleets that count rupees per kilometre.

Regulation sits close to the product. Battery safety requirements under AIS‑156 govern what Nabz may clamp to a pack; ARAI and ICAT certify; MoRTH sets the vehicle rules; PM E-DRIVE shapes what a fleet pays for a vehicle and so how long it keeps one. Two regulators bear on the options but not on today’s product. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs the rider-linked telemetry Nabz collects, and its consent notice names “service and warranty” as the purpose and nothing else. Were Nabz to sell assessments to financiers, those NBFCs answer to the Reserve Bank, and an insurer buying one answers to IRDAI.

Nabz is also, modestly, global. Deshingkar’s hardware group of nineteen sits in Pune; data science is one person in Toronto; fleet success is two in Singapore, covering India and the Gulf in one working day; sales is two in Edison, New Jersey. Of 61 employees, 33 are in Bengaluru. The largest prospect is Tawseel Rider Services in Dubai, which runs 6,200 electric two-wheelers and wants pack-health reporting its GCC insurer will accept.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

The pilot ran from February to September 2026. Kartikeya Sirur and Jocelyn Yeoh’s teams approached 68 fleets, signed 25 and completed 20; five fell away, two closures and three stalled installations. Exhibit 1 gives that funnel with the base for each rate.

The proposition contained three claims, and the pilot tested one of them cleanly. The first was that pack failure is predictable from telemetry. Simone Thibault’s evaluation, Exhibit 4, says it is — weakly, and only against one definition of failure. The second was that an operator can act on a warning, and here the pilots produced what nobody had written down in January: of the sixteen completed pilots that did not convert, ten gave Yeoh’s team a reason: four said the alerts told them what their mechanics already knew, three had no spare packs and so could not act on a warning, two cited price, and one said its financier owned the packs and wanted the data itself. Those are shares of the ten that answered, not of the sixteen; six said nothing.

The third claim was willingness to pay, and that is what the criterion measured. Four of twenty completed pilots converted: 20.0 per cent, against a threshold of 35.0 per cent that would have needed seven. But the twenty were not the population the hypothesis described. Sirur’s team, under pressure to fill the pilot, signed whoever would sign, and eight of the twenty ran fleets below the 500-vehicle floor the hypothesis itself had set. Exhibits 2 and 3 separate them: inside the hypothesis’s own population, one of twelve converted, 8.3 per cent; among the eight below the floor, three converted, 37.5 per cent. Three of the four fleets that bought were fleets the company had decided in January not to sell to.

A fourth thing is wrong, and Indraneel Varkey found it in October. At the floor price a converted fleet loses Nabz money: Exhibit 5 puts the cost to serve a vehicle at ₹147 a month against the ₹120 floor. Had all twenty fleets converted at ₹120, the hypothesis would have been validated and the company would have been worse off.

5. The people

Iravati Anklesaria, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. She wrote the criterion and told the board she would honour it; since 9 October she has said only that “we will decide with the data.” Her incentive is a second institutional round. She has not said that she thinks the 500-vehicle floor was the worst sentence in the document, accepted because Sirur’s pipeline looked better that way.

Kinshuk Deshingkar, co-founder and chief technology officer, Pune. He wants to persevere, narrowed: keep the monitor, sell small, fix precision, which he says is two chemistry generations from fixable. His incentive is nineteen people whose skills do not transfer to a software pivot. He has not told Anklesaria that a Tapti vice president asked him in September whether “the Pune group would ever come across as a team.”

Kimaya Shanbhogue, vice president, product, Bengaluru. She drafted the hypothesis and argues the verdict must stand: a company that renegotiates its criterion after seeing the result has none. She favours the certification pivot; her incentive is credibility, having fought for the criterion against Sirur. What she has not said is that the floor was her sentence, written to make recruiting easier, and that she now thinks it invalidated the test rather than the product.

Indraneel Varkey, chief financial officer, Bengaluru. He built Exhibit 6 and wants the wind-down kept on the table: ₹12.1 crore returned is defensible, ₹2.6 crore left after a fourth attempt is not. His incentive is the audit: he signed the Tapti treatment, and a hardware exit reopens it. He has not circulated how thin his pivot column is.

Simone Thibault, staff data scientist, Toronto. She evaluated the model and reported the parts that hurt. Her position is that twenty pilots cannot separate 20 per cent from 35 per cent, so no decision on Thursday is evidence-based. Her incentive is a paper on battery prognostics. She has not said that she raised the sample-size problem in January and nobody commented.

Jocelyn Yeoh, head of fleet success, Singapore. Closest to the operators, and least convinced by the three options. Her week-eight survey found thirteen of the twenty sponsors expecting to renew; four did, and she now says it asked operations heads, not the people who sign. Her incentive is the Tawseel relationship, which she owns. She has not said that she told two small fleets in July that Nabz would hold ₹149 for a year.

Kartikeya Sirur, head of enterprise sales, Edison, New Jersey. The test proves only that Nabz sold it badly: pilots run by engineers, a per-vehicle price quoted to fleets that budget per vehicle-year, the two largest never offered an enterprise contract. He carries a weighted pipeline of ₹9.4 crore, of which ₹4.1 crore is Tawseel, held at 60 per cent of a ₹6.8 crore gross value — a five-year term on a fleet he expects to reach 7,600 vehicles, against 6,200 today. His commission accrues on pipeline movement. He has not said that Tawseel needs GCC homologation nobody has costed.

7. Voices

“Four of twenty. On the normal approximation the 95 per cent band around 20.0 per cent runs 2.5 to 37.5 per cent: the standard error is the root of 0.2 times 0.8 over 20, which is 8.9 points, and 1.96 of those is 17.5. Your threshold sits inside the band. To tell 20 from 35 — one sample, five per cent two-sided, 80 per cent power — you needed about 72 pilots. We did not invalidate the hypothesis. We failed to test it.”

— Simone Thibault, review call, 9 October, 07:40 Toronto

“Read the reasons. Three of the ten who answered cannot act on an alert at all; they have no spare pack. For them it is not mispriced, it is unusable.”

— Jocelyn Yeoh, chat thread #pilot-readout, 9 October

— Kinshuk Deshingkar, email to Shanbhogue and Anklesaria, 13 October

— Kimaya Shanbhogue, reply, 13 October

— operations director, Tawseel Rider Services, Dubai, 16 October

— Idhika Bhansali, Satpura Growth Capital, 22 October

8. The options as Anklesaria sees them

She has three on the whiteboard, in the order Varkey’s exhibit uses, and has been staring at the ordering as much as the content.

A. Persevere, narrowed. Keep the monitor, abandon the 500-vehicle floor, sell to fleets under 500 vehicles at the ₹149 price, spend six months on precision. The evidence for it is Exhibit 3 and nothing else: 37.5 per cent of a sample of eight. The evidence against is Exhibit 5, where ₹149 leaves ₹2 a vehicle, and the knowledge that small fleets consume more support per vehicle, not less.

B. Pivot to pack-health certification. Sell assessments to whoever owns the residual value: NBFCs financing three-wheelers, lessors, insurers, resale platforms. The product is largely built. But the Tapti clause closes 11,400 vehicles to exactly this use, a credible residual-value model needs histories longer than the two years Nabz has, and the DPDP notice names service and warranty, so consent must be gathered again, fleet by fleet.

C. Perish, managed. Wind down over nine months, or sell the hardware business and the Pune team: ₹12.1 crore returned, on Exhibit 6.

What troubles her is that all three keep one thing fixed: the buyer is the fleet or nobody. Yeoh’s three fleets without spare packs, and the one whose financier owned the packs and wanted the data, point at a buyer in no column. Nor does the fourth possibility Deshingkar raised and dropped — selling the same alerts to Tapti as a warranty-reserve reduction, neither pivot nor perseverance but a change of customer for an unchanged product. And no option answers Thibault, whose objection is not that the answer is wrong but that there is none yet to be had.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets on Thursday 5 November. Bhansali’s ₹18 crore bridge expires on 20 November and requires a 2027 plan showing ₹6 crore of contracted revenue; Nabz has ₹27.07 lakh of annualised contracted subscription revenue plus the Tapti amortisation, which ends in August 2027. Cash is ₹24.6 crore, the burn ₹2.05 crore a month.

Discontinuing the hardware triggers the ₹3.20 crore clawback. A non-cancellable circuit-board order of ₹1.1 crore falls due on 15 January 2027, on top of ₹3.28 crore of finished monitors in the Nashik warehouse. The Pune lease needs ninety days’ notice at ₹14 lakh a quarter. Licensing line-fit data to a third party needs Tapti’s written consent; repurposing rider-linked telemetry needs fresh consent under the DPDP Act. Tawseel wants an answer on GCC certification by 30 November. Diwali falls on 8 November and half the Pune team is away from 4 to 12 November; fleets freeze procurement until the quick-commerce peak ends in mid-December, so Nabz cannot sell its way out of the decision before January.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What did the January hypothesis claim, and which of its claims did the pilot test?
  2. Using Exhibits 1, 2 and 3, state the conversion rate you would put to the board, and the base you are using.
  3. Exhibit 4 reports two definitions of failure. Which should the criterion have named, and would the verdict change?
  4. Thibault says the test was underpowered; Shanbhogue says the verdict must stand. Can both be right, and what follows?
  5. Given Exhibit 5, what should Nabz have learned in January, and whose job was it to notice?
  6. Anklesaria opens the offsite at nine on Monday. What should she say in the first ten minutes, and what one recommendation should she take to the board on 5 November, including what she tells Bhansali about the bridge?

At a quarter to eleven she closed the exhibit file and opened the January document again, the criterion in bold in the second paragraph. She had read it perhaps forty times since 9 October. The sentence was clear, and she had meant it. What she could not decide, with the generator finally silent and Monday nine hours away, was whether that clarity was the best thing the company had done or the most expensive.
exp20v2-prob.pivot:
Persevere, pivot or perish

1. The Monday after the pilot

At 3 p.m. on Monday 12 October 2026, Charvi Bhandari, co-founder and chief product officer of Bunkar Haat Exchange, walked into a Hyderabad meeting room with a single printed page. Bunkar Haat ran an online marketplace that sold handloom sarees directly from weaver clusters in Pochampally, Venkatagiri and Sambalpur to urban buyers. The company had raised a seed round of ₹9 crore in February 2026, and its bank balance stood at ₹3.6 crore. Monthly spending was ₹40 lakh, which meant nine months of life: ₹3,60,00,000 divided by ₹40,00,000.

The printed page held the result of a twelve-week pilot, run from Monday 20 July to Sunday 11 October. On 6 July, before the pilot began, Charvi had written the hypothesis into a one-page charter: at least 25 per cent of first-time buyers will place a second order within 28 days. The pilot drew 2,40,000 site visitors, of whom 7,200 bought for the first time, a conversion of 3.0 per cent. Of those 7,200, 832 ordered again within 28 days, a repeat rate of 11.6 per cent. The threshold had been 25 per cent. The pilot had cost ₹54 lakh in marketing.

Aniket Bhasin, the partner from the lead seed investor, would arrive in an hour. Arjun Chaudhary, who ran supply, wanted another six months of the same experiment. Aditi Bakshi, the analyst, had spotted something odd in the data. If Charvi persevered and was wrong, the company would burn ₹2.4 crore finding out. If she pivoted and was wrong, she would discard a consumer brand that might have worked. If she shut down, she might bury a real business. This page is about choosing among those three with a failed hypothesis in hand.

2. The idea

A hypothesis is a falsifiable belief about customers or markets, stated with a number that says what would count as success. It is invalidated when evidence gathered under a fair test lands on the wrong side of that number. Persevere, pivot or perish names the three responses. To persevere is to keep the strategy and change only how it is executed. To pivot is to keep the vision and the learning, and change one fundamental element: the customer, the problem, the solution, the channel or the revenue model. To perish is to stop, and return what remains to those who funded the work.

The idea counters two failures: the founder who never admits a result, and the founder who changes direction so often that nothing is learned. Steve Blank’s customer development method (2005) argued that start-ups should test beliefs outside the building. Eric Ries, drawing on his experience at IMVU, popularised the word pivot and defined it in The Lean Startup (2011) as a structured course correction designed to test a new fundamental hypothesis. Burbn, a check-in app, found users cared only about its photo feature and became Instagram in 2010. Glitch, a game, left behind a chat tool that became Slack in 2013. In both, something survived: a team, a technology, an insight.

The sentence Charvi could repeat in the meeting without sounding glib was this: the pilot did not tell us the company is wrong; it told us which of our beliefs is false, and we must now decide which beliefs it left standing.

3. How it works

The mechanics have six steps; practitioners perform the first three implicitly, which is where most errors enter.

First, reread the hypothesis and threshold exactly as written before the data arrived. Second, test the fairness of the test: was the sample large enough, the window long enough, the tracking correct? With 7,200 first buyers the sampling error on a rate near 12 per cent is under one percentage point, nowhere near the 13.4-point gap to the target. Third, decompose the failure. A chain of rates fails at one link, and a repair for the wrong link is wasted. Fourth, search for subgroups where the belief holds. Fifth, price each option in cash and months. Sixth, set a time box and a rule for what evidence would change the decision.

Every cohort had a full 28 days to repeat; the last, whose first orders ended on Sunday 13 September, was observed until 11 October, exactly 28 days later. The rate barely moves, from 11.0 to 12.0 per cent. This is a stable, low number, not a wobble that further weeks would cure.

4. A worked example

Aditi’s odd finding was in the buyer mix. Of the 7,200 first buyers, 400 were boutique owners who bought several sarees at once for resale. Splitting the pilot by segment changed the picture.

Table 2 prices each segment. Contribution per order is what Bunkar Haat keeps after variable costs. For a consumer order of ₹3,200 at an 18 per cent commission, revenue is ₹576; payment, packaging and returns handling cost ₹126; contribution is ₹450. For a reseller order of ₹24,000 at a 9 per cent wholesale commission, revenue is ₹2,160, costs are ₹360, and contribution is ₹1,800. The table counts each repeat buyer as one further order only, which is conservative. Customer acquisition cost (CAC) is the blended ₹750, the ₹54,00,000 spent divided by 7,200 first buyers, charged to every buyer alike.

Now the persevere case, line by line. A consumer yields ₹450 per order and costs ₹750 to acquire, so a buyer must place 750 divided by 450, or 1.67 orders, to pay back. The observed repeat share is 560 of 6,800, or 8.2 per cent. Suppose, generously, that each repeater placed three further orders over a year. Orders per consumer would be 1 + 0.0824 × 3 = 1.247, and contribution would be 1.247 × ₹450 = ₹561, a loss of ₹189 on each ₹750 buyer. To break even at three extra orders, the repeat share would need to reach 0.667 divided by 3, or 22.2 per cent, nearly three times the observed rate.

Second pass, one input changed. Hold everything else and let CAC fall. Break-even CAC is the ₹561 of lifetime contribution, a cut of 25 per cent from ₹750. At ₹400 the consumer line would earn +₹161 per buyer. Perseverance is therefore arithmetically possible, but only if Arjun can name what would cut acquisition cost by a quarter, and the pilot offered no such evidence. Resellers, meanwhile, recovered their ₹750 on the first order alone, since contribution of ₹1,800 exceeds it, and with the observed repeat orders the 400 accounts earned ₹12,09,600 against ₹3,00,000 of spend.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

A failed hypothesis is not a failed product

The pilot falsified one belief, about consumer repeat purchase. Whether the sourcing network or the logistics works is a separate question. A handloom saree is bought a few times a year, so 28 days may be the wrong clock; but the clock was part of the hypothesis.

The threshold must precede the data

Charvi wrote 25 per cent on 6 July. A threshold chosen after the result is a story, not a test.

A pivot changes one thing and keeps the learning

Changing ad copy or a discount is iteration, which leaves the hypothesis intact. A pivot swaps a fundamental element, here the customer, from urban consumer to boutique owner, while keeping the weaver network and catalogue. If everything changes at once, nothing carries over.

A segment signal is a lead, not a verdict

The resellers were 400 of 7,200 buyers, 5.6 per cent, but 272 of the 832 repeaters, 32.7 per cent, and 26.8 per cent of total contribution (12,09,600 of 45,21,600). Striking, yet small and self-selected: they found Bunkar Haat unprompted, and a subgroup found after the fact often looks good by chance. The test is whether the effect repeats in a fresh group recruited on purpose.

Perseverance needs a mechanism

“We need more time” is not a mechanism. A mechanism is a specific change plus a predicted effect, such as “a styling reminder will lift 28-day repeat from 8.2 to 22 per cent.” If nobody can write that sentence, the option is hope.

Sunk cost is not evidence

The ₹54 lakh is gone under every option; the pilot recovered ₹45,21,600 of contribution against it, 83.7 per cent. The live question is what the next rupee should buy.

Perishing is a decision

Each month of delay costs ₹40 lakh, and returning ₹3.2 crore to investors with reputation intact beats returning nothing.

What the verdict cannot tell you

The pilot says nothing about how many boutiques exist, how many Bunkar Haat can reach, or whether they will tolerate weavers’ lead times. Those are new hypotheses.

6. How it differs by product type and stage

In a consumer product, evidence arrives quickly in cohorts and the signal is retention, as here. In a B2B product, cycles are slow and customers large, so the evidence is signed pilots and reorders. In a marketplace, which Bunkar Haat is, a failed hypothesis may sit on either side: weavers supply, buyers demand. Charvi’s pivot swaps the demand side while keeping supply, which is why it is cheaper than it sounds. An early-stage company decides in one meeting; a large company must also move budgets, targets and people, the subject of the topic this one unlocks.

7. Common mistakes

Moving the goalposts. Symptom: the board deck shows a different success metric from the charter. Misunderstanding: the threshold is a target to be adjusted rather than a commitment. Cheapest diagnostic: place the dated charter beside the results slide.

Pivoting to the first bright spot. Symptom: a new strategy in each quarter, each built on a small group. Misunderstanding: a post-hoc subgroup is treated as a prediction. Diagnostic: ask how many, how chosen, and whether it repeats in a fresh cohort.

Extending the pilot. Symptom: “one more month” without a named question. Misunderstanding: more data will turn an unfavourable result favourable. Diagnostic: ask what result would change the decision; if the answer is none, the extension is a delay.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version has a charter that existed before the pilot, a verdict published within a day and unedited, and options priced in the same units.

Each option carries a pre-agreed test, and everyone knows the date of the next verdict.

9. Closing: what Charvi decided

Charvi told the board she would pivot, with a time box. Bunkar Haat would build a wholesale desk for boutiques, cut monthly spending to ₹32 lakh, and spend no more than ₹128 lakh, four months of the reduced burn, to the decision gate on Friday 19 February 2027. The pass bar: at least 300 new reseller accounts, of which at least 50 per cent reorder within 28 days. That bar is 18 points under the 68.0 per cent seen in the pilot, a haircut for self-selection. If it is missed, the company perishes in good order: cash of ₹232 lakh less ₹40 lakh of closure costs returns ₹192 lakh to investors. Her reasoning: persevering required a quarter off CAC with no mechanism to show, while the pivot kept the weavers, the catalogue and the learning, and cost ₹112 lakh less than six more months of the old plan.

Read next leading teams through reorganisations and pivots, because a decision is only half made until people reorganise around it. Revisit validating a problem hypothesis too, since the verdict is only as good as the test.

Two questions to sit with. First, if Charvi’s pilot had produced 24 per cent against a threshold of 25, what would have changed in the decision, and why does the answer expose how arbitrary any threshold is? Second, which belief in your own project would you least like to see a dated threshold attached to, and what does that reluctance tell you?

Companies and people in this case are fictional. Instagram, Slack and the cited frameworks are real.
exp40v2-prob.frequency:
Frequency and Intensity of the Problem

How often and how badly a problem occurs — and why the answer, properly measured, fixes the cadence, pricing metric and capacity plan of whatever gets built next.

1. Two decisions, six weeks apart

On 6 April 2026 Eshita Darekar, product head at Dhrupad Treasury Systems in Bengaluru, got a log extract she had wanted since January. Dhrupad's queue was where a mid-market manufacturer's finance team went when a supplier payment failed, duplicated or carried an unagreed deduction. It had 612 customers, an average contract value of ₹4.8 lakh and ₹29.38 crore of recurring revenue. Devdatta Fernandes, the chief revenue officer, wanted to reprice onto seats; the board met on 19 May. Ewa Dabrowska, the data lead in Warsaw, had reduced 40 consenting customers over the quarter to 31 March 2026 to one exhibit.

Six weeks later Dhanashri Ekbote faced the mirror image in Noida. Falak Air Works, which she co-founded in 2023, sold an indoor air-quality monitor at ₹12,400 with a ₹900 cartridge; by September 2026, 11,400 reported hourly from four cities. Dhariwal read that as an engagement failure; Ekbote did not.

2. The idea and its three traditions

Every argument here is a quarrel about definitions. The frequency of a problem, λ, is occurrences per unit of exposure time for a specified unit: 1,140 exceptions per customer-year. It is an incidence rate, not a prevalence share, and prevalence — the share of a population with the problem at all — cannot be multiplied by anything. The intensity, c, is one occurrence's cost in a single currency. Their product is the annual burden, B = λc; the reciprocal of λ is the cadence, τ.

From actuarial science came the identity: insurance is priced as expected claim frequency times expected severity. From Andrew Ehrenberg's repeat-buying work came the correction that individual rates are gamma-distributed, so the population mean describes almost nobody. From the burden-of-disease literature came the severity weight, making mild-and-frequent commensurable with rare-and-catastrophic. Customer development supplied the trigger: a product blind to an occurrence's cue cannot serve it.

Four positions contend over which term binds. The cadence-first school signs that a product cannot be used more often than its problem occurs, but not that low frequency bars a large business. The intensity-first school signs “rank by severity, then check feasibility” but not “frequency predicts retention”. The burden school signs “rank by annual burden” but not that the terms carry separate implications. The distribution school signs “never report a mean without its variance” but not that an average cadence is a design input.

3. Mechanics in depth

Expert practice runs seven steps; three are implicit, and those hold the errors. Fix the unit of analysis: in business software it is nested. A ₹200–500 crore customer's exceptions occur to the firm 95.0 times a month, to its finance function 4.52 times a working day, and to one of its four clerks about 1.13 — governing renewal, capacity, interface. The 40-customer panel pools lower, 69.1 a month. Fix the occurrence definition against the instrument: an occurrence is an event, a ticket an artefact of recording, and the ratio is neither stable nor one. Fix the window against the underlying cycle: Dhrupad's exceptions cycle monthly, so 90 days holds three, while Falak's cycle annually. Count with exposure in the denominator, and measure intensity by decomposition, since a pain score has no unit.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

State the conditions as testable claims. Usage cannot exceed occurrence: true for Dhrupad, and for Falak, where on matched monthly bases every monitored household met the problem in September — 11.86 high days a month in Delhi, 3.65 in Bengaluru — while 2,394 of the 11,400 monitors, 21.0 per cent, opened the app at all. It fails when the product serves a second job with its own frequency. Burden bounds willingness to pay: ₹4.8 lakh against a ₹9.57 lakh burden is comfortable, ₹11 lakh would not be, and Falak's ₹12,400 plus 3.1633 cartridges at ₹900, ₹15,247, against a ₹52,513 burden needs no defence. Cadence predicts the retention curve's shape, not its level. Frequency is stable enough to plan on: here it misleads. Readiness products such as backup and cyber cover have a near-zero occurrence rate and that is what is bought, so calling it no business is the category error. Calendar-generated occurrences are known a priori. And products that change the frequency they measure break the assumption from inside.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product. Frequency aggregates, and the union has a cadence no component has.

At the seams the number is owned by nobody: marketing quotes prevalence, product usage, finance burden, support peak-day volume.

6. Nine things that separate expert from competent

Prevalence is not incidence. The tell is a share with no time window. Ask how many times each, over what period — the room usually discovers it never measured.

The mean is a fiction when rates are gamma-mixed. The tell is an average-user persona: at a variance-to-mean ratio of 89.9, a typical customer at 285 exceptions describes none of the nine.

Measured frequency is endogenous to the instrument. The tell is a frequency that jumps the quarter a reporting feature ships: the world did not change, the microphone did.

Success destroys frequency. Dhrupad's 2024 cohort fell from 1,140 exceptions a year to 889, down 22.0 per cent, as the product fixed their master data: falling usage beside rising satisfaction.

Intensity has a tail that gets the budget. The modal exception puts ₹9,000 at risk and the median ₹18,000; a duplicate instruction puts ₹1,42,000 — one governs the interface, the other the business case.

Burstiness is a parameter separate from rate. Identical λ with different clustering needs different products: one capacity, one queueing. The tell is a team sized on the monthly mean, drowning on working day 17.

For rare, severe problems the metric is not frequency but the cost of being unprepared times the probability of needing to be. The tell is killing a category because it happens once in five years.

Whose frequency is being priced. Payer and user have different cadences, so a metric tracking sessions contradicts the payer's sense of value. The tell is seats on a product whose value scales with cash protected.

The trigger, not the rate, is the design object. Falak's Delhi households meet the problem on 142 days and open the app on 15: an unobservable cue yields a low-frequency product.

7. By product type and company stage

In consumer products frequency maps almost directly onto retention-curve shape. In enterprise products the unit is nested and the relevant occurrence is often the decision rather than the task: procurement happens annually even when the problem happens hourly, so burden must be annualised. In platforms the thinner side binds. In hardware cadences are physically determined, so the warranty window belongs against the failure hazard. In AI products only intensity moves. By stage: pre-seed teams count forty customers by hand; Series A builds the occurrence ledger, since definitions are cheap only once; growth-stage worries about endogeneity; a mature company mistakes usage frequency for problem frequency.

8. Three worked examples

Fursat Travel House: a rare problem served well. The Chennai company's 7,80,000 users took 1.3 leisure trips a year and it booked 2,34,000 of them in FY26, 23.1 per cent of the 10,14,000 trips taken. At a 6.2 per cent take rate on a ₹47,000 average trip, that is ₹2,914 a trip and ₹68.19 crore. A ₹9.6 crore engagement programme lifted app opens per user from 0.42 to 1.08 a month — 5.04 to 12.96 a year, up 157 per cent — while bookings per user a year moved from 0.300 to 0.302, up 0.7 per cent. Re-counting found eleven decision occasions per trip over a 38-day window, so the occasions that existed were 1.3 × 11 = 14.3 a year: opens had gone from 35.2 per cent of them to 90.6 and bookings had not moved. The ceiling was the trip, not the attention.

Dhrupad: pricing the right term. Darekar's case against seats was the cure paradox. A customer dropping from 1,140 to 889 exceptions would, on a ₹260 per-exception tariff, see its bill fall from ₹2,96,400 to ₹2,31,140 — 22.0 per cent less for having just received the full benefit. At 0.9 per cent of cash protected it pays ₹4,63,061 and then ₹3,61,106: still falling, but against a metric its treasurer recognises.

Dastak Home Safety Network: the failure. The Indore company sold monitored home safety at ₹249 a month, response included. Its FY25 plan rested on 1,42,100 support tickets across 96,000 subscribers, read as 1.48 incidents per subscriber a year. A 2026 audit found 49,000 distinct physical incidents, 2.9 tickets each, so true frequency was 0.51 a year. At 3,100 incidents an agent-year the centre needed 16 agents; it had 46.

9. Failure modes and early diagnostics

Counting artefacts instead of events. Early sign: a frequency that moves when the support tool does. Diagnostic: the ratio of recorded items to distinct events. Dastak caught it late, at ₹14.74 crore.

Estimating a seasonal rate from a short window. Early sign: a study period shorter than the cycle. Diagnostic: how many cycles does it contain? Falak would have overstated demand twofold from a winter quarter.

Chasing sessions the problem cannot supply. Early sign: notifications rising while occurrences per user stay flat. Diagnostic: divide the targeted monthly active rate by the measured occurrence rate; above one it is impossible.

Pilots shorter than the interarrival time of the event being demonstrated. Early sign: pilots converting erratically. Diagnostic: compute 1 − e−λt for the headline event — Dhrupad's was 15.5 per cent.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The live dispute is whether frequency or intensity is the primary screen, and argument cannot settle it, because the camps rest on different evidence. The cadence-first position rests on retention data: across large consumer portfolios the long-run plateau tracks problem cadence better than any feature or onboarding variable, so cadence is the parameter you cannot design around. It would be wrong if plateaus came mainly from switching costs.

The intensity-first position rests on the most valuable software categories serving problems of modest frequency and enormous severity — tax, litigation, security, settlement — where willingness to pay outlasts habit. It would be wrong if that margin advantage came from regulation and procurement.

The distribution school rejects the question: both camps argue about means that describe nobody, and what decides is the heavy decile and the burst profile — Dhrupad's top third carried 54.5 per cent. It would be wrong if heterogeneity were mostly measurement error.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this sorts problems into quadrants. Someone who has internalised it asks four questions of any frequency figure: whose unit, what counts as an occurrence, over what window relative to the cycle, and with which instrument. They quote a distribution, name the heavy decile, expect the number to fall when the product succeeds, and set pilot lengths from interarrival times. When an engagement target is proposed they divide it by the measured occurrence rate in front of the room.

12. The decisions

On 19 May 2026 Darekar opposed seats, not repricing. She proposed a platform fee plus a variable component tied to cash protected, since burden per customer was ₹9.57 lakh against a ₹4.8 lakh price, the exception rate varied 4.1 times, and seats price a quantity that falls 22 per cent when the product works. Fernandes accepted it and won a 90-day pilot: the headline event's demonstration probability rises from 15.5 per cent at fourteen days to 66.1 at ninety.

Ekbote declined the ₹7.4 crore air score. Her case was that the problem occurred 142 times a year in Delhi and 44 in Bengaluru, that 60.8 per cent of Delhi's high days fell in the 124 days from 15 October to 15 February, and that the measurable loss was ₹149.21 lakh of unserved cartridge demand, not the 75 per cent of accounts monthly inactive. The money went to exposure-triggered fulfilment: the monitor ordering its own filter once exposure crossed the threshold. Dhariwal's objection, unanswered: a household which never opens the app eventually cancels the card.

Three questions. First: the panel is 40 of 612 self-selected customers, so what would have to be true of the other 572 for the 1.96 per cent rate to mislead? Second: Falak applies ₹368.90 per high day unchanged to Bengaluru, where households meeting it on 44 days may be more sensitive, not less — if their intensity were double Delhi's, what changes? Third: if Dhrupad cuts exception rates by a fifth every two years, what does its own revenue model look like in a decade?

13. Going deeper

  • Writing a problem hypothesis — a hypothesis without λ and c is untestable.
  • Vitamin versus painkiller — asks whether a burden of this size converts into willingness to pay.
  • Retention curves and the PMF signal — turns cadence into the curve shape you should expect.
  • Surfacing assumptions — instrument, window and occurrence definition are all assumptions.
  • Riskiest assumption first — an uncertain, load-bearing frequency is the riskiest assumption.
  • Validating a problem hypothesis — the methods, including how long a window must run.
  • Persevere, pivot or perish — a frequency lower than planned is a clean pivot signal.
  • Opportunity solution trees — where opportunities, each with its λc, get compared rather than argued.
  • Problem framing and reframing — Fursat's eleven occasions per trip is a reframe: the same world yields a different λ.

Frequency and Intensity of the Problem

How often and how badly a problem occurs, and what that implies for how people will use the product built to solve it.

1. A Tuesday in Pune

On Tuesday, 14 July 2026, Bhumika Deshmukh, head of product at Aashray Home Repair Services, opened a spreadsheet that her data scientist, Callum Brennan, had sent overnight from Manchester. Aashray, headquartered in Pune, connected urban households with vetted plumbers, electricians and carpenters through an app, and it kept roughly 18 per cent of each job's value as commission. The company had 2,00,000 registered households in Pune and Hyderabad and a board meeting in fourteen days, on 28 July. At that meeting Bhumika would ask for ₹6 crore to fund two quarters of work by a fourteen-person engineering team.

The proposal competing for that money was popular inside the company. Ashok Bedekar, the chief executive, wanted a daily "home feed" of maintenance tips and offers, on the logic that consumer apps were won by habit. Bhumika suspected the premise was wrong. Households opened the app rarely because a leaking tap or a tripped switch is not a daily event. If she was right, a feed would burn six crore rupees chasing a cadence the problem could never supply.

Her instrument was a survey of 1,200 households, 600 in each city, which asked how many small home-repair incidents each had suffered in the previous twelve months and what each cost them. The first table is his result.

CityHouseholds surveyedWith at least one incidentShareIncidents reportedIncidents per household
Pune60046878%1,8603.1
Hyderabad60045676%1,7402.9
Total / average1,20092477%3,6003.0

Survey of 1,200 households, July 2026; incidents are small repairs (plumbing, electrical, carpentry) in the previous twelve months. Total row: counts are sums; the share and per-household columns are pooled averages (924 / 1,200; 3,600 / 1,200).

Seventy-seven per cent of households had the problem at least once, so it was widespread. But the typical household met it three times a year, once every four months. Bhumika had to decide what that implied for the product.

2. The idea

The frequency of a problem is how many times it occurs for one person or organisation in a defined period, such as a year. Its intensity is how much each occurrence costs them, counted in money, time and distress. Multiplied, they give the annual burden: the total cost the problem imposes on one customer in a year. A third quantity follows from frequency alone, the natural cadence, which is the average interval between occurrences.

The idea answers a question that a problem statement, however well written, leaves open. A hypothesis can say who has a problem and still be silent on whether they need help daily or once a decade. No single person invented the pairing. It surfaces in the customer-development tradition associated with Steve Blank in the early 2000s, in Ash Maurya's Running Lean (2010), which asks founders to rank problems by how much they hurt, and in the habit literature around Nir Eyal's Hooked (2014), which treats frequency as a precondition of habit.

The sentence Bhumika could repeat in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: "A product can be used no more often than the problem occurs, and no more willingly than the problem hurts."

3. How it works

Applying the idea takes five steps, and practitioners usually leave two implicit. The first step is to fix the unit: whose problem, and what counts as one occurrence. Callum and Bhumika agreed that the unit was the household and that an occurrence was a repair need that interrupted a day, whether or not it was ever fixed. The second, usually skipped, is to fix the period: twelve months, to capture one monsoon and one summer.

The third step is to measure frequency, which means counting occurrences and not asking how "common" the problem feels. The fourth is to measure intensity in a single currency. Aashray asked what the last incident cost in overpayment, lost wages and time at ₹300 an hour. The fifth, again often left implicit, is to translate the result into cadence and then into the implied usage pattern: how many days in a year the customer has a reason to open the product.

Aashray compared four problems, all measured the same way, because a number means little without a neighbour. The table sets them side by side, and the chart that follows draws the annual burden.

Annual burden = incidents per year x cost each time; cadence = 12 months / incidents per year.

The remarkable feature of the exhibit is how similar the burdens are and how different the rhythms. Problems A and D cost a household almost the same in a year, ₹2,700 against ₹2,800, yet one arrives every four months and the other once in five years. A is a repeated relationship; D is an emergency number kept in a drawer. Frequency told Bhumika that D could not support an app people opened often.

4. A worked example, and a second pass

To see what cadence means for usage, Bhumika followed the small-fix problem, A, through Aashray's funnel. The inputs were the 2,00,000 registered households, the survey's 3.0 incidents per household per year, the share of incidents Aashray captured (25 per cent, taken from its last twelve months of bookings), an average job value of ₹1,200 and an 18 per cent commission.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Frequency of the problem is not frequency of the product

They coincide only when the product is used at every occurrence and at no other time. A product can be used less often than the problem (customers solve some incidents themselves) or more often (a feed pulls them in with no underlying need).

Intensity is cost, not volume of complaint

Aashray therefore asked for rupees and hours, not a one-to-ten rating. A rating cannot sensibly be multiplied by a frequency.

The average hides the distribution

A mean of 3.0 incidents could be three for everyone, or twelve for a few old-building owners and none for most. The 924 of 1,200 households with an incident show breadth, but the mean cannot say how the burden is spread.

Recall is a distorted instrument

People remember dramatic incidents and forget routine ones, so a twelve-month survey tends to overstate intensity and understate frequency. Check surveys against booking logs.

Triggered and scheduled problems differ

A leak arrives unannounced; a vehicle service falls due on a calendar. The first calls for readiness at the moment of need, the second for a reminder.

Burden is not willingness to pay

Annual burden says what a problem costs, not what a customer will pay to remove it.

Substitutes cap the benefit

A household with a trusted neighbourhood plumber has the same incident rate as a household without one, yet far less need for Aashray. The problem's frequency sets the ceiling on usage; the quality of the existing alternative sets how much of it a new product can reach.

What it cannot tell you

Frequency and intensity do not say whether you can solve the problem, whether your solution is better than the alternatives, or whether the economics work. Before relying on the numbers, ask who was counted, over what window, and who was left out.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace

In consumer products, frequency translates almost directly into the shape of retention. A daily problem such as commuting supports daily sessions; an annual one, such as filing income tax, supports a seasonal spike and little between.

In B2B products, the unit is the organisation, and frequency can be hidden inside it. A finance team may close its books once a month, but the person who reconciles payments faces the problem every day. The account's cadence and the user's cadence differ, and the product must be sold to one and used by the other.

In marketplaces, there are two problems with two cadences, and they must be reconciled. Aashray's households need help three times a year; its plumbers need work every day. The marketplace must keep supply alive through the gaps in demand.

Company stage matters too. An early-stage team can measure frequency by calling forty customers. A large company already has behavioural data and the opposite risk: it can mistake frequency of usage, which it observes, for frequency of the problem, which it does not. Large players such as Urban Company can infer cadence from bookings, but only for customers who already booked.

7. Common mistakes

Chasing sessions the problem cannot supply

Symptom: a roadmap full of notifications, streaks and content for a rare-need product, with weekly active users falling after each push. Misunderstanding: that usage is a design variable independent of the problem. Diagnostic: divide the natural cadence into twelve months and compare it with the monthly active rate you are targeting.

Mistaking breadth for intensity

Symptom: the team cites that 77 per cent of households have the problem as evidence that it is serious. Misunderstanding: that prevalence measures pain. Diagnostic: ask for the rupee cost of the last occurrence from those who had it.

Multiplying unlike units

Symptom: an "annual burden" mixing ratings, hours and rupees. Misunderstanding: that any two numbers can be multiplied. Diagnostic: state the unit of the result; if it cannot be named, the product is meaningless.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of the same decision starts from the incident, not the session. The team measures frequency by counting, measures intensity in rupees, and cross-checks the survey against booking logs. It designs for the moment of need and treats the gaps between incidents as the place for light-touch reminders (a monsoon checklist, an annual electrical inspection), each justified by a real scheduled need and not by an engagement target. It reports usage as bookings per incident and shows the board a second pass at half the surveyed frequency.

9. What Bhumika decided

On 28 July she asked for ₹6 crore, but not for the home feed. She proposed a smaller investment in three things: faster rebooking of a plumber the household had already used, an annual maintenance plan that converted an unpredictable four-month cadence into a scheduled one, and supply-side tools to keep the 18 per cent commission flowing through lean weeks. Her reasoning was that the problem occurred three times a year, so the product's best possible behaviour was to be excellent three times a year and quiet in between. The board accepted it.

The natural next topics are Vitamin versus painkiller, which asks whether a problem of a given intensity is one customers will pay to solve, and Retention curves and the PMF signal, which shows how to read a usage curve once you know the cadence it should have. Two questions to sit with. First, which problem you are working on has a natural cadence you have never written down, and what would the roadmap look like if you did? Second, if the real frequency were half the figure you believe, which part of your plan would survive?
case40v1-prob.frequency:
Gamak Plant Diagnostics: How Often, and How Badly

A case on how often and how badly a problem occurs

Indian School of Business · Problem & Opportunity Definition

1. Sunday night, Coimbatore

At a quarter to eleven on the night of Sunday, 25 October 2026, Dhanashri Shaligram was still at her dining table off Avinashi Road in Coimbatore, with two printed pages face up and a third face down. The board of Gamak Plant Diagnostics Private Limited met at nine, and she was to open with the product plan for the two quarters to September 2027.

The first page showed how often her customers' machines broke. The second showed how often her customers opened her software. The two did not describe the same company. The third was a term sheet from Dubai worth more each year than Gamak's whole India subscription book, asking for a product Gamak's hardware could not produce.

Dhanashri had joined in October 2023 as the first head of product, and for three years had told investors one sentence: unplanned machine failure in Indian process plants was expensive, frequent and badly instrumented. In eleven weeks she had stopped being sure of the middle word. Whether the failures were frequent enough for anyone to form the habit of looking was the question due by nine.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2021

Gamak was founded in June 2019 by Elavarasan Thangavel, who had spent nine years designing submersible pump sets in Coimbatore. Its first product, a mains-powered vibration analyser for spinning mills in Tiruppur, worked: ₹1.9 lakh a machine installed, eighty-one units in two years.

In March 2021 came the decision that still governs everything. To reach the mid-market, Gamak abandoned the mains unit for a battery clamp-on sensor a technician could fit in four minutes without a licence. The bill of materials fell to ₹2,650. What bought the price was the duty cycle: the sensor wakes once an hour, samples four seconds, transmits and sleeps. Twenty-four observations a day, and the cell lasts thirty-six months.

By October 2026 Gamak had 11,400 sensors live across 312 plant accounts at ₹3,600 per sensor a year — ₹4.10 crore of India subscription revenue — plus 240 on pilot at three Dubai sites. Headcount was 112: 48 in Coimbatore, 32 in Bengaluru, 14 in Pune and 18 across Singapore, New Jersey, Toronto, Berlin and Dubai. A ₹46 crore Series A closed in September 2023; cash on 30 September 2026 was ₹19.2 crore against net burn of ₹1.28 crore a month, fifteen months to January 2028.

The second consequence went unexamined until this year. An hourly sample is a claim about how fast problems arrive. In August 2026 Dhruvesh Zala's team opened eleven failed chiller compressors; in three the bearing went from nominal to failure in under forty minutes, between two samples. Gamak was blind to those three because its product had decided, five years earlier, how often the world changes.

Figure A — The decisions behind the decision

Years are spaced 90 px apart from x=60 at 1 January 2019, so a marker's date inverts from its x-coordinate. Red marks the choices Dhanashri treats as binding.

3. The industry

India's installed base of rotating equipment in food and agri-processing is large, old and lightly instrumented. Cold storage has been built for two decades on subsidy — the cold-chain scheme under PMKSY, the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund — so capital arrives in lumps and maintenance budgets do not. The machines come from CRI Pumps and Texmo in Coimbatore itself, Kirloskar Brothers and Grundfos India, with Danfoss and Bitzer compressors. Ammonia plants answer to PESO and cold chain to FSSAI; the technician app that photographs plant staff sits inside the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

Gamak's competition is not one thing. Siemens, Schneider Electric and Honeywell sell condition monitoring inside automation contracts to plants that already have a control room; Altizon and Detect Technologies sell projects, not subscriptions; at the bottom, a man with a screwdriver and a feel for a bearing, paid in cash, right for thirty years. Gulf facilities management pays three to four times Indian prices and writes contracts with availability penalties, which is why a Dubai term sheet can outweigh 312 Indian accounts.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

Gamak grew on a belief: that plant managers would check the dashboard every morning in the hot months. In January 2025 it shipped the Plant Health Score — one number from 0 to 100 per plant, designed in Berlin by Dagmar Reinhold. Engagement rose for a quarter and settled. In September 2026, 108 of the 298 accounts live on 1 September opened the dashboard at least once that month (36.2 per cent); fourteen accounts went live during September and are excluded from both numerator and denominator.

In April 2026 Dhanashri commissioned two studies: Durairaj Ponnusamy's team interviewed the maintenance in-charge at 204 plants in June and July (Exhibit 1), and Eshita Kuruvilla counted what the system had flagged across every sensor live for the full year to 31 July 2026 (Exhibit 2). Exhibit 3 plots the two dimensions of Exhibit 1 against each other.

Three beliefs have since failed. That a flag meant a fault: Exhibit 2, panel B puts confirmed developing faults at a minority, with supply-voltage events from the local DISCOM behind much of the rest. That the stoppage logs were ground truth: Exhibit 5 finds sensors and logs barely agree, which indicts either one. And the seasonal story: the cohort in Exhibit 4 went live in April and stopped looking by week six.

On 12 October 2026 Falaj Industrial Services of Dubai sent a three-year term sheet: 4,100 sensors across 26 chilled-water plants at AED 490 per sensor per year, signature by 31 December 2026.

5. The people

Dhanashri Shaligram, 38, vice-president of product, Coimbatore. Position: the problem Gamak picks must have a rhythm matching the product's, and she suspects it is monthly. Incentive: her options vest against the Series B. Not saying: she now thinks the Plant Health Score was her mistake.

Elavarasan Thangavel, 46, co-founder and chief executive, Coimbatore. Position: customers who log in twice a quarter make you a maintenance contractor with an app. Incentive: he has told two Series B investors monthly active accounts will cross sixty per cent. Not saying: he wants Falaj more than that number.

Dhruvesh Zala, 41, vice-president of engineering, Bengaluru, with fourteen firmware engineers in Pune. Position: the only honest fix is a higher sampling rate on the machines that matter. Incentive: he would rather build a sensor than a screen. Not saying: his teardown found the forty-minute failures, and the board has not been told.

Dagmar Reinhold, 35, principal designer, Berlin. Position: habits are made, not found; alerts train avoidance, a ritual trains attention. Incentive: her influence runs through the dashboard. Not saying: she has never stood in a running ammonia plant.

Eshita Kuruvilla, 33, data scientist, Toronto. Position: Gamak must first decide what its ground truth is. Incentive: she is measured on model precision, which the unclosed alarms make unmeasurable. Not saying: she thinks Exhibit 1's severity field is unusable, and has told only Dhanashri.

Divita Marimuthu, 40, customer success lead, Singapore. Position: renewals turn on whether a plant can name one disaster Gamak prevented. Incentive: her bonus is on logo retention, which looks healthy. Not saying: the two accounts that cut sensors hardest (Exhibit 6) did so after Gamak flagged nothing; she booked both as renewals.

Durairaj Ponnusamy, 44, head of field operations, Coimbatore. Position: the logs are written on Monday for the previous week, from memory, by a man with eleven other jobs; the sensors beat the paperwork judging them. Incentive: utilisation falls if cells need replacing every five months. Not saying: his own technicians fill the severity field.

6. Two more exhibits
