7. Voices

“I am asking what we tell a Series B investor in March. If the answer is ‘our customers open us when something breaks’, we are selling insurance — and insurance trades at four times revenue, not fourteen.”Elavarasan Thangavel, board pre-read, 21 October 2026
“Kappa is 0.21. Our flags and their logs are strangers who pass in the corridor. That does not say the sensors are wrong. It says one of the two instruments is wrong, and nothing tells us which.”Eshita Kuruvilla, data review, 14 August 2026, 07:30 Toronto
“Please stop quoting the log at me. I have watched it being written: Monday morning, for the previous week, by an in-charge also chasing a spare part from Chennai. If a pump tripped on Thursday and ran fine on Friday, it never reaches the register.”Durairaj Ponnusamy, voice note to Dhanashri, 18 August 2026
“Twelve weeks of falling bars does not prove there is no habit. It proves we gave them no reason that outlasts novelty. Give me a Monday number that is different every Monday and I will give you a ritual.”Dagmar Reinhold, 3 September 2026, 14:20 Berlin
“Last December a compressor seized at our Krishnagiri store during the mango intake. Fourteen lakh of fruit. Your app did not warn us. We still pay you: the week after, your technician told my boss the second compressor was going the same way, and he was right. I open your app twice a month. I do not think that is your problem.”Devasena Velayutham, maintenance in-charge, Vaagai Agro Cold Stores, 9 September 2026
“Our towers have no season. The plant runs through Ramadan, through August, and when it stops a mall calls my chairman. I am not buying a diagnosis once an hour. I am buying the minute it starts.”Ebrahim Qureshy, asset services, Falaj Industrial Services, Dubai, 12 October 2026
“I can close Falaj in three weeks. I cannot close four hundred Indian plants in three years.”Dinyar Katrak, forecast call, 20 October 2026

8. The options as Dhanashri frames them

Option A: manufacture the cadence. Build Dagmar's weekly rhythm — energy per tonne, a Monday comparison, a league table across a group's plants — so Gamak is looked at when nothing is wrong. This moves the number Elavarasan has promised. It also asks an in-charge with eleven jobs to adopt a twelfth, and Exhibit 4 is the record of the last attempt.

Option B: build for the rare catastrophe. Take Exhibit 3 at face value: only refrigeration compressors combine real loss with real frequency. Put a mains-powered, minute-resolution sensor on those machines, charge four to six times the price for a tenth of the sensors, and let the Gulf fund the engineering. This is Dhruvesh's fix and Dinyar's contract. It makes a product opened rarely by design, and turns the investor story into one about severity rather than usage.

Option C: match the maintenance calendar. Attach to a rhythm that exists — the planned shutdown, the monthly review, the Deepavali despatch peak. Ship a monthly condition report a purchase head reads with the electricity bill, and route urgent findings through the technician already visiting. It concedes the engagement argument and makes Gamak a service with software attached.

Dhanashri's note to herself reads: all three assume the user is one person. The shift operator meets the problem several times a shift and cannot buy anything; the in-charge meets a real stoppage twice a year and feels the pain; the purchase head meets it as a number and signs. A frequency measured on the wrong person is a different product. And a fourth option is not on the agenda — charge for the repair, not the warning — for which the 37.8 per cent of alarms no technician closed out are either the best evidence or the reason it would fail.

9. The deadline and what cannot be moved

Of 46 engineers in Bengaluru and Pune, 31 are on platform and sustaining work; 15 are free for one new track. Falaj requires signature by 31 December 2026, with 99.5 per cent data availability, a penalty of AED 1,200 per site per day capped at AED 2,40,000 a year (₹57.6 lakh at ₹24 to the dirham), GCC exclusivity for 24 months; the channel partner takes 18 per cent of UAE revenue until March 2028, which on a ₹4.82 crore contract is ₹86.79 lakh a year. The mains variant's bill of materials is ₹9,400 against ₹2,650, and needs ₹62 lakh and seven months of certification: started 1 November 2026, it ships from end May 2027.

Raising the sampling rate is the cheapest technical answer and the costliest operational one: a sample every six minutes takes cell life from 36 months to about five months, which at ₹310 a visit and 2.4 visits a sensor a year across 11,400 sensors is ₹84.82 lakh a year gross, or 20.7 per cent of India subscription ARR of ₹4.10 crore. The 36-month cell already needs 12 ÷ 36 = 0.33 visits a sensor a year, or ₹11.78 lakh, so the increment is ₹73.04 lakh, 17.8 per cent of that ARR. Cash is ₹19.2 crore, burn ₹1.28 crore a month, and the Series B needs ₹12 crore of ARR by December 2027. The four people outside India — Dagmar at €1,02,000, Eshita at CAD 1,48,000, Divita at SGD 1,26,000, Dinyar at USD 1,95,000 — cost ₹4.47 crore a year at ₹95, ₹63, ₹68 and ₹88 to the currency, more than the India subscription book; a senior firmware engineer in Bengaluru costs ₹34 lakh.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. From Exhibits 1, 2 and 5, state how often the problem Gamak sells against occurs, and for whom. Give a number, name its unit, and say what its denominator was when the numerator was collected.
  2. Exhibit 1 reports 2.4 stoppages per plant-year, Exhibit 5's logs 1.33 stoppage-months, Exhibit 2 9.1 flag-events per sensor-year. What must be true for all three to hold at once, and which would you take to the board?
  3. Kappa of 0.21 is consistent with weak sensors and with weak logs. Design the cheapest study that separates the two, and price it in technician-days.
  4. Exhibit 4 shows attention collapsing by week six. Is that a failure of design, a failure of value, or correct behaviour for a problem of this frequency? What on the page distinguishes them?
  5. Options A, B and C imply different usage cadences, retention curves, prices and buyers. Pick one and name the metric you would put before the Series B investor instead of monthly actives.
  6. It is nine o'clock on Monday. What do you do, in what order, and what do you say to a board promised sixty per cent monthly actives, with Falaj to be signed in nine weeks and its hardware seven months from certification?

Dhanashri turned the third page back over at ten past midnight. Sixty per cent of accounts, every month: she had helped write that sentence. In Banaskantha a potato store was running nine compressors that would not fail this year, while a man wrote Thursday into Monday's register. In Dubai a plant had not stopped since February, which was exactly why Ebrahim Qureshy would pay for the minute it did. Twice a month, Devasena had said, and I do not think that is your problem. Dhanashri was no longer certain whose problem it was, or how often — and the meeting was in nine hours.
case20v1-prob.frequency:
Gaadiwale: The Rider Who Comes Back Every Few Months

A decision case on the frequency and intensity of a problem

1. Opening

On Monday, 19 October 2026, Deepak Shirsat sat in a glass meeting room on the fourth floor of Gaadiwale's office in Baner, Pune, with a single sheet of paper in front of him. It carried three project names and a date: Friday, 30 October, when the board would lock the roadmap for two quarters. Diwali fell on 8 November, when riders service their bikes before trips home.

Deepak was Gaadiwale's head of product. His squad of nine engineers in Pune and Bengaluru could build only one of three projects. The chief executive wanted monthly active users to rise. Deepak suspected that the number measured the wrong thing. Before Friday he had to decide which problem to build for, and defend it with evidence on how often riders felt it and how badly.

2. Company background

Gaadiwale was founded in 2021 by Eshaan Rege and two classmates. It lets owners of motorcycles and scooters book servicing, tyre and puncture repair and minor repairs at independent garages, at a price shown upfront. By October 2026 it had 4,10,000 registered riders, of whom 1,10,000 had made at least one booking in the previous twelve months, and 140 partner garages across five cities. A ₹38 crore Series A in 2024 funded the team of ninety-two.

The market is crowded and mostly unorganised. Authorised centres of Hero MotoCorp, Honda, Bajaj Auto and TVS handle warranty work, and lane-corner mechanics take cash or UPI. Park+ and the FASTag apps own the daily-use end of the owner's phone. Gaadiwale's pitch is the independent garage with a price shown in advance.

3. The situation

About 14,000 riders, all of them annual bookers, opened the app in a typical month, 12.7 per cent of the 1,10,000 annual bookers, and the board wanted 30 per cent. The chief executive's answer was to give riders a reason to open the app every week.

In August, Deepak had commissioned a survey of 1,200 riders drawn at random from the 1,10,000, asking what had gone wrong with their vehicle in the previous twelve months, how many times, how much it upset their week (1 to 5, where 5 meant it stopped them reaching work or home) and what it cost (Exhibit 1). Emeka Okafor, the data scientist in Toronto, also followed an 18,000-rider cohort who first booked between January and March 2026, and asked when they came back (Exhibit 2).

From Toronto, Emeka read the second chart as a verdict on the weekly-app idea: riders returned in a bunch, at roughly four months. From Berlin, Dieter Hartmann, the designer, had been prototyping a "Rider Club" with fuel-price alerts, parking and rewards, and believed a daily habit could be manufactured. From Pune, Dilnaz Daruwalla, who ran the garage network, saw idle garages on weekdays and needed bookings that could be planned.

4. The people

Eshaan Rege, co-founder and chief executive, in Pune. He wants the monthly active figure to rise before the mid-2027 fundraise.

Dilnaz Daruwalla, vice president of operations, in Pune. She wants predictable demand for the 140 garages and fewer disputes at the counter.

Dieter Hartmann, senior designer, in Berlin. He wants a product riders love enough to open without a reason. His prototype tested well with five riders, though he concedes that shows opinion, not behaviour.

Emeka Okafor, data scientist, in Toronto. He wants the roadmap to follow what riders do.

5. Exhibits

Missed or late service was reported by 840 of the 1,200 riders (70 per cent), about three times a year each, giving 2,520 episodes. Punctures reached 660 riders (55 per cent) at 2.5 episodes each, 1,650 in all. A breakdown was reported by only 288 riders (24 per cent), 432 episodes in all, but scored 4.6 on intensity and cost ₹1,800 per episode.

Exhibit 1. Problems reported by 1,200 surveyed riders, previous twelve months (August 2026 survey)

Multiplying episodes by intensity gives a rough ranking: 5,610 for punctures (1,650 × 3.4), 5,292 for service (2,520 × 2.1), about 1,987 for breakdowns (432 × 4.6) and 1,440 for disputes (480 × 3.0). On frequency alone, service leads; on intensity, breakdown. Weighted by both, punctures and service are close, and breakdown is a distant third.

Exhibit 2 says the same thing from behaviour. Only 6 per cent had returned by day 30, and 31 per cent by day 90. Between day 90 and day 120, another 3,780 riders, 21 per cent of the cohort, came back, taking the cumulative figure to 52 per cent. By day 180 it was 61 per cent, so 7,020 riders (39 per cent) had not rebooked. This is consistent with a roughly four-month rhythm for the 52 per cent who return by day 120.

Option C sells at ₹2,999 a year for three services, with 80 per cent paid to garages, which also covers the included puncture repair. Contribution = revenue less direct cost. All figures are planning assumptions.

6. The options

Option A: build the Rider Club. Fuel-price alerts, parking and rewards would give riders a reason to open the app weekly. It answers the chief executive's metric directly. It addresses no problem in Exhibit 1, competes with apps that own those moments, and contributes ₹10.56 lakh against a ₹90 lakh build.

Option B: build a breakdown SOS plan. Breakdown is the most intense problem, scoring 4.6, so riders feel the value at once. But only 24 per cent have it, so it behaves like insurance: buyers are those most likely to need it, and the planning case loses ₹5.37 lakh in year one. Live location tracking also brings Digital Personal Data Protection Act obligations.

Option C: build a service-cadence plan. Riders pay ₹2,999 a year for three services, spaced about four months apart, with reminders at each interval and puncture repair included. It follows the cadence the data shows. The cost is a 20 per cent margin and little movement in monthly active users: a rider reminded three times a year opens the app about three times a year.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. In Exhibit 1, which problem has the highest frequency, the highest intensity, and the highest combination? Why does the ranking change?
  2. What does Exhibit 2 imply about the natural usage cadence of Gaadiwale's product, and what does it imply about the monthly-active-user target?
  3. Why does Option B lose money in Exhibit 3 despite addressing the most intense problem? What would make it break even?
  4. Which option would you take to the board on 30 October, and what would you tell Eshaan to measure instead of monthly active users?

8. A note for the learner

The lens is a simple question: how often does the problem occur, and how badly? Frequency sets the natural usage rhythm of any product built around it; intensity decides what a customer will pay to make the problem go away. A frequent but mild problem supports habit but little price. An intense but rare one supports price but little habit, and is easily mistaken for a business when it is really an insurance risk. The chief executive's metric assumed a weekly problem, and nothing in the survey shows one.

A well-reasoned answer starts from the rider's year, not the dashboard. Service and punctures dominate, and Exhibit 2 shows a four-month rhythm, so build for it and judge by it. One defensible path is Option C, with the Option B decision deferred. Option C is the only plan in Exhibit 3 that recovers its build cost within two years, on the year-one planning figures and assuming year two repeats year one (₹65.98 lakh a year against ₹70 lakh of build),.

Deepak should also reframe the board metric. A cadence product should be judged on the share of riders who rebook within 120 days and on plan renewals at twelve months, not on monthly opens. Exhibit 2's baseline is 52 per cent by day 120. A target of 65 per cent for the next cohort can be read within four months. He should be candid that Option C will leave monthly active users near where they are, a feature of the problem, not a failure of the plan. Option B can return later as a small add-on priced with claims data; Option A should wait.
exp40v2-prob.framing:
Problem framing and reframing

A frame is a bet about where the loss lives. Make it name its slice.

1. Two companies, two one-line problems

On Tuesday 25 August 2026, Balwant Sahni, chief executive of Bandhak Credit House in Coimbatore, sent his credit committee a one-page note. Bandhak lends against property to small manufacturers across Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Assam, average ticket ₹20 lakh, 41 branches. The note said one thing. "Our median file-to-sanction is 19 days. The four lenders we lose to are at 11. I want 10 days by March." Beneath it sat a ₹14 crore programme: a rules engine, a valuation panel, a document-upload app. The committee would decide on Thursday 17 September.

Bhargavi Kalyanaraman, Bandhak's head of product, did not think him wrong; 19 days is slow and the competitive figure was real. What troubled her was that the sentence had already settled three things — that the loss was to delay, that the delay was Bandhak's to remove, and that ₹14 crore was the right order of magnitude.

Six weeks later, on Wednesday 7 October 2026, Bela Ganguly put a similar sentence to her own product head. Ganguly is chief operating officer of Bakhiya Apparel Works, a Tiruppur platform on which knitwear exporters post stitching jobs and job-work units bid for them. In the September quarter exporters posted 6,250 orders and only 2,400 found a unit. Her reading: "We are short of supply. Four hundred more units, ₹1.6 crore, and the match rate fixes itself."

Both sentences are frames. A frame is not a description of a problem but a choice of which problem to have, and that choice fixes the solutions anyone brings. The discipline that separates an audit of such a choice from a debate: every frame must name the slice of measured loss it claims, and the fraction of it it can reach.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Problem framing fixes four things: whose problem it is, what counts as relief, which part of the causal chain is treated as given, and how general the statement is. Reframing restates it — wider, narrower, or from another party's vantage — to see whether a different solution set appears. A frame is a question, not a claim: the test is whether it admits a better solution than you would otherwise have built.

Two traditions produced it. The empirical one: Getzels and Csikszentmihalyi in 1976 found that the art students later judged original were distinguished by how long they spent arranging the still-life — "problem finding"; Simon in 1973 argued that ill-structured problems arrive without a defined space, so defining the space is the work; Kahneman and Tversky in 1981 showed a choice reversing when described as lives saved or lives lost. The professional one: Ackoff on the error of the third kind; Schön in 1983 on "problem setting"; Dorst after 2011 on frames that must be invented; Rittel and Webber in 1973 on wicked problems, where statement and solution cannot be separated.

Five schools sit on this material. The root-cause school (Ohno) signs "a well-measured symptom plus causal digging beats restatement", not "the symptom may be the wrong thing to measure". The design school (Schön, Dorst, Rittel) signs "a frame is judged only through the solutions it generates", not "the correct frame is discoverable before any design". The jobs-and-outcomes school (Christensen, Torres) signs "outcome frames outlive product-behaviour frames", not "widening is always worth its cost". The decision-analytic school (Howard, Raiffa, Ackoff) signs "the right frame maximises the expected value of a decision you can take", not "framing is primarily creative". The constraint school (Goldratt) signs "the frame belongs at the binding constraint", not "the constraint is a matter of interpretation".

3. Mechanics: the frame ledger, worked

The technique that marks expert practice is not a ladder of abstraction: climbing one tells you how general a statement is, not how much money stands behind it. Experts build a frame ledger — decompose one measured loss into exhaustive, mutually exclusive slices, then make each frame point at the slices it claims.

Bhavya Lunawat, Bandhak's analyst in Indore, built the June-quarter ledger in four days. Between 1 April and 30 June 2026 Bandhak logged 18,000 enquiries; 9,000 became files; 5,400 were credit-approved; 3,510 accepted the sanction; 3,159 were disbursed, worth ₹631.80 crore at the ₹20 lakh ticket. Finance values a disbursal at ₹1.35 lakh of lifetime contribution.

The step almost always skipped comes next. A lost enquiry is not worth ₹1.35 lakh, because it still had to survive every later stage. Each slice is valued at contribution times the downstream conversion from that stage: 3,159 ÷ 9,000 = 35.1 per cent for an abandoned file, 3,159 ÷ 5,400 = 58.5 per cent for an approved borrower, 3,159 ÷ 3,510 = 90.0 per cent for an accepted sanction, 100 per cent at disbursal. Skip it and the lost files come to 14,841 × ₹1.35 lakh = ₹200.35 crore against ₹98.78 crore — twice the true figure, with the first slice alone overvalued nearly threefold, ₹121.50 crore against ₹42.65 crore.

Two reason codes turn the ledger into a frame audit. Of the 9,000 who never completed a file, Bhavya's coding of field notes gave 51 per cent (4,590) to property documents unavailable, unregistered or disputed and 18 per cent (1,620) to income documents; the remaining 31 per cent split between a decision not to borrow, rate shopping and other causes. Of the 1,890 who walked away after sanction, an exit survey of 400 of them gave shares rather than counts: 42 per cent to borrowing faster elsewhere, 19 per cent to a low valuation, 11 per cent to a late title dispute. Applied to all 1,890, those shares are 794, 359 and 208 borrowers.

The chief executive's frame can now be priced rather than argued with. "Cut turnaround" reaches at its ceiling the 794 speed-driven walk-aways (794 × 0.90 × ₹1.35 lakh = ₹9.65 crore) plus the 211 of 351 ready-to-disburse files attributed to internal delay (₹2.85 crore): ₹12.50 crore, 12.6 per cent of ₹98.78 crore. The title frame — "a creditworthy borrower cannot prove a clean claim on the asset we insist on" — reaches the 4,590 document-blocked abandonments, ₹21.75 crore or 22.0 per cent. A wider frame, pricing risk without property, adds the 1,584 rejections for collateral shortfall (₹12.51 crore) and the 359 valuation walk-aways (₹4.36 crore): ₹38.62 crore, 39.1 per cent.

Exhibit 2. Scale: 600 pixels = ₹98.78 crore, so the reach bars are 76, 132 and 235 pixels (12.6, 22.0 and 39.1 per cent); the stacked segments are 259, 173, 139 and 29 pixels and sum to 600.

Two second-order effects follow. First, 13 of the median 19 days were spent waiting for borrower documents (9) and on legal and title vetting (4), against 3 for valuation and 3 for credit — so 68.4 per cent of the delay the chief executive wanted removed is the title problem wearing a stopwatch. Second, F1 moves two teams' roadmaps, F2 three, F3 five plus a policy clearance; a frame needing five teams needs a planning cycle.

4. When the audit applies, and when it misleads

Claim one: the loss is measured, exhaustive and attributable. True for Bandhak — every enquiry has a stage and a reason code and the slices sum to the whole. True for Bakhiya on the demand side, false on the supply side, because a unit that looked and silently declined leaves no record. Where it fails, name the dark slices instead.

Claim two: last quarter's shares predict next quarter's. True of Bandhak's title problem, a feature of land records rather than of fashion. False where market structure is moving: a ledger built on 2016 behaviour would have put a payments company's loss in card-entry friction, months before UPI made the question obsolete.

Claim three: a wider frame can be executed by this organisation at this size. F3 is arithmetically the best frame here and was, in August, unavailable: no cash-flow underwriting capability and no appetite to build one before March. A frame the organisation cannot execute is a criticism, not a frame.

The method misleads in three situations. With no loss to decompose — a new category, a zero-revenue line — the honest route is the design school's: sketch solutions to discover the frame. Where the problem is regulated, the slice is small and the tail catastrophic: the ledger priced Bandhak's 208 late title disputes at ₹2.53 crore and said nothing about a disputed security interest costing a lender its standing in a state. And where a frame's value is option rather than recovered loss: F3's argument was never the ₹38.62 crore but survival against a competitor who lends without property.

5. Hard edge cases

Two-sided. Ganguly's supply frame and Vora's spec frame claim slices of the same 3,850 unmatched orders from opposite sides, and relief on one side can load the other. Binoy Karunakaran, Bakhiya's data lead in Kochi, audited the no-quote orders against the capacity ledger.

Exhibit 3. At risk = orders × ₹18,000, the contribution per matched order: a 12,000-piece order at ₹46 a piece is ₹5.52 lakh, 4 per cent of that is ₹22,080, less ₹4,080 of servicing = ₹18,000. The quarter's loss is 3,850 unmatched orders of 6,250 posted, ₹693.00 lakh: ₹405.00 lakh here, ₹288.00 lakh in the 1,600 that drew quotes but no match.

Ganguly's frame reaches 414 orders — ₹74.52 lakh of ₹693.00 lakh, 10.8 per cent. Vora's reaches the 1,746 spec-blocked orders (₹314.28 lakh) plus the 655 unmatched orders in the widest quote-spread band (₹117.90 lakh): ₹432.18 lakh, 62.4 per cent. The residual ₹186.30 lakh, 26.9 per cent, belongs to neither. And 480 units were live while only 192 quoted at all, a 40.0 per cent participation rate: the supply frame reads that as a reason to recruit, the spec frame as evidence that 288 units could not price.

Multi-product, and the organisational seam. The frame that matters most usually belongs to no single team. Bandhak's title problem sits between credit policy, legal operations and field sales; none owns it, so each has a narrower frame it can own and the narrow frames win by default. Done well, the wide frame gets one named owner and a budget outside any function's plan; done badly, it goes in a strategy deck.

Regulated. Here the frame has a legal perimeter: Bandhak cannot frame its problem as "lend without security" when its approvals, cost of funds and recovery rights all assume security. The expert move is to state the perimeter inside the frame — "within a secured product, the borrower's claim must be provable in 72 hours" — narrower than F3, and still admitting title resolution and machinery as collateral.

Hardware plus software. Bhatti Kiln Industries, which instruments brick and ceramic kilns in Morbi, framed its 2025 problem as "operators ignore our alarms": 1,180 instrumented kilns, alarm action rate 23 per cent. The frame was wrong in a way only hardware makes visible — the damper an alarm asks you to adjust within twenty minutes was a hand-wheel two floors up. Software frames assume the user's action is cheap; hardware must price it.

AI-native. Here the frame writes the evaluation set, and so what "working" means. Bodhini Diligence Labs in Bengaluru framed its problem as "extract twelve clause types accurately", reached 96.2 per cent accuracy, and found only 31 per cent of credit officers used the tool more than twice. Reframed as "a credit officer must decide whether a security interest is enforceable", the output became a four-line enforceability note and repeat use rose to 74 per cent. The accuracy number never moved.

6. Eight distinctions between an expert and a competent practitioner

Reachable loss, not altitude, ranks frames. The competent practitioner climbs to the most abstract statement everyone can applaud; the expert ranks frames by the money behind each and whether it can be reached within a planning cycle. The tell is a wide frame arriving with a number and a date, not the word "fundamentally". F3 holds 78 per cent more reachable loss than F2 and pays back three times slower.

Value each slice at its downstream rate. Shown a 9,000-enquiry drop-off, an expert asks what those 9,000 would have converted at. Biggest drop-off, biggest problem is wrong: early losses are thinner per unit, and those who dropped early are less qualified than those who stayed.

A frame has an owner and a vocabulary. "Whose problem is this?" precedes "what is the problem?". Sahni's frame was competitive position; Basavaraj Hiremath, the Belagavi foundry owner whose father's name is still on the property, had a problem of proof; Bhupen Kakati's officers in Guwahati had a problem of wasted visits. A statement fitting all three fits nothing.

The frame creates the measure, and the measure then defends the frame. Once "19 days to 10" was the sentence, a dashboard was built and every later discussion conducted in days. Experts ask what metric a frame will create before adopting it, because within a quarter that metric is the only evidence anyone brings.

Dark slices are named, not estimated. Bakhiya cannot see units that looked and declined; Bandhak cannot see manufacturers who never enquired because they knew they had no papers. Experts will not let a percentage of the visible loss pass as a percentage of the problem: the darkest slices are the ones the current frame caused.

Frames borrow the shape of the data collection. Reason codes are written by officers rewarded for file completion, so "customer not interested" absorbs everything inconvenient. The expert asks which code an officer picks when the real reason embarrasses them; at Bandhak the tidy 31 per cent residual earned a week of listening first.

A narrow frame can be bought as information about a wide one. This move most distinguishes experts. F2 pays back in 0.75 quarters and yields data on which properties are unprovable and which borrowers would still have repaid — what F3's case needs. The tell is a practitioner who sequences frames.

The cost of a wrong frame is not the programme cost. If Bandhak spends ₹14 crore on turnaround and the loss sits in title, the cost is ₹14 crore plus four quarters of foregone F2 recovery at ₹8.70 crore — ₹48.80 crore. For Bakhiya it is ₹1.60 crore plus three quarters of the spec frame's forgone yield of ₹129.96 lakh a quarter: ₹5.50 crore.

7. Product type and company stage

In consumer products the frame is written as an observed behaviour — "users drop at the OTP screen" — and reframing means finding the task attempted; the loss is easy to measure, hard to attribute: consumers file no reason codes. In B2B and enterprise the first act is separating user, buyer and payer: Bandhak's branch officer, credit committee and borrower. In platforms and marketplaces the frame must name a side and the ledger be built twice; hardware must price the user's action, and AI products write their own eval. Where the difference is asserted but not real: consumer products do not reframe more often than enterprise ones — release cost differs, framing does not.

Stage changes the economics, not the method. A twelve-person company reframes almost free: twenty conversations move the statement and no budget defends the old one. At Bandhak's scale a statement has a team, a target and somebody's variable pay, so reframing is political. At very large scale frames become institutionalised, and reframing is done by competitors.

Exhibit 4. Vertical scale 5.6 pixels per percentage point, horizontal 135 per quarter: F2 at 22.0 per cent and 1 quarter, F1 at 12.6 per cent and 2 quarters, F3 at 39.1 per cent and 3 quarters. Bubble radii go as the square root of cost.

8. Three worked examples

One: the cheap frame that bought the wide one. Bhargavi put three numbers to the committee. F1: ₹14 crore against ₹12.50 crore reachable at an assumed 35 per cent capture — ₹4.37 crore a quarter, payback 3.20 quarters. F2: ₹6.5 crore against ₹21.75 crore at 40 per cent — ₹8.70 crore, payback 0.75. F3: ₹22 crore against ₹38.62 crore at 25 per cent — ₹9.66 crore, payback 2.28. F3 recovers most per quarter and is still the worse first move: its first credible signal is three quarters away.

Exhibit 5. Shares are of the ₹98.78 crore loss in Exhibit 1. Rows are not additive: F3's slice contains all of F2's. Recovered = reachable × capture; payback = cost ÷ recovered. F1 to F2 adds ₹9.25 crore of reachable loss for one extra team, F2 to F3 ₹16.87 crore for two more — ₹8.44 crore per team.

Two: the reframe that moved a marketplace without buying supply. Vora's ₹85 lakh programme made a fabric-in date and a trim list mandatory and published a quote-spread indicator. Of 4,000 quoted orders, the 1,500 with a spread of 15 per cent or less matched 1,275 times (85.0 per cent); the 1,600 in the 16–30 per cent band matched 880 times (55.0 per cent); the 900 above 30 per cent matched 245 times (27.2 per cent) — blended, 2,400 of 4,000, or 60.0 per cent. Spread measures how differently units price the same unknown: specification quality, not supply. Moving the widest band to the middle band's rate yields 495 matches against 245, a gain of 250; converting 45 per cent of the 1,746 spec-blocked no-quote orders into quoted orders (786) and matching them at 60.0 per cent yields 472 more. Together 722 extra matched orders at ₹18,000 — ₹129.96 lakh against ₹85 lakh, payback 0.65 quarters, against 4.29 quarters for Ganguly's ₹1.6 crore at 50 per cent capture of its 414-order slice (₹37.26 lakh a quarter).

Three: the reframe that failed, and the recovery. Bhatti Kiln did everything this page recommends and lost two quarters. It rejected "operators ignore alarms" as a frame with a solution folded inside, climbed to "kiln owners need certainty about fuel cost", and built a fuel-price advisory that reached 41 of 1,180 kilns, 3.5 per cent, for ₹3.4 crore. The failure was not insufficient width but a frame naming a problem the company had no asset for and no measured loss behind. Recovery came from narrowing to what the ledger could see: the damper is manual. An auto-damper retrofit at ₹46,000 a kiln was piloted on 120 kilns; alarm action rose from 23 to 68 per cent and fuel saving averaged ₹18,400 per kiln per month — ₹22.08 lakh a month against ₹55.20 lakh of cost, payback 2.5 months.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late

One frame, many optionsEvery alternative is a variant of one ideaWhat would someone rejecting our premise propose?Bandhak's ₹48.80 crore
Climbing past the executableApplause, and no metric for this quarterWhat will we know by 31 December?Two quarters, as at Bhatti Kiln

One-sided frame, two-sided marketOne side improves, liquidity does notWhat does this do to the other side?Bakhiya's ₹5.50 crore

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

First, whether framing should be valued at all. The decision-analytic position, taken here, says a frame is a bet with an expected value; its evidence is cases like Bandhak's, where a priced audit flipped a ₹14 crore decision in three weeks. The design school's reply, steelmanned, is that this is circular: you can price a frame only against solutions you have already imagined, and no ledger built on Bandhak's funnel could have produced F3. To be wrong, it would need the best frames to be routinely those with no measurable slice.

Second, the constraint school against the outcomes school on altitude. Goldratt: the frame belongs at the binding constraint, Bakhiya's spec problem simply is its constraint, and most reframing is undisciplined measurement. The outcomes reply: constraints are artefacts of the current design, so optimising at one perfects a product nobody wanted.

Third, who should frame. One camp holds framing to be the product manager's irreducible job, and that distributing it yields a statement nobody holds. The other holds that single-owner frames are the main source of organisational blindness, and that the corrective is three framings from three functions before any costing.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied framing produces more statements; someone who has internalised it produces fewer, each with a number and an owner. They ask what the loss is before what the problem is, and state their own frame as a choice, aloud, with the alternatives rejected and why. Bhargavi's memo of 11 September carried the marker: "If the pilot lifts file completion in the title-blocked cohort by less than four percentage points in one quarter, the problem is not provability and I will say so."

12. What each of them decided

On Thursday 17 September, Bandhak's committee approved ₹6.5 crore against F2 — a paralegal title-resolution service in 14 branches, a machinery-and-receivables collateral option where property proof failed, and a 72-hour provability check at the first field visit — and cut F1 to ₹3.2 crore of operations work on the 211 ready-to-disburse files, worth ₹2.85 crore a quarter. F3 was given a date: a paper in April 2027 on the F2 cohort's repayments.

On Friday 30 October, Bakhiya took Vora's ₹85 lakh programme and 60 of Ganguly's 400 units — those in machine classes where the 414-order slice showed genuine absence of capacity. Bashir Rowther, who runs a 46-machine unit in Tiruppur and had quoted on four orders all quarter, got it first. Ganguly's summary: "I was not wrong that we need units. I was wrong that it was the biggest thing we were short of."

Three questions. First: the audit valued every slice at observed downstream rates, assuming the 4,590 document-blocked borrowers would have converted like everyone else — what if they were systematically better credits, or worse? Second: F3 had the largest reachable loss and was still not chosen first; when would deferring it be the mistake rather than the discipline? Third: Bakhiya's residual ₹186.30 lakh, 26.9 per cent of the loss, belongs to no frame on the table — whose job is it to look there?

13. Going deeper

Writing a problem hypothesis gives the frame a falsifiable form. 'How might we' questions open a settled frame into solution directions. Five whys on user problems works beneath a frame, not across frames. Problems with conflicting stakeholders handles the Bandhak triangle of officer, committee and borrower. Surfacing assumptions exposes what a frame takes as given. Riskiest assumption first sequences tests inside a frame. Validating a problem hypothesis sets the evidence standard reason codes cannot meet. Frequency and intensity of the problem sizes a slice with no funnel. Vitamin vs painkiller is the same judgement qualitatively. Persevere, pivot or perish is what a reframe forces when the ledger stops explaining the loss.

Charaiveti Workshops: Twenty-Five Per Cent Overnight

A case for discussion. Do not circulate.

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday, 18 October 2026, Udita Purandare was still at her dining table in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with two documents that could not both be true. The first she had signed on 15 September, headed Problem statement, FY2027 H2: Riders do not come back to Charaiveti because we keep their vehicle overnight. We will cut the share of jobs taking longer than 24 hours from 25 per cent to 8 per cent by 31 March 2027. The second was a four-page note from Toronto, timed 19:40 that evening: re-cut by job type — please read before the pack is frozen.

Purandare was chief product officer of Charaiveti Workshops Private Limited, which ran from Pune a branded network of 1,124 independent two- and three-wheeler service garages in fourteen cities. The board met on 29 October. The pre-read, already circulated, asked for ₹14.5 crore and six of the nine remaining release slots to attack the overnight number. Diwali fell on 8 November, and nothing structural could ship into the fortnight before it. Eleven days.

2. How Charaiveti came to be shaped this way

Charaiveti was founded in 2019 by Ulhas Wankhede, a former after-sales manager from Nagpur, with two colleagues. India's two-wheeler owners mostly service at independent garages, starved of genuine parts, working capital and shop-floor systems. Charaiveti offered a signboard, a tablet application, next-day parts from a regional hub and a rider app, earning a commission on parts, a garage subscription and a fee on app-booked jobs (Exhibit 1).

Two earlier decisions governed October 2026. In November 2023, facing a hiring freeze, the founders built one mobile application covering the rider's booking journey and the garage's shop floor, on a single codebase and a single fortnightly release train, rather than fund a second mobile team. Every change has competed for the same slots since. In July 2024 Charaiveti signed a five-year exclusive supply agreement with Mrudang Spares Distribution, to 31 July 2029. Mrudang gives 60-day credit on hub inventory — the reason Charaiveti can hold parts without equity — and a 2.0 per cent rebate on routed value, worth ₹2.48 crore in the quarter to 30 September 2026 on ₹40.50 crore routed in July, ₹42.20 crore in August and ₹41.28 crore in September. In return at least 85 per cent of parts value must route through Mrudang; September's routed share was 86.0 per cent, leaving ₹48 lakh a month of headroom.

3. The industry around it

The Indian two-wheeler after-sales market was being pulled two ways. Hero MotoCorp, TVS, Bajaj Auto and Honda were extending authorised networks into tier-two towns with branded turnaround promises; Ather Energy and Ola Electric had built experience centres, and Mahindra's Treo came with service contracts. Yet the independent garage was still where most older vehicles were repaired, and demand had been reshaped by fleets: quick-commerce operators and last-mile contractors serving Flipkart and Meesho sellers ran captive fleets whose downtime cost money by the hour.

Regulation touched the product at three points. Labour carried 18 per cent GST, invoiced separately from parts. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 had put a consent screen into the garage tablet in June 2026 before a walk-in rider's number could be stored. And the PM E-DRIVE scheme had accelerated electric three-wheeler adoption in the fleet segment, with BIS standards limiting what a garage could touch. Charaiveti also licensed its software abroad: Khareef Fleet Services ran 2,400 two-wheelers from seven Dubai depots on it (Exhibit 6b).

4. What happened, and what has since come apart

A February 2026 retention review put first-service repeat near 28 per cent on the 2025 cohorts, against a target of 40, and Wankhede asked for a problem statement by the September board. Theresa Nolte, the Berlin designer, visited fourteen garages in June and wrote a memo: riders did not choose a Charaiveti garage; a garage joined Charaiveti and served whoever walked past. In September, 1,04,000 of the 3,20,000 jobs on the network (32.5 per cent) came through the rider app; the other 2,16,000 were garage-entered, with a mobile number captured on only 1,25,280 of the 2,16,000 (58.0 per cent). The memo was praised and not acted on.

The April 2026 cohort's 120-day window closed on 28 August for the last of them, and in the first days of September Tanmayi Wagle, a data scientist in Toronto, built what became Exhibit 3: repeat purchase against turnaround for the 52,000 riders whose first identified paid service fell that month. Between 1 and 7 September an exit survey went to all 37,440 of them who had not returned. There were 5,616 single-select replies; the leading reason, chosen by 2,078 of the 5,616 respondents (37.0 per cent), was that the service took too long. On 15 September Purandare signed the statement built on it.

Three things have since turned out differently. First, the base: the pre-read took the survey as though 37 per cent of churned riders had left over speed. As a share of the 37,440 who did not return, the 2,078 who said so are 5.6 per cent. Second, on 12 October Wagle found an untabulated free-text box: 1,904 of the 5,616 respondents (33.9 per cent) had written something, 812 about a part — 42.6 per cent of the 1,904 who wrote anything, 14.5 per cent of all respondents. Parts is a larger problem than speed, or a much smaller one, depending on the denominator.

Third, the gradient itself. Wagle's October note split the same jobs by type (Exhibit 4a). Accident and major-repair work takes longer and brings riders back less often for reasons unconnected to impatience, and it concentrates in the slow bands. Separate it out and the like-for-like gap either side of 24 hours narrows from 12.0 percentage points to 9.9: the prize falls from three points of repeat rate to a little over one.

Two more things arrived that fortnight. On 6 October Khareef's renewal terms reached Singapore: ₹6.2 crore for calendar 2027, conditional on a multi-depot module live by 15 December 2026, sized at ₹3.8 crore and four slots. On 14 October, at a garage owners' council in Nashik, nine of twenty-two owners said the catalogue showed stock the hub did not have — and Exhibit 5 had just told finance that 176 garages had left in six months.

5. The people

Udita Purandare, 41 — chief product officer, Bengaluru
Joined January 2025 from logistics software. Position: one number beats three. Incentive: 40 per cent of a ₹1.1 crore package rides on repeat rate reaching 36.0 per cent. Not saying: she signed before Wagle's job-type work existed.
Ulhas Wankhede, 53 — co-founder and chief executive, Pune
Position: Charaiveti is a consumer brand and the Series D story needs rider numbers that move. Incentive: he has told two investors consumer will be 40 per cent of ₹150 crore FY2028 revenue. Not saying: a lead investor asked whether the rider app was "a distribution cost pretending to be a product".
Bijal Soparkar, 47 — chief financial officer, Bengaluru
Position: the cheapest crore defends contracted revenue. Incentive: the Khareef renewal and the Mrudang rebate sit in his plan. Not saying: a FY2028 scenario thins the rider app to a booking layer, taking ₹11 crore of annual cost out.
Bhumika Kharbanda, 44 — head of network operations, Nagpur
Position: turnaround is an operations problem she can own, given nine hubs. Incentive: the hub plan expands her remit and budget. Not saying: the catalogue stock her team publishes refreshes once daily at 04:30 IST from a file Mrudang sends overnight; she has known since July that it overstates availability.
Tanmayi Wagle, 33 — staff data scientist, Toronto
Position: most of the gradient is job mix; the honest prize is near one point. Incentive: an earlier churn model of hers was overturned in 2025. Not saying: the job-type label comes from a keyword classifier (Exhibit 4b) that over-calls accident work.
Theresa Nolte, 34 — principal designer, Berlin
Position: the problem is mis-owned, not mis-measured; two-thirds of jobs never touch the rider app. Incentive: she wants a funded research function. Not saying: all fourteen visits were in Pune and Nashik, never a fleet depot.
Serene Khoo, 36 — regional customer success lead, Singapore
Position: the fleet frame is the only one with contracted revenue. Incentive: ₹9.5 crore of the ₹13.0 crore international line is her renewal book. Not saying: Khareef's operations director mentioned a rival's demonstration on 2 October, unrecorded.
Wendell Driscoll, 49 — head of enterprise sales, North America, Princeton
Position: Charaiveti is a fleet-operations software company that owns a garage network. Incentive: a FY2027 quota of ₹18 crore of new international revenue. Not saying: two of his three live deals need labour-compliance reporting that is on no roadmap.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

"Nine slots left, thirteen slots of asks, and a Diwali freeze between. I am not going to the board with three problems. Pick the one with a number."

Ulhas Wankhede, leadership call, 13 October 2026

"The gradient in Exhibit 3 is real. What I can no longer say is that waiting caused it. Build nine hubs on that assumption and we have bought a parts-logistics business for a one-point retention gain — which may still be right, for other reasons."

Tanmayi Wagle, note to U. Purandare, 18 October 2026, 19:40 IST

"We are arguing about a metric that reaches seven jobs in ten. Two jobs in three are garage-entered, and for two in five of those we have no number. We are measuring the loyalty of people who do not know we exist."

Theresa Nolte, comment on the board pre-read, 16 October 2026

"Catalogue showed 6 clutch plates at Nashik hub this morning. Hub had none. Customer went to the authorised centre. Do not send me a faster booking screen."

Upendra Pokale, garage owners' council group, 14 October 2026

"Khareef is ₹6.2 crore of 2027 revenue and a reference we cannot replace. The module is four slots. If it slips past 15 December I have no January conversation."

Serene Khoo, email to B. Soparkar and U. Purandare, 7 October 2026

8. The options, as Purandare currently sees them

Hold the frame. Fund the turnaround programme: ₹9.2 crore of pre-staged parts inventory across nine hubs, ₹5.3 crore of product and field work, six of nine slots, 25 per cent to 8 per cent. The organisation believes it — but her own arithmetic puts the prize near 1.1 points against a bonus metric needing eight.

Re-aim at the garage. Reframe it as a garage cannot promise a date it cannot see stock for: catalogue accuracy, a live stock interface, a local sourcing pilot — ₹6.1 crore and three slots. But the Mrudang floor leaves only ₹48 lakh a month of headroom, and Pokale's garages already buy 22 per cent of their parts outside the application, so a pilot at scale breaches the contract funding the hubs.

Re-aim at the fleet. Build the multi-depot module, keep Khareef, serve the three Indian fleet accounts that asked. ₹3.8 crore and four slots for ₹6.2 crore of contracted revenue is the best ratio on the table — but it makes the rider app a channel, not a product, before a consumer-story Series D.

Split the frame. Reverse the 2023 decision: a second mobile team at ₹7.4 crore annualised, relieving no slot before Q1 FY2028.

Reframe the measurement. Tell the board that first-service repeat rate is the wrong instrument: it is computed on the 2,29,280 September jobs carrying a rider identity, not the 3,20,000 that exist, and is blind to fleets. Which means saying in writing that the pre-read rests on a misread base.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets on 29 October 2026. Cash at 30 September was ₹96 crore; the approved H2 FY2027 envelope is ₹24 crore. The three programmes total ₹24.4 crore and thirteen of the nine available slots: both bind, neither clears by trimming. The Mrudang agreement runs to 31 July 2029 with an 85 per cent routing floor, and the 60-day credit inside it makes ₹9.2 crore of hub inventory affordable — so the garage option attacks the contract funding the turnaround option. The Khareef condition expires on 15 December 2026, the DPDP consent screen cannot be removed to lift identity capture, and Purandare's variable pay is written against the number she is minded to call wrong.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. State, in one sentence each, the four problems Charaiveti could be solving, naming whose problem each is and the evidence that it matters.
  2. Exhibits 2 and 4a describe the same 52,000 riders. What does each license you to claim, and what does neither?
  3. The footnotes to Exhibits 3 and 4a compute the same prize and get 3.0 and 1.1 points. Reconstruct both. Which assumption does each make?
  4. Exhibit 5 reads as "the tail churns" or as "we are quietly losing our best garages". Which does it support, and what absent data would settle it?
  5. Nolte says the metric misses the jobs it cannot identify; Khoo says it ignores a quarter of the jobs and a third of the parts value. What statement survives both, and is it narrow enough to build against?
  6. It is Monday morning, 19 October, and Purandare has the 9:30 with Wankhede. What does she say, what does she stop, and what goes into the board pack about the sentence she signed on 15 September?

11. Still Sunday

Just before midnight Purandare read her own sentence back. Riders do not come back to Charaiveti because we keep their vehicle overnight. It was clear, measurable and had survived a leadership review; and colleagues in four time zones had offered sentences that fitted the evidence as well. In the margin she wrote: whose problem is this? — and under it, who pays if I am wrong about whose it is? The pack was due.
case20v1-prob.framing:
Cardamom Kitchens: The Lunch That Arrived on Time

A case on problem framing and reframing

1. Opening

On the morning of Thursday, 15 October 2026, Bhavna Pasricha, chief product officer of Cardamom Kitchens, sat in the company's Kharadi office in Pune with a one-page problem statement she had signed a week earlier. It read: "Subscribers are leaving because our lunches arrive too slowly. Cut median delivery time from 34 minutes to 25." The board of directors would meet on Friday, 23 October, and expect her to ask for money against that sentence, before the Diwali ordering surge made any change risky.

This week, reading customer complaints one by one, she had begun to doubt it. She had eight days to decide whether to ask the board for a fast-delivery network, to ask for something different, or to say that the problem had been wrongly stated.

2. Company background

Cardamom Kitchens was founded in 2021 by two former hotel chefs and a logistics engineer, selling weekday lunch subscriptions to office workers. A subscriber picks a menu each week, pays through UPI or a card on Razorpay's checkout, and receives a hot meal in a sealed box at the office reception or desk. The kitchens, licensed by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, sit in Pune (serving Hinjewadi and Kharadi) and Bengaluru (serving Whitefield and Bellandur). On 1 September 2026 the company had 48,000 active subscribers.

The market around it is crowded. Swiggy and Zomato will deliver almost any restaurant lunch in under thirty minutes, and Zepto Cafe has made speed its brand. Cardamom has never competed on speed. Its pitch was a home-style meal at a predictable price of about ₹280 per order, with a contribution of about ₹60 per order after food, packaging and delivery costs, roughly 21 per cent of the order value.

3. The situation

In September the company noticed that it was losing subscribers. Of the 48,000 subscribers active on 1 September, 9,600 (20.0 per cent) placed no order at all in September and were counted as lapsed. The remaining 38,400 placed 3,84,000 orders in September, exactly ten orders each on average. At ₹60 contribution per order, a retained subscriber was therefore worth about ₹600 a month.

Every lapsed subscriber received an exit survey on 1 October, and 2,400 of them, one in four, replied by 6 October. Exhibit 1 shows the answers. Delivery that was too slow led the list at 37 per cent of respondents, and that figure became the problem statement. Exhibit 2 shows September orders by delivery time and the complaints each band produced. Complaints rise with delay: 3.0 per cent of orders up to thirty minutes drew one, against 10.0 per cent of those over fifty.

Then Bhavna read the complaint tickets themselves rather than the bands. Exhibit 3 sorts all 17,280 by what the customer wrote. Late arrival accounts for 40 per cent. But 30 per cent say the box came on time and nobody was there to take it: the subscriber was in a meeting, on a call, or at a client site, and the lunch sat at reception, often until it was cold.

The 28 per cent in Exhibit 1 who chose "arrived when I was away" were not complaining about speed at all.

4. The people

Uday Rajguru, vice president of operations in Pune, runs the kitchens and the delivery partners. He believes the speed diagnosis. A fast-delivery network of six satellite hubs, he argues, is the fix that hands him a number he can manage, and the 10.0 per cent complaint rate over fifty minutes proves it.

Bipasha Dutta, who leads customer success from Singapore, reads the tickets daily. She has been pressing Bhavna to look at the "not available" tickets. She wants the product to let subscribers say when they will be at their desk.

Ulrike Sommer, the product designer in Berlin, observes that the app asks what the subscriber wants to eat but never when they want to eat it. She would prefer to redesign the whole lunch moment, including office lockers.

Bhaskar Kurup, head of sales in New Jersey, sells corporate meal plans to human-resources managers at large employers. He wants any option that can be shown to a prospect before December.

5. The options

Bhavna sketched what each framing would ask the board for, summarised in Exhibit 5. The monthly figures that follow are upper bounds: they assume the exit survey's shares hold for all 9,600 lapsed subscribers, not just the 2,400 who answered, and that every subscriber who lapsed for the addressed reason could be won back.

Option A: build the fast-delivery network. Six satellite hubs in Pune and Bengaluru would target a twenty-five minute median. The cost is ₹180 lakh upfront and ₹9 lakh a month in running cost. It addresses the 37 per cent who named speed, 3,552 subscribers, worth up to ₹21.31 lakh a month in contribution. After running cost, that nets at most ₹12.31 lakh a month, a payback of about fifteen months, on the most generous reading. It would also not touch the 5,184 tickets where the food arrived on time.

Option B: let the subscriber choose the arrival window. Subscribers would pick a thirty-minute slot for each day, and kitchens would plan batches around the slots. The cost is ₹35 lakh upfront, ten weeks of build, and ₹6 lakh a month for slot planning. It addresses the 28 per cent who said the lunch came when they were away, 2,688 subscribers, worth up to ₹16.13 lakh a month, or ₹10.13 lakh net, a payback of about three and a half months. It leaves the speed complaints untouched.

Option C: put a place for lunch in the office. Cardamom would install lockers or sponsor pantry shelves in forty partner offices, so the box lands somewhere safe and warm. It costs ₹90 lakh upfront and ₹4 lakh a month, takes six months, and needs approval from building managers and employers. The exit survey cannot size it, and Bhaskar doubts it can be sold before December.

Exhibit 5. The three options (upper-bound figures)

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Read Exhibits 1 to 3 together. What might "too slow" mean to a subscriber, and how far should the team trust the 37 per cent?
  2. How might the 7,200 who did not reply differ from the 2,400 who did, and how would that change the figures in Exhibit 5?
  3. Rewrite Bhavna's problem statement at the three levels in Exhibit 4. Which solutions appear or vanish at each?
  4. Which option would you take to the board on 23 October, what would you test first, and what result would make you change your mind?

7. A note for the learner

This topic asks one question: have I framed the problem so narrowly that I have excluded the best solutions? Bhavna's sentence named a cause (slowness), a metric (median minutes) and a solution (faster delivery) in a single breath. That is a solution wearing a problem's clothes, and it forecloses everything else. The tickets suggest that the cause may be mismatch between when lunch arrives and when the subscriber is free, which a faster van does nothing about.

A well-reasoned answer widens before it commits. The reframing "lunch arrives when I am away" takes in both the on-time complaints and part of the survey, and it can be tested cheaply. The widest frame, a place for lunch to land, cannot yet be sized; it is a hypothesis to learn about.

One defensible path is Option B, with a small test of C. Ask the board for the ₹35 lakh build, ship slot selection to a pilot of two Pune offices in the first weeks, and compare four-week lapse against matched offices without slots. In parallel, spend a fraction of Option C's budget on lockers in three offices to learn what building managers will accept. Hold Option A back, not because speed is irrelevant, but because its payback is the longest of the two sized options and it leaves the 30 per cent of tickets about on-time boxes untouched. Before presenting, Bhavna should also re-sample the 7,200 silent lapsers with a two-question message, because every figure in Exhibit 5 depends on them being like the respondents. If slots fail the pilot, the speed case returns with better evidence.
exp20v2-prob.framing:
Problem framing and reframing

Widening or narrowing the problem until the best solutions become visible

1. A one-line problem and a ₹1.2 crore request

On Monday 5 October 2026, Usha Narayanswamy, head of product at Urvara Soil Labs in Hyderabad, had eleven days before the board met on Friday 16 October. Urvara sells a soil test to smallholder farmers. A field agent collects a sample, a laboratory analyses it, and an app sends a report with fertiliser advice in Telugu, Hindi or Marathi. Chief executive Udayan Bhattacharjee had put the problem into the board paper in four words: "Reports take too long." Beside it sat a request for ₹1.2 crore (₹120 lakh) to build two regional labs and a courier network that would cap turnaround at four days.

The sentence was not invented. Upasana Dhillon, who runs field operations from Jaipur, had a folder of complaints; a dealer in Sikar said the sowing was over before the report arrived. Umang Tripathi, the data analyst in Vijayawada, had pulled the third quarter. Between 1 July and 30 September, agents collected 40,000 samples and the lab delivered 36,000 reports. Farmers who changed what they bought as a result numbered 10,800. Urvara had ₹4.8 crore of runway, so the request was a quarter of everything the company had. If the framing was wrong, the money would buy a faster lab that few more farmers used.

Third-quarter fact (1 July to 30 September 2026)Figure
Samples collected40,000
Reports delivered36,000
Farmers who acted on the advice10,800
Action rate (acted ÷ delivered)30.0%
Request: ₹120 lakh against runway of ₹480 lakh25%

Source: Urvara internal data, as assembled by U. Tripathi. "Acted" means the farmer bought at least one recommended input within 30 days.

Nobody was wrong; delay was real. But the sentence had chosen a cause and a cure before anyone asked what the farmer was short of.

2. The idea

Problem framing is the act of choosing how a problem is stated: whose problem it is, what outcome is wanted, and how general the statement is. That choice quietly fixes the list of solutions anyone will consider. Reframing is deliberately restating the problem, wider or narrower, to see whether a different list appears. A frame is not a fact about the world; it is a decision, and can be made badly unnoticed.

The idea has several parents. Karl Duncker's 1945 experiments showed people fixating on the familiar use of an object. S. I. Hayakawa's "ladder of abstraction" in the early 1940s described statements moving between concrete and general. Donald Schön, in 1983, called the framing work "problem setting" and argued that skilled professionals spend more effort there than on solving. Horst Rittel and Melvin Webber, writing in 1973 about wicked problems, observed that stating the problem and finding the solution cannot be separated.

Exhibit 1. A ladder of problem statements for Urvara. The board paper began on rung 1.

The ladder shows that "reports take too long" is not the problem at all; it is rung 1, a goal with a solution folded inside it. Usha could repeat one sentence in the meeting without sounding glib: "Before we decide how to make the report faster, let us check that faster is what the farmer is short of."

3. How it works

The mechanics run in six steps, and practitioners usually skip the second and the last. First, write the problem as a full sentence naming a person, an outcome and an obstacle. Second, strip out anything that smuggles in a cause or a cure; "too long" asserts that time is the obstacle, and "build labs" asserts the remedy. Third, climb the ladder by asking "why does that matter?" until the answer is outside the company's control. Fourth, descend from each rung by asking "how could we achieve that?" and listing what appears.

Fifth, attach evidence and a price to each rung: what is known, what it would cost to learn more, and what the business could measure within a quarter. Sixth, and most often left implicit, choose a rung and say aloud that you have chosen it. The chosen altitude is a judgement about what the team controls and can verify; stating it invites others to challenge it, which is the point.

RungWhat the team could do from hereMeasurable by Urvara within a quarter?
5 Incomes riseFund crop-advisory partnershipsNo; seasons and prices intervene
4 More farmers actRedesign the whole advice journeyYes; action rate was 30.0%
3 Farmers can actVoice explanation, dealer stock linksYes; from survey and app events
2 Report before sowingSeasonal sampling calendarPartly
1 Faster labRegional labs, couriersYes; days to delivery

Exhibit 2. Rungs, solution families and measurability. Rung 3 and rung 4 offered the widest set of options that Urvara could still test.

The table does not say rung 1 is wrong. It shows rung 1 was the only rung anyone had costed, which suggests the others were excluded by neglect rather than analysis.

4. A worked example

Umang split the 36,000 delivered reports by days to delivery and counted, in each band, the farmers who acted.

5 to 814,0004,20030.0%

Exhibit 3. Action rate by turnaround band, third quarter 2026.

Speed barely moves behaviour: the slowest band acts at 28.8 per cent and the fastest at 31.0. Suppose the ₹120 lakh programme brought every report to the fastest band's rate. The 14,000 reports in the middle band gain 1.0 point, or 140 farmers; the 10,000 in the slowest band gain 2.2 points, or 220. That is 360 extra farmers acting, so each costs ₹1,20,00,000 ÷ 360 = ₹33,333. Urvara earns a ₹600 commission per acting farmer from input retailers, so 360 farmers yield ₹2.16 lakh a quarter.

Now widen to rung 3. Umang and Upasana's team phoned a sample of 600 farmers and scaled the answers to the 25,200 who received a report and did not act (36,000 minus 10,800).

Exhibit 4. Why 25,200 farmers did not act. Bar length is 8 pixels per percentage point; counts sum to 25,200.

Two causes, unreadable reports (9,828) and missing stock (6,300), account for 16,128 of the 25,200, and neither is a speed problem. A ₹90 lakh programme of spoken explanations plus a live feed of nearby dealer stock is assumed to convert one third of the first group (3,276) and half of the second (3,150), giving 6,426 extra farmers acting. Halving the assumed conversion halves the benefit, yet the reframed option still beats the lab programme nearly nine to one. The decision survives the change in input.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Framing is not root-cause analysis

Root-cause methods dig down from a symptom you have already accepted. Framing questions the symptom itself. Five whys applied to "reports take too long" would produce a very good account of lab bottlenecks, and would never ask whether the report mattered.

Wider is not better

Rung 5, "incomes rise", is unarguable and undecidable. A frame is useful only if it is wide enough to admit a better solution and narrow enough that the team can act and measure. The right altitude is the highest one you can still test.

A frame belongs to someone

"Whose problem is this?" comes before "what is the problem?" The chief executive's frame was about reputation; the farmer's was about a sowing date; the dealer's was about stock. Reframing without naming the owner yields a tidier statement nobody holds.

Reframing is not pivoting or scope creep

A reframe changes the problem statement before work starts. A pivot abandons a strategy after evidence; scope creep adds work without a decision. Mixing them lets sceptics dismiss a framing exercise as indecision.

Data informs the frame but cannot choose it

Exhibit 3 showed speed mattering little. It did not show that interpretation mattered more; the telephone survey did. Even then, choosing between rungs rested on judgement about what Urvara is for.

Your data covers only those who stayed

Every figure above concerns farmers who gave a sample and received a report. The 4,000 whose samples never reached a report, and the farmers who never tested, are invisible. A frame built only on current users inherits their selection.

Questions before relying on it

Who wrote this statement, and what did they already believe? Which solution is hidden inside it? What would we do if the stated cause disappeared tomorrow? What evidence would make us climb, and what would make us descend?

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace; early and large

SettingTypical narrow frameWhat reframing usually reveals
Consumer"Users drop at sign-up"The user never wanted the account; the job was one task
B2B"The buyer wants feature X"The user, buyer and payer hold different problems
Marketplace"Not enough supply"Supply exists but is not discoverable or trusted by demand

Exhibit 6. Typical narrow frames and the wider question each hides.

In consumer products the frame is usually about the person's immediate behaviour, and reframing means finding the larger task. In B2B the first act is separating whose problem it is, because the signing customer and the daily user often disagree. In marketplaces the problem sits between two sides, and a frame that improves one side can worsen the other. Urvara has all three: the farmer uses, the retailer pays commission, and both must be present for the market to clear.

Stage matters too. An early company reframes cheaply, because it has few commitments and a conversation with twenty customers can change the problem. A large company reframes expensively, because a problem statement has become a budget line, a team and a target. There the discipline is to reframe before the funding cycle, not after.

7. Common mistakes

Solution in disguise. The symptom is a problem statement containing a verb such as "build", "add" or "integrate". The misunderstanding is that naming the solution makes the problem concrete. The cheapest diagnostic is to delete the solution words and read what remains: if nothing is left, there was no problem statement.

One frame only. The symptom is a review meeting where every alternative is a variation on the same idea. The misunderstanding is that a frame is neutral. The diagnostic is to demand at least three statements at different rungs before any option is costed.

Climbing to the clouds. The symptom is a statement everybody applauds and nobody can act on. The misunderstanding is that wider is more strategic. The diagnostic is to ask what the team could measure by the end of the quarter.

Framing by the loudest voice. The symptom is a problem written in the vocabulary of one function. The misunderstanding is that urgency means importance. The diagnostic is to ask whose problem it is and to interview one person from the other side of it.

8. What good looks like

Good practice produces a one-page memo with three problem statements, each on a different rung, each with its evidence and its cost to test. The memo names the author of each frame, shows the numbers behind the choice, and says what result would send the team back up or down the ladder. It also states plainly what remains unknown, here whether the survey's reasons were stated honestly. A board member can disagree with the rung and still see why it was picked.

9. What Usha decided

On 16 October she asked the board for ₹90 lakh in place of ₹120 lakh, in two tranches: ₹30 lakh for an eight-week pilot of spoken reports and dealer stock links in two districts, then ₹60 lakh if the pilot lifted the action rate. She kept the tail of nine-day reports on the agenda as an operations fix, since those 10,000 reports cost about 220 acting farmers and did not justify new laboratories. Rung 3 offered the largest test she could run quickly, and even the cautious case beat the labs.

The next topics follow naturally. "How might we" questions turn a chosen frame into a set of openings without collapsing them into one solution. Five whys on user problems tests the cause beneath a frame. Problems with conflicting stakeholders handles the situation in which the dealer, the farmer and the chief executive will never share one statement.

Two questions to sit with. Think of a statement you have written this month: which solution is hidden inside it, and what would the problem look like with that solution deleted? And whose problem did you frame, and have you spoken to them?
case20v1-prob.sizing:
Tessera Pharma Desk: Is Expiry Loss Worth a Team?

A decision case on sizing an opportunity before staffing it

1. Opening

On the evening of Tuesday, 13 October 2026, Nisha Gawde, head of product at Tessera Pharma Desk, sat in the company's Baner office in Pune and looked at a number she did not yet trust. It was ₹602.28 crore, and it appeared in a message from Ethan Menezes, the company's data scientist in Toronto, under the heading "annual expiry write-offs, all stores, extrapolated".

The company's quarterly roadmap would be locked on Friday, 23 October. Until then, five engineers and a designer were unassigned, and three proposals sought them. Nisha had to recommend one. Her founder-CEO wanted one page: what the problem was worth, and what chasing it would cost. Chemists were about to stock up for Dhanteras on 6 November and Diwali on 8 November.

2. Company background

Tessera sells billing, inventory and GST software to independent chemists. It had 38,000 paying stores on subscriptions averaging a little over ₹7,000 a year.

Competition was crowded: Marg ERP and GoFrugal held large installed bases among small chemists, while Tata 1mg, PharmEasy and Apollo Pharmacy pulled customers toward organised retail. Regulation set the frame: the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation and state drug controllers forbid the sale of expired medicines, and GST requires every return to be documented.

That prohibition is the root of the problem Nisha was weighing. Stock that expires on the shelf is a straight loss, but stock noticed a few months early can often be returned to the distributor for a credit note. The window varies by manufacturer, and most shops track it with a notebook or memory.

3. The situation

Over two months, 60 larger stores in Pune and Nashik used a prototype that flagged batches 90 to 120 days before expiry and generated the return note for the distributor. Those stores recovered about 20 per cent of the value that, on their prior-year records, they would have written off. The pilot stores were large volunteers, a limit Nisha had noted.

Ethan's number came from a different source. About 9,200 of the 38,000 stores, or 24.2 per cent, record expiry write-offs in a dedicated voucher type. He took the twelve months to September 2026 from those stores, grouped them into three sizes, and applied segment averages to every store in the band. His caveat: stores that log write-offs are the careful ones, and he could not say whether they lose more or less than the rest. Exhibit 1 sets out his arithmetic; Figure 1 shows how the pool divides.

In Berlin, Ellora Mallick, the product designer, had interviewed eleven chemists by video and heard the same sentence repeatedly: "I know it is expiring, I just do not have time to look." In Toronto, nine and a half hours behind Pune, Ethan worried that "extrapolated" would be read as measured. In Edison, New Jersey, Navdeep Bose, who runs channel sales to distributors, had a rival claim on the team.

4. The people

Nisha Gawde, head of product, Pune, owns the recommendation. She wants an answer that survives the founder's follow-up questions.

Ethan Menezes, data scientist, Toronto, built the pool estimate. He wants the page to say plainly what is measured and what is projected.

Ellora Mallick, product designer, Berlin, wants to ship the pilot's alert experience properly, since a busy shopkeeper must act within a minute of seeing a flag.

Navdeep Bose, head of channel sales, Edison, New Jersey, wants the team put on GST reconciliation. Stores sent 2,300 tickets last quarter about matching purchase invoices to GSTR-2B, from 1,150 distinct stores. He believes a chemist who cannot reconcile invoices will leave.

5. The numbers behind the options

Exhibit 2 turns the pool into a revenue estimate for Tessera. The adoption rates and prices are Nisha's own working assumptions, not observations. Only the 20 per cent recovery comes from the pilot. The add-on would cost ₹6,000, ₹4,000 or ₹2,400 a year by segment. For a large store, ₹6,000 is under 12 per cent of the ₹51,840 it would recover if the pilot's 20 per cent holds on Ethan's average. If Ethan's loss figures were halved, recoverable value would be ₹25,920 and the price 23.1 per cent of it.

Segment A matters most. Its stores are 36.8 per cent of the base, but they supply ₹210.0 lakh of the ₹320.4 lakh, or 65.5 per cent. The cheapest option aims at them alone. Exhibit 3 sets the three proposals side by side, and Figure 2 places them against the calendar.

6. The options

Option 1: build the full expiry module. All six people work for twelve months on an expiry-recovery module covering every segment, with distributor-specific return rules and reports. It targets ₹320.4 lakh a year against ₹192 lakh of cost. The risk is a year without learning whether mid-sized and small chemists will pay, and those assumptions are the weakest in the model.

Option 2: ship a narrow product for large stores. Two people, an engineer in Pune and Ellora, build the pilot's alerts and return-note generator for segment A over three months, at a cost of ₹16 lakh. It targets ₹210.0 lakh a year, 65.5 per cent of Option 1's revenue, for about 8 per cent of its cost. 267 paying large stores at ₹6,000, under 2 per cent of the segment, recover the build cost in the first year of revenue, before run costs. The cost is that segments B and C are not served.

Option 3: put the team on GST reconciliation. The tickets are real, and the 1,150 stores asking are 3.0 per cent of the base. The cost is that the claim is unsized: nobody has measured how many of those stores might leave.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, state the problem as reach, frequency and value. Which is best evidenced and which weakest?
  2. Ethan's pool rests on 9,200 stores that log write-offs. In what direction might that bias the ₹602.28 crore, and what single piece of evidence would you ask him for?
  3. The pilot covered 60 volunteer large stores. What does it show about segment A, and what does it not show about segments B and C?
  4. Choose among the options. What would change your mind, and when would you find out?

8. A note for the learner

Sizing asks whether a problem is worth a team by multiplying reach, frequency and value. Here reach is 38,000 stores, frequency is 3 to 12 expiry events a month, and value is ₹1,000 to ₹1,800 per event. A good answer does three things. It separates the size of the problem (₹602.28 crore a year) from the size of Tessera's prize (₹320.4 lakh at assumed adoption), because a pool is not a revenue. It labels what is measured, what is extrapolated and what is assumed. And it compares the cost of finding out with the cost of being wrong.

One defensible path is Option 2. Evidence is strongest for large stores: the pilot is real, loss per store is high, and the price is under 12 per cent of recoverable value at base figures, and under a quarter if losses are halved. The 3 months buy evidence on adoption before any 12-month commitment. A sensible gate would invite 2,000 large stores to a trial and extend to segments B and C only if at least 400 of them (20 per cent) convert at the stated price, a rate below the 25 per cent assumed in Exhibit 2.

The GST proposal should not be dismissed. It should be sized the same way before the next roadmap; the four people left over can start. The loudest signal is not the biggest, and the cheapest experiment that could prove an estimate wrong beats the largest build that assumes it is right.
