Sizing an opportunity

Reach × frequency × value: is this problem worth a team?

1. Two companies, two deadlines

On Tuesday 14 July 2026 Tanvika Kshirsagar, vice-president of product at Utsaah Wellness House in Bengaluru, was given a question and a date. Utsaah sells a consumer subscription app for musculoskeletal recovery. Of its 24,80,000 monthly active users, 3,16,000 paid: 2,21,000 monthly at ₹249 and 95,000 annually at ₹1,990, worth ₹66.0348 crore and ₹18.905 crore a year, ₹84.9398 crore together. Blended annual revenue per paying subscriber, ₹84.9398 crore ÷ 3,16,000, was ₹2,687.97; revenue per monthly active user, a different denominator, was ₹342.50.

Varad Agnihotri, the founder, wanted to know whether knee osteoarthritis deserved a standing team of nine. The board met on Friday 11 September 2026, fifty-nine days away. An engineer cost ₹34 lakh fully loaded, so nine meant ₹3.06 crore, and Varad's rule was that a team must return at least 1.8 times its annual cost in gross revenue by the end of year two. Nobody disputed that knee pain hurt; the question was whether it hurt enough people, often enough, expensively enough.

Three weeks later, on Thursday 6 August 2026, Vikram Herlekar faced the same question in a different shape. Vikram ran product at Tulaadhar Weighing Industries in Rajkot, which makes industrial weighbridges and load cells; 12,600 were in service across India. Tanmayi Nadgouda, the commercial director, had heard one complaint from cement and fertiliser depots for two years: trucks arrive short. The proposal was a retrofit sensor kit plus software to detect under-loading — eleven people at ₹38 lakh, ₹4.18 crore a year. Upendra Belsare's capital committee met on Friday 2 October 2026, fifty-seven days later, applying the same 1.8 times hurdle but on gross profit, since hardware carries cost of goods.

2. The idea, and what it was invented to fix

Sizing an opportunity estimates, before a team is committed, the annual magnitude of a problem as the product of three quantities: reach, the units — people, accounts, machines — meeting a stated qualifying definition; frequency, how often each unit meets the problem in a period; and value, what one encounter costs or is worth over that period. A separate second step asks what share the firm could convert into revenue or gross profit, and whether that clears its hurdle for a team.

Two lineages merged here. The older is strategic market sizing, formalised in consulting practice through the 1970s and 1980s, splitting a market into a total addressable market, a serviceable subset and an obtainable share. The younger is the engineering habit of pricing a defect as rate of occurrence times cost per occurrence. Product management fused them in the 2010s, when schemes such as Intercom's RICE put reach and frequency beside value. Hence the confusion: market sizing asks how big is this market, opportunity sizing asks is this problem worth a team. The practice exists to defeat one pathology — teams commit to problems that are vivid rather than large.

Two schools disagree about what the output is for. The decision-gate school treats a size estimate as a hurdle test whose value lies in comparability: it will sign that a uniform method beats a bespoke estimate per candidate, and not that the absolute number means anything. The falsification school treats the output as a list of the assumptions it rests on, ranked by how far the answer moves when each is wrong: it will sign that the only useful product of a sizing is naming the input to measure next, and not that two proposals can be compared on point estimates.

3. Mechanics: the chain worked through

The step most often left implicit is where the estimate is decided: the qualifying definition. Tanvika refused to size “knee pain”. A qualifying user was aged 45 or over, reported knee pain on four or more of the previous fourteen days and named a daily activity it prevented. That definition, not the data, sets reach.

Conversion matters as much. At three in seven rather than one in three, the first cohort yields 10,602 payers, year two holds 15,903, and at ₹3,600 the multiple is 1.87 — a pass. So the sizing says neither yes nor no: it says the answer turns on price and conversion, and nothing else is worth another week.

4. When the method applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions are testable claims. The problem must already be validated: three numbers multiplied for an unconfirmed problem give a precise fantasy. Utsaah passes on 1,240 diaries; Tulaadhar passes weakly, having complaints rather than measurements, and that proves decisive. The unit must be countable in a system of record: Utsaah counts qualifying users from its database, while Tulaadhar counts bridges but counts loads only on the 60 per cent with telemetry. Value per encounter must be observable rather than inferred from stated willingness to pay. Capture must be bounded by something other than ambition — a measured conversion rate, a channel capacity, a sales cycle.

The method misleads where the product creates a behaviour rather than relieving a cost, leaving no frequency to measure; where value is so concentrated that three averages describe nobody; and where the problem is a precondition — onboarding, identity, trust — so those who suffer most never arrive.

5. Hard edges: platforms, hardware, regulation, AI

Multi-product firms hit the attribution seam: if knee users renew the main Utsaah subscription at a higher rate, part of the gain belongs to a product nobody is sizing. Size incremental revenue at constant base behaviour and log retention as unquantified upside — which committees quietly treat as quantified.

Two-sided businesses size both sides and take the minimum. Upvan Harvest Works, a Nashik marketplace linking grape and onion growers to exporters, has 74,000 growers transacting 2.4 times a season on average and 1,860 exporters capable of 180 lots each. Exporters could absorb 1,860 × 180 = 3,34,800 lots; growers can generate 74,000 × 2.4 = 1,77,600, so growers bind. At ₹1.85 lakh a lot that is ₹3,285.6 crore of gross merchandise value, and at a 1.8 per cent take rate — ₹3,330 a lot — ₹59.1408 crore of fee revenue if every grower used the platform: a ceiling, not a forecast.

Hardware changes the arithmetic twice: gross profit rather than revenue must clear the hurdle, and the install base caps reach. Regulated markets insert gates that stay invisible unless written as lines, as Udyot Solar Services discovered expensively below. AI-native products face a moving denominator. Tatsam Scribe Services in Hyderabad sized its medical scribe against 1,24,000 private-practice specialists, each holding roughly 3,840 consultations a year (16 a day over 240 working days) and saving 4.2 minutes per note at ₹1,800 an hour — ₹126 a note, ₹4,83,840 a clinician a year, ₹5,999.616 crore across the reach. The problem held; capture moved. Inference cost per note fell from ₹14 to ₹2.10 in fourteen months, 85 per cent, and three rivals priced to the new floor.

6. Eight nuances that separate the expert

The size of the problem is not the size of the prize

Utsaah's qualifying users lose ₹115.52 crore a year; Utsaah can collect ₹4.45284 crore in year two, about 26 to one. The tell is a deck whose headline and revenue figures differ by an order of magnitude with nothing explaining the gap: value the user keeps, value a substitute captures, value lost to people who will not change.

The qualifying definition is the estimate

Move Utsaah's bar from four painful days in fourteen to two, and reach rises while average value per user falls, in opposite directions and by different proportions. The tell is a sizing produced in an afternoon: nobody argued about the definition. Experts fix it first.

Frequency is a distribution, not a mean

Utsaah's 6.4 painful days in fourteen averages a diary in which three-eighths of users — 37,107 of the 98,952, or 37.5 per cent — reported eight or more. The tell is a product that delights the heavy tail and bores the rest: the mean describes nobody.

Capture rates are behavioural, not geometric

Twelve per cent, ten per cent, one per cent: round capture assumptions are a signature of invention. Utsaah's 8.33 per cent is the product of two measured rates, one in four starting and one in three converting. Ask which observed rates a capture figure multiplies.

Units must cancel

Monthly frequency times annual value overstates by twelve; a per-truck value times per-site frequency overstates by the trucks per site. The tell is a result wrong by a suspiciously clean factor; the cure is writing the unit beside every multiplier.

Expected loss is not loss

Tulaadhar's short-loading figure is an expectation over all loads: 2.4 per cent are short by 0.9 per cent of a 24.5-tonne load at ₹4,200 a tonne — ₹926.10 when it happens, ₹22.23 per load on average. Depot managers remember the ₹926; quoting that conditional loss where the sizing needs the unconditional one inflates the value step about forty-two times.

The install base is a ceiling, and sometimes a low one

Tulaadhar's qualifying reach is 2,772 bridges. At ₹24,000 a bridge a year and 82 per cent software margin, every one would yield ₹5.455296 crore of gross profit against a team costing ₹4.18 crore — 1.31 times, below the hurdle. Compute the hurdle in units first: 1.8 × ₹4.18 crore ÷ ₹19,680 a bridge is 3,823 bridges against a reach of 2,772.

The useful output is the next measurement

Both estimates ended by naming one input: price and conversion for Utsaah, the value driver and breadth of reach for Tulaadhar. The expert's document closes with an experiment, not a conclusion: the deciding inputs are the ones the firm has not yet paid to observe.

7. Across product types and company stages

For consumer products reach is enormous and value per encounter small, so the build-down dominates and the risk is definition drift. Two estimates of one quantity — Indians who would pay for a digital knee programme in a year — show what reconciliation looks like.

Business and enterprise products invert the shape — small reach, large value per encounter, extreme concentration — so the honest method names accounts, not averages. Platforms take the minimum of two sides; hardware clears its hurdle on gross profit inside a fixed install base. For AI products the chain is ordinary, but capture assumptions decay fast.

Stage changes the purpose rather than the method. A seed-stage firm sizes to learn whether a market can hold a company and wants only an order of magnitude. A firm of Utsaah's size sizes to allocate between proposals, so comparability beats precision. Tulaadhar, with a factory and an install base, sizes to decide whether to open a product line at all, and its constraint is reach. Stage never changes the units: most audit findings are unit errors made in a hurry.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

The first, Utsaah's, is worked above: the base case fails at 1.46. The second is Tulaadhar's, which fails for a reason the method is unusually good at exposing. Vikram built reach down from 12,600 installed bridges: 60 per cent on a live service contract with connectivity gives 7,560; 55 per cent of those in sectors exposed to short-loading gives 4,158; two-thirds of those handling at least 40 third-party inbound loads a month gives 2,772 qualifying bridges, a compound 22.0 per cent. Telemetry on 214 bridges gave 62 third-party loads a month, 744 a year, so 2,772 × 744 = 20,62,368 load events. He then priced three candidate losses per event.

The driver everyone talked about was worth 18.0 per cent of the problem; the one nobody had named — trucks idle while a disputed weight is re-checked — was worth four times as much. Capture then showed the proposal could not work at any adoption rate. At one-third adoption, 924 of 2,772 bridges or 33.3 per cent, the kit at ₹46,000 yields ₹4.2504 crore of one-time hardware revenue and ₹1.615152 crore of gross profit at 38 per cent margin; software at ₹24,000 a bridge yields ₹2.2176 crore of recurring revenue and ₹1.818432 crore of gross profit at 82 per cent. Recovery had two moves. Make the product brand-agnostic, reading the serial output of any manufacturer's indicator, widening reach from 2,772 to the 22,880 qualifying bridges in India's estimated installed base of 1,04,000 — Tulaadhar's 12,600 being 12.1 per cent of it. Then price against the dispute value rather than pilferage: ₹36,000 a bridge a year is 51.4 per cent of the ₹70,040 disputes cost each bridge, and yields ₹29,520 of gross profit. Winning 2,860 bridges, one-eighth or 12.5 per cent of the national qualifying base, over 36 months gives ₹8.44272 crore of annual gross profit, 2.02 times the ₹4.18 crore team cost.

The third example is the failure. Udyot Solar Services of Jaipur sized residential rooftop solar in March 2024 from urban households in Rajasthan, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh with monthly electricity bills of ₹2,500 or more: 46,20,000 households saving about ₹31,000 a year each, a problem worth ₹14,322 crore. Udita Bhagwatkar's team claimed one per cent, ₹143.22 crore, hired fourteen people at ₹35 lakh — ₹4.9 crore a year — from June 2024 and committed ₹22 crore to installers. The error was not optimism about capture but an unwritten definition, and the decisive gates were regulatory and financial, not behavioural. 9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Sizing the nation. The sign is a headline from a market report with no line connecting it to the firm's own customers. Ask which of our accounts it describes. At Udyot that cost ₹7.4 crore.

Unwritten gates. The sign is a reach figure produced faster than the argument about its definition. Ask what must be true of a unit for it to count, then check each condition against data. Udyot's gates compounded to 2.09 per cent.

Sizing the loud driver. The sign is a value step built on the loss customers complain about rather than the one they incur most often; Tulaadhar's was 18.0 per cent of the problem. Price every candidate.

Stating the hurdle in rupees rather than units. The sign is a sizing with no line saying how many units the hurdle needs; one division answers it. Tulaadhar needed 3,823 bridges and had 2,772.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is whether to size at all before a prototype exists. The measure-first position holds that the cheapest way to resolve a sizing is to ship a crude version to a few hundred users and read the conversion, because the deciding inputs are behavioural and cannot be surveyed; its evidence is the over-statement of intent, visible in Utsaah's data as 9.00 per cent surveyed against 8.33 per cent observed. The size-first position holds that the estimate's function is to stop work on problems whose arithmetic cannot close — Tulaadhar's reach ceiling, found in ten minutes, would have cost two quarters to discover by building. For measure-first to be wrong, prototypes would have to be dear relative to estimates; for size-first to be wrong, reach ceilings would have to be rare.

The second is about precision. One camp holds that any figure beyond one significant digit is false confidence, and the output should be an order of magnitude plus a ranked list. The other holds that precision makes an estimate falsifiable: a stated 8.33 per cent conversion can be checked in a quarter, while “roughly ten per cent” cannot be shown wrong. It turns on whether the firm punishes being wrong or being vague.

11. What mastery looks like

Four observable habits. They argue about the qualifying definition before asking for data, writing it so a sceptic could disqualify a unit with it. They keep the problem table and the capture table separate, and will not let a committee quote one as the other. They compute the hurdle in units before anything in rupees. And they close with the one measurement that would change the answer, so the next quarter never surprises them.

12. The decisions, and three questions

On 11 September 2026 Tanvika did not ask for nine people. She showed the base case at 1.46 times, the price sensitivity of Exhibit 4, and a narrower proposal: target only the 37,107 severe users, three-eighths of the qualifying base, at ₹4,800 rather than ₹3,600, with a team of six costing ₹2.04 crore. Three in seven of the severe segment, 15,903, would start; one in three of those, 5,301, would pay — ₹2.54448 crore in year one, 1.25 times. In year two, two-thirds renew, 3,534 users, and a second cohort of 15,903 starters from the 21,204 severe users not yet reached adds 5,301, giving 8,835 payers and ₹4.2408 crore: 2.08 times, a pass. Varad funded six, if the price was tested first.

On 2 October 2026 Vikram told Upendra's committee the proposal as written was impossible, showing the 3,823 bridges the hurdle required against the 2,772 the install base contained, and asked for seven people and two quarters to build the brand-agnostic product and test the ₹36,000 price on 40 bridges. Tanmayi disagreed: selling against a dispute depots had never quantified would be harder than selling against pilferage they complained of weekly. Her objection remains unresolved, and it is right.

Three questions. First: Tanvika's narrowing raises the multiple from 1.46 to 2.08 by shrinking the addressable population by five-eighths — when is a smaller, denser opportunity better, and when is it merely easier to defend? Second: Tulaadhar's reach ceiling was computable on 6 August, yet the proposal had circulated for two years — what made a ten-minute division hard? Third: Udyot's revised reach was 2.09 per cent of the original — which of the four gates would you have written down in March 2024, and which could you not honestly have known?

13. Going deeper

Validating a problem hypothesis comes first: sizing an unvalidated problem gives precision without truth. Market sizing (TAM / SAM / SOM) supplies the build-down grammar of Exhibits 1, 5 and 9, keeping each rate attached to the right population. The opportunity brief is where a sizing becomes a document others can attack. Quantifying the cost of the problem deepens the value step of Exhibits 2 and 7. Writing a problem hypothesis and Surfacing assumptions give the ranked list the falsification school calls the real output; Riskiest assumption first turns it into experiments, as with Tanvika's price test and Vikram's 40-bridge pilot. Frequency and intensity of the problem is the distributional treatment Utsaah's severe three-eighths demands. Vitamin vs painkiller explains why a large expected loss can still fail to sell, and Persevere, pivot or perish is what Udyot faced in May 2025.

Sizing an opportunity

Reach, frequency and value: is this problem worth a team?

1. A number due in fourteen days

On Friday 25 September 2026, Mugdha Kalelkar, head of product at Nishkarsh Billing Works in Pune, was handed a deadline. Her chief executive, Onkar Bendre, wanted one figure on the table at the board meeting on 9 October, fourteen days away: what is it worth to spend a team on late payments? Nishkarsh makes GST invoicing software for small manufacturers. Its 1,60,000 monthly active accounts issue invoices to larger buyers, and many of those buyers pay late.

The idea on the table was an "early pay" feature: a manufacturer taps a button on an unpaid invoice and a partner lender advances most of the money within a day. Manoj Pimparkar, who ran sales, had already written the pitch. Interviews with twenty-six of thirty manufacturers had confirmed that waiting for money hurt, and he quoted an industry estimate of overdue receivables running into lakhs of crores of rupees. Onkar replied that the figure belonged to all of India, not to Nishkarsh. The proposed team was eight people, and Mugdha costed each at ₹30 lakh a year including salary, cloud and management time.

What the board must weighFigure

Exhibit 1. The decision frame. The hurdle is Nishkarsh's own rule of thumb for funding a standing team: it must plausibly return at least twice its annual cost once the product matures.

If Mugdha sized too generously, the company would commit eight engineers and designers to a feature that cannot repay them, at the expense of work with a surer return. If she sized too timidly, a real problem would be left to a rival. Neelesh Sapre, her analyst, had pulled the account data on Monday 7 September, eighteen days earlier. The method she chose is the subject of this page.

2. The idea

Sizing an opportunity means estimating, before building anything, how many people have a problem (reach), how often each meets it (frequency) and what each occurrence costs or is worth (value). Multiplying the three gives the yearly size of the problem. A second step then asks what share of that problem the company could actually capture, and whether the resulting income justifies a team. The method descends from older market-sizing practice, in which analysts split a market into a total, a served part and an obtainable part; the product-management habit of putting reach and frequency explicitly beside value was popularised by prioritisation frameworks such as Intercom's RICE scoring in the 2010s.

It exists to solve one recurring failure: teams fall in love with a problem because it is vivid, not because it is large. The sentence Mugdha could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib was this: "We are not asking whether the pain is real; we are asking how many people feel it, how often, and how much it costs them each time, and then how much of that we can collect."

3. How it actually works

The first step, often left implicit, is to fix the unit of the problem. Mugdha refused to size "late payment" in general. She defined a qualifying invoice as one of at least ₹1 lakh that is paid after its due date, and a qualifying account as one with at least three such invoices in the last twelve months. Everything downstream depends on this definition; change it and every figure moves.

The second step is to narrow the population in stages, each stage a stated percentage of the one before. Of Nishkarsh's 1,60,000 active accounts, 62 per cent issue credit invoices to other businesses, which is 99,200. Of those, 35 per cent meet the qualifying test, which is 34,720 accounts. That figure is the reach.

The third step is to measure frequency and value from transaction records rather than from interviews, because people recall their worst invoice, not their typical one. The fourth, again often skipped, is to price the pain in the user's own terms. Neelesh found that qualifying invoices were paid on average 40 days after the due date, and that manufacturers financed the gap at about 1.5 per cent a month, a common rate for informal and cash-credit working capital. Over 40 days, using a 30-day month, that is 1.5 × 40 ÷ 30 = 2.0 per cent of the invoice. The last step separates the size of the problem from the size of Nishkarsh's slice, covered below.

4. A worked example

Neelesh split the 34,720 accounts into three tiers by annual turnover, because averaging across them hid a great deal. Exhibit 3 shows the arithmetic row by row. Invoices are accounts times invoices per account; invoice value is invoices times average invoice size; the cost of waiting is 2.0 per cent of invoice value.

The size of the problem is therefore ₹438.4 crore a year, or about ₹1.26 lakh per affected account. That is large, but it is a cost to manufacturers, not revenue to Nishkarsh. The averages deserve a second look. The small tier holds 57.6 per cent of the accounts but only 9.9 per cent of the cost; the large tier holds 13.6 per cent of the accounts and 64.6 per cent of the cost.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

The size of the problem is not the size of the prize

The ₹438.4 crore is what manufacturers lose; Nishkarsh earns a fee on advances. Confusing the two inflates a case more than eighty-fold here, since 438.4 ÷ 5.2608 is about 83.

Sizing is not market sizing, though it borrows from it

Market sizing asks how large a revenue pool is. Opportunity sizing asks whether a specific problem justifies a specific team.

Only validated problems are worth sizing

Multiplying three numbers for a problem nobody has confirmed produces a precise fantasy. Mugdha's interviews came first, and sizing came second.

Averages conceal where the value lives

Exhibit 3 shows a blended 17.74 invoices per account, yet no tier has that figure. Segment before you multiply, particularly when a few heavy users dominate.

Definition drift

Move the qualifying threshold from ₹1 lakh to ₹50,000 and reach rises while average value falls.

Willingness to act is not measured

The method counts people who have the problem, not people who will change behaviour to solve it. Twelve per cent obtainable is a judgement, and it needs testing with a prototype.

Questions a newcomer should ask

Which of these inputs was measured and which guessed? Who else already solves this, and at what price? Which single input, if wrong by a third, reverses the answer?

6. How it changes by product type and by stage

Consumer products usually have enormous reach, modest value per event and a long tail of casual users, so the reach step dominates and the tiering work is about engagement, not turnover. B2B products, like Nishkarsh, have smaller reach but steeply skewed value, as Exhibit 4 shows: a handful of large accounts carry most of the money,. Marketplaces must size two sides and the link between them. Here the lender side is the binding constraint, which is exactly what the sensitivity table revealed: supply of approved buyers, not demand from manufacturers, set the ceiling.

Stage matters as much. An early-stage company with five engineers has a hurdle of survival: it needs one problem large enough to build a company on, so it sizes aggressively and tolerates rough inputs. A large company has many competing projects and a formal hurdle, so its sizing is a comparison tool, and consistency of method across proposals matters more than the precision of any one estimate. Nishkarsh sits between the two, which is why Onkar set a fixed multiple.

7. Common mistakes

Starting from the top. The symptom is a slide quoting a national figure, such as all overdue receivables in India. The misunderstanding is that a big market implies a big opportunity. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask which of our own accounts this number describes, and to refuse any figure that cannot be traced to one.

Multiplying unmatched periods. The symptom is a total that looks too high by a factor of twelve or four. The misunderstanding is mixing monthly frequency with annual value. The diagnostic is to write the unit beside every multiplier and check they cancel.

Treating the blended average as typical. The symptom is a feature that delights small accounts and earns nothing. The diagnostic is to recompute the answer for the top ten accounts alone.

Hiding the weakest input. The symptom is a tidy, single-number answer with no range. The misunderstanding is that precision signals rigour. The diagnostic is the one-input sensitivity table of Exhibit 7: if no row changes the decision, the weak input was perhaps not that weak; if one does, you have found where to spend your next week.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the same decision looks like this. The problem is stated as a single sentence naming the user and the moment. The qualifying definition is written down. Reach comes from system data, frequency and value from transaction records, and each is tagged measured or assumed. The answer is a range with the decisive input named, and the capture step is separate from the problem step.

ElementWeak versionStrong version
Reach"All 1,60,000 accounts"34,720 qualifying accounts, definition stated
ValueOne averageThree tiers, averages recomputed
Result"Huge"₹3.288 to ₹6.576 crore of fee, with the swing input named

Exhibit 8. The target for the brief Mugdha writes next.

9. What Mugdha decided

Mugdha took two numbers to the board. The problem was real and large: ₹438.4 crore a year, concentrated in 4,720 large accounts that hold 64.6 per cent of the cost. But at 25 per cent lender coverage the fee was ₹3.288 crore, only 1.37 times the cost of an eight-person team, and the hurdle of 2.0 was missed. A squad of four costs ₹1.2 crore, and at the same pessimistic coverage that is 2.74 times. She therefore asked for four people for two quarters, a spend of ₹60 lakh, with one purpose: to have Mwajuma Njoroge, her engineering lead in Nairobi, match buyer GST numbers against the lenders' lists and measure the true coverage. If it reaches 40 per cent, she would ask for the second four. Onkar agreed, because the request was sized to what the evidence supported and told him which result would change his mind.

Read next the opportunity brief, which turns this sizing into a document that others can challenge, and the cost of the problem, which refines the value step with better evidence of what users truly lose.

Two questions to sit with. Which input in a sizing you made recently was assumed rather than measured, and what would it take to measure it? And if your estimate of a single input were wrong by a third, would your decision change?
case40v1-prob.sizing:
Tirpal Garage Exchange: How Many Bikes, How Often, Worth How Much?

A parts-and-software network for India's independent two-wheeler garages must decide whether the arrival of electric scooters is an opportunity worth a team, a threat worth a team, or neither.

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday, 22 November 2026, Enakshi Gharat sat on the floor of her flat in Aundh, Pune, with three printed versions of one slide. Each carried a different size for the same opportunity: ₹47 crore, ₹13 crore, ₹80 crore. All three were hers.

Gharat was vice-president of product at Tirpal Garage Exchange, the Wakad company that sold spare parts and workshop software to 11,400 independent two-wheeler garages. In nine hours she would ask the board for eight people, 6.9 FTE, costing ₹4.23 crore a year, to build the EV Desk: a diagnostics, job-card and parts flow for electric scooters.

The money was not what unsettled her. It was that she no longer trusted her own estimate of how many electric scooters would reach those garages, how often each would come, or what Tirpal would earn when it did. Her data scientist in Toronto had written a sentence she had read thirty times: the three builds are not three estimates of one quantity.

The deadline was not really Monday. Barzan Dispatch, the Dubai delivery fleet that was Tirpal's largest software customer, had to be given notice of any change by 15 December; the covenant was tested on 31 December; the Toronto contract ended on 31 March.

2. How Tirpal came to be shaped this way

Ninad Halbe founded Tirpal in 2017, after eleven years selling accounting software to automotive dealers in Maharashtra. The independent garage that services most of India's two-wheelers buys brake pads, clutch plates, filters and sprockets from sub-distributors, pays cash and keeps no records. Tirpal put the catalogue in an Android app, delivered next morning and settled on UPI through Razorpay; garages paid nothing for the app and Tirpal earned a margin on parts.

The decision that still shapes every argument was taken in November 2021, eleven weeks from running out of money: stay asset-light, routing orders to distributors for a fee, or go asset-heavy. Halbe went heavy — 14 depots costing ₹62 crore, financed by a ₹48 crore facility secured against inventory and carrying two covenants tested quarterly: net debt to EBITDA no higher than 3.0, and inventory turning at least 5.5 times a year.

It worked. In the year ended 31 March 2026 parts gross merchandise value was ₹268 crore, on which net revenue at an 11.6 per cent take rate was ₹31.1 crore, with ₹4.9 crore of subscriptions: ₹36.0 crore in all. Of the 11,400 garages onboarded, 7,860 had transacted in the previous 30 days (69 per cent).

It also set a trap. Every new category competes for depot slots, working capital and the turns the covenant watches, so a part that sells 1.2 times a year is a covenant risk. And because Tirpal spent 2022 and 2023 laying concrete rather than writing diagnostics software, it has no telemetry capability at all.

3. The industry around the decision

India's electric two-wheeler market stopped being a curiosity around 2023. Ola Electric, Ather Energy, TVS, Bajaj with the Chetak, Hero MotoCorp's Vida, Greaves' Ampere and a tail of regional assemblers put enough scooters on the road that the trade's question became when rather than whether. FAME-II lapsed in March 2024 and was succeeded by PM E-DRIVE; by FY26 electric models approached a tenth of new two-wheeler registrations in the metros, far less in the small towns where most of Tirpal's garages sit.

The service economics did not follow. An electric scooter has no engine oil, clutch, air filter or spark plug. Its expensive component, the battery pack, is sealed, carries an OEM warranty of three years or more — several manufacturers moved to five-year cover in 2025 — and under the AIS 156 regime and OEM warranty terms cannot be opened by an independent garage without voiding the customer's cover. What is left is tyres, brakes, suspension, wiring and bodywork.

Regulation touches Tirpal elsewhere too: VAHAN, the source of any top-down sizing here, does not cover every state uniformly, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act governs the consent behind service reminders.

Tirpal's exposure is not only Indian. Barzan Dispatch in Dubai, with 9,200 two-wheelers, pays ₹2.1 crore a year for the software — ₹2.1 crore of the ₹4.9 crore subscription line (42.9 per cent) and 5.8 per cent of total revenue — and is converting its fleet at 3,000 vehicles a year. Evan Rebello, in Edison, New Jersey, has two North American fleets that ask about electric support in the first meeting.

4. What happened, and what has since been shown to be wrong

In January 2026 Nabeel Darwish, operations director at Barzan Dispatch, told Natalie Teo that renewal would require electric support "by the middle of 2027". In April Halbe told investors electric was "an FY28 story for parts and an FY27 story for software", which committed nothing.

In June, Elodie Rochon pulled the first network-wide count of electric work from the records: 9,240 EV-tagged jobs in May 2026 across 7,640 active garages, or 1.21 per garage a month. The July deck opened with "the EV job is already on the shop floor".

Two things have since been shown wrong about that number. The tag fired on a list of part numbers, 11 of which were also fitted to petrol scooters, among them a 90/90-12 tyre common to four ICE models; re-tagged in September on fitment data, May's count fell 18 per cent to 7,577 jobs, or 0.99 per garage per month. And the tag sees only jobs in which a part was billed through Tirpal: a 2025 reconciliation, in which 96 garages opened their purchase books for February to April, found that 61 per cent of their parts spend flowed through Tirpal — measured on petrol-era spend, a year before the first electric SKU was listed in any depot.

In July, Nihal Bhoite began stocking 42 electric-specific parts in three depots without a category approval; by 31 October that shadow inventory stood at ₹1.9 crore, of which ₹72 lakh had not moved in 90 days (38 per cent). Between 5 and 19 October Gharat's insights team surveyed garage owners by telephone (Exhibit 2), drawing its frame from the 60 pin codes with the highest electric registrations in Tirpal's depot cities — chosen so the survey would find electric work at all, and fatal to generalising its rates. On 20 October Rochon pulled the logs for the same 412 garages (Exhibit 3); the two disagreed in both directions at once.

On 28 October Gharat circulated the deck with three builds (Exhibit 4). The figure that escaped into the board pack was "a ₹47 crore parts pool" — the gross merchandise value of the middle build, not revenue and not a forecast of capture. Rawool's note of 3 November asked for the low build only; on 9 November Teo reported that Barzan's renewal terms would reference an EV milestone; on 14 November Rochon sent her memo.

5. The people

Enakshi Gharat, vice-president of product, Pune, wrote all three builds and argues the team must be funded now, because the parc ages whether Tirpal is ready or not. Unsaid: she wrote the question behind the 6.8 figure, and has promised an engineer in Pune the lead.

Ninad Halbe, co-founder and chief executive, Pune, wants an EV announcement before the Series C closes: "electrification-ready" is worth more in a valuation conversation than a year's revenue. Unsaid: a fund has asked in writing for a board-approved EV plan before diligence.

Nupura Rawool, chief financial officer, Pune, holds the covenant and argues that no category may be funded on a frequency never measured on the vehicle in question. Unsaid: she has modelled the facility's headroom with the EV Desk approved, and it holds.

Nihal Bhoite, head of depot operations, Nashik, says the constraint is depot slots and turns, not money or people: electric SKUs turn at a third of the ICE rate, and his bonus tracks turns. Unsaid: his 42 SKUs were stocked at his own discretion.

Elodie Rochon, senior data scientist, Toronto, endorses no build: "how often" has been borrowed from petrol behaviour and discounted rather than measured. Unsaid: her contract ends on 31 March 2027, she holds a Montreal offer, and only the re-tagging keeps her.

Nils Hoffmann, product designer, Berlin, at half an FTE, argues that a module bolted onto the job card will fail, because the card assumes an interval of kilometres and oil. Unsaid: he has prototyped a rebuilt card, and wants a full-time role.

Natalie Teo, customer success lead, Singapore, carries the Gulf accounts, reports to Rebello and is paid on retention; Barzan's ₹2.1 crore, she says, is at risk without an EV commitment. Unsaid: in September she told Darwish "June 2027 is achievable".

Evan Rebello, head of sales, Edison, New Jersey, wants the Desk because it opens the North American fleet conversation. Unsaid: two of the four opportunities he has shown the board as new logos are renewals under new names.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

"I am not asking the board to believe ₹80 crore. In every version the parc gets older and the work arrives. We are arguing about the year, not the direction."

Enakshi Gharat, leadership review, 28 October

"Three builds in one deck is not rigour, it is hedging. Pick the one you would bet the covenant on. If it is build B, the answer is no team."

Nupura Rawool, note to the board pack, 3 November

"6.8 is the average among owners who said yes; multiplying it across 7,860 garages assumes the ones who said no also do 6.8, and they do zero. And 1.92 came from the pin codes we picked for having the most electric scooters. I can tell you what the logs saw, not how often an electric scooter needs a garage."

Elodie Rochon, memo to Gharat and Rawool, 14 November

"Everyone is counting the jobs we might win. Last year 41 jobs a month came through an average West garage, nearly all petrol. Tell me what that is in 2030, then tell me whether this is growth or an evacuation."

Nihal Bhoite, depot review, Nashik, 11 November

"Electric scooters come, yes. One puncture, one brake, sometimes a wire. For anything serious the owner goes to the showroom, for the warranty. I will not refuse the work, but I am not buying a machine for it."

Ejaz Khatib, garage owner, Kalyan, survey field notes

8. The options as Gharat currently sees them

Option 1: fund the team. Eight people, 6.9 FTE, from 1 January 2027: ₹423 lakh in year one and ₹372 lakh thereafter. Defensible only against build A, which clears the team's cost by ₹4 lakh a year on a frequency borrowed from petrol scooters.

Option 2: buy information first. A two-person wedge for one quarter — the Pune field app engineer and the training lead, about ₹13 lakh — plus ₹51 lakh of diagnostic kits in 300 garages, instrumented so every electric visit is recorded whether or not the part is billed through Tirpal. By March 2027 that yields the number nobody has: paid visits per electric scooter per year at an independent garage. It also means telling Darwish nothing.

Option 3: serve Dubai and stop. Protect the ₹2.1 crore with a patch to the fleet workflow, built by the platform team in two sprints, and decline the parts opportunity until FY29. Cheapest; it leaves Bhoite's stock stranded.

Option 4: partner rather than build. Carry a diagnostics vendor's or an OEM network's tooling into Tirpal's garages for a share of the job: a hiring question becomes a contracting one, at the price of the data the depots were built to collect.

A fifth possibility sits in none of the four, and it is the one Bhoite circles. Every option sizes the electric pool. Tirpal's petrol parts GMV is ₹268 crore, which, if GMV tracks the parc, is about ₹2.7 crore a year for each percentage point of the two-wheeler population in its depot cities that goes electric — and electric models already approach a tenth of new registrations there. The pool the company argues about adding is of the same order as the pool it is quietly losing, and the question may be one of defence rather than growth. Nobody has built that sizing.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at 9.30 am on Monday, 23 November 2026, and four constraints are not negotiable. Barzan's contract requires 90 days' notice of any material change, so Darwish must be told something by 15 December, before the 15 March renewal. The covenant is tested on 31 December — net debt to EBITDA no higher than 3.0, inventory turning at least 5.5 times — and Bhoite's electric SKUs turn at a third of the ICE rate. Any role above ₹60 lakh needs board approval, which the Toronto ₹94 lakh does. And the service-reminder feature cannot ship until customer consent has been re-papered under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, work that has not started.

Halbe's Series C timetable is softer but louder. Gharat knows that a plan approved to satisfy diligence is not the same artefact as a plan built to be right, and that both would look identical in Monday's minutes.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. State the reach, the frequency and the value each build in Exhibit 4 assumes. Which of those nine quantities has been measured on an electric scooter?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 disagree in two directions at once: the log finds electric work in more garages, the survey more jobs per garage. What would make each right, and what single measurement would separate them?
  3. If the three builds are not estimates of one quantity, what should the board see on one slide, and what is lost by showing build B alone?
  4. Bhoite's ₹72 lakh of unapproved stock predates this analysis. How should a board treat a sunk, ageing, unauthorised position when sizing a forward opportunity?
  5. Option 2 spends ₹64 lakh to buy one number, 15 per cent of build-A contribution. When is a frequency measurement worth that — and what does waiting cost with Barzan, the Series C and Rochon?
  6. It is Monday morning. Gharat has fifteen minutes and one slide. What does she ask for, what does she say about the ₹47 crore already in the pack, and how does she frame a problem whose honest size she does not know?

At half past midnight Gharat deleted the three slides and typed one line on a blank one: How many, how often, worth how much — and which of the three do we actually know? Under the question was an answer about electric scooters, and under that, she suspected, a different question about petrol ones. The board met in nine hours.
case20v1-prob.hmw:
Jhilmil Home Energy: Choosing the Question

A teaching case on writing “How might we” prompts

1. Opening

On the morning of Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Gargi Vasaikar, chief product officer of Jhilmil Home Energy, sat in a glass-walled meeting room at the company’s Baner office in Pune with a single sheet of paper and a Friday 23 October deadline. By 5 p.m. on 23 October she had to circulate the opening prompt for a two-day ideation workshop beginning on Monday, 26 October. Fourteen people would build their week around whatever sentence she chose, and the 2 November engineering sprint would be scoped from the ideas that survived.

Three candidate sentences lay before her, each beginning “How might we” and each from a colleague she respected. She suspected they answered three different questions, and that only one matched what the research had asked.

2. Company background

Jhilmil was founded in 2021 by two former Tata Power Solar engineers. It designs, finances and installs rooftop solar plants for housing societies in Pune, Thane and Nashik, the resident-run bodies that pay the electricity bill for lifts, water pumps and corridor lights. A typical Jhilmil plant is 40 kW and costs ₹20 lakh installed, or ₹50,000 a kilowatt. In western Maharashtra a plant of that size generates about 1,460 units per kilowatt a year, so 58,400 units. At a common-area tariff of ₹9 a unit, the society saves ₹5.26 lakh a year and recovers its outlay in about 3.8 years, before any subsidy.

Revenue in FY26 was ₹38 crore across 140 employees. The competition is crowded: Tata Power Solar, Waaree, Loom Solar and dozens of local installers who quote on a phone call. The PM Surya Ghar scheme, run through MNRE, has made rooftop solar a household phrase, and net-metering approval from the distribution company, MSEDCL, remains a step every installation must clear.

3. The situation

Between 1 April and 31 July 2026 Jhilmil’s field teams approached 480 societies. Exhibit 1 shows where they were on 30 September. Of the 96 societies that received a written quote, only 24 passed a general-body resolution, which is 25.0 per cent of quotes. Delivery after approval was reliable: 18 plants, 75.0 per cent of the 24 approvals, were commissioned, and the other six were scheduled. The drop that matters is between quote and approval, where 72 societies had been quoted and had not approved by 30 September.

In September, Greta Hallberg, a senior designer based in Berlin, interviewed committee members from 30 of the 72 societies, chosen by willingness to talk, that had been quoted and had not approved. She coded each conversation by the single reason the interviewee returned to most. Exhibit 2 shows the result. It describes only those 30; the 42 societies not interviewed may differ.

None of the 30 gave price as the main reason. Yet the internal problem statement, written in August, read: “Societies cannot afford the upfront cost of solar.” Gargi had signed it herself.

4. The people

Gopal Shirodkar, head of sales, works from Edison, New Jersey, and leads the channel that sells to non-resident Indians who own flats in societies and vote by proxy. On his calls, owners keep asking for a lease with no money down. He wants the workshop to open with: “How might we offer societies a zero-down-payment solar lease?”

Osman Bakhtiar is a director of Bakhtiar Developments, in Dubai, a family-run builder whose 14 Thane societies are a major Jhilmil account group. He wants a flagship ambition and proposes: “How might we make every home we build energy-independent?” His group has offered to co-fund a pilot.

Greta Hallberg in Berlin did the interviews. Her set of three prompts, drawn directly from Exhibit 2, is listed in Exhibit 3. She has not asked for a particular solution, and she worries that her prompts sound abstract to a sales team.

Gargi Vasaikar herself owns the decision. The Pune engineering team, weary of workshops that end in vague sticky notes, will judge her by the result.

5. Exhibit 3 and the six-minute test

On Tuesday, 13 October, Greta ran a small test. Six Jhilmil colleagues each spent six minutes sketching ideas for one statement at a time, and she grouped the sketches by approach. Exhibit 3 gives the results.

Prompt A produced 31 ideas but only four approaches, and nearly all were variants of leasing: tenor, interest, who holds the asset. Prompt B produced 58 ideas and 17 approaches, but few concerned housing societies at all. The set in C gave 44 ideas in 11 approaches, and every one of the 44 was about the committee’s decision.

6. The options

Option 1: open with Gopal’s lease prompt. The upside is concreteness: engineers can scope a lease within the sprint, and the NRI channel has real demand. The cost is that the prompt already contains its answer. Exhibit 2 codes one main reason per interview and none was upfront cost, so the sprint could deliver a financing product that those 72 societies have no reason to prefer.

Option 2: open with Osman’s ambition. The upside is energy and a co-funding partner. The cost is that nothing constrains the room: Exhibit 3 shows the breadth, yet the output would be hard to turn into a two-week sprint, and the 72 non-approving societies would stay where they are.

Option 3: open with Greta’s three prompts, but test them first. Use Thursday 22 and Friday 23 October to rewrite C1 to C3 in plainer commercial language with Gopal and Osman, rerun the test with two sales colleagues, and keep the 26 October date. The prompts trace to Exhibit 2, and each admits many answers. The cost is two days and the risk that Gopal and Osman feel overruled.

The workshop itself costs ₹6.5 lakh in flights and venue, and an idle sprint costs about ₹7 lakh a week, so moving the date is expensive. Option 3 keeps both date and discipline.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Read Exhibits 1 and 2 together. Where in the funnel is the problem, and what does the August statement assume that the interviews do not support?

2. Apply a simple test to each prompt in Exhibit 3: remove the “How might we” words and ask whether only one product could answer it. Which sentences pass?

3. Prompt B generated the most ideas. Why is idea count a poor measure of a good prompt?

4. Which option would you take to the 5 p.m. deadline, and how would you present it to Gopal and Osman so that each sees his concern preserved?

8. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. A “How might we” question is the hinge between a framed problem and a room full of ideas. Its job is to open solutions without smuggling one in. A prompt that is too narrow, like Gopal’s, names the answer, so people fill in details instead of thinking. One that is too broad, like Osman’s, names no constraint, so people drift. A good prompt is tied to evidence about a real person’s difficulty, specific enough to guide and open enough to surprise.

One defensible path. Option 3. Exhibit 2 shows that doubt about payback, unequal gains and the committee cycle account for 24 of the 30 interviews, or 80.0 per cent of that sample. Each of C1, C2 and C3 corresponds to one of those themes, and none names a product. The test in Exhibit 3 supports the choice but, with six people, does not prove it.

She should then keep Gopal’s lease as one of the ideas the room can reach through C2 or C3, since a lease may well make payback and fairness easier to explain. That keeps his demand signal without letting it dictate the question. For Osman, the energy-independence ambition becomes the stated purpose of the pilot, with the three prompts as the route. She should also write down what evidence would make her revisit the frame, for example if the 42 un-interviewed societies cite price.
exp20v2-prob.hmw:
'How might we' questions

Turning a problem into generative prompts without embedding a solution

1. A Tuesday review in Pune

On Tuesday 6 October 2026, Ila Hosamani, head of product at Haveli Stays Network, sat through a quarterly review that ended with a sentence she had been dreading. Haveli Stays runs a marketplace of heritage homestays, havelis and farmhouses, mostly in Rajasthan, and its guests book through an app and pay through UPI. Between July and September the platform had taken 12,400 bookings. Of those, 1,240 had been cancelled by the host, not the guest: exactly 10 per cent. Finance had costed each such cancellation at an average of ₹4,000 in refunds, rebooking credit and support time, so the quarter's bill was 1,240 × ₹4,000 = ₹49.6 lakh.

The founder, Hitesh Doshi, who ran host operations from Jaipur, closed the meeting by saying: “Put this on Monday's sprint plan: how might we penalise hosts who cancel?” Everyone nodded. Diwali fell on 8 November, five weeks away, and a fix that failed would be discovered in December, when guests were already stranded.

The sentence began with the three words her design lead, Gitika Saxena in Kolkata, kept on a sticky note, but it contained a solution. Penalties are an answer; the question had already been closed, and the sprint would produce a penalty ladder without anyone asking whether penalties touched the causes. Before sprint planning on Monday 19 October she had to restate the problem so that ideas would be wide enough to find a better answer, and narrow enough to be useful.

2. The idea

A “how might we” question, usually abbreviated HMW, is a one-sentence prompt that invites ideas about a problem. “How” assumes a solution exists. “Might” makes an idea provisional, which lowers the cost of saying something odd. “We” makes the answer collective. The device is usually credited to Min Basadur, who used it in the 1970s while working on creative problem-solving at Procter & Gamble, and it spread through design consultancies such as IDEO and later through the Stanford d.school and large technology companies.

It was invented to solve a specific difficulty: a team that has understood a problem has a statement of what is wrong, not of what to do. Turning it directly into a task (“build a penalty system”) skips ideation; leaving it as a complaint (“hosts cancel too often”) gives people nothing to push against. The HMW sits between the two: it takes a finding and reshapes it into an open invitation.

The test, in one sentence Ila could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: a good HMW names the person and the tension, and leaves the solution blank. If you can answer the question with a single feature, it was an instruction in disguise. If any answer is possible, including answers about pricing, communication or policy, it was too vague to start a conversation.

3. How it works, step by step

Ila's first step was one that practitioners usually leave implicit: she went back to the evidence. An HMW is only as good as the finding it is made from. She asked Indrajit Sen, the data lead who worked from Chennai, to classify all 1,240 host cancellations by the reason the host gave when cancelling, or by the reason support recovered afterwards. Exhibit 1 shows the result.

Exhibit 1. Host cancellations, July to September 2026, by cause. Shares are rounded to one decimal place (150/1,240 = 12.1; 160/1,240 = 12.9).

The second step is to choose a frame, a sentence about whose problem it is. Ila wrote: “Hosts who accept a booking they later cannot honour, because something in their own world changes.” The third step is to state the tension, the pair of things that pull against each other. Here, hosts want full calendars and flexibility to say yes to a good offer; guests want certainty. The fourth step is to write the HMW, and the fifth, usually skipped, is to adjust its altitude. Exhibit 2 shows the idea.

The ladder is the implicit step. Any HMW can be made broader by asking “why does that matter?” and narrower by asking “what specifically?” Ila's task was to climb until the solution fell out of the question, and stop before it went soft.

4. A worked example, with a second pass

Ila's team wrote four candidate questions and sized each against Exhibit 1. For each, the cancellations “in scope” are those whose cause the question could plausibly touch. An assumed reduction was applied to those, and each avoided cancellation was valued at the ₹4,000 finance figure. The reductions are guesses to be tested.

Read line by line: question A touches only the 160 price disputes; a penalty does nothing for a host whose haveli is being repainted. At a 25 per cent cut it avoids 40 cancellations, worth 40 × ₹4,000 = ₹1.60 lakh. Question B reaches 496; halving them avoids 248, worth ₹9.92 lakh. Question C reaches 248 + 186 = 434 cases; half is 217, worth ₹8.68 lakh. Question D reaches 150 + 160 = 310, and 40 per cent of that is 124, worth ₹4.96 lakh. On this pass the order is B, C, D, A, and the penalty framing comes last by a wide margin.

Now change one input. Ila asked Jaipur's host team to review all 496 double-booked cases. They reported that the 496 were not one group. In 310 cases the host's other calendar, usually a rival booking site or a family WhatsApp group, had not been synced and the host had honestly lost track. In the other 186, the host had knowingly accepted a higher offer elsewhere. Check: 310 + 186 = 496. A calendar tool cannot help the second group, so B's scope falls from 496 to 310. At the same 50 per cent cut it avoids 155 cancellations, worth 155 × ₹4,000 = ₹6.20 lakh.

The lesson is not that C is correct. It is that the ordering moved when one piece of evidence moved, and that the 186 deliberate cases are the one residue where a penalty might belong.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

A question can hide a solution without using a solution word

“How might we get hosts to use our calendar?” has no feature name in it, yet it presumes that the calendar is the answer. The test is whether you can imagine a good response that does not involve the thing named. If you cannot, the thing named is the solution.

Narrow is not the same as specific

People blur the two. A narrow HMW prescribes the means; a specific one names a particular person in a particular situation. “How might we help a Jodhpur host with a daughter's wedding in February keep a booking promise?” is specific and still open.

An HMW is not a problem statement

A problem statement says what is true and for whom; an HMW is a question derived from it. Keep the statement, and attach each HMW to it, so readers can see which finding each question came from.

One finding yields many questions, and the set matters

Good practice is to write five to ten HMWs from one problem, at different altitudes, and then choose. Writing only one means defending it by default.

It cannot tell you that the problem is worth solving

However well phrased, the HMW says nothing about whether a ₹49.6 lakh quarterly cost deserves attention against other costs. That comes from sizing the opportunity, which precedes the question. It also cannot tell you whether the diagnosis is right; the phone calls to hosts changed the answer more than any rewording did.

Ask who is excluded

Ask whose voice the word “we” leaves out. Ila's first draft was written without a single host in the room. Ask too whether a stranger would read the question the way you do.

6. How it differs by product type and stage

In a consumer product, the person in the question is usually one individual with a recognisable moment. In B2B, the user and the buyer differ, and a question for the user alone may be unfundable. In a marketplace like Haveli Stays, there are two sides with opposed interests, and the sharpest questions sit on the seam between them. Question D asks what the two sides agree, not about either alone. A one-sided HMW pushes cost onto the other side, as question A did.

Stage matters too. In an early-stage company an HMW session might be one afternoon and the answer tried the next day. In a large organisation the HMW travels through approvals, and an open question can harden into a requirement as it is repeated. Attaching an HMW to a named metric and owner helps it stay a prompt and not become a mandate.

7. Common mistakes

The disguised solution

Symptom: the ideation session produces five variations of one feature. Misunderstanding: the question named the mechanism. Cheapest diagnostic: before the session, ask three colleagues to answer in one line each; if all three give the same answer, rewrite.

The boil-the-ocean question

Symptom: ideas that range from app redesigns to hiring plans, none comparable. Misunderstanding: breadth was mistaken for creativity. Diagnostic: can you name the person and the moment? If not, climb down one rung.

The question with no evidence behind it

Symptom: the room agrees quickly and nobody asks for a number. Misunderstanding: fluency was taken as understanding. Diagnostic: ask which row of which table the question came from. Ila's penalty question had none.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the same Tuesday would have ended differently. Hitesh would have stated the ₹49.6 lakh cost and asked the team for questions, not penalties. Indrajit would have produced Exhibit 1 within a day. Gitika would have run a thirty-minute session producing eight or nine HMWs, and Ila would have sorted them by altitude, struck out any that named a feature, and sized the survivors as in Exhibit 3. The team would have phoned a sample of hosts before ranking, found the 310 and 186 split, and planned the sprint around two or three questions with explicit scope, each tied to a cause and to a number that could be re-measured after launch.

9. Closing: what Ila decided

On Friday 16 October Ila took three questions to Hitesh and Gideon Ochieng, the engineering manager who led the platform team from Nairobi: B (know what is already promised), C (cheap early closing dates) and D (agree what was booked). She kept A out of the sprint, and explained why in a sentence: it reached 160 of 1,240 cancellations and could damage host goodwill in the busiest weeks. She parked the 186 deliberate cases as a policy question for Hitesh, for after Diwali. C led after the second pass, ₹8.68 lakh against B's ₹6.20 lakh, and the two share calendar infrastructure, so building both cost little more than one.

What to learn next: ideation methods such as brainstorming and Crazy 8s, in which a good HMW becomes raw material. Revisit problem framing too: an HMW is no better than its frame.

Two questions to sit with. First, take a project you are currently working on and write its HMW in ten words; can a colleague name a solution that your wording rules out? Second, which of your team's HMWs would survive being rewritten for the person who is most affected by the problem, in their own words?
exp40v2-prob.hmw:
'How might we' questions

Turning a problem into a generative prompt without smuggling in the answer

1. Two rooms, six days apart

On Thursday 1 October 2026, Priyamvada Walvekar, head of product at Pratyay Lending Systems in Pune, heard her founder close a quarterly review with a sentence that would cost a quarter. Pratyay sells field-collections software to thirty-four non-banking financial companies regulated by the Reserve Bank of India, on contracts worth ₹28.4 crore a year, licensed to 18,500 agents. In September 2026 those agents logged 9,25,000 visits, of which 3,70,000 reached a borrower, a contact rate of 40.0 per cent. Of the contacts, 1,29,500 ended in a recorded promise to pay, or 35.0 per cent. Of the promises, 51,800 of the 1,29,500 were honoured (40.0 per cent) recovering ₹8,400 each on average: 51,800 × ₹8,400 = ₹43,51,20,000, or ₹43.51 crore.

Purnendu Lavate, the founder, looked at the kept rate and said: “Next quarter's theme is one line. How might we add a WhatsApp reminder module?” The room liked it; it had the three words on it. Priyamvada counted the rest and found a specification: a channel, a mechanism, an implied cause. Planning closed Monday 12 October.

Six days later, on Wednesday 7 October 2026, Raghunandan Tilvekar, chief product officer at Ritu Appliance House in Rajkot, faced the mirror image. Ritu rents water purifiers across Gujarat, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh: 1,42,000 subscriptions at ₹420 a month, against ₹150 of filters and service, leaving ₹270 of contribution. Its devices carry a Bureau of Indian Standards mark and a cellular module reporting filter life. In July–September, 8,520 were cancelled. Finance costs each at the contribution forgone over the fourteen months it would otherwise have run: 14 × ₹270 = ₹3,780. The quarter cost 8,520 × ₹3,780 = ₹3,22,05,600, or ₹322.06 lakh. Rutvik Dhurandhar, the founder, proposed the theme himself: “How might we reward customers who stay two years?” A loyalty discount is a lever he can pull by Monday, and the most expensive answer available.

2. The idea, and who disputes it

A “how might we” question (HMW) is a one-sentence prompt, derived from an evidenced problem statement, that invites solutions without naming one. The grammar carries three loads. How presupposes an answer exists, licensing search. Might marks every answer provisional, lowering the cost of a bad idea. We makes the search collective and, less innocently, fixes who may answer. The device traces to Min Basadur's problem-solving work at Procter & Gamble in the 1970s, carried into design consulting by IDEO, formalised at the Stanford d.school, and absorbed by product organisations as the hinge between research and ideation.

It was invented against a specific failure: findings generate no options. Converted into work (“build the reminder module”) they skip the search; left as complaints they give a room nothing to push against. The HMW occupies the gap — a finding restated as an invitation, narrow enough to answer and wide enough that the answer is not yet known.

Four schools disagree about how much work the sentence itself does. The design school signs that a prompt's quality is the variety of mechanisms it elicits and that grammar is causal — “might” changes who speaks — but not that a prompt be priced before the session, since premature valuation kills the odd idea that proves large. The outcome school, from jobs-to-be-done, signs that neutrality comes from an outcome with a metric and a direction, not a softened verb, and denies that “might” adds anything a good outcome statement lacks. The hypothesis school signs that the only artefact worth a sprint is a falsifiable assumption with a named risk, not an open question carrying none. The constraint school, common among engineering leaders, signs that a space opens fastest when you name the constraint you refuse to relax, and that unconstrained breadth produces unbuildable suggestions.

The test: a good HMW names a person and a tension, specifies its population, and leaves the mechanism blank. If one feature answers it, the sentence was an instruction; if every feature answers it, a mood.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Expert practice begins a step earlier than the literature: the population is decomposed before anyone writes a question. Priyamvada asked Rameshwari Pandhare, Pratyay's data lead in Kochi, to classify all 77,700 broken promises by recorded cause.

Cause of a broken promise, September 2026CountShare (%)

Exhibit 2. Counts sum to 77,700.

The decomposition is the real artefact, and it prices the founder's sentence. A reminder addresses forgetting, which is 9,324 of the 77,700 broken promises, or 12.0 per cent; nothing in the other 88 per cent is touched by a timely message.

The second step is the frame: whose problem this is. Priyamvada wrote: “A borrower who means to pay and an agent who needs the promise on record agree a date neither controls.” The third is the tension: agents are paid on promises captured, borrowers on their employers' calendars. The fourth transforms the frame into a family of questions: remove the bad, amplify the good, question an assumption, invert it, attack an adjective, borrow a resource. The fifth, almost always skipped, sizes each candidate against that decomposition as N × c × v less the cost of answering: N the population reached, c the conversion an answer achieves, v the value of one conversion. The result is Exhibit 3. The discipline is that N comes from a row of Exhibit 2, v is computed per cause rather than borrowed from the headline, and c is the only guess.
