The founder's question is not wrong; it is small. Question A is worth ₹3.92 crore of ₹21.17 crore, or 18.5 per cent of the sized total, and ranks third behind B and C. Question B (how might a borrower name a date on which their money will actually exist?) reaches the largest cause, is worth ₹9.14 crore, and needs no new channel, only that the date field stop being whatever the agent types.

Two second-order effects matter more than the ranking. First, once a table exists nobody proposes a question they cannot attach to a row, healthy discipline or occasionally a loss. The loss is row D: a phantom promise recovers nothing, so a disciplined team deletes it. But if 15,540 of the recorded promises were never made, the real promise base is 1,29,500 − 15,540 = 1,13,960, and the kept rate is 51,800 of 1,13,960, or 45.5 per cent, not 40.0 per cent. Answering D moves the headline metric by 5.5 points without recovering a rupee, and every target negotiated off the old number is wrong. The expert keeps one unsizable question alive, labelled measurement so its zero is not read as worthlessness.

Second, a point estimate invites argument where a break-even ends it. Asked what rate A would need to beat B, Priyamvada divided: 10,878 ÷ 9,324 = 1.167, so A must convert 116.7 per cent of its population. A cannot overtake B under any assumption, and the quarrel over 50 per cent becomes irrelevant.

4. When it applies, stated as tests

Three conditions make the device earn its place. First: the population decomposes and no single cause dominates. If one cause were 80 per cent there is nothing to open up, only a thing to fix. Pratyay's largest cause is 35.0 per cent, Ritu's 30.0 per cent, so both pass. Second: the team holds discretion over more than one mechanism. Pratyay controls the workflow, the data model, the payment rails and client reporting. Ritu passes partly: its moulding tooling is committed for eighteen months, so a question needing a new housing is not live. Third: searching costs less than being wrong. A week of discovery is cheap against ₹322.06 lakh a quarter.

The device is actively misleading in two situations. One is where the answer is externally determined: a regulator's conduct norms, a contract, a store policy. Asking how we might contact borrowers more often, when frequency is bounded by norms Pratyay's clients observe, stages a search whose result is fixed. The other is where the finding is a defect, not an opportunity: of Ritu's 852 mandate failures, 639 of the 852 (75.0 per cent) follow one deterministic path, an expiring e-mandate the app never prompts anyone to renew. That is a bug with one correct answer; the 75 per cent conversion in Exhibit 5 is high because no creativity is required.

5. Hard edges

At Ritu the hard edge is the hardware–software seam. Firmware ships over the air in a window Qadir Modak's team opens twice a year; mechanical change needs tooling. Raghunandan runs two registers, one answerable in software this quarter and one held for the next device cycle, refusing to downgrade a good hardware question into a bad software one. Rhiannon Tudor, Ritu's designer in Bristol, gets the second, never the first.

In a two-sided market the sharpest questions sit on the seam: Rivayat Crafts Network, a marketplace for handloom and brassware sellers, found that a question written for one side pushes cost to the other, faster delivery for buyers landing as an unfunded obligation on weavers. In regulated products the constraint belongs inside the question, or the room re-invents impermissible mechanisms; Pratyay writes “within the contact norms our clients are held to, how might …”. In AI-native products the mechanism is a model, which corrupts the sizing more than the wording: Qudrat Agri Labs, grading cotton bales from photographs, found its v term depends on model accuracy, itself the thing being decided, so it states a threshold as a condition: at 92 per cent precision what does this unlock, at 78 per cent what breaks?

At multi-product seams, mature companies do this far less well than they describe. Stated practice is a reviewed register with evidence attached; observed practice is that an executive's sentence becomes a planning line, the line a requirement, and nobody can name the row. The defence that works is a one-page sizing table travelling with it.

6. Eight distinctions that separate command from competence

The solution hides in the noun, not the verb. “How might we make the collections app faster?” names no feature, yet has decided the app is where the problem lives. The tell: ask for an answer not involving the named object. If none exists, that object is the solution.

Altitude is set by who must act, not by taste. Competent practitioners argue about breadth; experts ask whose backlog an answer lands in. A question spanning payments, agent incentives and client contracts is unassignable, not inspiring.

The denominator is the artefact; the sentence is packaging. The tell is sequence: an expert wants the decomposition before the wording, delaying a workshop a week for it. Exhibit 2 priced the reminder module at 12.0 per cent of the problem, which no rewording could have done.

The most valuable question is sometimes the one that cannot be sized. Row D looks worth nothing. It is worth 5.5 points of a metric the board tracks. The tell is a register still holding one question labelled measurement.

Value per conversion differs by cause. One rupee figure across every row flatters the largest cause; row E recovers ₹3,200, not ₹8,400. The tell: the expert interrogates the per-unit column before the conversion column.

“We” is a scoping decision disguised as a pronoun. Does Pratyay's “we” include the field agent, the client's branch manager, or the borrower? Each reading yields different answers, and rooms assume the narrowest. The tell is asking who is inside it.

The conversion column is where dishonesty accumulates, so experts use break-evens. Nobody can defend 50 per cent; everybody can evaluate “A needs 116.7 per cent to beat B”. The tell is contested questions carrying thresholds, not estimates.

A question has a shelf life, because its decomposition moves. Priyamvada's September table will be wrong by February: if B succeeds, cash timing shrinks and forgetting becomes a larger share of a smaller problem. The tell is a date-stamped question naming its exhibit. Teams also mistake synonyms for breadth: if two candidates touch one row and nothing else, the family is one question in eight hats.

7. How the practice shifts by product type and stage

In consumer products the person is an individual in a recognisable moment and the decomposition comes from instrumentation; Ritu's customer is a household, and the subscriber who signs is not the person who complains about the taste. In B2B the user and buyer diverge, so a question serving only the user may be unfundable: question B helps borrowers and agents, but is sold to a credit head who cares about the kept rate, so it travels with a metric or not at all. In hardware the binding difference is the cadence of what can change. In AI products it is narrower than claimed: the grammar is unchanged, while the value term becomes conditional on a capability threshold.

Stage changes the risk, not the method. In a company of twenty an HMW is a conversation on Monday and an experiment on Wednesday, and over-formalising it is the error. At Pratyay's scale the question crosses three planning layers and the error reverses: an open prompt hardens into a commitment because repetition confers authority. Sector folklore is a claimed difference that is not real — nothing distinguishes how a fintech and a logistics firm write these sentences, only teams that size them from those that do not.

8. Three worked examples

A success, by reframing. In March 2025 Pratyay had 12,000 licensed agents, of whom 4,800 of the 12,000 opened the app that month, a 40.0 per cent login rate. The executive question was how to make the home screen faster. Radhika Khanvilkar, the design lead, reframed it after four days of ride-alongs: how might an agent finish a route without opening a second tool? The tool was paper: the app could not show a route offline. Offline download shipped in June 2025 and logins rose to 8,400 of the 12,000, or 70.0 per cent: 3,600 more agents, from a question never mentioning speed.

A partial success, measured honestly. Ritu tested its appointment-window question in the Rajkot and Jamnagar cluster, 18,600 subscriptions, in April–June 2026, where Prasad Nerurkar's team re-sequenced routes and offered two-hour slots. Of 6,200 service requests there, 3,720 of the 6,200 had previously been met within forty-eight hours, or 60.0 per cent, matching the company rate; after the change 4,960 of the 6,200 were met in window, or 80.0 per cent. Service-driven cancellations in the cluster fell from 186 in January–March to 93, protecting 93 × ₹3,780 = ₹3,51,540.

A failure, and what recovery cost. Prabodh Transit Works, an intercity bus-ticketing company in Nagpur, took 6,40,000 bookings in April–June 2025 and received 19,200 complaints, 3.0 per cent of bookings. Pranita Ambegaonkar's team read 1,728 of the 19,200 tickets, a 9.0 per cent sample, of which 1,080 of the 1,728 mentioned a bus that did not arrive, 62.5 per cent. The question was textbook: how might a traveller be certain their bus is coming? Six engineers, fully loaded at ₹1.75 lakh a month each, worked from Monday 7 July 2025 to Monday 29 September 2025 (twelve weeks, or three months, costing 6 × ₹1.75 lakh × 3 = ₹31.50 lakh) and shipped live vehicle tracking with push alerts. In the eight weeks before launch there had been 2,700 “bus did not arrive” complaints; in the eight weeks after, 2,592, a fall of 4.0 per cent.

The question was fine; the frame beneath it was false. The evidence base was 1,728 of 6,40,000 journeys, or 0.27 per cent, and tickets are written by people who already believe they know the cause. In late November 2025 Pranita telephoned 150 complainants: 96 of the 150 had been standing at the wrong pickup point, watching their bus pass a corner they could not see. The reframed question (how might a traveller recognise the exact spot where the bus will stop) took two engineers six weeks, Monday 8 December 2025 to Monday 19 January 2026, at 2 × ₹1.75 lakh × 1.5 = ₹5.25 lakh. Over the next eight weeks the category fell to 1,431, down 47.0 per cent from 2,700: a sixth of the money, twelve times the effect. The ₹31.50 lakh bought not a bad question but an unexamined frame, which no phrasing detects.

9. Failure modes and their early signs

The embedded solution. Sign: the candidate list is five variants of one mechanism. Diagnostic: which rows of the cause table does this reach? Cost late: a quarter of engineering aimed at 12.0 per cent of the problem.

The uniform per-unit value. Sign: one rupee figure down the whole value column. Diagnostic: what does a success recover here? Cost: at a flat ₹8,400, row E would have been sized at ₹5.87 crore rather than ₹2.24 crore.

The sample-shaped frame. Sign: the evidence is a channel: tickets, reviews, the last three sales calls. Diagnostic: what fraction of the population is this, and who selected into it? Cost: Prabodh's twelve weeks.

The unsizable question quietly dropped. Sign: every surviving question has a rupee figure. Diagnostic: which changes a denominator rather than a numerator? Cost: a year of targets set against a 40.0 per cent kept rate that was really 45.5 per cent.

10. Where the disagreement is genuine

The design school's strongest form is not that words are magic but that participation is causal: where the prompt is provisional, more people speak and the spread of mechanisms widens. That claim is supported in Basadur's problem-finding work, falsified if a metric and decomposition alone generate the same variety.

The outcome school's strongest form is that the sizing table does all the work and grammar is ceremony. Its evidence is the class of well-run sessions producing thirty ideas and no decision, and that Exhibit 3, not the sentence, killed the reminder module. It is falsified if teams working from outcomes alone converge on the incumbent mechanism, what “make the app faster” looks like.

The hypothesis school's strongest form is that the unit of discovery is a falsifiable assumption, and Prabodh is its best case: a well-formed question, a false frame, ₹31.50 lakh. Had the team written “we assume complainants know why their bus did not come”, the 150 calls would have come in July. It is falsified if starting from assumptions stops teams finding non-obvious mechanisms, since an assumption inherits the model that generated it.

No synthesis is honestly available. The positions bet differently on where error enters: the room's imagination, the missing metric, or the unexamined premise. All three are real; none can be primary.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this writes better sentences. Someone who has internalised it asks for a table before a workshop, computes value per conversion for each cause, replaces contested estimates with break-evens, keeps one unsizable question in the register, states what each excludes, date-stamps its exhibit, and, hardest, tells an executive his sentence reaches 12.0 per cent of the problem, arithmetic on one page, the only form in which it can be said.

12. What each of them decided

On Monday 12 October 2026 Priyamvada took Exhibit 3 to Purnendu and to Pei-Chun Lo, who leads Pratyay's platform team from Taipei. She proposed B and C, which touch the same promise-capture and payment-rail code and together cost barely more than either alone, with D funded as a two-week measurement task because the board's kept rate is understated by 5.5 points. She did not reject the reminder; she put it behind those three with the break-even written down, so the decision read as arithmetic, not a verdict on whose idea it was.

On Thursday 15 October 2026 Raghunandan put one comparison to Rutvik, taking care both sides were the same kind of rupee. A ₹50 monthly discount across all 1,42,000 subscriptions costs 1,42,000 × ₹50 = ₹71,00,000 of cash every month it runs. The benefit is not cash: price-driven cancellations run at 1,704 a quarter, or 568 a month, and each one avoided earns ₹3,780 of contribution over fourteen months, so 568 × ₹3,780 = ₹21,47,040 is a stock of future contribution, not a month's income. Put on the discount's own basis, 568 subscriptions saved a month, each surviving fourteen months, leave 568 × 14 = 7,952 extra live subscriptions once the stock has built, worth 7,952 × ₹270 = ₹21,47,040 a month, the same figure now genuinely monthly. At best the question destroys ₹71,00,000 − ₹21,47,040 = ₹49,52,960 a month in the steady state, and more while the stock builds.

Discussion questions. First: Priyamvada put the founder's question behind B, C and D rather than striking it: defensible use of evidence, or an accommodation costing Pratyay a quarter in nine months? Second: Ritu's row of 750 unestablished reasons carries no question and no value; what would you spend to turn it into evidence, and how would you know it was worth it? Third: Prabodh's question passed every stylistic test here and still failed. What must be added to the method, not the sentence, to catch that in July?

13. Going deeper

Problem framing and reframing sits beneath this: the frame is what a question inherits, and Prabodh shows a good question cannot survive a false one. Ideation: brainstorming, Crazy 8s, HMW is what a sized question feeds, unlocking the search the table makes worth running. Writing a problem hypothesis makes a question falsifiable. Surfacing assumptions is the missing step in the Prabodh sequence. Riskiest assumption first orders the work, putting the 150 calls before twelve weeks of engineering. Validating a problem hypothesis fills the N column instead of guessing. Frequency and intensity of the problem is where v comes from, the column most often borrowed rather than computed. Vitamin vs painkiller is the judgement after the arithmetic: Ritu's 1,278 improved-supply households stopped being either.
case40v1-prob.hmw:
Jalpaan Foodservice: The Sentence Due at Nine

An ambiguous case on framing a design sprint

1. Sunday night, Aundh

At twenty to ten on Sunday, 18 October 2026, Gitika Vengsarkar sat at her dining table in Aundh, Pune, with a cold plate of poha she had forgotten and a document nine words short of finished. By nine the next morning she had to circulate the framing question for a three-day design sprint. Fourteen people would fly, dial in or drive across Pune for it on Wednesday, 21 October, and whatever sentence topped that brief would decide which ideas were in scope.

She had four candidate sentences, one from each of four colleagues she trusted, and a fifth of her own she could not get under thirty words. Each began “How might we”, and each, read slowly, already contained its answer. Behind all five sat a worry she had written nowhere: that what she was asked to frame was not what had gone wrong.

On 11 December, Northline Financial Services’ sourcing committee would meet in Jersey City to decide whether to extend Jalpaan’s master services agreement, which covered 12 of its 41 cafeterias and almost a third of revenue. Girisha Gogte, Jalpaan’s founder, had put it plainly on 14 October: the sprint must produce something nameable in the renewal deck.

2. Jalpaan Foodservice

Jalpaan Foodservice Private Limited was founded in Pune in 2014 by Girisha Gogte, after eleven years in hotel food and beverage. The business is institutional catering: Jalpaan runs cafeterias inside other companies’ offices, buys the vegetables, employs the cooks and bills the employer per meal. Exhibit 1 is the FY26 portfolio.

FY26 EBITDA was ₹13.64 crore, 6.0 per cent of revenue. Twelve of the 41 cafeterias — ten in India, both Dubai sites — serve Northline Financial Services, a US-headquartered insurance and asset-management group with capability centres in five Indian cities and a regional office in Dubai. Those twelve serve 31,000 meals a day and produced ₹74.80 crore: 32.9 per cent of revenue, ₹96.52 a meal.

One decision from March 2023 constrains Gitika now. To win Northline, then 14 sites, Jalpaan accepted two terms the sales team called cosmetic. The first was a waste pass-through cap: Jalpaan absorbs plate waste above 60 grams a meal at the Indian sites, at the agreed food-cost rate of ₹168 a kilogram. The second put the employee app, Thali, inside Northline’s single sign-on, with consent scoped under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act to meal fulfilment alone, and the kitchen tablets under Northline change control. Both were signed because a 2022 audit at two Pune kitchens measured waste at 54 grams a meal.

3. The industry

Indian institutional catering is a volume business with thin margins. Jalpaan competes against the Indian arms of Sodexo and Compass Group, and against regional caterers who quote ₹15 a meal lower and mean it. GST on canteen service billed to an employer is 5 per cent without input tax credit, so a kilogram of wasted dal is a kilogram nobody reimburses. FSSAI licensing sets the floor; the Kharadi licence renews on 28 February 2027.

The sharper force is substitution. A Northline analyst in Hinjawadi can have lunch at her desk from Swiggy, Zomato or Zepto in under half an hour, and need not decide at half past nine. In 2023 the competition was the canteen across the road; by 2026 it was the phone in her pocket, and the comparison was not price but the cost of committing early.

Jalpaan’s exposure is global in an awkward way. The two Dubai cafeterias earn the most per meal in the portfolio and sit under another inflation and inspection regime. The product team spans five time zones and five salary bands: Kadaba’s seat in Toronto costs about ₹1.42 crore a year fully loaded, against roughly ₹38 lakh for a senior analyst in Pune. Figure 2 shows the wiring.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Thali went live in June 2024 with one promise: if employees pre-ordered before the kitchen locked its production plan at 09:30, Jalpaan could cook closer to demand and shorten the one o’clock queue. Pre-ordering was free and voluntary. Adoption rose for two quarters and stopped. Exhibit 2 is the end of August 2026.

Two figures reset what the team believed. 9,272 people have pre-ordered at some point, so low usage is not ignorance of the feature; and 5,220 of the 14,112 activated employees, 37.0 per cent, pre-ordered at some point but not in August. In August the ten sites served 2,73,000 lunches over 21 serving days, of which 38,451 were pre-ordered, 14.1 per cent — what the facilities deck calls “app adoption”, unmoved in five quarters.

In February 2026 Northline cut its employer meal subsidy from 70 per cent to 55 per cent. On a ₹110 lunch the employee’s share went from ₹33.00 to ₹49.50 overnight. Footfall fell and campus delivery orders rose. Jalpaan’s revenue per meal did not change, because Northline pays the balance; the number of meals did. The month before the cut, Northline’s workplace team had fielded its annual survey, and Exhibit 3 is its cafeteria block.

In July 2026 Mariana Melo flew from Lisbon and ran fifty interviews at Hinjawadi and Kharadi. She and Madhura Sundararajan coded every transcript independently against eleven codes; Exhibit 6 is the code that mattered. What Mariana brought back was not on the January list: people were not declining the canteen, they were declining to decide at half past nine. On Wednesday, 23 September 2026, 3,772 of 8,200 badge-ins at the two largest sites, 46.0 per cent, came after 09:30.

In August, Oormila Pagnis’s kitchen audit produced Exhibit 4, which nobody has yet explained.

Read naively, Exhibit 4 says pre-ordering causes waste: waste rises monotonically with pre-order share across all six sites. Oormila does not believe the causal reading — the three worst sites are also the three largest, four counters each — but she cannot separate the two, and the audit collected nothing that would. At 86.0 grams against a 60-gram cap, 26 grams of excess across 26,000 meals a day and 250 serving days is 169 tonnes a year, ₹2.84 crore at ₹168 a kilogram: 20.8 per cent of FY26 EBITDA.

From the end of August the team ran a pilot: a nudge at Hinjawadi A, a push at 08:40 and a one-tap reorder, with Gachibowli as control. Exhibit 5 is Kadaba’s read-out.

Saumitra’s interval is narrow and his arithmetic is right; whether it licenses any claim about the nudge is another question, and he has said so twice in writing. Feroze Kanga’s deck quotes the 6.0 points without either footnote.

5. The people

Girisha Gogte, founder and CEO, Pune. Position: the sprint must yield a named commitment for 11 December. Incentive: a Series C round paused since July, in which the Northline renewal is the largest line of diligence. Not saying: he has already described a “smart pre-order assistant” to investors.

Oormila Pagnis, COO for kitchens, Pune. Position: the only problem worth three days is the 26 grams, the only one with an invoice attached. Incentive: her cost line carries the ₹2.84 crore. Not saying: she approved the 2022 audit that weighed waste only on Tuesdays and Wednesdays, never a Friday, when waste peaks.

Suhas Bellur, head of engineering, Bengaluru. Position: pre-order is the only lever Jalpaan controls end to end, so the question should be about pre-order. Incentive: two of his fourteen engineers are free in Q4, and a scoped feature protects that capacity. Not saying: he thinks the 09:30 lock is a kitchen constraint dressed as a product rule.

Mariana Melo, product designer, Lisbon. Position: start from the employee’s 12:40 decision, not Jalpaan’s 09:30 one. Incentive: her fifty interviews are the first research Jalpaan has commissioned. Not saying: fourteen of the fifty transcripts are from employees who never installed Thali, which she believes is the point.

Saumitra Kadaba, data scientist, Toronto. Position: nothing in Exhibits 4 and 5 supports a causal claim, so the sprint should commission a clean test, not a feature. Incentive: a clean test is a quarter of his own work. Not saying: he cannot separate site size from pre-order share in Exhibit 4, and the counter opening sat in release notes he read on 2 September.

Madhura Sundararajan, customer success lead, Singapore. Position: the quarterly satisfaction score is the live risk, not waste and not adoption. Incentive: the service-credit clause sits in her review. Not saying: she second-coded Mariana’s transcripts and disagreed on the ones carrying the reframe.

Feroze Kanga, enterprise sales, New Jersey. Position: the renewal needs a number and a feature name by end-November. Incentive: Northline is 32.9 per cent of revenue and most of his variable pay. Not saying: his deck reports Exhibit 3’s nine per cent as a share of all 28,000 with access rather than of the 4,312 who answered the block — 1.4 per cent — and argues from a January survey about a February price change.

Mazin Al Suwaidi, director of workplace services at Northline, Dubai. Position: he wants a credible plan, and he is not unfriendly. Incentive: he recommended Jalpaan in 2023, and the subsidy cut was his own group’s policy. Not saying: a second caterer has approached his team.

6. Agreement on the code that matters

Exhibit 6 is the one piece of research hygiene the team did properly, and the most uncomfortable. Mariana and Madhura coded all fifty transcripts for whether the employee raised the timing of the lunch decision rather than its price.

A kappa of 0.64 is respectable for eleven codes and two coders on different continents. The problem is where the nine disagreements sit: the reframe rests on five transcripts, and those five are the ones the co-coder read as being about money.

7. Voices

“Everyone keeps saying adoption. Twenty-six grams a meal is ₹2.84 crore. Adoption is a slide; the grams are a cheque I write every quarter.”

Oormila Pagnis, product council, 9 October

“I asked a woman in Kharadi why she had stopped pre-ordering. She said: at nine-thirty I don’t know what kind of day it is yet.”

Mariana Melo, research debrief, 28 July

“Treated site up 8.0 points, interval ±0.52. I will not sign the word ‘because’. A counter opened at the treated site in week two; the control lost its servery for six days.”

Saumitra Kadaba, chat thread, 29 September

“Only nine per cent of Northline’s people want a cheaper lunch. Their own survey says it. Price is not our problem — the app is.”

Feroze Kanga, renewal review, 12 October

“Feroze, that nine per cent is of the four thousand three hundred who answered the block, not of the twenty-eight thousand. And we ran it in January.”

Madhura Sundararajan, same thread, unanswered

“Bring the committee a plan you believe. The subsidy is a Northline decision, and it is settled.”

Mazin Al Suwaidi to Feroze Kanga, 2 October

8. The four sentences, and the fifth

Gitika had written the candidates on one page, which is how she came to distrust them all.

A, from Suhas and Feroze. “How might we get more Northline employees to pre-order on Thali?” Buildable, measurable, and it names the only metric in the renewal deck. It also assumes pre-ordering is the behaviour worth having — the proposition Exhibit 4 embarrasses and that, on Exhibit 2, 9,272 have tried and 5,220 did not order in August.

B, from Oormila. “How might we bring plate waste below 60 grams a meal without shrinking portions?” The only candidate attached to an invoice. It also writes the 2023 cap into the premise — a cap set from a baseline that excluded Fridays — and forbids, in its second clause, the one move most caterers reach for.

C, from Mariana. “How might we help someone decide what to eat at 12:40 without walking to the counter first?” It moves the unit of analysis from Jalpaan’s production plan to the employee’s afternoon, where the competition sits. It also smuggles a solution in four words: without walking to the counter.

D, from Saumitra. “How might we forecast tomorrow’s demand well enough to cook less?” Honest about what Jalpaan controls. It also presumes the answer is a model, puts the work in the most expensive seat on the team, and produces nothing nameable by 11 December.

E, Gitika’s own, unfinished. “How might we make the canteen the easiest good decision on a Northline campus?” She likes that it names no feature. She cannot defend scoping three days and fourteen people against it, and Girisha would ask what the noun is.

What she had noticed at about nine o’clock, and told no one, was that all five sentences take the cafeteria as the unit. None asks whose problem the 14.1 per cent is. The subsidy moved 15 percentage points onto the employee in February; the pre-order window shuts before 46.0 per cent of people arrive; and the January survey everyone quotes predates both facts.

9. The deadline and the hard edges

The brief goes out at 09:00 IST on Monday, 19 October. The sprint runs 21–23 October in Pune, with Toronto and New Jersey nine and a half hours behind, Lisbon four and a half, Dubai an hour and a half and Singapore two and a half ahead; the only window in which all seven cities overlap is 18:30 to 20:30 IST. The budget is ₹9.40 lakh: ₹4.20 lakh of travel, ₹1.80 lakh for a facilitator and ₹3.40 lakh of costed time.

Engineering capacity in Q4 is two of fourteen engineers. Any new data field or tablet software goes through Northline change control, which has run ten to fourteen weeks all year; a request raised on 23 October returns in January 2027, after the committee meets. Using Thali order history to personalise anything needs fresh notice and consent under the DPDP Act, because the 2023 consent is scoped to meal fulfilment, and Northline’s legal team has twice declined to push a consent prompt mid-contract. The 60-gram cap stands until the MSA is renegotiated, which is not on the December agenda. Northline’s satisfaction score was 3.58 out of 5 for the quarter to September, below the 3.60 floor; a second consecutive quarter below it, measured on 30 November, forfeits 2.5 per cent of the quarter’s Northline billing, which on ₹18.70 crore is ₹46.75 lakh. Diwali falls on 8 November, and the kitchens will run festive menus on half-strength rosters.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. State, in one sentence and without naming a feature, the problem Jalpaan is solving at the Northline sites. Whose problem is it?
  2. Exhibits 3 and 4 point in different directions and Exhibit 2 fits neither. Which would you trust, and what evidence would change your mind?
  3. Saumitra’s interval is ±0.52 percentage points. What does it license you to say about the nudge, and what does it not?
  4. Take sentences A to D and name the solution each already assumes. Which assumption is most expensive if wrong, and for whom?
  5. The 60-gram cap rests on a 2022 audit that never weighed a Friday. Does that change what the sprint should ask, or only what Jalpaan should renegotiate — and who must be told?
  6. It is 09:00 on Monday. What sentence does Gitika send, who is in the room on Wednesday, and what does she tell the committee on 11 December if the sprint produces nothing Northline can name?

11. Ten past eleven

She had moved sentence C to the top twice and moved it back both times. At ten past eleven she typed a sixth line, read it, and deleted it. Outside, somebody three floors down was testing a string of Diwali lights; they came on all at once, and went out.
exp20v2-prob.brief:
The Opportunity Brief

Making the case for a product opportunity on one page: who, what problem, evidence, size, why us, why now.

1. A message on a Monday

On Monday, 6 July 2026, Girija Mandrekar, a product manager at Gudam Storage Exchange, read a message from the chief executive, Gopinath Ravichandran. Gudam, based in Pune, is a marketplace on which owners of warehouses in Bhiwandi, Chakan and Hosur list space and small businesses rent it. Gudam keeps 12 per cent of every rental, and until then the minimum rental was three months.

Gaurang Pitale, who ran operations from Nagpur, had been forwarding a pattern. Between 1 January and 30 June 2026 the support desk had logged 312 enquiries for storage of under four weeks, and every one had been declined. Gulshan Tirkey, who led sales from Kochi, added that direct-to-consumer brands needed pallets mainly for the run-up to Diwali on 8 November. Engineering had estimated that a short-term pallet booking product would cost ₹180 lakh and five months of work. Gopinath wanted a decision at the board meeting on Thursday, 16 July, ten days away, and he would read one page.

The company applied one rule to new products: steady-state revenue of at least ₹200 lakh a year. The risks ran both ways. If Girija overstated the opportunity, Gudam would spend ₹180 lakh on a feature few brands used. If she understated it, a build started after the board meeting could not reach the festive season, and the next chance would be a year away. Her task was to write what product teams call an opportunity brief.

FactFigureSource
Short-term enquiries declined, 1 Jan to 30 Jun 2026312Support desk log
Build estimate₹180 lakhEngineering
Revenue hurdle for new products₹200 lakh a yearCompany rule
Gudam's share of each rental12 per centCurrent terms

2. The idea

An opportunity brief is a single page that answers six questions in a fixed order: who has the problem, what the problem is, what evidence shows it is real, how large it is, why this company should solve it, and why the moment is now. Its purpose is to let a decision-maker say yes, no or not yet to an opportunity before anyone designs a solution.

It was invented to cure a familiar failure. Proposals reach executives as solutions ("let us build a booking engine") carried by enthusiasm, with the problem implied and the evidence anecdotal. Two proposals cannot be compared because each argues in a different shape. The lineage is mixed. Barbara Minto's "pyramid principle", taught at McKinsey from the 1970s, insisted that the answer come first. Amazon's "working backwards" memos, in use from the early 2000s, forced teams to write the customer's story before building. Marty Cagan, the product leader, popularised the "opportunity assessment", a short list of questions a team answers before work begins.

The sentence Girija could repeat without sounding glib: "Here is who is hurting, how we know, what it is worth, and why we should fix it now, on a page you can argue with."

3. How it actually works

The sequence matters because each answer constrains the next. The first step is to name the who narrowly enough to count. "Small businesses" is not a segment; "direct-to-consumer brands with a festive peak, shipping from Bhiwandi, Chakan or Hosur" is. The second step is to state the problem in the customer's words, not in the shape of the product. Girija wrote: "I need forty to two hundred pallets for ten weeks, and nobody will rent me less than three months."

The third step is evidence, which the brief arranges by strength. Girija and her colleagues interviewed 40 brands, and 26 of them, or 65 per cent, said they had turned away or delayed peak orders for want of space. That is what people said. The 312 declined enquiries are what people did. A brand that agreed to pay a premium would be evidence of what people paid, the strongest kind, and she did not yet have it.

The fourth step is size, worked through in the next section. The fifth, why us, names a specific asset: Gudam already listed 1,420 warehouses, so the supply side of a short-term product existed without being recruited. The sixth, why now, needs a dated external reason, and Diwali on 8 November supplied it.

Two steps are usually left implicit, and they are the ones Exhibit 1 places in the strip. The first is the decision requested: approve ₹180 lakh, approve a pilot, or decline. The second is the kill criterion: the result that would make the team stop. A brief without them describes an opportunity but asks nothing of anyone.

4. A worked example, line by line

Girija sized the opportunity from the bottom up, multiplying a chain of counts and rates, each with a stated source. The table shows the chain for the first pass.

At ₹246.24 lakh a year the opportunity clears the ₹200 lakh hurdle with room to spare, and a careless brief would end there. But the "25 per cent willing" figure was the weakest in the chain. It came from interviews, where people are polite, and it had never been tested with money. Girija therefore ran a second pass in which only that input changed, falling to 15 per cent.

The second pass flips the verdict. Each one percentage point of willingness is worth 72 brands, or ₹9.85 lakh of revenue, so the hurdle is met only if the willing share reaches 200 ÷ 9.8496, about 20.3 per cent. The honest statement for the page is therefore not "₹246 lakh" but "the opportunity is worth building if slightly more than one brand in five (20.3 per cent) of those with a peak will actually book, and today we have no better evidence than interviews."

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

A brief is not a business case

A business case commits to a solution, costs it in detail and forecasts returns. The brief argues only that a problem deserves attention, and it should survive a change in solution. Mixing the two produces pages that defend a design rather than test an opportunity.

One page is a constraint, not a summary

The limit forces choices about which evidence is strongest. A thirty-slide deck compressed to one page keeps its padding and loses its ranking.

What people said, did and paid are different evidence

Opinions are cheap and behaviour is costly. A declined enquiry shows someone went to the trouble of asking. A paid deposit shows more. The brief should label each item with its rung and be candid about how few rungs it has climbed.

Size is a range with a named swing input

A single figure invites false confidence. A range invites the useful question, "which input moves it?" Girija's range was ₹147.74 lakh to ₹246.24 lakh, and the swing input was willingness to book.

"Why us" is an advantage, not a compliment

"We are good at logistics" is not an answer. A valid answer names something a competitor would need months to copy, such as 1,420 listed warehouses. If any well-funded start-up could say the same sentence, the section is empty.

"Why now" needs a dated cause

A trend ("e-commerce is growing") has always been true. A cause with a date, such as the festive window opening on a known week, creates urgency that a board can verify.

Bottom-up and top-down answer different questions

A top-down figure, a percentage of a large market, is easy and unfalsifiable. A bottom-up chain, as above, is auditable line by line. The first persuades; the second can be wrong in a way someone can point to.

What the brief cannot tell you

It cannot say whether the product will be loved, whether customers will pay a premium, or whether the team can build it. It reduces the chance of working on a non-problem; it does not guarantee a solution. Before relying on one, ask who wrote it, which line is the weakest, and what would change the author's mind.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and large

The six questions are constant, but the weight on each shifts with the kind of business.

SettingWhat dominatesTypical weak spot
ConsumerWho and size: segments are huge and behaviour changes slowlyMistaking downloads for need
B2BEvidence: few buyers, so each interview is a large share of the totalConfusing a user's wish with the buyer's budget
MarketplaceWhy us: both sides must appear togetherSizing one side and assuming the other

Gudam's brief is a marketplace brief. Girija's chain sizes demand, but the supply side matters just as much: warehouse owners must be willing to carve out weekly pallet capacity, and the brief should say so. Stage matters too. An early-stage company has little data and writes briefs that are mostly thinking; a large firm has plenty of data but competing priorities, so its brief is chiefly an instrument for comparing opportunities fairly.

7. Common mistakes

The solution in disguise. The symptom is a "problem" statement that names a feature, such as "customers lack a booking engine". The misunderstanding is that the brief is a pitch. The cheapest diagnostic is to delete the product name and see whether the sentence still describes a customer's difficulty.

A single-point size. The symptom is one confident figure with no sensitivity. The cause is the belief that a precise number looks credible. Diagnostic: change the weakest input by half and see whether the verdict flips. Girija's did.

Borrowed evidence. The symptom is a slide quoting an analyst report in place of customer contact. The cause is confusing market data with proof of this segment's pain. Diagnostic: ask how many named customers the author has spoken to this quarter.

Missing request. The symptom is a meeting that ends with "interesting" and no decision. The cause is omitting the strip in Exhibit 1. Diagnostic: look for a sentence beginning "We ask the board to".

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Girija's page would open with one line of problem and one line of request. It would name the segment and its 7,200 brands, quote the customer's sentence, and rank the evidence: 40 interviews, 312 declined enquiries, no payments yet. It would show the sizing chain with both passes, state that the verdict turns on a 20.3 per cent willing share, and name the assumption least tested. It would end with a pilot and the number that decides it. A reader could disagree with any line, because every line is specific enough to be wrong, and that is the mark of a good brief.

9. What Girija decided

On 7 July, Girija sent Gopinath a page that asked for something smaller than ₹180 lakh. She proposed a manual pilot: Gaurang's team in Nagpur would book pallets by spreadsheet for brands approached by Gulshan's sales team, before Diwali, at a cost of ₹12 lakh in staff time and fees. The team would approach 200 of the 7,200 brands. If at least 41 booked, a willing share of 20.5 per cent against the 20.3 per cent threshold, she would return with a full build request. If fewer, the idea would be shelved with the evidence on record.

The reasoning was that the pilot bought the one input the whole case depended on at about one-fifteenth of the cost, and could finish within the festive season rather than after it. The board accepted the page on 16 July.

To learn next, study sizing an opportunity in more depth, since the brief is only as honest as its size, and then how to design a test that produces evidence of payment rather than opinion. Two questions to sit with. Which line on your own latest proposal would you least like a sceptical director to probe, and what would you need to learn to defend it? If your best estimate sits close to the hurdle, is the right move to refine the estimate or to run a small test?
case40v1-prob.brief:
Anupaat Credit Rails: Three One-Page Briefs

An ambiguous case on defining an opportunity, set in Hyderabad, November 2026

1. The night before

At twenty to ten on the night of Sunday, 15 November 2026, Irawati Mhasalkar had three sheets of paper side by side on the dining table of her flat in Kondapur, Hyderabad, and a fourth, blank, underneath them. The three were opportunity briefs, printed on the template her own team had built two years earlier: six boxes on one page, in a fixed order — who, what problem, evidence, size, why us, why now. She had twice begun a fourth brief and twice stopped.

Mhasalkar was vice-president of product at Anupaat Credit Rails, and by nine the next morning she had to send one of the three pages to Anirvan Yerneni, the co-founder and chief executive. The board pack closed on Wednesday, 18 November; the board met on Friday, 20 November, to allocate the FY28 platform budget. Yerneni wanted one page. "If an opportunity needs two pages," he had written on 3 November, "it isn't an opportunity yet. It's a research programme."

What troubled her was not that the pages were weak. All three were complete; every box was filled. It was that the page which read best was the one she believed least, the page she believed most could not be built in FY28, and the number which made the first page persuasive was the same number as a field note reading half as large.

2. The company, and a signature from 2021

Anupaat was founded in June 2016 by Yerneni, a chartered accountant, and Advaith Beliappa, an engineer who had built billing systems for a telecom operator. Its first product was unglamorous: accounts-payable automation for mid-market Indian manufacturers — firms of ₹300 crore to ₹1,500 crore of turnover, below the Mahindras and Asian Paints of the market, running Tally or SAP Business One. The connectors into those two ledgers are still the company's deepest piece of engineering. The second product came from a crisis: when factories stopped in March 2020 and suppliers began asking to be paid early at a discount, Beliappa's team wired that into the platform. Anupaat did not lend; it arranged.

To arrange, it needed a lender, and on 1 September 2021 it signed one: a five-year exclusive financing agreement with Dhanakshi Finserv, a Mumbai non-banking financial company. Dhanakshi funded the early payments; Anupaat took 0.42 per cent of discounted volume; and clause 11.4 extended the exclusivity to any "credit or credit-like facility offered by the company to participants on the network". In February 2023 Anupaat raised ₹310 crore at a post-money valuation of ₹2,050 crore, on a plan promising a second revenue line by FY28 and revenue of ₹520 crore by FY29. In FY26 it recorded revenue of ₹198 crore (Exhibit 2) and employed 611 people, 528 in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune.

Clause 11.4 ran to 31 August 2026, endable on ninety days' written notice. None was given, and on 3 June 2026 it renewed itself for twenty-four months, to 31 August 2028 — the whole of the year the board is about to fund (Figure 1).

3. The industry

Anupaat sells into the plumbing of Indian working capital, and the plumbing had been rebuilt around it. Electronic invoicing under the Goods and Services Tax became compulsory for firms above ₹5 crore of turnover in August 2023, and from 1 April 2025 firms above ₹10 crore had to report an invoice to the Invoice Registration Portal within thirty days of issue: for the first time the date and amount of a mid-market invoice were on record within a month. The Reserve Bank's TReDS platforms — RXIL, M1xchange, Invoicemart — had made receivable discounting normal for suppliers to large buyers, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act had given consent teeth.

Competition came from three directions, none of them like Anupaat. The TReDS platforms owned the large-buyer end. Payment companies such as Razorpay and software houses such as Zoho were absorbing the small end of payables. Specialist supply-chain lenders were going at distributors directly. Abroad, the United Arab Emirates had legislated an e-invoicing mandate and Saudi Arabia's ZATCA phases were running, so Gulf industrial distributors — Anupaat's exposure ran through one, Mirqab Industrial Supplies LLC of Jebel Ali — were being told to digitise the documents Anupaat already parsed.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In August 2026, with FY26 growth at 21 per cent against 49 per cent two years earlier, Yerneni commissioned three opportunity briefs and told Mhasalkar to bring him one. Brief A, Distributor Float, proposed financing the working-capital gap of the distributors who buy from Anupaat's anchors. Brief B, Compliance Cockpit, proposed selling the anchors a reconciliation and e-invoicing control room built on data Anupaat already held. Brief C, Gulf Payables, proposed following Mirqab into the UAE and Saudi Arabia.

Between 6 July and 21 August a four-person team ran a distributor study already under way, which became Brief A's evidence box (Exhibit 4). In September, Indranil Palepu returned from Dubai with a non-binding letter of intent from Mirqab worth ₹14 crore over three years, lapsing on 31 December 2026. In October, Ileana Rego's team in Toronto restated the three size boxes on one basis (Exhibit 5). On 28 October, while costing Brief A, Ambika Lalwani read clause 11.4 and found the renewal of 3 June. On 6 November, Beliappa sent the capacity note that became Exhibit 6A.

Four things believed in August are no longer safe. Brief A's evidence box says 62 per cent of distributors named the cash-flow gap unprompted; the field note by the same team reports 34 per cent, and both are the same 139 people on different bases. Everyone working on Brief A assumed the exclusivity lapsed in August 2026. The Mirqab pilot was thought representative of Gulf support economics, and Quek's ticket data says it is not. And Brief A's size box rests on an average of 180 distributors per anchor, where the median among them is 110.

5. The people

Eight people carry a stated position into the decision, from seven Anupaat offices (Figure 2).

Irawati Mhasalkar, product, Hyderabad, owns the template and the decision, and holds that Brief A has the only first-hand evidence. Her bonus rides on the second line. Unsaid: she wrote clause 11.4's summary into the 2021 board note without reading the clause.

Anirvan Yerneni, co-founder and chief executive, Hyderabad, wants one page and says the Gulf is "the story a Series D buys"; his incentive is the ₹520 crore FY29 line. Unsaid: an investor asked him in October about non-India revenue, and the board has not been told of the renewal.

Advaith Beliappa, co-founder and chief technology officer, Bengaluru, argues for Brief B: it reuses the ledger and ships in one half-year. He is losing people in Pune. Unsaid: the Tally rewrite must happen in FY28 regardless, and he has put its 38 person-months in Exhibit 6B's committed column rather than asking for them.

Ambika Lalwani, partnerships and risk, Mumbai, says Dhanakshi will consent "as a formality" and that Brief A should be costed at 1.10 per cent; her target depends on that relationship alone. Unsaid: the manager who promised her flexibility left in July, and she had a diary reminder for the notice date.

Ileana Rego, data science, Toronto, will endorse no size box until the three are in one unit. Overruled once in FY25, she intends not to be again. Unsaid: her restatement's 12 per cent adoption rate comes from one anchor's loyalty programme.

Imke Brandhoff, principal designer, Berlin, says the "who" box is the broken one: a distributor is three people — the owner who borrows, the accountant who reconciles, the sales officer judged on collections — and the box holds one line. Unsaid: she drew the template and now thinks it does harm.

Aileen Quek, customer success, Singapore, opposes Brief C on cost to serve and has the tickets to argue it; she carries the 91 per cent retention target. Unsaid: two of her six team leads have resigned, and no Gulf desk can be staffed before April 2027.

Indranil Palepu, global accounts, New Jersey, holds the Mirqab letter of intent and argues that a signed customer outranks a survey; his commission counts letters of intent at half weight. Unsaid: Imad Shaheen's committee has made the unscoped Arabic annexure a condition.

7. Voices

Brandhoff, design review, 9 November: "The box is called 'who' and it takes one line, so the line says 'distributors'. Lalwani, partnership review, 11 November: "Clause 11.4 renewed on 3 June. It is a formality and we will undo it; we put ₹3,500 crore through Dhanakshi last year." Asked whether she had consent in writing: "I have a relationship."

Quek, in the same review: "Mirqab's 1,100 suppliers filed 212 tickets in the January to March quarter — 0.19 per supplier. Across the network's 41,800 suppliers, Mirqab included, we had 1,672 tickets in the same quarter, which is 0.04. Nearly five times the load per supplier, from the account we treat as proof that the Gulf works."

Beliappa, at the end: "I can give you 72 person-months. Brief A needs 94. You can have B, or C, or an argument with me about Tally that you will lose in FY29."

8. The options as Mhasalkar sees them

She had written the options on the back of the blank sheet, and did not trust the list. First, send Brief A as written: the only first-hand evidence, the clearest "why now", and a size that matters if Lalwani is right about Dhanakshi — ₹27.38 crore rather than ₹10.45 crore. It does not fit FY28 H1, and quotes a percentage without its base.

Second, send Brief B: it fits capacity with twenty person-months spare, rests on demand already turned away, and raises no regulatory question. It also answers a question the board did not ask — ₹10.5 crore of ARR against an FY29 ambition of ₹520 crore.

Third, send Brief C: a customer, a mandate-driven "why now", a size box no director will query, four person-months spare — if the Arabic annexure is free, which nobody has checked.

Fourth, send Brief A rewritten: the 34 per cent base in evidence, clause 11.4 in "why us", the median rather than the mean in "size", which takes the number to ₹6.38 crore — an honest page that reads as a case against itself.

Fifth, send no brief, and ask for six weeks and ₹1.2 crore to pilot with forty distributors recruited without an anchor's help — asking the board to fund a question, not an answer.

Three things about the list bothered her. All five options assume the "who" is a distributor, which Brandhoff disputes; 81 of the 181 who were asked, 45 per cent, already paid for a workaround, with 13 more volunteering it where the question was not put — which could mean the demand is proven or that it is served. The list treats the briefs as mutually exclusive, which is true of a one-page format, not of the work: Brief B's reconciliation engine is the underwriting data Brief A needs. And no option changes the page itself.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board pack closes at 6 p.m. on Wednesday, 18 November; the board meets on Friday, 20 November. One page, by nine on Monday morning. ₹26 crore of incremental FY28 operating expense is approved in principle, no more. Cash at 30 September 2026 stood at ₹138 crore against net burn of ₹6.2 crore a month — twenty-two months — and the board wants a breakeven quarter inside FY28. Of the 156 person-months in FY28 H1, 84 are committed, and a hiring freeze holds until that quarter.

Under the RBI's digital lending rules Anupaat arranges and does not lend, so any float product needs a lender, and clause 11.4 makes that lender Dhanakshi until 31 August 2028, with ninety days' notice required. Moving from 0.42 to 1.10 per cent needs Dhanakshi's written consent and, under clause 14, a ₹6 crore exit payment. Lending on Anupaat's own book would need an NBFC licence and, on a ₹400 crore book at fifteen per cent capital adequacy, ₹60 crore of equity. The DPDP work cannot slip past FY28 H1, and the Mirqab letter lapses on 31 December 2026.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Read the six boxes of each brief in Exhibit 1 as claims. For each brief, which box persuades, and which carries the risk?
  2. Exhibit 4 supports both 62 per cent and 34 per cent. Which belongs on a one-page brief, and what must the page say about the base?
  3. Exhibits 2 and 3 disagree about discounted volume. Which figure belongs in a "why now" box, and what does the choice reveal?
  4. Exhibit 5 restates the three size boxes into near-identical revenue. Does that make the opportunities equivalent? What does it destroy?
  5. Where does clause 11.4 belong — in "why us", in "why now", or nowhere? Argue that an artefact which cannot hold it is the wrong artefact here.
  6. What should Mhasalkar send at nine on Monday morning, and what should she say to the board on 20 November about how she chose — including what she now knows about the page she did not send?

11. A quarter past eleven

She picked up Brief C, read the size box — ₹11.6 lakh crore — and put it face down. It was the only number on the table nobody in the company could check, and the only one no director would question. Brief A's page was marked twice in her own hand: a circle round "62 per cent" and, in the margin of "why us", four words written on Thursday and not acted on — whose balance sheet, though?

The blank sheet was still blank. She drew six boxes on it, labelled the first one who, and stopped. Rego would be awake in Toronto; Brandhoff asleep in Berlin; Palepu wanting an answer about the annexure. Before nine the page would go to Yerneni, and it would say one thing, and the company would believe it.
case20v1-prob.brief:
Arogya Pantry: One Page for the Board

A decision case on the opportunity brief

1. Opening

On the morning of Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Anwesha Mahadik, head of product, sat in the glass-walled product room on the second floor of Arogya Pantry's office in Baner, Pune, with a printed one-page brief. The brief proposed a range of low-glycaemic breakfast mixes for households managing diabetes or pre-diabetes, and it asked the board for ₹2.4 crore. The board would meet on Friday, 30 October. Founder-CEO Amitabh Sabnavis wanted the brief in his inbox by Monday, 19 October, and had said he intended to back it.

Mahadik thought the brief read well. That worried her. Each of its six boxes (who, what problem, evidence, size, why us, why now) was filled, and none was empty. But she knew that two of the boxes were filled with confidence rather than proof. She had sixteen days to decide what to carry into the boardroom: the brief as written, a better-evidenced brief, or something smaller.

2. Company background

Arogya Pantry was founded in 2017 by Sabnavis, a former food technologist, to sell ready-to-cook millet breakfast mixes: ragi dosa batter powder, jowar upma, bajra porridge. In the year to 31 March 2026 it recorded revenue of ₹86 crore, about 180 employees, and contract plants near Pune and Nashik. Its channels were its own site (22 per cent of revenue), marketplaces such as Amazon (31 per cent), quick-commerce apps such as Blinkit and Zepto (29 per cent) and general and modern trade (18 per cent).

Saffola, from Marico, and Kellogg's owned the supermarket breakfast shelf; Soulfull and Slurrp Farm had made millets a recognisable aisle. Arogya's edge was taste and a short ingredient list, not scale. Growth had slowed from 41 per cent two years earlier to 19 per cent last year, and Sabnavis wanted a second line.

3. The situation

The idea had come from three places. Customer comments kept saying “sugar”. The ICMR-INDIAB study had reported over ten crore Indians living with diabetes. And Arogya's own Low-Sugar Ragi Mix, launched quietly in January 2026 with no campaign, had begun to reorder well.

Mahadik asked her remote colleagues to test the draft. Aryan Venkatesh, the data scientist in Toronto, pulled the reorder data: Low-Sugar buyers came back more often, but people who pick a low-sugar mix may simply be a different kind of customer. Alisha Gomes, the customer-success lead in Singapore, made fourteen call-backs in her evenings. Nine of the fourteen said they were already buying a national brand’s product for the purpose, and most said they would try Arogya’s if it tasted better. Zainab Kaul, the designer in Berlin, argued the opposite worry: that a “diabetic” label would shrink the appeal of the whole brand, since many families buy for one person and cook for all.

Exhibit 1 sets out the evidence Mahadik held. A survey had gone to 5,150 repeat buyers, meaning customers with two or more orders, in September; 412 replied, a response rate of 8.0 per cent. Of the 412, 206 (50.0 per cent) said someone in the household had diabetes or pre-diabetes. Of those 206, 124 said they would pay at least ₹20 more per pack. That is 60.2 per cent of the 206, but only 30.1 per cent of all 412 respondents, and the two should not be confused. The reorder rows record what people did. Among first-time buyers between January and June 2026, 31.0 per cent of Low-Sugar buyers reordered within 60 days, against 22.0 per cent of buyers of the other mixes.

4. The people

Amitabh Sabnavis, founder-CEO in Pune, wants a second growth line before the next funding conversation,. Aryan Venkatesh, in Toronto, wants no claim in the brief that the data cannot carry. Alisha Gomes, in Singapore, wants customers’ own words in the brief, and fears overpromising on health. 5. Exhibits

Exhibit 2 shows how the draft sized the opportunity and what it asked for. The draft started from the 1,80,000 customers who bought in the twelve months to 30 September 2026. 6. The options

Option A: carry the brief as drafted. Mahadik submits it on 19 October and asks the board for the full ₹2.4 crore. The upside is speed: the January window stays open and Sabnavis is supportive. The cost is that ₹2.4 crore, including ₹80 lakh that is hard to reverse, rests on a survey with an 8.0 per cent response and a sizing step that carries an untested assumption.

Option B: hold the brief and validate first. She runs a ten-week pre-order test with a landing page and sample packs, at an estimated ₹18 lakh, returning to the board in January. The upside is evidence resting on purchase behaviour. The cost is a missed January launch.

Option C: take a staged brief to the board on 30 October. The brief asks for ₹55 lakh now for formulation and nutrition validation, with a four-week pre-order test funded from within that sum, and sets out in advance the results that would release the remaining ₹1.85 crore at a December review. The upside is that the board decides on 30 October, the work starts, and the commitment follows the evidence. The cost is that the January launch probably slips to March,.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Of the six boxes in the brief (who, what problem, evidence, size, why us, why now), which are supported by what customers did and which only by what they said? How would you grade each?
  2. Read Exhibit 1 closely. What does the 31.0 per cent against 22.0 per cent tell you, and what does it not? What would you need to see before treating it as evidence of demand?
  3. Look at the sizing chain in Exhibit 2. Which single assumption moves the answer most, and how would you test it cheaply?
  4. Whose problem is this, the person with diabetes or the household that cooks for them? How does Kaul’s framing change the first box, and does it change the size?

8. A note for the learner

An opportunity brief is a decision artefact, not a summary. Its six boxes force a team to say, on one page, whose problem this is, what the problem is, what evidence exists, how large it is, why this company should be the one to solve it, and why now. A good brief marks each box as seen, heard or assumed, so a reader finds the weakest in seconds.

A well-reasoned answer here does three things. It separates stated intent from behaviour, noting that the survey (an 8.0 per cent response, self-selected) and the reorder gap (a non-random comparison) are different strengths of evidence. It names the assumption doing the most work in the size, which is the leap from respondents to all 1,80,000 buyers. And it matches the size of the commitment to the quality of the evidence.

On those grounds Option C is the most defensible path. It does not spend ₹80 lakh of irreversible money on a weak box. It turns the weakest boxes into a four-week test with go and no-go numbers written before the results arrive. Option A suits small or reversible money; Option B suits a world with no board date. Neither holds. Mahadik’s task is to write the page so Sabnavis, who reads only the first page, can see exactly what the board is buying on 30 October, and what it is not.
exp40v2-prob.brief:
The Opportunity Brief, in Depth

Why the six answers on the page are coupled — and why the expert's real work is finding the narrowest "who" for which size and advantage hold at once.

1. Two decisions in one September

On Monday, 7 September 2026, Tejashri Lotlikar was given seventeen days. She is senior product manager at Tulya Elevator Services, an Ahmedabad firm holding annual maintenance contracts on 11,400 lifts across Gujarat, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu and Rajasthan. Thangam Velusamy, who runs service operations from Coimbatore, had argued for two years that a vibration-and-door-cycle sensor on each lift could predict failures before they stranded anyone. Engineering costed the programme at ₹340 lakh and seven months. Trilochan Mokashi, the managing director, would hear it at the investment committee on Thursday, 24 September, and his rule for new products was fixed: contribution of at least ₹75 lakh in year two, payback within thirty months.

Tejashri had the operational facts. Lifts averaged 4.2 emergency callouts a year at a loaded cost of ₹1,250 — 47,880 callouts, ₹598.5 lakh of service cost a year that Tulya bore under its own contracts. What she lacked was a page that would survive Trilochan reading it twice.

A different decision was being framed 900 kilometres south. On Wednesday, 9 September, Tilottama Navalkar, group product manager at Tatkshan Payout Network in Bengaluru, was asked by Toshan Vichare, the co-founder, to settle an argument before the product forum on Tuesday, 29 September. Tatkshan's app lets gig workers draw earned wages before payday: 8,60,000 registered, of whom 1,92,000 — 22.3 per cent — take an advance monthly at a fee of 1.9 per cent. On 1 July 2026 its two largest aggregator partners moved riders from daily to weekly settlement, widening the gap the product fills. The next population was factory payrolls in Sanand, Halol, Pithampur, Oragadam and Ludhiana. Tirthankar Zambre, the credit risk lead in Nagpur, wanted workers to pay the fee, as today; Tvisha Pardeshi, in partnerships from Jaipur, wanted employers to pay instead.

Both faced the same artefact: one page answering who has the problem, what it is, what evidence exists, how large it is, why this firm, and why now. And both found what this page argues — that the six answers are not independent. Widening the "who" to make the size clear weakens "why us"; tightening it until the advantage is undeniable usually shrinks the size below the hurdle.

2. The idea, and the four schools that disagree about it

Precisely: an opportunity brief is a single page that names a bounded population, states their problem in their terms, ranks the evidence that it is real, estimates the value of solving it through a visible chain of arithmetic, asserts a durable reason this firm should solve it, names a dated external change making now the moment, and requests a decision with a condition under which the author would abandon it.

It was invented against one pathology: proposals arriving as solutions. Theodore Levitt's 1960 argument that railways declined by defining themselves through their product rather than their customers' transport problem is the ancestor of the "who and what problem" half. Barbara Minto's pyramid principle, taught at McKinsey from the 1970s, supplied answer-first discipline with an inspectable structure beneath; Amazon's working-backwards memo, the conviction that prose exposes muddled thinking; Christensen's jobs-to-be-done, a countable "what problem"; Marty Cagan's opportunity assessment, the short question set; and Richard Rumelt's insistence that strategy begins with diagnosis, the reason a good brief reads as diagnosis rather than forecast.

Four schools now claim the artefact. The diagnosis school holds that its only real content is the problem statement and the causal account beneath it: it will sign "a brief with no monetary estimate can still be decisive" and refuse "an unsized opportunity should never be funded". The portfolio school, descended from stage-gate practice, holds that the brief exists to make unlike opportunities comparable: it will sign "every brief must end in a figure computed the same way as every other" and refuse "the number is less honest than the diagnosis". The experiment-first school treats the page as a register of hypotheses whose figures are placeholders: it will sign "the size is whatever next quarter's test says" and refuse "approve the build on this page". The narrative school holds that the discipline lives in the prose: it will sign "a template is a crutch" and refuse "six headings are enough".

3. Mechanics: Tejashri's page, line by line

Each answer constrains the next, and the arithmetic is done in public. Tejashri began with the only question she could count: not "building owners", not "our customers", but lifts whose maintenance is bought by a facility-management agency or a society committee with a written uptime expectation — buyers who have shown they will pay for availability rather than repair. Of the 11,400 lifts, Thangam's team classified 35 per cent, or 3,990, as meeting that test. At an assumed attach rate of 30 per cent, 1,197 lifts would sign in year one at ₹450 per lift per month.

She then built contribution per lift from first principles rather than quoting a price. Subscription contributes ₹5,400 a lift a year. The sensor sells at ₹7,500 against a landed cost of ₹5,200, so hardware contributes ₹2,300 once. Avoided callouts contribute 4.2 × 20 per cent × ₹1,250 = ₹1,050 a lift a year, the 20 per cent being engineering's estimate of failures a vibration signature catches early. Connectivity and cloud cost ₹55 a lift a month, ₹660 a year; retrofit labour ₹900 once. First-year contribution is ₹7,190 a lift, every later year ₹5,790.

Blended over three years the programme earns (₹7,190 + ₹5,790 + ₹5,790) ÷ 3 = ₹6,256.67 per lift-year, computed from the per-lift lines rather than read back off the annual totals.

Here the brief turned on its author. Year-two contribution of ₹69.3063 lakh misses the ₹75 lakh hurdle: the attach that clears it is 7,500,000 ÷ 5,790 = 1,295.34 lifts, so 1,296 lifts — 32.5 per cent of the 3,990 rather than 30. That is a small miss. Payback is not. Against ₹340 lakh of build, year one returns ₹86.0643 lakh and each later year ₹69.3063 lakh, so the remaining ₹253.9357 lakh takes a further 44.0 months: payback at 56 months, not 30. Thirty-month payback needs ₹340 lakh ÷ (₹7,190 + 1.5 × ₹5,790) = ₹340 lakh ÷ ₹15,875 = 2,142 lifts — 53.7 per cent of the SLA-sensitive population, or 18.8 per cent of every lift Tulya maintains.

Two steps are usually left implicit, and they separate competent practice from expert practice. The first is the decision requested, sized to the cheapest decisive experiment rather than to the ambition: Tejashri asked for ₹46 lakh, being 400 rented sensors at ₹5,200 (₹20.8 lakh), retrofit labour at ₹900 (₹3.6 lakh), three months of connectivity at ₹55 a lift a month (₹0.66 lakh), two engineers and an analyst for the quarter (₹18 lakh) and ₹2.94 lakh of contingency. The second is a kill criterion that can fire: of the 400 lifts offered the subscription at ₹450, at least 130 committees — 32.5 per cent — must sign, and callout reduction must reach 20 per cent.

4. When the brief helps, and when it misleads

Four conditions, each testable. One, the population can be counted before the product exists. True for Tulya: the 3,990 lifts sit in a maintenance database with contract terms attached. Weaker for Tatkshan, whose 1,900 employers come from dated association directories. Two, the problem is stable enough that this quarter's evidence holds next year. True of lift breakdowns, governed by physics and duty cycles; only partly true of wage timing, which moved under Tatkshan on 1 July. Three, sufferer and payer can be named separately, as Tulya's residents and their society committee can. Four, a decision is actually available — where a regulator or a signed contract has removed the choice, the brief is theatre.

It becomes actively misleading in three situations. Where the opportunity is a platform investment whose value appears only through products not yet conceived, the demand for a sized population punishes the right decision: the brief for a general-purpose data layer always loses to a feature. Where the problem is a compliance obligation, "why us" is vacuous. And where the market is being created rather than served, bottom-up sizing anchors on a population that does not yet exist.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Multi-product firms hit the attribution seam. Tulya's avoided-callout line of ₹12.5685 lakh is a reduction in the service division's cost, not revenue in the new product's ledger, and whether it may be counted is a political question dressed as an accounting one. Mature firms write briefs in contribution, name the division whose budget moves, and let two general managers argue in front of the committee, not inside the document.

Two-sided situations break the single-population assumption: a brief that sizes demand and assumes supply is half a brief. Regulated products invert the evidence hierarchy, because what customers would pay for may be unlawful to sell; Tatkshan's page must carry the Reserve Bank's digital lending expectations about who the lender of record is, and that belongs in "why now", not in a risk appendix. Hardware imposes a second clock: the ₹5,200 sensor has lead times and a field failure rate, so Tulya must commit to volume a software brief would never mention. AI-native opportunities strain "evidence" hardest, since capability improves between writing and decision; the honest author dates the assumption.

At the seams, practice differs from policy. A brief endorsed in advance by the business-unit head arrives with its conclusion pre-agreed and functions as a record, while a brief from an unsponsored team is read as a request for permission to find a sponsor.

6. Eight distinctions between a competent brief and an expert one

The six answers are coupled, not six fields

The competent author fills the sections in order and treats a weak "why us" as a writing problem. The expert knows "who" is the only free variable and that moving it moves everything else. The tell is a brief whose population definition changed three times between drafts while the "why us" paragraph survived word for word. Tejashri's page reports the coupling: the lift count that justifies the build is nearly double the count for which Tulya's installed base is a real advantage.

The sufferer and the payer differ, and size belongs to the payer

A page that quotes a resident trapped between floors and then sizes from society maintenance budgets has crossed a seam without noticing. The expert names both parties in the first two lines, sizes from the payer's budget, and keeps the sufferer's words as evidence. The obvious reading — that strong user pain implies willingness to pay — fails wherever the budget holder is insulated from the pain.

"Why now" needs a clock, not a trend

"Urbanisation is driving lift installations" has been true for twenty years and will be true for twenty more, which makes it an argument for doing this sometime. Tatkshan's "why now" is a date: the settlement change of 1 July 2026. The expert's test is to re-date the sentence twelve months earlier and ask whether it still reads as true; if it does, the section is empty.

Evidence is ranked by what it cost the customer

Said, did, paid and kept paying are four rungs, and a thousand survey responses sit below one cancelled contract. Tulya's 47,880 logged callouts are a "did"; its committee interviews a "said"; it has no "paid" at all, which is what the ₹46 lakh pilot buys. Tatkshan starts two rungs higher: 1,92,000 workers already pay 1.9 per cent every month.

State the size as the threshold the decision turns on

A point estimate invites a debate about the estimate. Tejashri's page does not lead with ₹69.3063 lakh; it leads with "this clears the hurdle if 32.5 per cent of SLA-sensitive committees sign, and pays back in thirty months only at 53.7 per cent." A break-even can be tested; a forecast can only be defended.

Time windows must match, in both directions

A result measured over a quarter and compared against an annual hurdle is a defect even when the arithmetic inside each is right, and the error runs both ways: annualising a festive quarter overstates, judging a seasonal product on a lean quarter understates. The related discipline is the unit of analysis: Tulya's is a lift-year, because technicians are dispatched per lift and contracts renew yearly.

Ask for the cheapest experiment that moves the swing input

Tejashri's ₹46 lakh pilot is 13.5 per cent of the ₹340 lakh build and buys the two inputs the case rests on. The competent brief asks for what it wants; the expert brief asks for what would make the next request answerable. The diagnostic is "what is the smallest sum that would change your mind?"

"Why us" is a stock with a half-life

Tulya's advantage is 11,400 lifts it already visits monthly, which no competitor can assemble quickly. But two national lift majors were shipping monitoring hardware as standard on new installations, so the advantage applies only to the existing base and drains as buildings are replaced. The expert gives the advantage a date by which it will no longer hold.

7. How this differs by product type and stage

The six questions are constant; the binding constraint moves. In consumer products the hard question is "who", because segments are enormous and the work is finding the subpopulation whose behaviour already differs. In B2B and enterprise it is "evidence", because twelve conversations can be a meaningful share of the market and the tempting error is reading a user's enthusiasm as a budget holder's intent. In platforms it is "why us", since both sides must be sized. In hardware it is "why now", because tooling imposes a calendar software briefs ignore. In AI products it is "size", because the population servable in month nine differs from the one measured today.

Exhibit 5. Where the brief usually breaks, by setting

Hardware and physical goodsWhy nowVolume committed before attach is known
