Stage changes the reader, not the questions. In a firm of thirty people the brief is mostly thinking, written to stop the founders building the third idea of the month. At Tulya's size it compares one opportunity against others competing for the same seven months of engineering. In a large listed company it becomes a governance document, and authors write to survive review rather than to be right.

8. Three worked examples

Tatkshan, and the brief that was really about who pays. Tilottama wrote one page per option with identical chains. Of 1,900 employers, 6 per cent — 114 — would sign within twelve months. Their headcounts were not uniform: 66 sites of 250, 34 of 600 and 14 of 1,400, which is 56,500 workers and an average of 495.6 a site, not the 500 her first draft assumed. Eighty per cent, 45,200, were eligible; half installed, 22,600; and 65 per cent of those activated, 14,690, which is 32.5 per cent of the eligible base. On worker-pays, 60 per cent of activated workers transact in a month — 8,814, being 39.0 per cent of installs and 19.5 per cent of eligible workers — taking 1.8 advances of ₹2,450, so ₹4,410 a worker a month, ₹388.6974 lakh of monthly volume and ₹7.3853 lakh of fee at 1.9 per cent: ₹88.623 lakh a year on a ₹60 lakh build of four months. On employer-pays the fee disappears, transactions rise to 80 per cent of activations (11,752 workers), and revenue is ₹18 per eligible worker per month, ₹216 a year, ₹97.632 lakh — on a ₹185 lakh build of nine months. The second is 10.2 per cent larger and pays back in 22.7 months against 8.1.

Tulya's earlier success, where the brief was small and right. In 2024 Thangam briefed a dull opportunity: pre-kitted spare-parts pouches for the eleven commonest failures. The population was 340 technicians; the evidence was 47,880 callouts of which 31 per cent needed a second visit for a part; the arithmetic was that removing a second visit saves ₹1,250. It asked for ₹18 lakh and passed in one meeting, because every line referred to a report the company already produced.

Toran Dental Network, where the approach failed. Toran runs 128 clinics in nine cities, 6.2 lakh patient visits a year at an average realisation of ₹1,850 — ₹114.7 crore. In 2024 Tanaya Belvalkar's team briefed a patient app top-down: a large dental market, a 3 per cent capture, a ₹212 lakh build over fourteen months. It shipped to 1,86,000 installs and 21,100 monthly actives — 11.3 per cent — and the assumed nine-point lift in repeat bookings measured 1.4 points. The brief had failed at "who": its population was every patient, a group with no shared problem. The recovery narrowed the unit from patient to treatment plan. Of 7,400 multi-visit orthodontic and implant plans issued in the six months to 30 June 2026, 3,219 — 43.5 per cent — lapsed before the second appointment. At ₹46,000 average plan value and 32 per cent contribution, a completed plan is worth ₹14,720, so those lapses carried ₹473.8368 lakh of forgone contribution in that half-year. The intervention was ₹26 lakh for a calling desk, a financing tie-up and one reminder flow. In the quarter to 30 September 2026, of 3,600 plans issued, lapse fell from 43.5 to 33.5 per cent — 360 plans saved, ₹52.992 lakh of contribution in one quarter, which Tanaya refused to annualise because that quarter held the school-holiday peak for orthodontic starts.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

The solution in disguise. Sign: the problem statement contains a noun the company does not sell yet. Diagnostic: delete every product name and see whether a customer's difficulty remains. Caught late, the team cannot change course, because the brief specified the artefact.

The borrowed population. Sign: the "who" is a number from an industry report rather than a query someone can re-run. Diagnostic: ask for the list. Tulya's 3,990 lifts exist as rows; Tatkshan's employers do not.

The uncrossable gap between sufferer and payer. Sign: strong interview quotes and no named budget line. Diagnostic: ask who signs the invoice and what they spend on this today. Caught after launch it is the most expensive failure of all: the product works and nobody buys it.

Hurdle gaming. Sign: a base case clearing the hurdle by one to three per cent, or a kill criterion phrased as "if adoption is disappointing". Diagnostic: recompute at the hurdle. Tejashri's year-two figure missed by ₹5.6937 lakh, and she wrote the miss into her first paragraph rather than lifting the attach rate to 33 per cent.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether a brief should carry a monetary estimate at all. The diagnosis school at its strongest: early estimates are not merely uncertain, they are anchors, and every later debate is then conducted in units the first guess chose; its evidence is that the sizing of successful new categories was usually wrong by an order of magnitude, in both directions. The portfolio school at its strongest: an organisation with twelve teams and seven months of capacity must choose, and refusing comparable units does not remove the comparison, it moves it into the corridor where seniority decides. It would be wrong if firms that size late allocated capital as well as firms that size early.

Bottom-up versus benchmarked sizing. Bottom-up chains like Tejashri's are auditable line by line and therefore falsifiable; their weakness is that plausible rates compound multiplicatively, and 35 per cent × 30 per cent is a product of two guesses. The benchmarking position holds that a comparable firm's observed attach rate beats your own survey, because it is a "did". It would be wrong if the comparable's pricing, channel or regulation differ enough to invalidate the transfer.

Whether hurdle rates belong in briefs. Against: thirty-month payback rules systematically kill platform and option-like investments, and several of the largest businesses of the last two decades would have failed such a test at inception. For: without a hurdle every brief clears, and firms that abandoned hurdles mostly discovered pet projects rather than options. What would settle it is evidence about which error a given firm actually makes.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied the brief writes the six sections well. Someone who has internalised it spends most of the available time on the definition of the population and treats the other five answers as consequences. They quote break-evens rather than forecasts, and they know which line of their own page is weakest and say so before being asked.

12. What each protagonist decided

On 24 September, Tejashri asked the committee not for ₹340 lakh but for ₹46 lakh and one quarter. Her page said the opportunity was real; that at 30 per cent attach it missed the ₹75 lakh hurdle by ₹5.6937 lakh and missed thirty-month payback by 26 months; and that the build justified itself only at 2,142 lifts, a number reachable only by selling to lifts Tulya does not maintain, where its advantage is weak. Trilochan approved the pilot.

On 29 September, Tilottama recommended worker-pays, on the ground that the employer-pays option's 10.2 per cent revenue advantage was not worth a build three times larger, a payback 14.6 months longer and a second buyer Tatkshan had never sold to. She wrote the condition under which she would be wrong: if employer sign-on in the first two clusters materially exceeded 6 per cent, the constraint was her own assumption, not demand.

Discussion questions. First, Tejashri's brief concludes that the build pays back only at a population where her "why us" is weakest: is that a reason to decline, to build a cheaper version, or to acquire the advantage she lacks? Second, under what conditions is a 10.2 per cent larger opportunity worth a three-times larger build? Third, Toran's first brief passed review and its second probably would not have, since ₹26 lakh for a calling desk is not a product proposal: what does that tell you about what review processes select for?

13. Going deeper

Sizing an opportunity — the brief is only as honest as its chain, and this is where compounding rates are treated properly. Writing a problem hypothesis — the one sentence the page rests on, in the customer's units. Surfacing assumptions — the discipline by which Tejashri found that 20 per cent callout reduction was an engineering opinion. Riskiest assumption first — the rule that turns the weakest line into next quarter's work. Validating a problem hypothesis — moving evidence from "said" to "paid" without building the product. Frequency and intensity — whether 4.2 callouts a year is an annoyance or a crisis. Vitamin vs painkiller — the test separating a problem people pay to remove from one they report.
exp40v2-prob.riskiest:
Riskiest assumption first

Which single assumption, if wrong, kills the idea — and have I tested it?

1. Two companies, one mistake in two shapes

On Tuesday 8 September 2026 Parimala Sundarrajan, head of product at Panna Grid Works in Coimbatore, opened the plan she had helped write. Panna sold a retrofit kit — meter, motor controller, dashboard — to Tiruppur knitwear units for thirty per cent of verified electricity savings over thirty-six months, nothing up front. The plan put 450 kits into the field over fourteen months and ₹9.20 crore of capital before the first savings invoice, against ₹17.5 crore of cash and ₹38 lakh a month of burn; the board met on Friday 9 October.

Eleven pilot kits had run seven months, saving between 3.2 and 14.8 per cent of a unit's bill, median 9.6, mean 9.31, which Prabhakar Ghorpade, the co-founder, read as settled. Rachit Deodhekar worried about the hardware, Purvi Jhalani about the sample, and Paulina Gorska, the firmware contractor in Kraków, about nothing unwritten. On Tuesday 15 September, a week later, Sundarrajan sat in a Tiruppur shed while an owner explained that her measured saving was no saving: his production was down that month, and he would not pay a share of a number he could not rebuild from his own books. Nobody had written that sentence down as an assumption.

The same morning in Jaipur, Roshni Bhimani, vice-president of product at Pukhraj Jewel Systems — store software for 240 jewellery chains across 3,100 stores, ₹96 crore of recurring revenue — received a proposal for a module to estimate the karat of exchanged gold from photographs, replacing the counter manager's eye. Prachi Sehgal's team in Pune costed the build at ₹5.03 crore; Qurban Tyabji had three willing chains and Rutger Pauwels in Antwerp the assay workflow. At one 22-store chain, 792 of 4,400 quarterly valuations ended in a karat dispute and 297 of those 792, or 37.5 per cent, walked out: at ₹13,490 of margin a basket, ₹1.60 crore a year, of which the module claimed two-thirds. Every assumption on Sehgal's list concerned the model; none concerned the manager.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

An assumption is a belief the plan's outcome depends on that has not been checked against evidence. The riskiest is not the one the team feels least sure about; it is the one with the largest expected loss — the probability it is false times the money that would be unrecoverable when its falsity becomes visible. Testing it first is a claim about sequence: spend the next rupee of discovery where it averts the most expected loss per rupee and per day, seldom where uncertainty feels thickest.

The history runs down two channels that never merged. The engineering channel begins with Barry Boehm's spiral model of 1988, which ordered each iteration by the highest remaining risk and treated testing as the purchase of information. The decision-analytic channel is older: Frank Knight's 1921 split between measurable risk and unmeasurable uncertainty, Ronald Howard's decision analysis of 1966, and Howard Raiffa's 1968 value of information, still the only rigorous answer to whether a test is worth running. Rita McGrath and Ian MacMillan married the two for managers in 1995 — write the plan as a reverse income statement, list the assumptions its numbers depend on, and retire them in order of leverage.

The start-up literature rediscovered it with better marketing: Eric Ries's leap-of-faith assumptions in 2011, Ash Maurya's riskiest-assumption ranking in 2012, Rik Higham's 2018 claim that such a test precedes the minimum viable product, Teresa Torres's continuous discovery in 2021 — all against one pathology: teams test what is cheap and enjoyable, then find the fatal flaw after the money is gone.

Exhibit 1. Five schools: what each would and would not sign
SchoolWould signWould refuse
Risk sequencing (Boehm, Maurya)Order tests by loss averted per rupeeThat the most uncertain goes first
Decision analytic (Raiffa, Howard)Test only where information is worth its costThat the riskiest always goes first
Sensitivity (McGrath, MacMillan)Rank by how far the key number movesThat invented probabilities belong in it
Continuous discovery (Torres, Cagan)Assumptions attach to solutions; test weeklyThat building stops for one assumption

3. Mechanics, worked through

Expert practice has six steps, two of them usually implicit and one usually skipped.

Step 0, write the plan as a number. A median unit draws 42,000 kWh a month at ₹7.90, a bill of ₹3,31,800. A kit costs ₹1,58,000 landed, ₹22,000 to install and ₹900 a month to service: ₹2,12,400 over thirty-six months. Panna earns thirty per cent of the saving, so contribution per kit is 36 × 0.30 × 42,000 × 7.90 × r − 2,12,400, or ₹35,83,440r − ₹2,12,400, where r is the saving rate.

Step 1, surface what is not on the list. The four assumptions Panna's team wrote down were all things it controlled or measured. The one Sundarrajan found in a shed — that an owner would accept the method by which the saving was computed — belonged to no function, which is exactly why it was absent. Gary Klein's pre-mortem is the reliable technique: assume the money is gone and write the obituary privately.

Step 2, convert each belief into a threshold, then a probability. "The kit saves enough" cannot be false. Set contribution to zero and break-even is 2,12,400 ÷ 35,83,440 = 5.93 per cent of the bill; the pilot median of 9.6 per cent clears it, and two of the eleven units, 18 per cent, did not. Five colleagues then put the chance that owners would reject the measurement method at 0.30, 0.40, 0.45, 0.55 and 0.60 — mean 0.46, median 0.45 — privately, because the first number spoken in a room becomes the room's number.

Step 3, price the failure at the moment it becomes visible. Damage is not programme size but capital sunk when the truth arrives. Panna committed in four tranches: ₹110 lakh of firmware and dashboard in months nought to two, then 150 kits at ₹1.80 lakh each in months three, seven and eleven. A refusal to sign surfaces in month three, with ₹380 lakh committed and 150 uninstalled kits worth ₹148.5 lakh at 55 per cent resale: a loss of ₹231.5 lakh. A refusal of the measurement method surfaces at the first invoice in month ten and costs ₹610.4 lakh: a factor of 2.6 between them.

Loss if false is capital committed by the month of visibility less recoveries at 55 per cent of cost: A2 ₹650 lakh less 40 kits (₹39.6 lakh), A1 ₹650 lakh less 60 kits (₹59.4 lakh). Expected loss is chance false times loss; rows are not summed.

Step 4, state what the test cannot tell you. No test resolves an assumption completely, so experts carry a resolution fraction: the share of uncertainty removed. Asking twenty-five owners to sign a verification protocol, before any kit is offered, resolves perhaps seventy per cent of A2 — it cannot say what an owner does when a real invoice lands, only what he signs when nothing is at stake.

Step 5, charge the delay to the tests that block. Panna burns ₹38 lakh a month, so a test that holds the build twelve days costs ₹15.2 lakh on top of ₹1.8 lakh of fieldwork. Tests beside the build are charged nothing, because they stop nothing, so sequencing is only ever about the two or three that do. And because probabilities are not independent — a method the owner accepts also fixes the number Panna is paid on — the ranking is rerun after every result.

4. When the rule applies, and when it misleads

The conditions are four claims, each testable before an experiment is designed.

Exhibit 5. Four conditions, applied to both
ClaimPannaPukhraj
C1. One failure makes the others irrelevantTrue: refused measurement makes revenue uncollectableTrue: an overridden model earns nothing
C2. A test costs less than the loss it averts and ends before the next commitmentTrue: ₹1.8 lakh, before the tooling commitTrue: ₹9.5 lakh against ₹5.03 crore
C3. Both outcomes lead to different actionsTrue: refusal means a flat feeTrue: high override shrinks the build
C4. It is about the world, not our executionPartly: reliability is execution, retired by doingTrue: manager behaviour is a fact

Where the rule misleads matters more than where it works. First, the two-way door: if the commitment is reversible for less than the test costs, act and watch. Second, the endogenous assumption: a network good's value to the hundredth user does not exist before the ninety-ninth arrives, and a test at zero liquidity measures the test. Third, the legal fact: whether a device may sit in series on a metered supply is a question for counsel, not an experiment. Fourth, when no instrument exists at the fidelity required. Fifth, when the team knows the assumption is false and intends to change it.

5. Hard edge cases

In a two-sided market the fatal assumption is rarely a belief; it is a product of rates. Raunaq Events Exchange, matching wedding clients to vendors in Indore, carried 1,200 enquiries a month, of which 468 cleared a ₹3 lakh budget; 164 of those 468, or 35 per cent, were matched to a vendor set, and 41 of the 164, or 25 per cent, booked. At ₹27,600 of take on a ₹4.60 lakh booking that is ₹11.32 lakh a month, and multiplying any one rate by 0.6 ends the business, so the ranking runs over the links rather than the chain. The weak link was matching, where supply was thin and exclusive — and exclusivity lived in the vendor contract.

In multi-product companies the riskiest assumption often sits on another team's roadmap: Pukhraj's module needed an override log the platform team had deprioritised, a belief both fatal and unowned, and at such seams the honest test is a written commitment with a date. In hardware plus software lead times constrain sequence: Panna's housing tooling took fourteen weeks, and a test finishing after the commit is a post-mortem with a budget. In regulated settings it is often binary and cheap to resolve, as with the Bureau of Indian Standards hallmarking rules governing how Pukhraj may describe a karat estimate. In AI-native products the trap is structural: accuracy is measurable, so it gets measured, while the fatal assumption is that a human acts on the output. Mature companies say they test first and mostly reverse it: budget approved, then the test run as insurance and called a pilot.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

The riskiest assumption is usually not on the list. A competent team writes four or five, all about what it can measure or control. The tell is homogeneity: if every item belongs to a function in the room, the dangerous one lives in a counterparty's head.

Riskiest is not least certain. Expected loss is probability times money, and the two get conflated. The tell is a list sorted by how anxious people sound: Panna's team feared the saving rate, which had the second-largest expected loss and the worst information per rupee.

The threshold is computed, not chosen. A kill condition of about ten per cent is a preference; 5.93 per cent follows from the cost structure. The tell is a round number, which survives the data because it was never derived.

Damage depends on when you would find out, since what you lose is what is sunk at discovery. The tell is a damage column with one figure repeated, or a one-to-ten score, which hides that a late-visible assumption is far dearer.

The resolution fraction is the most fudged number in discovery, because nobody writes down what a test cannot tell them. The tell is the absence of a sentence beginning "this will not tell us whether"; Panna's test resolved seventy per cent of A2 at best, and the residual thirty is where the money was.

Assumptions are correlated, and resolving one can promote another to fatal, since a test that passes changes the plan and the changed plan has different assumptions. The tell is a ranking produced once in a workshop. This is what killed Rath Tyre Industries below.

Who runs the test determines what it finds. The plan's owner recruits the friendly sample, asks the leading question and reads ambiguity kindly, usually without noticing. The fix is to specify the sample before anyone knows who is in it.

In outcome-priced businesses, measurement is the product. Wherever revenue is a share of a saving, the counterfactual is unobservable, and the assumption that the counterparty accepts your construction of it outranks every technical one. The tell is a contract with no baseline clause.

7. How the practice changes with product type and stage

The arithmetic does not change by product type. What changes is the ratio of test cost to loss and the speed of the cheapest honest test, which decide whether sequencing matters. In consumer products tests are cheap and fast against the loss — a pin-code launch with a repeat threshold runs six weeks for ₹26 lakh — so the debate is moot. In enterprise software a priced contract offered to a named list costs ₹2.4 lakh and three weeks, but the answers arrive one buyer at a time, which is why enterprise teams parallelise more. In marketplaces it is concierge matching on the weakest link, in hardware bench ageing against a costed bill of materials, in AI products shadow mode with an override log, as Pukhraj ran for ₹9.5 lakh in twenty days.

Stage changes who can afford to be wrong. A seed-stage company risks time, so crude tests are rational. At scale the loss column grows faster than the test column — Pukhraj put ₹5.03 crore at risk against a ₹9.5 lakh test, 53 to 1 — but the political cost of a fail rises too, and the large firm's characteristic failure is running the test after the budget is approved.

8. Three worked examples

Panna Grid Works. Contribution per kit is linear in the saving rate, so the mean suffices for a go decision. At the pilot mean of 9.31 per cent contribution is ₹1.21 lakh a kit; at 4 per cent it is a loss of ₹69,062, which over 450 kits is ₹3.11 crore.

Qulfi Dessert House: a plan killed for ₹26 lakh. A Bengaluru frozen-dessert brand planned a ₹4.20 crore quick-commerce launch. Its riskiest assumption was repeat, not trial: the plan needed 1.9 orders per acquired customer in sixty days. A six-week test in three pin codes produced 2,60,000 impressions, 31,200 first orders at 12 per cent, 6,864 second orders at 22 per cent and 2,265 third orders at 33 per cent — 40,329 orders from 31,200 customers, or 1.29 each. At ₹46 of contribution an order and ₹18.2 lakh of media, acquisition cost ₹58.33 a customer, so 1.27 orders merely repaid acquisition and the observed 1.29 covered the customer and nothing else.

Rath Tyre Industries: the approach applied correctly, and failure anyway. The Nashik retreader ranked its assumptions in March 2024 and tested the top one in April: would fleet owners pay a monthly per-tyre fee instead of buying retreads? Eight of nine fleets signed, so ₹5.60 crore went into fourteen months of sensors and software. By October 2025, 62 fleets paid ₹28,000 a month, ₹17.36 lakh in all, and 41 per cent of sensor readings were missing against a contractual billing threshold of 85 per cent: drivers removed sensors and workshops refused to refit them. Twenty-three of 62 fleets, 37 per cent, churned within four months. Two failures compounded: the nine test fleets were Rath's own retread customers, so the sample was selected for willingness, and data integrity, ranked second, was never re-ranked once the first passed. The recovery was a three-week study in November 2025 costing ₹4.2 lakh — available nineteen months earlier — which found 9 per cent loss at the 1,240 fleets with in-house workshops. Rath re-priced to that segment: 48 fleets at ₹38,000 a month, ₹2.19 crore of recurring revenue.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Each mode has a signature weeks before the loss, and a question that surfaces it.

Exhibit 7. Five failure modes
Failure modeEarly warningDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Testing the comfortable assumptionThe first experiment prototypes the fun featureIf this is negative, do we stop?Panna: ₹610.4 lakh by month ten
Unfalsifiable assumptionsThe list reads as slogans about valueWhat number would prove this wrong?Discovery that cannot conclude
Friendly sampleThe sample comes from existing accountsWho is in it, and who chose them?Rath: ₹5.60 crore, fourteen months
Ranking produced onceNo new ranking after the first resultWhat became fatal when that passed?Rath: 23 of 62 fleets churned
Accuracy measured, adoption assumedAn evaluation dashboard, no override logWhat does the human do when it disagrees?Pukhraj: ₹5.71 crore a year over-paid

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Sequential against parallel. The sequencing school holds that attention is scarce: a team running six tests resolves none. The parallel school answers that most tests do not block, that delay is a real cost, and that one cheap test rarely justifies stopping. The disagreement turns on the blocking fraction: three of Panna's five tests blocked, so sequencing mattered; where nothing blocks, the argument is a category error.

Do subjective probabilities belong in the ranking? The sensitivity school says no: rank by how far the key number moves, because moves are computable and probabilities invented. Applied to Panna, a ten per cent adverse move in each parameter ranks cleanly and exposes the weakness: three parameters have identical leverage, and the assumption that threatened the company does not appear, because a binary belief has no ten per cent move.

The last row is not a sensitivity but a binary, which is why ranking cannot be left to sensitivity alone.

Can desirability be tested for something that does not exist? The commitment school, strongest in hardware and deep technology, argues that a test asks people about a thing they cannot imagine, citing products that failed every survey and succeeded anyway. The sequencing answer is that this confuses testing demand with testing a falsifiable mechanism: nobody could have surveyed demand for Panna's kit, but a protocol an owner will or will not sign costs ₹1.8 lakh. The position is wrong wherever such a mechanism exists and right where the fatal assumption concerns a world the product creates.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied the idea ranks assumptions in a workshop and tests the top item. Someone who has internalised it spends the effort on assumptions not on the list, prices damage at the moment of visibility rather than at programme size, charges delay only to blocking tests, and reruns the ranking after each result, because the question is never what is riskiest but what is riskiest now.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Panna's protocol test ran from Monday 21 September to Friday 2 October — ten working days, ₹1.8 lakh. Of 25 owners approached, 19 signed a written verification protocol, but only 7, or 28 per cent, accepted a baseline normalised for production volume, against a pre-registered threshold of 15. A2 failed. On Friday 9 October Sundarrajan did not ask for ₹9.20 crore. She proposed a flat ₹7,500 a month per kit for thirty-six months in place of the savings share — ₹2,70,000 of revenue against ₹2,12,400 of cost, ₹57,600 of contribution — and funding for 120 kits: ₹2.16 crore of capital for ₹69.12 lakh of contribution. The flat fee moves measurement risk to the owner, who stays ahead unless his saving falls below 2.26 per cent of his bill; the worst pilot unit saved 3.2 per cent.

Pukhraj's shadow mode ran twenty days in six stores: managers wrote their estimate, saw the model's, then recorded the final number. Across 1,042 valuations, 458, or 44 per cent, were overridden, and 371 of the 458, or 81 per cent, upwards, towards a higher payment to the customer. Of the 212 overrides with a reference assay, the model was closer in 164, or 77 per cent. At ₹9,400 a gram of 22-carat gold and nine grams a transaction, a 0.6-carat upward adjustment costs ₹2,307, so 371 of them cost ₹8.56 lakh in twenty days — ₹49,933 per store-week, which annualises crudely to ₹5.71 crore a year across 22 stores, against a dispute prize of ₹1.07 crore. On Friday 2 October Bhimani cancelled the ₹5.03 crore module and funded ₹1.15 crore for a second-opinion tool that keeps the manager's number primary and logs every override — the instrument that makes the real assumption, whether owners will enforce a machine valuation against their managers, testable.

Riskiest assumption first

Which single assumption, if wrong, kills the idea, and has it been tested?

1. A plan with six months of build in it

On Monday 3 August 2026, Hemlata Sirohi, head of product at Imarat Nirman Exchange in Hyderabad, opened a roadmap that ran to six months and a spend of ₹3 crore. Imarat was a start-up with ₹14 crore of seed funding and fixed costs of ₹9 lakh a month. Its idea was to let small building contractors order TMT steel bars (the ribbed rods used in concrete) through a phone app, receive them at the site, and pay 45 days later. Imarat would buy from mills and large stockists, sell at a 2.5 per cent spread, and borrow working capital at 13 per cent a year from a non-banking finance company (NBFC), a lender regulated by the Reserve Bank of India.

The co-founder and chief executive, Gurmeet Lamba, had spent a decade selling steel. Harshada Pawar, who handled mills and stockists, held letters of intent for supply. Ishwar Dongre, the credit analyst, had drafted a scorecard. Everyone could explain why it would work; nobody had been asked which part they could least afford to have wrong.

Sirohi asked, and five answers emerged: contractors might not leave their usual dealer, mills might not hold price, contractors might not repay, the NBFC might charge more, deliveries might miss 24 hours. The board would meet on Friday 28 August and was expected to release the first ₹1.5 crore. If the build began on the wrong belief, Imarat would spend most of a crore learning what a cheap test could have said in a fortnight.

2. The idea

An assumption is a belief the plan depends on but nobody has checked. The riskiest assumption is the one most likely to be false and most destructive if false. Testing it first is a rule about sequence: before building or hiring, find the belief whose failure ends the idea and spend the first money trying to break it. If it fails, the team has lost days, not quarters.

The habit has two ancestors. Software engineers, notably Barry Boehm with his 1980s spiral model, argued that projects should attack their highest risks early because late discovery of a fatal flaw is the costliest. Start-up writers then carried it into new ventures: Eric Ries popularised "leap-of-faith assumptions" around 2011, and Ash Maurya urged founders to rank risks and test the worst first. All were solving one problem: teams tested what was easy rather than what mattered.

Sirohi's sentence for the meeting: "Of everything we are assuming, which one, if false, makes the rest irrelevant, and what is the cheapest way to find out?" It holds two questions.

3. How it actually works

Step one: write each assumption as a falsifiable statement. "Credit matters" cannot be wrong. "Contractors will pay within 45 days, with losses below 0.9 per cent of sales" can be, because it names a behaviour, a threshold and a population.

Step two: estimate how likely each is to be false. This is judgement. Sirohi had five colleagues write numbers privately and averaged them, so the most senior voice could not set the figure.

Step three, usually implicit: estimate the damage if it is false. A delivery promise slipping to 48 hours is a nuisance; a repayment failure that eats the spread is not survivable. Imarat scored damage from 1 to 10, where 10 means the idea cannot continue.

Step four: multiply and rank. The product is a crude score whose job is to order the list, not price it.

Step five, also usually implicit: attach a cost and duration to the cheapest honest test. The riskiest assumption is not automatically tested directly, because a fatal assumption with a ruinous test may deserve a cheaper proxy first.

Exhibit 1. Imarat's five assumptions, ranked (average of five private estimates)
AssumptionChance false (%)Damage (1-10)Risk score (% x damage)Direct test cost (₹ lakh)Days
A3. Contractors repay on 45-day credit within the loss limit45104506.060

Risk score is chance of being false, in per cent, multiplied by damage. It is an ordering device with no rupee meaning.

Repayment scores 450, which is 67 per cent above the next item (270), and the gap is the story. The other four are real risks, but each has a workaround that costs money rather than the business. Only repayment attacks the spread directly.

4. A worked example, line by line

Testing repayment directly meant lending real money for 60 days, at ₹6 lakh. Dongre proposed a proxy: dealers already sold steel on credit to the same kind of contractor, and their ledgers held repayment history. Forty contractors agreed to share dealer records and GST filings. Cost ₹0.8 lakh, time 12 days.

Before opening any ledger, Sirohi wrote down what would count as failure, the step most teams skip. She needed the break-even loss rate: the share of sales that can be lost before the spread stops covering the cost of money. A typical contractor buys 18 tonnes a month at ₹58,000 a tonne, so monthly sales are 18 x 58,000 = ₹10,44,000. The 2.5 per cent spread earns ₹26,100. Funding for 45 days at 13 per cent a year costs 10,44,000 x 0.13 x 45 / 365 = ₹16,733. The remainder, ₹26,100 less ₹16,733, is ₹9,367, which is 0.90 per cent of sales. Any credit loss above that and the contractor costs Imarat money.

Exhibit 3. Monthly economics of one contractor at three credit terms (₹, nearest rupee)

Margin before credit loss is spread less cost of funds. The 45-day column is the first pass; the others change only the credit term. Credit loss is 1.25 per cent of 10,44,000.

The ledgers arrived on Monday 17 August, thirteen days after work began on Tuesday 4 August. Dealers had sold these 40 contractors ₹48 crore of steel on credit in twelve months and written off ₹60 lakh. The loss rate is 60 lakh divided by 48 crore, which is 1.25 per cent. Against the 0.90 per cent limit, the assumption failed: at 45 days each contractor would cost Imarat ₹3,683 a month.

The second pass changes one input. Hold spread, funding rate and losses fixed, and cut credit from 45 days to 30. Funding falls to ₹11,155, margin rises to ₹14,945, and break-even becomes 1.43 per cent, clearing the observed 1.25 per cent by 0.18 points. Net is ₹14,945 less ₹13,050, or ₹1,895 a month. At 60 days the idea is hopeless. The same contractors pass or fail on one term-sheet number, which is worth learning before building.

With fixed costs of ₹9 lakh a month, ₹1,895 per contractor means 9,00,000 / 1,895, rounded up, which is 475 contractors to break even.

5. Nuances worth knowing

Riskiest is not the same as least certain

Risk is uncertainty multiplied by consequence; teams that rank by anxiety test the wrong thing.

The kill condition comes before the test

Sirohi computed 0.90 per cent before opening a ledger. Had she looked first, 1.25 per cent could be rationalised either way. A threshold fixed in advance converts a result into a decision.

A proxy is not the thing itself

The ledgers recorded losses to customers who knew their dealer personally; Imarat's would owe an app. Failure on a proxy is informative. Success on a proxy only earns the right to a more direct test.

Losses are concentrated, so averages mislead

The ₹60 lakh came from four contractors, an average of ₹15 lakh. Thirty-six of forty, 90 per cent, paid in full. A portfolio rate of 1.25 per cent can hide a flawless majority and a ruinous tail, and screening the tail may matter more than pricing.

Assumptions interact

Thirty-day credit helps repayment but may hurt switching, since contractors who value 45 days may stay with the dealer. Re-rank after every test.

It is not an MVP, and it cannot say the idea is good

A minimum viable product is the smallest build that teaches something; this principle decides what to learn, and Imarat's test needed only a spreadsheet. Surviving it removes one way of dying and leaves the rest. Before relying on the ranking, ask who produced the probabilities and whether the first speaker anchored them.

6. How it changes by product type and stage

In consumer products the riskiest assumption is usually behavioural: will people change a habit and keep the change? Tests are cheap, since a landing page reveals intent within days. In B2B it is more often a buyer who is not the user, or procurement time, and each data point is a conversation. Imarat is B2B with a lending core, where the risk is the counterparty's behaviour and a mistaken test costs real money.

In a marketplace the classic fatal assumption is the cold start, a chain rather than a single belief, so the test should find the weakest link. Pawar's letters of intent were not treated as evidence of price stability; a price held through a month of rising steel costs is a fact.

Early-stage companies risk little but time, so tests can be crude. A large company has reputation to protect, and its fatal assumptions are often a regulator's tolerance or another unit's cooperation. Reserve Bank of India rules on digital lending constrain how an app may route money, and an engineer would never list that risk.

7. Common mistakes

Testing the comfortable assumption. Symptom: the first experiment is a prototype of the exciting feature. Misunderstanding: confusing interesting with dangerous. Diagnostic: ask of each experiment, "If this comes back negative, would we stop?"

Writing assumptions that cannot fail. Symptom: a list of phrases like "customers value convenience". Misunderstanding: treating a slogan as a hypothesis. Diagnostic: write the number that would prove each item wrong.

Moving the goalposts. Symptom: a test fails and the team explains why it does not count. Misunderstanding: treating the threshold as a negotiating position. Diagnostic: compare the date on the threshold document with the date of the data.

Stopping after one pass. Symptom: the team declares the idea validated. Misunderstanding: believing there is only one assumption that matters. Diagnostic: re-run the ranking with the result in hand and see what rises.

8. What good looks like

The five assumptions sit on one page as falsifiable statements, with independent probabilities and a cost and duration beside each. The failure threshold is written and dated before data arrives. The first test is the 12-day, ₹0.8 lakh proxy rather than the ₹6 lakh lending experiment, and its result is taken seriously whichever way it falls. Then the ranking is redone and the next test chosen. The roadmap is reordered, not abandoned.

9. The decision

On Friday 28 August Sirohi did not ask for the ₹1.5 crore. She proposed a 90-day pilot with 25 hand-picked contractors on 30-day credit, with a rule to stop if losses ran above 1.43 per cent of sales. Twenty-five contractors at ₹10,44,000 meant ₹2.61 crore of sales a month, or ₹7.83 crore over three months. At 1.25 per cent, expected losses would be about ₹9.79 lakh, the price of the test and a fraction of the build avoided. Dongre would use the pilot to see whether screening out the four-in-forty tail pushed losses well below 1.25 per cent. The board funded the pilot, not the build.

Study the four product risks next, which supply the categories assumptions are drawn from, then scoping the minimum viable product, which turns a surviving assumption into the smallest thing that can test the next.

Two questions to sit with. The ledger test could only fail the assumption, never confirm it: what result would have persuaded you that a direct lending test was safe, and what threshold would you have written first? And in your own work, which assumption would you rather not test, and is the reluctance a clue to its score?

Rujuta Dental Devices: What to Fund First

Which belief to test first, when the clock belongs to somebody else.

1. Sunday night, Hyderabad

On the night of Sunday, 29 November 2026, Lasya Chaganti sat in the Rujuta Dental Devices product office in Jubilee Hills, Hyderabad. On Thursday, 3 December, the board's product committee would meet in Mumbai and ask one question: what should Rujuta spend the next ten weeks and ₹6.5 crore finding out?

Chaganti, the chief product officer, had spent ten months building Rujuta Lite: a ₹29,000 clear-aligner course for mild crowding, planned from photographs the patient took on a phone, with no technician visit and no clinic appointment. The full product, at an average realisation of ₹62,000, began with a technician arriving at the patient's home with an intraoral scanner. Lite dropped that visit; the Chakan line, the Mumbai orthodontists, the resin contract and the 340-strong field force stayed.

On her desk were four proposals, each from a colleague she trusted, each answering a different question. Zinal Khamkar wanted to prove the scan; Dr Suhasini Taskar the screen; Lahari Mallavarapu wanted to treat patients and wait; Mitchell Boone wanted to sell. Between them they had named five things that could be false, and nobody had shown which would end Lite rather than merely slow it.

What made the night long was a sentence in Mallavarapu's memo: the number that decided whether Lite was a business could not be observed before month seven of treatment, and every deadline fell earlier.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2022

Rujuta was founded in March 2019 by Anuradha Devdhar, six years in category management at Lenskart, and Dr Suhasini Taskar, an orthodontist practising in Dadar. The idea borrowed the eyewear playbook: take the inconvenient part of the purchase to the customer's home, keep the clinical judgement in-house. FY2026 revenue was ₹148.0 crore: ₹130.2 crore from 21,000 aligner courses at an average realisation of ₹62,000, and ₹17.8 crore from retainers, whitening and accessories.

The decision that shaped everything after it came in June 2022. Rather than buy from a contract manufacturer, Rujuta committed ₹58 crore to a captive printing and thermoforming line at Chakan, outside Pune, sized for 42,000 course-equivalents a year, and signed a five-year resin agreement to June 2027 with a minimum purchase of ₹11.4 crore a year. The line bought four-day turnaround and a device margin no competitor matched. It also created a fixed cost that wanted volume, and in FY2026 ran at half capacity (Exhibit 5).

Two later decisions narrowed the room further. In November 2023, after a patient's treatment was stopped at stage nine and reverted, the board adopted a Clinical Governance Charter: a named orthodontist signs every plan, and any case above 4 mm of crowding needs an in-person examination before the first aligner ships. In January 2024 the company put its scan technicians on payroll rather than franchising them; by 2026 there were 340, at ₹11.6 crore a year and ₹3.4 lakh each. Lite would make most of their visits unnecessary.

3. The industry

India's clear-aligner market in 2026 split three ways. Orthodontists prescribed Invisalign and its clinic-channel rivals at ₹1.5 lakh and above. Chains such as Clove Dental and Apollo White Dental sold mid-priced in-clinic treatment. A direct-to-consumer tier — makeO toothsi, Illusion Aligners and Rujuta among them — sold at ₹55,000 to ₹80,000 with a home scan, performance media and EMI through Bajaj Finserv or UPI AutoPay mandates via Razorpay. Nobody had yet sold a planned course in India below ₹35,000, or one with no clinician in the room.

Regulation sat unevenly. Aligners are notified medical devices under the Medical Device Rules and Chakan held its licence, but advisers had not closed whether software that proposes tooth movements is itself a device. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act made Lite's weekly selfies a consent problem of a particular kind: facial images, held seven months, processed by a model in Toronto. The National Dental Commission's position on who may supervise orthodontic treatment was argued about in Rujuta's compliance notes, never settled.

In October 2026 Marsa Dental Group, fourteen clinics in Dubai and Sharjah, signed a term sheet to white-label Lite: ₹24.6 crore over three years, a ₹3.2 crore advance against a working remote-scan product by 31 January 2027, and a ₹48 lakh penalty — 15 per cent — on default. Behind it, Mitchell Boone in Edison, New Jersey, had US brands wanting Rujuta's manufacturing but needing an FDA route nobody had begun.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Lite began in February 2026 as a research note (Figure 1). Mallavarapu, a data scientist in Toronto, built a model that reconstructed an arch from twelve phone photographs. Against the intraoral scan of the same mouth, across 180 arches from 96 patients, the mean deviation was 0.41 mm. Taskar read that as below the tolerance that mattered for mild cases, and the note circulated with the word equivalent in its title. Nobody recorded that the 180 sets had been shot by Rujuta's own technicians, in good light, with someone else holding the phone.

In June 2026 Mathilde Vogt's capture flow — a guided sequence with retractors shipped in advance — went to internal testers, where 71 per cent of staff attempts produced a usable set first time. It reached real prospects in Hyderabad and Jaipur in August: of 9,600 leads offered the photo option, 4,128 produced a usable set, or 43.0 per cent (Exhibit 3). The company had budgeted for 65 per cent.

In September, Taskar ran the eligibility study. Four hundred cases already scanned intraorally went through the photo pipeline, and the algorithm's call was set against a three-orthodontist panel's consensus on the same sets. The two agreed on 325 of the 400 cases; Cohen's kappa, from the cells in Exhibit 2, was 0.62. In 46 of the 234 cases the algorithm called eligible — 19.7 per cent — the panel would have refused remote treatment.

In November, Mallavarapu re-ran the measurement on photographs patients had taken themselves. Mean deviation was 0.68 mm, 1.12 mm in the posterior region. The February figure was not wrong; it had measured a different thing. Six days later the Series C term sheet arrived: ₹310 crore at ₹1,860 crore pre-money, conditional on a second product line showing paid traction by 31 March 2027.

5. The people

Lasya Chaganti, 38, chief product officer, Hyderabad. Owns the recommendation. Position: test the one assumption whose failure ends Lite first. Not saying: she suspects that assumption cannot be tested by 31 January, and cannot see how to tell a board so.

Anuradha Devdhar, 44, co-founder and chief executive, Mumbai. Position: Lite is the second product line the term sheet demands, and a study is not traction. Incentive: a valuation resting on growth, with idle Chakan capacity the first thing investors ask. Not saying: she has told Marsa January is achievable and not told her own committee.

Dr Suhasini Taskar, 51, co-founder and clinical director, Mumbai. Position: the screen is the risk; if a case that needs a clinic gets an aligner, the Charter has failed. Incentive: her signature is on every plan, and her registration. Not saying: she wrote the February note that said equivalent, and has not retracted it.

Zinal Khamkar, 36, vice-president of engineering, Pune. Position: reconstruction fidelity is the root cause, and ₹1.1 crore settles it in six weeks. Incentive: a scan problem is one her team can fix. Not saying: her November diagnostics put the posterior deviation down to how patients hold the phone — Vogt's problem, not hers.

Mathilde Vogt, 33, design lead, Berlin. Position: 43.0 per cent of leads producing a usable set is the cheapest way to kill Lite, and nobody has proposed testing it. Not saying: she thinks June's 71 per cent was presented in a way that invited the mistake.

Lahari Mallavarapu, 31, staff data scientist, Toronto. Position: refinement and abort rates are unmeasured, and no accuracy work substitutes for treating patients. Incentive: she designed the pilot. Not saying: her role costs ₹1.42 crore a year fully loaded against ₹38 lakh for the same hire in Hyderabad.

Serena Lim, 40, head of customer success, Singapore. Position: the plan has no answer for a Lite patient whose treatment stalls in month four. Incentive: her team absorbs every failure, against targets set on the full product. Not saying: three of her seven team leads will not stay if Lite ships at this ratio.

Mitchell Boone, 49, head of international sales, Edison, New Jersey. Position: Marsa signs in January or the pipeline behind it closes for a year. Incentive: variable pay on contracted value, not outcomes. Not saying: Marsa's counsel has advised their chief operating officer, Tariq Haroon, that a licensed dentist must examine a patient before treatment begins there — making Dubai clinic-assisted, not remote. Rujuta's counsel has not seen it.

7. Voices

“Zero point six two is not a bad kappa for a screening instrument. It is a terrible one for a gate. And the panel was two-thirds my own people.”

— Dr Suhasini Taskar, clinical review, Mumbai, 18 November

“Everyone is arguing about millimetres on arches we never received. Fifty-seven per cent of the people we offered it to never got us a usable set. Fix that and you are at least choosing from people who can operate the product.”

— Mathilde Vogt, design review, Berlin, 20 November, 09:14 CET

“Tariq's counsel is clear with him that a dentist in their clinics sees the patient first. He is treating us as a lead engine for his chairs. If that is what we sell, Dubai tells us nothing about whether remote works.”

— Serena Lim, message to Chaganti, 22 November, 11:02 SGT

“And if a patient in Indore is at stage eleven with teeth that have stopped moving and no clinic that will take her? Who does she call, and what do we pay the clinic?”

— Serena Lim, committee pre-read, 27 November

8. The options as Chaganti sees them

Chaganti had written the four proposals in the order of what they cost (Exhibit 6). Option A, at ₹1.1 crore, is the only one that reports before the Marsa milestone of 31 January 2027. Option B is the one Taskar will accept, and speaks to the Charter. Option C is the only one that observes the number Lite's contribution depends on, and it reports in July. Option D, at ₹14.0 crore, exceeds the committee's authority by ₹7.5 crore and alone yields a board-ready read on paid traction, nineteen days after its date; Option C's 1,200 patients are treated at the discount its ₹2.8 crore absorbs, so they are not paid conversions.

The page had a property she had not noticed while drawing it: each proposal tested one assumption, as though the beliefs were independent. But Exhibit 4's mild-band rate came from cases screened off intraoral scans; Lite would screen the same mouths with a worse instrument, so assumptions one, two and three are one chain, and a clean result on the first says little about the third. Vogt's point cut the other way: if only 43.0 per cent of willing leads produce a usable set, Lite's population is not the one these studies sample. And Lim's patient in Indore was not about the product at all: it was an assumption about a referral network that did not exist, that no proposal costed, and that the Charter would require the moment a remote case needed a chair.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The committee meets on Thursday, 3 December 2026, in Mumbai, with discretionary authority of ₹6.5 crore; anything larger waits for the full board in February. The Marsa advance of ₹3.2 crore is contingent on a working remote-scan product by 31 January 2027, which Boone reads as a product, not a study. The Series C term sheet requires paid traction from a second product line by 31 March 2027. The resin agreement runs to June 2027 at a minimum of ₹11.4 crore a year against ₹8.9 crore consumed in FY2026. Cash stood at ₹61.4 crore on 30 September 2026 against net burn of ₹4.3 crore a month: 14.3 months of runway. The Charter, amendable only by the board, requires an orthodontist's signature on every plan and an in-person examination above 4 mm of crowding. Three hundred and forty technicians sit on payroll at ₹11.6 crore a year, and Lite would make their visits unnecessary. The consent position on facial images held for seven months has never been tested by a regulator.

At one in the morning Chaganti wrote a line in her notebook and underlined it twice: which of these, if it is false, means we never ship at all? She could not get the list below three.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. List every assumption Rujuta Lite depends on, and for each, what evidence the case offers and what it does not.
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 are both offered as support for Lite. Read each against the population it came from: what does each license you to believe, and what has it been used to imply?
  3. What would have to be true for Exhibit 4's 28.0 per cent mild-band rate to transfer to Lite — and what would make it understate Lite's experience?
  4. Figure 3 asserts that each proposal tests one assumption. Redraw it, and say what your version implies about the order of the work.
  5. Suppose the assumption whose failure would end Lite cannot be observed before any deadline the company faces. What are Chaganti's choices then, and what does each cost if she is wrong?
  6. What should Chaganti do on Monday morning, 30 November, and what should she say on 3 December? Write the three sentences she opens with, and name what she is asking the board to accept.

The office lights went off at twenty past one. Her recommendation was due in the committee pack by nine on Tuesday, under a heading that read What we will know, and when. She had not filled it in.
case20v1-prob.riskiest:
Ranikhet Orchards: The Box That Must Be Reordered

A decision case on testing the riskiest assumption first

1. Opening

On Monday, 19 October 2026, Leher Chaturvedi sat in Gurugram with a 41-slide launch plan for a weekly fruit subscription open in front of her. The board of Ranikhet Orchards would meet on Friday, 23 October. The founder, Aakash Dhillon, wanted to say "go" with Diwali on 8 November only three weeks away and the winter apple season about to peak. Chaturvedi, the company's head of product, had to tell him what to fund first.

The plan was good, and everyone who had read it could name something to worry about, though no two people named the same thing. Chaturvedi had to decide which worry, if true, would end the idea, and test that one first.

2. Company background

Ranikhet Orchards buys apples, plums, pears, kiwi and walnuts from about 1,400 grower families in Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, grades and packs them at two facilities, and sells them under its own label. Revenue in FY2026 was ₹64 crore. Most came through partners such as BigBasket, Flipkart Grocery and Zepto, and the rest from its own site and app. The founder started the company in 2017 after watching growers in Kotgarh accept thin auction prices; the pitch is the farm gate, a named valley and a fair price.

Amazon Fresh and Reliance Retail's JioMart sell similar fruit at discounts Ranikhet cannot match. Ranikhet's own site has a loyal but small audience: an email list of 9,400 subscribers and a blended customer acquisition cost of ₹1,100 per new household.

3. The situation

In August Dhillon asked for recurring revenue. Chaturvedi's team proposed the "Orchard Box": a weekly crate of six varieties of seasonal fruit, packed in Gurugram, delivered chilled in Gurugram and Bengaluru, at ₹949 per box, paid by UPI AutoPay or card through Razorpay. The plan assumed a custom app, cold-chain contracts and a marketing push, for ₹2.4 crore.

Three pieces of evidence existed. A survey of the email list drew 1,150 responses from 9,400 invited (12.2 per cent), and 598 respondents said they would "definitely" or "probably" subscribe at ₹949, which is 52.0 per cent of respondents. A one-off Kinnaur apple crate sold in December 2025 had 3,200 buyers that month, of whom 410 ordered again within 60 days (12.8 per cent). And of 18,400 crates shipped from Shimla to Bengaluru partners last year, 386 arrived damaged (2.1 per cent).

In Exhibit 1, each box earns ₹260 after fruit, packing, freight, fees and support, which is 27.4 per cent of the ₹949 price. Against an acquisition cost of ₹1,100, a household must take 4.23 boxes on average before Ranikhet recovers what it spent to win it. Nobody had ever measured how many boxes a household would take.

Exhibit 1: Economics of one Orchard Box (₹)

Bar runs from x = 40 to x = 514.5, that is 474.5 px for ₹949. Segments sum to ₹949. Figures are the team's FY2026 estimates for a Gurugram-packed box; fruit is exempt from GST.

Lorenz Weidner, the Berlin designer, argued that a box a household cannot skip or pause is a box it will cancel, so the app comes first. Arman Tandon, the data scientist in Toronto, pointed out that the survey measured intention and the crate a one-off purchase, and neither measured a subscription. Anushka Bhatnagar, the customer-success lead in Singapore, had run a meal-kit subscription elsewhere and said households are lost in the first month.

4. The people

Aakash Dhillon, founder, Gurugram. He wants a launch announced before Diwali and sees the app as proof that Ranikhet is a consumer brand.

Abhinav Pradhan, head of sourcing, Shimla. He answers to 1,400 growers and wants the cold-chain contracts signed first: bruised fruit in Bengaluru, he argues, no app can rescue.

Lorenz Weidner, designer, Berlin. He wants the app flows finished.

Anushka Bhatnagar, customer success, Singapore. She wants real households before anything is built; in her experience the retention curve was set by the second delivery.

5. The assumptions

Chaturvedi spent the weekend listing what the plan took for granted, asking of each what happens if it is false and what it costs to find out (Exhibit 2).

Exhibit 2: What the launch plan assumes

A. Growers can supply six varieties every week for 16 weeksRanikhet already supplies BigBasket and Zepto year-roundSubstitute varieties; a nuisanceLow
B. Fruit reaches Bengaluru in 72 hours with under 3 per cent damage386 of 18,400 crates damaged (2.1 per cent)Pay more for freight or change partnerMedium
C. A household will pay ₹949 for a box598 of 1,150 survey respondents (52.0 per cent) say they probably wouldLower the price; contribution fallsLow
D. A household will keep ordering for 4.23 boxes or moreNone for subscriptions; 410 of 3,200 reordered a one-off crate (12.8 per cent)Acquisition cost is never recovered; the idea has no economicsLow if run by hand

Base for the survey figure is respondents (1,150), not the 9,400 invited. Base for the crate figure is the 3,200 households that bought in December 2025, each followed for 60 days.

A, B and C could each be wrong without ending the idea: supply can be patched, freight repriced, a price lowered. D is different. If households take two boxes and stop, nothing repairs the arithmetic in Exhibit 1, and D was the one assumption with no direct evidence.

If a household stays from one week to the next with a constant probability, it takes 1 ÷ (1 minus that probability) boxes on average. Setting this to 4.23 gives weekly retention of 76.4 per cent, so the share of first-box households still ordering in week four would be 44.5 per cent (0.764 cubed). Chaturvedi rounded this to 45 per cent, which is 135 of 300 households, and wrote it on the whiteboard as the bar the pilot must clear.

6. The options

Chaturvedi saw three distinct courses, summarised in Exhibit 3.

Option 1: Build and launch. Approve the ₹2.4 crore plan: ₹95 lakh for the app, ₹60 lakh of minimum cold-chain commitments and ₹85 lakh of marketing. Its upside is speed and a Diwali announcement. Its cost is that the money is spent before anyone knows whether households reorder, and the cold-chain commitments are not refundable.

Option 2: Secure supply and cold chain first. Sign the freight contracts and trial reliability before recruiting anyone. It protects the brand, but costs ₹60 lakh in commitments, and the 2.1 per cent damage rate suggests B is largely met. It leaves D untouched.

Option 3: A hand-run pilot to test repeat ordering. Recruit 300 households in Gurugram and Bengaluru, half from the email list and half from paid social media so that the loyal list does not flatter the result. Take orders on WhatsApp, collect payment through Razorpay links, and run six weekly boxes at ₹949 from 30 October with no app. Acquisition at ₹600 a household costs ₹1.80 lakh; if every household took all six boxes, 1,800 boxes at an all-in delivered cost of ₹759 each would cost ₹13.66 lakh, against ₹17.08 lakh of revenue. Cash at risk is ₹15.46 lakh, and week four falls on 20 November.

Exhibit 3: The three options

OptionMoney committed (₹ lakh)Time to a reading on DWhat it leaves untested
1. Build and launch240.00Only after launchNothing is tested first; D is learned last
2. Cold chain first60.00None before launchC and D

Option 1: ₹95 + ₹60 + ₹85 lakh = ₹240 lakh. Option 3: ₹1.80 lakh acquisition + ₹13.66 lakh delivered cost (1,800 boxes × ₹759, being ₹689 of Exhibit 1 costs plus ₹70 extra courier cost), gross of ₹17.08 lakh revenue (1,800 × ₹949) if every household took all six boxes.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, what does the 4.23-box figure depend on?
  2. Why is the 52.0 per cent survey result weaker evidence for D than it first appears?
  3. Rank assumptions A to D in Exhibit 2 by damage if false and cost to test.
  4. Which option would you take to the board on 23 October, and what result in week four would make you stop?

8. A note for the learner

This topic asks one question: which single assumption, if wrong, ends the idea, and have we tested it? Teams usually test what is easiest or what the loudest person fears. Instead, list assumptions, ask what each failure costs and what finding out costs, and run first the test that is fatal and cheap.

By that logic Option 3 is defensible. Assumption D is fatal, unmeasured and cheap to test by hand. Options 1 and 2 spend ₹240 lakh and ₹60 lakh on assumptions that are patchable (A, B, C) or partly evidenced (B). Pradhan is right that bruised fruit damages the brand, but a 2.1 per cent damage rate can be priced; two-box households cannot be priced away.

A good answer also designs the test honestly. The threshold of 135 of 300 households in week four is a screening bar under constant weekly retention, not confirmation of 4.23 boxes, and recruiting beyond the email list guards against a flattering sample. It notes that a hand-run pilot cannot show whether an app would raise retention. And it states the miss in advance: below 135, Chaturvedi returns to the board with the reasons households stopped.

Option 3 costs Dhillon a Diwali announcement and gives him a number on 20 November.
exp20v2-prob.assumptions:
Surfacing assumptions

What must be true for a problem statement to hold, ranked by how uncertain it is and how much it matters.

1. A Monday in June

On Monday 9 June 2025, Chirantan Basu opened the weekly leadership meeting at Chitrakoot Pulses Exchange with a single sentence on a slide: "Small dal mills in central India lose six to nine per cent of their selling price because wholesalers outside their district cannot find them." Chitrakoot, headquartered in Nagpur, was a seven-year-old business-to-business marketplace for pulses. Chirantan, its head of product, had written it after eleven weeks of work, and the chief executive, Chaitanya Rao, liked it.

The decision on the table was a nine-month build of a "mill discovery" product, in which a mill in Latur or Akola would list its graded stock and a wholesaler in Hyderabad or Kolkata could find it, request a sample and place an order. Chaitanya wanted to commit ₹1.8 crore, or 180 lakh. Engineering in Indore would take 96 lakh, field operations run from Coimbatore by Chellam Pillai would take 42 lakh, mill onboarding incentives 24 lakh, and a reserve to guarantee early payments to mills 18 lakh. The four lines sum to 180 lakh.

Chellam, a fourteen-year veteran of mills, asked a question that Chirantan could not answer: "If a wholesaler in Kolkata has never tasted this mill's toor dal, what makes you think he will buy it because he can now see it?" The slide said mills were hidden. It did not say what had to be true for visibility to turn into orders. If the sentence was wrong in any one place, the company would spend most of a year building a catalogue nobody ordered from.

2. The idea

An assumption is a belief that a plan silently relies on and that has not been checked. A problem statement is a plan in compressed form: it names a person, a pain and a reason the pain persists. Every one of those clauses leans on other beliefs, and the leaning is invisible because the writer shares the beliefs. To surface assumptions is to write down, in testable language, everything that must be true for the statement to hold, and then to rank that list by two things: uncertainty, meaning how little the team actually knows, and impact, meaning how badly the plan fails if the belief is false.

The practice answers a specific failure: managers plan new ventures with confidence suited to old ones. Rita McGrath and Ian MacMillan proposed in a 1995 Harvard Business Review article on "discovery-driven planning" that a venture team should keep an explicit assumption checklist and revisit it as evidence arrives. Eric Ries popularised the "leap-of-faith assumption" from 2011, and David Bland and Alex Osterwalder later drew the ranking as an "assumptions map". The common thread: find the weakest belief before signing the largest cheque.

The sentence Chirantan could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib was this: "Before we spend ₹1.8 crore, let us list what has to be true and find out cheaply which of those beliefs we are least sure of and can least afford to get wrong."

3. How it works

The mechanics have seven steps, and practitioners usually leave the second, fifth and sixth implicit. First, state the problem in one sentence with a named customer. Second, split the sentence into its clauses, because assumptions hide in conjunctions: "mills lose money because wholesalers cannot find them" contains a claim about loss, a claim about cause and a claim about what removing the cause would do. Third, ask of each clause "for this to be true, what else must be true?" until the answers can be observed.

Fourth, rewrite each answer so it could be proved wrong: not "wholesalers will try new mills" but "at least a quarter of wholesalers offered a sample from an unknown mill will place a trial order". Fifth, record who believes it and why. A belief held because three mill owners said so differs from one nobody has thought to ask about. Sixth, give each belief a confidence, a percentage the team agrees honestly, and an impact, a score from one to five for how much of the plan collapses if the belief is false. Seventh, rank, and attach to the top items the cheapest test that could change the team's mind.

Exhibit 1. The seven steps compressed into five boxes. The work lives in the arrows: the second arrow is where hidden beliefs are made visible, and the fourth is where the team is forced to put a number on what it knows.

The sequence is not optional. Teams that jump from sentence to tests test whatever is easiest; teams that rank without falsifiable rewriting end up scoring slogans.

4. A worked example

Chirantan, Chellam and Chandrasekhar Naidu, the Indore engineering lead, spent two days producing six assumptions, each with an agreed confidence that it is true and an impact score; uncertainty was then computed. Using one minus confidence would treat a belief held at 10 per cent as highly uncertain, when the team is fairly sure it is false. This page instead uses a measure highest at 50 per cent confidence: uncertainty = 1 − |2 × confidence − 1|. At 40 per cent confidence, 2 × 0.4 − 1 = −0.2, whose absolute value is 0.2, so uncertainty is 0.8. The risk score is uncertainty multiplied by impact.

#What must be trueConfidenceUncertaintyImpact (1-5)Score
A1Distance, not price or quality, is why unknown mills stay unsold40%0.854.0
A2Wholesalers will place trial orders with a mill they have never used50%1.055.0
A3Mills will keep stock and price listings current60%0.843.2
A4Grade and quality can be judged from samples and certificates30%0.642.4
A5Wholesalers will pay within 15 days70%0.631.8

Exhibit 2. First-pass scoring. Scores sum to 5.0 + 4.0 + 3.2 + 2.4 + 1.8 + 0.8 = 17.2. Confidence figures are team judgement, not measurement.

The ranking is A2 (5.0), A1 (4.0), A3 (3.2), A4 (2.4), A5 (1.8), A6 (0.8). The top two account for 9.0 of 17.2, or 52.3 per cent of the total score. The surprise is that A2, which everybody had treated as obvious, was a coin toss on a belief whose failure would sink the plan, while A4, held at only 30 per cent, ranked fourth because the team was fairly sure it was false.

Next came cost. Each belief got its cheapest decisive test.

#Cheapest testCost (₹ lakh)

A2Concierge trial: Chellam's team hand-brokers orders for three weeks6.0

Exhibit 3. All six tests together cost 15.0 lakh, which is 8.3 per cent of the 180 lakh build budget (15 ÷ 180).

Second pass. The interviews finished first. Seventeen of the twenty mills, 85 per cent, named buyer reach as one of their top two problems. The team did not adopt 85 per cent, because the mills were reached through Chitrakoot's own contacts and would skew friendly. It moved A1 to 80 per cent. Only that one input changed. Uncertainty becomes 1 − |2 × 0.8 − 1| = 1 − 0.6 = 0.4, and the score becomes 0.4 × 5 = 2.0, down from 4.0. The total falls to 17.2 − 4.0 + 2.0 = 15.2, and the new order is A2 (5.0), A3 (3.2), A4 (2.4), A1 (2.0), A5 (1.8), A6 (0.8). A2 now carries 5.0 of 15.2, or 32.9 per cent.

Exhibit 4. The same six beliefs ranked before and after one new input. A1 drops from second to fourth; nothing else changed.

The 1.5 lakh spent on interviews reordered a 180 lakh decision and pointed the next 6 lakh at A2.

5. Nuances to become aware of

An assumption is not a fact, a risk or a hope.

A fact has been observed. A risk might happen to a plan that otherwise holds: "a competitor may launch". An assumption is a condition the plan requires: "wholesalers want new suppliers".

Uncertainty is not the same as low confidence.

As the worked example showed, a belief held at 10 per cent is not uncertain; the team has effectively concluded it is false. Treat it as a decision to drop the clause, not a test.

The scores are judgement.

Confidence of 40 per cent has no frequency behind it. Its value is that it can be argued with. Have members score privately; the spread is information. Chirantan scored A3 at 80 per cent and Chellam at 40: the mills Chirantan had met were tidy, those Chellam knew were not.

Assumptions must be falsifiable.

"Customers will like it" cannot be wrong, so it cannot be tested. A usable one names a population, a behaviour and a threshold.

Assumptions depend on each other.

A2 requires a wholesaler to trust an unseen mill, which leans on A4. If A4 fails, A2 fails whatever its own score, so a cheap test of A4 may go first.

It is not an experiment hypothesis.

Surfacing produces a ranked list. A hypothesis turns one item into a specific prediction with a method.

It cannot find what nobody thought of.

A list contains only beliefs someone could name. The unknown unknowns, such as a state-level change in dal procurement policy, stay invisible. Invite people who disagree, and interview customers first.

Questions to ask before relying on it.

Who wrote the list, and who was absent? Is every item testable within weeks? Are the tests cheap against the cost of being wrong?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and late

In consumer products the dominant assumptions concern attention and habit, and large samples make tests fast. In B2B they concentrate on the buying process, who signs and who pays; samples are small, so interviews and concierge trials substitute for statistics. In a marketplace, as Chitrakoot discovered, assumptions come in pairs, one about each side, plus a third about whether they will transact once matched. The riskiest belief is usually about the harder side to attract, here the wholesaler.

Stage changes the stakes. An early-stage company can run the exercise in an afternoon but has little data. A large company has data but suffers from institutional confidence: beliefs held because never challenged. There the fifth step, recording who believes each item and why, matters most, because "everybody knows" is where weak assumptions hide.

7. Common mistakes

Listing only the comfortable. Symptom: every assumption on the list has confidence above 70 per cent and no one is nervous. Misunderstanding: the list is an inventory, not a search for weakness. Diagnostic: ask each person which belief would make them quit, and check it is listed.

Vague assumptions. Symptom: items read "users want a better experience". Diagnostic: ask what number would make you drop it; a blank answer marks a slogan.

Testing the easy item. Symptom: the team ships a landing page and reports signups while the pricing belief is untouched. Diagnostic: compare the item tested with the top of the ranking.

Doing it once. Symptom: the list is dated three months ago and unchanged. Diagnostic: check when confidence figures last moved.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the Monday meeting looks different. Chirantan arrives with six falsifiable assumptions, each with a threshold, a named owner, a confidence agreed after private scoring, an impact and a costed test. The 180 lakh request is replaced by a 15 lakh request for tests, and a rule is written down in advance: if fewer than a quarter of offered wholesalers place a trial order, the build does not start.

9. What Chirantan decided

Chaitanya did not approve the full build. He approved 15 lakh of testing and asked Chirantan to return with results. Chellam's team ran the three-week concierge trial from Monday 16 June to Monday 7 July; the formal review took place a week later, on Monday 14 July. The reasoning was simple: 8.3 per cent of the money bought a real chance to learn that the other 91.7 per cent should not be spent as planned.

The next topic, riskiest assumption first, takes the ranked list and decides what to test in what order, including cases like A4 where a lower-ranked belief should go earlier. After it comes writing an experiment hypothesis, which turns a chosen assumption into a prediction that evidence can contradict.

Two questions to sit with. Think of a plan you are working on: which clause in its one-sentence justification would you least like to hear questioned by a sceptical colleague from the field, and why? And if your most confident belief turned out to be wrong, how would you find out, and how long would it take?
